en: Now begins the second chapter:
Learn that dharma which is practiced by the wise, by the virtuous, and always by those free from hatred and passion, and which is approved by the heart. 2.1.

The first chapter, which was intended to reveal the true nature of the subject matter to be expounded in this treatise, has been concluded. Furthermore, the description of the creation of the world and so forth was explained merely as a supplement to that. Now, the treatise itself begins. Since the matter promised therein might have been forgotten due to the intervention of the description of the world's creation and other topics, he now informs the students once more for the sake of reconnection.

"Listen attentively and hear that Dharma which you have desired to learn, as it is now being spoken by me. In the first chapter, five or six verses are intended to establish the purpose (*prayojana*) and other preliminary matters; the remainder is in the form of explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). If that [explanatory portion] is not perfectly grasped, there is no great loss regarding the full comprehension of Dharma. However, here Dharma itself is directly taught. Therefore, the result of this restatement is that this subject matter must be firmly grasped by those who possess attentiveness. The word *dharma* has the meaning already stated, referring to the performance of the *Aṣṭakā* and other such rites. But outsiders (*bāhyadarśinaḥ*) consider even the wearing of ashes, carrying of skulls, and so forth, to be Dharma. To exclude that, the qualifying words beginning with "by the learned" (*vidvadbhiḥ*) are used. The "learned" (*vidvāṃsaḥ*) are those whose minds are refined by the scriptures and who are skilled in the knowledge of the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of cognition (*prameya*). And these "learned" ones are those who know the meaning of the Veda, and none others. For those who accept authority (*prāmāṇya*) for anything other than the Veda regarding Dharma are indeed unlearned, because they grasp the means and objects of cognition in a contrary manner. And this is determined according to reality through Mīmāṃsā."

The "good" (*santaḥ*) are the virtuous; they are those who practice the objects determined by the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and who exert effort for the sake of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful. The beneficial and the harmful are both the visible, which is well-known, and the invisible, characterized by injunctions and prohibitions. Those who stand outside the practice of these are called "not good. Therefore, both are included here: knowledge and practice. It is not possible that the word *sat* expresses mere existence, because that would be purposeless; for whatever is practiced by someone must indeed already exist.

"Service" (*sevā*) refers to the habit of performing [the prescribed rites]. By using the suffix denoting a present participle (*bhūtapratyaya*), he indicates that this has been in practice since beginningless time. This Dharma of the *Aṣṭakā* and other such rites was not initiated by anyone in the present age like other [non-Vedic] dharmas. He demonstrates this very point with the word "eternal" (*nitya*). This Dharma exists as long as *saṃsāra* endures. All external dharmas, however, are initiated by foolish and ill-behaved men; even if they find an opportunity for a certain period of time, they disappear again. For delusion does not persist for a thousand ages. Even though right knowledge is obscured by ignorance, upon the destruction of that [ignorance], it attains only purity. Indeed, its purity cannot be destroyed.

"By those free from hatred and passion. This is the second cause regarding the performance of external religious duties (*bāhyadharmānuṣṭhāna*). Confusion (*vyāmoha*) has been mentioned previously; by this term, greed and the like are indicated, since the mention of passion and hatred is intended to be illustrative. Through greed, people engage in *mantras*, *tantras*, and so forth. Alternatively, greed is included within passion and hatred. Attached to those means of enjoyment that exist for themselves, and being unable to live by other means, they subsist by wearing [ascetic] marks (*liṅgadhāraṇa*) and the like. As it has been said: "Wearing ashes, carrying skulls, nakedness, and saffron robes—these are the livelihoods of those devoid of intelligence and manliness. Hatred is the cause of contrary performance. For those dominated by hatred are not at all capable of determining the truth; therefore, they resolve what is actually non-dharma to be dharma. Alternatively, both passion and hatred are obstacles to the determination of truth. Even when there is some mere knowledge of the scriptures and one has attained the designation of a learned man (*vidvat*), contrary performance is possible due to the presence of passion and hatred. Even though they know the scripture correctly, they practice non-dharma such as false testimony for the purpose of harming someone they dislike or for the benefit of someone they love. It is impossible to determine with certainty that their performance is rooted in the Veda, because another cause characterized by passion and hatred is possible. Therefore, there is a prohibition of that.

Here an objection is raised: [7] The word *sat* in the phrase "by the *sadbhiḥ*" has been described as signifying goodness (*sādhutā*). But what kind of goodness does he possess, if it is possible that he might engage in unrighteousness (*adharma*) due to passion and hatred? Therefore, one should not have said "by those free from hatred and passion."

In that case, it is stated as a reason: because they are free from passion and the like, they become virtuous (*santa*). Here, what is being demonstrated is the absence of the predominance of passion and hatred. It is not the case that the cause—which has reached a state capable of the absence of those [passions]—is utterly annihilated without remainder. And thus says the Śruti: "For one who possesses a body, there is indeed no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant" (ChU 8.12.1).

Attachment (*rāga*) is greed for the enjoyment of sense objects. Aversion (*dveṣa*) is the activity of opposing that [attachment]. Greed (*lobha*) is stinginess, a desire for exclusivity, thinking, "May this [wealth, fame, and so forth] not belong to another. These are mental factors (*cittadharma*). Alternatively, attachment (*rāga*) is affection toward sentient beings such as wife, son, friend, and kinsman; greed (*lobha*) is the desire even for insentient things such as wealth.

By "heart" (*hṛdaya*); by the word "heart," he expresses the mind (*citta*). And the approval of the heart is its serenity; for this is the established state. The principles beginning with the intellect (*buddhi*) reside within the heart. Even though fools engage in external acts such as violence or the eating of forbidden food under the impression that they are dharma, nevertheless, their hearts are reproached [by conscience]. But in the performance of Vedic rites, the mind is fully satisfied.

This is the meaning of all this: I do not teach such a Dharma in which these faults exist; rather, it is that which is practiced by great beings of such a kind, or wherein one’s own mind inclines. Therefore, it is appropriate to show exceptional reverence for the Dharmas being taught.

Alternatively, the *veda* is the heart (*hṛdaya*), for when it has been studied, it resides in the heart in the form of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and thus it is the heart. Consequently, a triad is here included. Even if some person were to engage in action based merely on their own preference without inquiry, even then such engagement is appropriate precisely in this case; this is what is expressed by the phrase "authorized by the heart. Furthermore, there is this maxim: "The path is that which the great man has taken" (MBh 3. App. 32.68), and that too applies here. For in this matter, the learned are free from desire, have previously engaged in it, and are irreproachable in the world. Moreover, if the engagement were without a valid source of authority (*aprāmāṇika*), even that is established through the authority of the Veda. In every respect, this [verse] generates a disposition toward engagement.

Others, however, explain this verse as defining the general characteristic of Dharma: "That which is practiced by such persons is to be understood as Dharma. This definition applies to everything—whether prescribed by the direct revelation (śruti), by the tradition (smṛti), or obtained through customary conduct (ācāra). In this context, however, the reading "Learn that Dharma which is practiced by these" is more appropriate. (2.1)
To have desire as one’s sole essence is not praised, yet here there is no such thing as being without desire;
for the study of the Vedas and the performance of Vedic ritual action are themselves objects of desire.

One whose nature is characterized by desire (*kāmātmā*) is one for whom the longing for a fruit is the cause of engaging in action; the state of being such is *kāmātmatā*. By the word "self" (*ātman*), it is indicated that this is the primary motive. This is not praiseworthy, but rather censured. Consequently, through this censure, an inference of prohibition is understood: "It should not be done. Thus, this is effectively a prohibition of all optional rites (*kāmya-karma*), such as the *Saurya* sacrifice and others. Alternatively, why should we specify [the Saurya and other rites]? Every performance of action is for the sake of achieving a result, not for the mere completion of its own form. Nor is there any action whatsoever that is fruitless. Even regarding the statements, "One should not perform useless exertion" (MDh 4.63), "An offering poured into ashes" (MDh 3.181), or "Seeking news of the country or the king in another region," even there a result of the action exists. However, because of the absence of the principal fruit—such as heaven or a village—which is useful to a person in terms of both seen and unseen benefits, it is called "useless exertion."

Now it is argued: "Let it be that action bears fruit; however, one should not form a desire for its object, for the fruit will arise from the very nature of things. To this we reply: even in this case, rites such as the *saurya* sacrifice would be fruitless. The fruit is known as something desired; it will not come to pass for one who lacks the desire for it. Furthermore, no worldly activity is observed to be independent of the expectation of a result. Nor is there any specific distinction stated in the Veda to the effect that "in Vedic rituals, the fruit should not be expected. In that case, since desire is prohibited regarding those fruitful rites explicitly mentioned in scripture, if one refrains from acting, there is a contradiction with the scripture. As for obligatory (*nitya*) rites, there is simply no possibility [of desiring their fruit]. Moreover, because no distinction is made, if worldly activities were to cease, there would be a contradiction with what is perceived. Thus, this would follow: nothing at all should be done by anyone, and everyone should remain silent.
It is said in reply: as for what was stated regarding the contingency of a prohibition applying to optional rites such as those dedicated to Sūrya, he will state there:
"In this world, one enjoys all desires exactly as they were intended" (MDh 2.5).

For if there were a prohibition, from where would there be a *saṃkalpa* (volitional resolve), and from where the attainment of desire? As for the argument that because no specific qualification is mentioned, the rule would apply even to worldly actions—that too is incorrect, for a specific qualification is indeed implied here, since Dharma is the subject under discussion in the statement, “Learn that which is Dharma” (MDh 2.1). Furthermore, regarding the claim that since no fruit is heard of in the case of obligatory (*nitya*) rites, there can be no possibility of an intention toward a fruit, and thus what need is there for a prohibition—there too it is said: Someone who does not correctly understand the meaning of the scripture might not engage in these rites simply because they lack a visible fruit. Moreover, having observed that engagement in rites such as the *Saurya* sacrifice—which have fruits explicitly stated in the texts—is preceded by an intention toward a fruit, one might, through general inference (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), conclude that “whatever is to be done is done for the sake of a fruit,” and thus intend a fruit even where none is heard. To prevent this, this [prohibition] is undertaken. Even though this is the logical principle: “Whatever is heard to have a fruit must be performed exactly so; and as for that which is understood from the scripture as being merely obligatory through terms like ‘throughout life’ (*yāvajjīvam*)—without assuming a fruit via the *Viśvajit* logic—there is no possibility at all of performing it otherwise,” nevertheless, one who is incapable of grasping this principle is instructed by means of a direct statement (*vacana*). For while grasping it through logic involves effort (*gaurava*), comprehension from a direct statement is easier and more pleasant; thus, acting as a friend, the author teaches a matter established by valid authority (*pramāṇa*).

[12] Although this word *kāma* is seen to denote "desire" (the fire residing in the heart), nevertheless, because that meaning is impossible here, *kāma*, *icchā*, and *abhilāṣa* are synonymous. In this context, through consideration of what is to be explained later, the sense will be established as follows: one should not engage in every activity out of a longing for results.

But the opponent, considering the meaning of the term *kāmātmatā* (being characterized by desire) to be merely the state of being connected with mere longing, objects: "And there is no such thing here as the absence of desire. The meaning is that in this world, no activity whatsoever exists for one who is devoid of desire. Let us set aside for a moment such things as agriculture and trade performed by those of mature intellect; even the acquisition of the Vedas—that is, the study of the Vedas—which is made to be done by a child under the lash of his father and others, does not occur without desire. For study consists in the utterance of sounds, and utterance does not arise without desire, like the sound of a thunderclap. If he desires it, why is he beaten? That very desire is produced in him by the beating; the only difference is that in the case of a desired object, the desire arises spontaneously. Furthermore, this "application to action" (*karmayoga*) prescribed by the Veda—such as the performance of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, which is understood as obligatory—would also fail to be attained. For the renunciation of one's own property for the sake of a deity is not possible for one who lacks desire. Therefore, if the state of being characterized by desire were prohibited, it would follow that all actions prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis are prohibited. (2.2)
Desire indeed has its root in volition; sacrifices are born of volition;
vows, restraints, and duties—all are traditionally held to be born of volition.

And therefore, having clarified what was stated—that the essential nature of a sacrifice cannot be accomplished without desire—he explains it as follows: "The mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is the root of sacrifices and the like, and of desire. One who wishes to perform sacrifices and so forth necessarily forms a mental resolve. And when that resolve is being made, desire—its cause—must necessarily be present, even if it is undesirable. Just as for one seeking to cook who produces fire, smoke—which shares the same cause—is produced even though it is undesirable. In that case, it is impossible [to claim] that "the sacrifices and such will be performed, yet desire will not arise."
Now, what is this so-called *saṃkalpa* (volitional construction), which is the root of all action?

It is said: That which is called the "mental vision" (*cetaḥ-saṃdarśana*) is that immediately after which aspiration (*prārthanā*) and determination (*adhyavasāya*) arise in succession. For these mental operations constitute the very root of all engagement in action. Indeed, physical activities do not occur without it. To illustrate: first is the discernment of the nature of an object—the cognition that "this object accomplishes this purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*). This is what is intended here by "volition" (*saṃkalpa*). Following that, there arises aspiration, which is desire; this itself is *kāma*. When this desire exists—thinking, "How may I accomplish this by means of this?"—one determines, "I shall do it," and resolves upon it; this is "determination" (*adhyavasāya*). Thereafter, one proceeds toward the employment of the means, which is the domain of external activity. For example, a hungry person first perceives the act of eating; then he desires, "May I eat"; then he determines, "Having desisted from other activities, I shall eat"; then he addresses the agents, instruments, locations, and authorities, saying, "Prepare the kitchen! Bring [the food]!"

Now, if this is so, sacrifices and the like do not arise from mere intention (*saṃkalpa*) alone, but rather from intention, prayer, and resolve. In that case, why is it said that "sacrifices are born of intention"? There is no fault here, because intention is the primary cause. For this very reason, he will state later on: "No action whatsoever is seen in one who is devoid of desire."

Vows (*vrata*). A vow is a mental resolve (*adhyavasāya*) regarding what has been enjoined: "This must be performed by me for as long as I live," such as the vows of a *snātaka*. The duties of self-restraint (*yamadharmāḥ*) are of the nature of prohibitions, such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth. Engagement in what ought to be done and withdrawal from what is forbidden do not exist without a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). 2.3.
No action whatsoever is ever seen here in this world that is performed by one who is free from desire;
for whatever one does, all that is the movement of desire. (2.4)

In the preceding [verse], scriptural engagement and withdrawal were explained as being dependent upon volition (*saṃkalpa*). By this [verse], it is stated that even in worldly activities, they are dependent upon that [volition]; this is the distinction. In this world, at any time whatsoever—even during the waking state—no action can ever occur as something to be performed for one who lacks the desire to do so. Whatever action one performs, whether worldly or Vedic, whether enjoined or prohibited, all that is the movement of desire. || 2.4 ||

And it has been stated that all activity is caused by desire alone. This situation is extremely precarious: being "of the nature of desire" is not praised, yet there is no performance of any rite whatsoever without it. To this, he provides the following remedy: "By conducting oneself properly toward those [desires], one goes to the world of the immortals;
and here, one enjoys all desires exactly as they were intended. (2.5)

One should engage correctly with those desires. What, then, is correct engagement? It is that whatever has been heard [in scripture] should be performed exactly as such. In the case of obligatory (*nitya*) rites, no fruit should be intended, because no such fruit was heard [prescribed]. In the case of optional (*kāmya*) rites, however, there is no prohibition, because they were heard [in scripture] in that way; they are understood through injunction precisely as means to a fruit. For one who does not desire the fruit, performing them would constitute the performance of what was not heard [prescribed]. In the case of obligatory rites, the intention for a fruit is merely delusion; for a fruit does not arise from mere intention when the status of being a means to a fruit is not established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). By acting thus, "one goes to," that is, attains, "the state of the world of the immortals. "Immortals" (*amarāḥ*) are the gods; their "world" (*lokaḥ*) is heaven (*svargaḥ*). Because they dwell there, the word "world" (*loka*) is applied to the inhabitants, due to the non-difference between the location and the occupant, as in the expression "the beds cry out" (*mañcāḥ krośanti*). Thus, this is a compound: "immortals and worlds" (*amarāś ca te lokāś ca*); the state of that is "the state of the world of the immortals" (*amaralokatā*). The meaning is that one attains the condition of being among the divine folk, or attains divinity. This was stated in this way for the sake of metrical conformity. Alternatively, "one who sees the immortals" is *amaralokaḥ*. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied in the sense of the object [of the action] (Pāṇini 3.2.1). From that, the suffix denoting state (*bhavapratyaya*) is added. Thus, he becomes a beholder of the gods. Even by this method, it is simply the attainment of heaven that is expressed. Or else, he is regarded in the world as if he were an immortal (*amara*).

This is an *arthavāda* (an explanatory or glorificatory statement). Here, heaven is not enjoined as a fruit, because there is no fruit for obligatory (*nitya*) rites, and because various fruits are heard of in the case of optional (*kāmya*) rites. Therefore, by the attainment of heaven, it is simply the successful accomplishment of the performance of the scriptures that is expressed through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). The meaning is: "That for the sake of which the performance of actions [is undertaken], that is accomplished. In that regard, for obligatory rites, the purpose is either the non-occurrence of transgression (*pratyavāya*) or the fulfillment of the injunction's purpose. But in the case of optional rites, one attains—that is, reaches—all desires, all objects of longing, having formed a resolve at the time of performance according to what was intended and according to what was heard; having resolved upon whatever fruit is heard for whichever rite, having aimed at it and desired it mentally, thinking, "May I obtain this fruit from this," one then enjoys all those desirable objects.

Therefore, the contingency of a logical impasse is avoided, because it is not desire for all objects that is prohibited. What then? It is the desire characterized by the longing for results regarding obligatory rites (*nitya*). However, the acquisition of the means of accomplishment is indeed subject to desire. But the proponents of Brahman (*brahmavādins*) consider the phrase "being of the nature of desire" (*kāmātmatā*) to be intended as a prohibition of the *saurya* sacrifice and others. Actions performed with a view toward results become the nature of bondage; however, one who acts without desire, following the principle of offering everything to Brahman, is liberated. This was stated by the Blessed Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana: "Do not be motivated by the fruit of action" (BhG 2.47). Likewise:
"Because the means of accomplishment are incomplete, because of ignorance, because of the performance of ritual action, and because of the intention for a fruit, the rite is recorded as impure.
There are many alternative interpretations here, but they have not been shown because they lack substance. (2.5)
The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the Smṛtis and the conduct of those who know it, the practice of the virtuous, and also the satisfaction of one’s own self. (2.6)

What is the connection of this [treatise]? Since it was promised that *dharma* is to be explained here, and since that *dharma* is characterized by injunction and prohibition, one might ask: why is the fact that the Veda is the source of *dharma* not enjoined as "The Veda should be known as the source of *dharma*; it should be relied upon for the authority regarding *dharma*"? This is because its status as such is established even without such an instruction. Indeed, the Veda’s status as the source of *dharma* is not something to be understood through the instructions of Manu and others; rather, it is established by its own nature: (1) because it produces cognitions of objects that are not sublated; (2) because, being authorless (*apauruṣeya*), there is no suspicion of false representation due to defects arising from human contact; and (3) because a word is inherently faultless. Thus, like perception, its intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) is established.

Now it is said: having restated that the authority of the Veda is established by logical reasoning, the fact that the Smṛtis of Manu and others have that [Veda] as their source is made known by means of a scriptural statement.

That too is not the case; for even there, [the memory] depends upon a prior cognition. Since errors, deceptions, and the like have been refuted by the acceptance of the tradition by great men (*mahājana*), and since it is impossible for a person to perceive supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārtha*), and because the person's own experience is established, the memory of the meaning of the Veda is understood to be rooted solely in the Veda itself. Indeed, a memory regarding matters of duty (*kāryārtha*) is not possible for those who know the Veda. And since the Veda is the root, there is no occasion for postulating another root.

Nor is it appropriate to say: "And [the authority of] the Smṛtis and Śīlas of those who know them [is accepted]. This too is merely restated for the purpose of showing the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of the external Smṛtis, since their lack of authority is established by logic itself. For there is no possibility of a connection with the Veda for the Śākyas, Bhojakas, Kṣapaṇakas, and others, such that they could be authoritative regarding their own subject matter on the basis of having the Veda as their source; this is because they do not themselves accept it, because they declare the Veda to be unauthoritative, and because they teach matters that contradict the perceptible Veda. In that regard, the impossibility [of a Vedic source] exists in those Smṛtis because of the prohibition against the study of the Veda. For if Buddha and the others were students of the Veda, then a deliberation might arise as to whether or not [their works] have the Veda as their source. But where that connection is far removed, what suspicion can there be of having the Veda as a source? Furthermore, they themselves accept other sources handed down through tradition: "O monks, with my divine eye I see the good and bad destinies. In this way, all the outsiders—the Bhojakas, Pāñcarātrikas, Nirgranthas, Ānarthavādas, Pāśupatas, and so forth—accept the authors of their own systems to be superhuman beings or specific deities who perceive those objects directly, and they do not consider Dharma to have the Veda as its source. Moreover, matters taught therein are contradicted by the perceptible Veda. For instance, if violence is declared to be Dharma by the Saṃsāramocakas and others, it is here [in the Veda] explicitly prohibited. Likewise, elsewhere bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) is accepted as non-Dharma, whereas here there is the injunction: "One should bathe every day" and "One should resort to sacred fords. Similarly, the killing of the animal in the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is in some places held to be a cause of sin, yet that is contradicted by the injunction for the Jyotiṣṭoma. Likewise, others maintain that all sacrifices and oblations are for one's own sake, whereas they are understood from various rules concerning the distinction of deities to have diverse divinities as their objects. Therefore, there is a contradiction.

As for those who say: "Just as in the case of accepting or not accepting [certain gifts], or like the times for the *udita* and *anudita* oblations, since we observe contradictions with direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), it is possible that there exists another Vedic branch—whether lost or not lost—that contains injunctions for matters contrary to those [revealed texts]. For the branches of the Veda are infinite. How could they all be directly perceived by a single person? Furthermore, their disappearance is possible. In that regard, there might exist such a Vedic branch in which this practice of eating from a vessel made of human bone, wandering naked, and so forth, would be taught.

It is said in reply: We do not claim that it is impossible for the Veda to teach contradictory meanings. Rather, because those two [options] are of equal status, there is no conflict between their alternative applications (*vikalpa*). In this case, however, the Veda would have to be inferred; and there is no occasion for inferring something that contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Nor can certainty be established by mere possibility alone. On the contrary, the injunction of direct perception which contradicts it is already certain; and what is uncertain does not sublate what is certain. Furthermore, we shall elaborate upon the position regarding the disappearance of Vedic branches (*śākhā*) later in this very verse. Moreover, in all cases, the Smṛtis of Manu and others are interconnected with directly revealed Śruti texts—sometimes through a mantra, sometimes through a deity, and sometimes through rules concerning ritual materials (*dravya*). Since such a connection is not possible in the case of external (non-Vedic) traditions, they lack authority.

In this way, conduct (*ācāra*) also possesses authority, just like the *smṛti*, when it is practiced by those learned in the Vedas for the sake of an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), because its source is possible. However, improper conduct lacks authority because visible causes and the like are possible, and because error and the like are possible for the ignorant.
The same applies to self-satisfaction (*ātmanas tuṣṭi*).

If the authority of the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and established customs is derived from the instructions of Manu and others, then how is the authority of Manu and others established? For in their case as well, it must be from another instruction, such as "And Manu declared the Smṛti," and so forth. How then is that [instruction] established? Therefore, whether this is authoritative or unauthoritative is to be determined through reasoning, not through mere instruction. Thus, this verse is useless; the subsequent verses are of the same nature.

To this it is replied: Here, those authors of *Dharmasūtras* who compose textual treatises with the intent of providing the substance of categories for the sake of instructing unlearned persons—just as they record the performance of the *Aṣṭakā* and other rites after having themselves understood their obligation from the Veda for the purpose of making others understand them—likewise [record] the authority of the Veda and so forth, which are established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). There are certain learners who are incapable of discerning the truth through logic due to a lack of the intellectual capacity for reasoning, deliberation, and so on; for their sake, even a matter established by logic is taught like the advice of a friend. In that context, the very fact that the Veda is the root of Dharma, which is established by logic, is restated by this [sūtra]: "The Veda is the root of Dharma. The Veda has been established as the root of Dharma through inquiry and reasoning; one should not entertain a doubt regarding its lack of authority here. Furthermore, in the world there are instructors of matters established by other means of knowledge, such as: "You must not eat while suffering from indigestion, for diseases arise from indigestion. Nor should it be said: "Those who are unable to grasp the Veda's status as the root of Dharma through logic will not believe it even from a verbal statement. For it is observed that some people accept the word of those renowned for their reliability without even investigating it. Thus, this entire section is rooted in logic, not in the Veda. We shall demonstrate elsewhere, in the case of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), traditional law (*smṛti*), and so forth, where the basis is logic, as the occasion arises. As for how the *Aṣṭakā* and other rites have their basis in the Veda, that will be pointed out right here.

By the word *veda*, the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* [Vedas] together with the *Brāhmaṇas* are denoted. These possess well-known distinctions for students from other sentences; having been refined by a tradition of oral instruction, students recognize them upon merely hearing them as "this is the Veda," just as they recognize "this is a Brāhmaṇa. In that collection of sentences, the term *veda* is applied to the whole beginning with "I praise Agni" (*agnim īḷe*, RV 1.1.1) and "Agni is indeed the lowest of the gods" (*agnir vai devānām avamaḥ*, AitB 1.1.1), and ending with "Thou enkindlest [the fire]" (*saṃ sam id yuvase*, RV 10.191.1) and "Now the Mahāvrata" (*atha mahāvratam*, AitĀ 1.1.1), as well as to the individual sentences that constitute its parts. Furthermore, there is no distinction between primary and secondary usage here, as there is in words like *grāma*. For the principle is that words functioning for a whole may also function for its parts. The word *grāma* is most commonly used for the whole collection, yet through connection with phrases such as "the village is burnt," it refers to a part thereof. Even when only a few huts are burning, common people say, "the village is burnt. Alternatively, even in that case, the word denotes the whole; the burning, though occurring in one part, is designated as belonging to the whole. Indeed, the connection of the whole with an action occurs precisely through its parts, for it is impossible to see or touch the whole while setting aside its parts.

And the word *veda* is etymologically explained: it is called *veda* because from it people know (*vidanti*) the object characterized as *dharma*, which is not cognizable by any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And that cognition arises from each individual sentence, not from the entire collection of chapters and sections denoted by the term *Ṛgveda* and so forth. Thus, the penalty stated in the rule "the tongue shall be cut off for reciting [a forbidden mantra]" (GDh 12.5) refers even to a single sentence; likewise, the inclusion of the word "entire" in the rule "it must be mastered in its entirety" (MDh 2.165) is intended to ensure the study of every sentence of the Veda. Otherwise, one might consider himself successful after studying only a few sentences, rather than the whole Veda. We shall examine this point further below.

And that Veda is divided in many ways: the Sāmaveda has a thousand paths through divisions such as the Sātyamugri and Rāṇāyanīya; the Yajurveda has one hundred and one branches through divisions such as the Kāṭhaka and Vājasaneyaka; the Ṛgveda has twenty-one branches through divisions such as the Āśvalāyana and Aitareya; and the Atharvaveda is ninefold through divisions such as the Maudaka and Paippalādaka.

Now, it may be objected that some do not even consider the *Atharvaveda* to be a Veda; for [it is said], "The triple knowledge (*trayī vidyā*) consists of the *ṛc*s, the *sāmans*, and the *yajus*s," and "The sun moves with the three Vedas, never devoid of them" (*TB* 3.12.9.1). Likewise, in such passages as "One should observe the vow pertaining to the three Vedas" (*MDh* 3.1), the name "Ātharvaṇa" does not appear anywhere at all. Furthermore, a prohibition is heard: "Therefore, one should not recite [the *brahmayajña*] with the *Atharvaṇa*. Consequently, they declare the followers of the *Atharvaṇa* to be heretics (*pāṣaṇḍin*) excluded from the triple Veda (*trayībāhya*).

That is incorrect, because the learned (*śiṣṭas*) employ the term "Veda" without making distinctions. There is also usage [of the term] in the passage: "the *Śrutis* of the Atharvans and Aṅgirases" (MDh 11.33); here too, *śruti* and *veda* have the same meaning. Furthermore, being denotable by the word "Veda" is not the sole cause for the sentences concerning the *agnihotra* and so forth to be authoritative regarding *dharma*, since we observe the usage of the term "Veda" even for the *Itihāsas* and *Āyurveda*, as in: "The *Itihāsa-Purāṇa* is the fifth Veda among the Vedas" (ChU 7.1.2). What then [is the cause]? It is the state of being authorless (*apauruṣeya*), combined with the capacity to make known the objects to be performed and the absence of error. All of this exists in the Atharvaveda as well, because rituals such as the *jyotiṣṭoma* are taught there just as they are in the Yajurveda and others. The misconception of some that it is not a Veda because of the frequent teaching therein of rituals rooted in malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) is mistaken; for such magic is prohibited because its result is the severance of another's life-force. Yet those very rites are primarily practiced by the followers of the Atharvaveda when serving as royal priests; therefore, they are censured.

As for the claim that in passages such as "not devoid of the Vedas" (*vedair aśūnyaḥ*, TB 3.12.9.1), the *Atharvaveda* is not mentioned, these are merely explanatory statements (*arthavāda*). What does it matter whether it is mentioned there or not? This statement—"the three Vedas" (*trayo vedāḥ*, MDh 2.230), "the triple knowledge" (*trayī vidyā*), and so forth—has the different classes of mantras in mind. Indeed, there is no fourth class of mantras apart from the *Ṛk*, *Yajus*, and *Sāman*, because the *praiṣas*, *nivids*, *nigadas*, *indragāthās*, and so on, are included within these very categories. In the *Atharvaveda*, only the *carcas* are recited as mantras; therefore, this [Veda] is simply the *Ṛgveda* with respect to the category of mantras. As for the prohibition [of mixing], it serves as a proof of the opposite, since a prohibition is only logical when there is a prior possibility of occurrence. Or rather, this is its meaning: one should not mix the ritual acts prescribed by the three Vedas with the mantras studied in the *Atharvaveda*. In the *Vācaḥstoma* sacrifice, all *ṛcs*, all *yajūṃṣi*, and all *sāmans* are employed; therein lies the prohibition of those mantras studied in the *Atharvaveda*.

That Veda is a distinguished collection of words, not of human origin, known as the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, divided into many different recensions; it is the root of Dharma, its authority, and the cause for its full understanding. "Root" here means the cause. And that [Veda] serves as the source for Dharma only by way of making it known—through the Veda and the Smṛtis—not by way of producing it, nor by way of being its sustaining cause, as in the case of a tree.

The word *dharma* has already been explained. That which is to be done by a person (*puruṣa-kartavya*)—which is a means to the highest good (*śreyas-sādhana*) by a nature distinct from what is cognizable through perception and other means—is [Dharma]. Agricultural labor, service, and so forth are things to be done by a person, and their nature as a means to that [good] is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Furthermore, the manner in which the production of rice and other crops results from agricultural labor and so forth is also indeed cognizable through perception and other means. However, the fact that sacrifice (*yāga*) and the like are means, and the specific form by which they produce the *apūrva* (unseen potency) through an intervention and so forth—that is not cognizable through perception and other means. And "highest good" (*śreyas*) is, in general, the attainment of desired fruits such as heaven or a village, denoted by the word "pleasure" (*sukha*); it is also the attainment of fruits such as freedom from disease, wealth, and the absence of unhappiness, as well as the avoidance of hell and the like, denoted in general by the word "pain" (*duḥkha*).
Others, however, [hold that] the highest good consists of the nature of supreme bliss and so forth.

This Dharma is understood from the words of the Brāhmaṇas containing injunctive suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like, and in some cases also from mantras such as, "One should sacrifice *kapiñjala* birds to Vasantā" (MS 3.14.1). Among these, sentences connected with words expressing desire (*kāmapada*) make known that performance is for the sake of a fruit, such as: "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya" (TS 2.3.2.3); "One desiring a village should offer a *sāṃgrahiṇī* oblation to the Viśvedevas" (TS 2.3.9.2). These are not performed by one who does not desire the fruit.

Other [rites], which are enjoined as obligatory by terms such as *yāvajjīvam* ("as long as one lives") and so forth, are not performed for the sake of a result, because no result is mentioned [in the scriptural injunction]. Nor can a result be postulated for them—even in the absence of a stated result—as in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," since they are understood to be duties to be performed even without a result due to terms like *yāvajjīvam*. In that regard, there is the fault of transgressing the meaning of the scripture (*śāstrārthātikrama*) if they are not performed; therefore, those rites are performed in order to avoid that fault.

The same principle applies even to prohibitions, such as "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed" and "Liquor must not be drunk. For the avoidance of what is forbidden is not for the sake of a [desirable] fruit, but rather for the sake of avoiding sin (pratyavāya). "Entire" means complete; there is not a single word, syllable, or vowel that does not lead to dharma.

Here they raise an objection: Is it not said that the Veda consists of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), mantras, and names (*nāmadheya*), while Dharma has the nature of being something to be performed (*kartavyatā*)? In that case, it is appropriate that injunctive sentences should be the authority for Dharma, for from them the necessity to perform actions such as sacrifices is understood—such as: "One offers the *agnihotra*," "One offers with curds," "That which one offers in the evening to Agni and Prajāpati," and "One desiring heaven offers [the sacrifice]. For here, the ritual act called *agnihotra* is understood as something to be performed; "with curds" indicates the substance therein; "to Agni and [Prajāpati]" indicates the deity; and "one desiring heaven" indicates the qualification (*adhikāra*). However, as for passages such as "Agni indeed is all the deities," "Agni alone is the divine *hotṛ* priest," and "He invites the gods and offers the oblation," as well as "Prajāpati cut out the omentum from his own body," and so forth—nothing to be performed is taught by these. They merely recount past events or other matters that are not currently applicable. For instance: "In the past, the omentum was cut out by Prajāpati from himself"; let him have cut it out, what is that to us? Likewise, Agni’s identity as the self of all deities is of no use in the ritual dedicated to Agni, since the purpose of the designation is fulfilled by the word "Agni" itself. If there were another deity, then because of that difference, there would be no designation of Agni at all. Furthermore, since the invocation is already prescribed by another text, such as "O Agni, bring Agni hither" (*agnim agna āvahe*), the statement "He invites the gods and offers the oblation" and so forth is redundant. As for the mantras, such as "Death did not exist, nor immortality then" (*na mṛtyur āsīd amṛtaṃ na tarhi*) and "May the good god fall today, never to return" (*sudevo adya pated anāvṛt*), which express meanings such as descriptions of past events or lamentations—what Dharma do they authorize? At that time, death had not arisen, nor was there immortal life. Since beings had not yet been produced prior to creation, there was no life for anyone, nor was there death, as everyone was already dead during the dissolution (*pralaya*). Whether death existed or not, nothing to be performed is taught by this. Similarly, "that good god"—meaning a highly meritorious person equal to a deity—who might fall today, throwing himself down from a precipice, "never to return," where there is no returning or reviving. This refers to Purūravas, who, deceived by Urvaśī, uttered lamentations. Likewise, regarding names: "One should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," "One should sacrifice with the *balabhid*," and so forth—these do not enjoin any purpose, action, or substance, because the action is enjoined by the verb (*ākhyāta*) and words like *balabhid* do not denote a substance. Moreover, since Soma is obtained through the archetype (*prakṛti*) due to its being an unmanifest injunction (*avyakta-codana*), the status of denoting a substance is not to be assumed with difficulty. Therefore, Dharma is not taught by means of a name. Consequently, how can it be said that the entire Veda is the root of Dharma?

It is said: It was precisely with this concern in mind that the term "all" (*akhila*) was employed, because all of these [scriptural elements] are intent upon the exposition of *dharma*. For instance, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) do not have meanings separate from the injunctive sentences such that they would fail to provide knowledge of *dharma*. Since they are understood to be subservient to injunctions when they are divided and found to be syntactically expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*), and since their unity of sentence (*ekavākyatā*) is established in being subservient to that [injunction], they must be interpreted in such a way that they conform to the purpose of that [injunction]. Therefore, the statement regarding Prajāpati’s evisceration does not terminate in its own literal meaning; rather, it is a supplement to an injunction. Nor is a substance, quality, or other thing to be enjoined perceived directly from the explanatory passages; instead, they attain the status of being supplements by praising the matter to be enjoined through a different mode of expression. That [matter] is indeed perceived therein: namely, that the animal sacrifice must be performed in such a way that, in the absence of actual animals, Prajāpati fashioned his own self into an animal because there was no other way out, and his omentum was eviscerated. For wherever explanatory passages exist, the injunctive statements are accompanied by them. Even though the understanding of the meaning of the injunction occurs even without them—as in the case of the injunction itself, "He sacrifices the *kapiñjala* birds for spring" (MS 3.14.1)—nevertheless, they are not useless. For when they are present, the understanding does not arise from the injunction alone. Nor was the Veda created by anyone, such that one could say, "Just as they do not exist elsewhere, let them not exist here either. When explanatory passages are present, we must state how they function; and that has been stated. Furthermore, this is not an extraordinary matter; for even in the world, words of praise are seen to be merely supplementary to injunctions. For example, when a master is about to give wages, a certain servant might affectionately say, "Devadatta is good, always attentive, knows the ground for service, and is dedicated to it. Therefore, by means of praising the matter to be enjoined, explanatory passages are indeed injunctive. Likewise, in some cases, the specific details of what is to be enjoined are understood from the explanatory passage alone. For example: "He places the smeared pebbles" (TB 3.12.5.12). Here, the injunction requires some means of smearing, such as clarified butter or oil; however, by the praise of clarified butter in the explanatory passage, "Clarified butter is indeed splendor" (AitB 8.20), clarified butter is determined [as the required substance]. Similarly, from the explanatory passage regarding the nights, "Those who perform these nights find a firm foundation" (cf. TāṇB 23.2.4), the qualification [of the performers] is understood. Therefore, explanatory passages are also a source of *dharma*.

Some mantras, however, are indeed prescriptive, such as "For the spring, [offer] kapiñjala birds" (MS 3.14.1). In the case of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*), the injunction regarding the deity is based solely on the wording of the mantra. For in that instance, the deity is neither heard in the original injunction of the ritual action (*karmotpattivākya*), nor is it enjoined by another separate statement. Yet, a mantra—such as "From here, Indra... (TS 1.1.12.1)—is prescribed and employed. Therefore, the cognition of the deity arises from this wording of the mantra. There are thousands of such injunctions regarding deities based on the wording of mantras. Furthermore, even those other mantras which are recited as descriptive restatements (*kriyamāṇānuvādinaḥ*) bring to mind a duty characterized by traditional law (*smṛti*); thus, by illuminating the matters to be performed, they constitute a source of Dharma.

A noun, however, has a meaning not distinct from that of the verb; like the meaning of the verb, it possesses a well-established status as the root of dharma. Furthermore, injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) are for the most part based precisely upon nouns, as in: "In autumn, one should sacrifice with the Vājapeya" (ĀpŚ 18.1.1) and "One desiring self-sovereignty [should sacrifice] with the Vājapeya" (TB 1.3.2.3).
Therefore, it is established that the entire Veda is the root of dharma.

Others, however, suspecting that sentences such as those concerning the *śyena* sacrifice lack the quality of producing *dharma*, maintain that the term "entirety" (*akhila*) refers to prohibitions such as "one should not eat garlic. For the *śyena* and similar rites consist of killing and are of the nature of violence; because violence is cruel and because these magical rites (*abhicāra*) are prohibited, they are non-*dharma*. Therefore, the entire Veda is not the source of *dharma*. Furthermore, *dharma* has been described as something to be performed, whereas acts such as the killing of a Brahmin are not to be performed; how then could sentences prescribing them be the source of *dharma*? Moreover, even animal sacrifices such as the *agnīṣomīya* are far removed from the state of being *dharma* because they are means for accomplishing violence. Indeed, it is accepted in all traditions that violence is sin. And it has been said: "Where the killing of living beings is *dharma*, what kind of thing is non-*dharma* there?"

But how is this doubt dispelled? By the inclusion of the word "entire" (*akhila*). For it has no other purpose. If it is argued that the reason (*hetu*) has not been stated, [we reply]: this is a scriptural text (*āgama-grantha*) which states an established fact; those who seek the reason are instructed by means of Mīmāṃsā. We have stated that this is said for the sake of those who understand through scripture alone.

The authors of the *Vivaraṇa*, however, demonstrate merely a fraction of the underlying reasoning. As for what was said—that the *śyena* sacrifice and others are *adharma* because they are prohibited—that is true. Nevertheless, even among those [acts] that are prohibited, there is one whose hatred is extremely intense, who has transgressed the prohibition by virtue of the qualification [for the rule] "one should not harm living beings. For such a person, these [sacrifices], when performed, bring about the satisfaction characterized by the killing of an enemy; in this respect alone, the Veda’s status as the root of *dharma* is not undermined even in sentences concerning the *śyena* and other such rites. Even regarding prohibitions, one who is impelled toward killing by passion is enjoined to the prohibition. This very non-performance of that which is being prohibited is precisely what constitutes the performance of the prohibition. In the case of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice and the like, there is no prohibition against *hiṃsā* (harming) at all, because only worldly *hiṃsā* characterized by hatred is prohibited by the prohibition. Scriptural *hiṃsā*, however, which is characterized by injunction, does not fall within the scope of the prohibition, since the prohibition finds its application only in the worldly case. Nor can it be established through an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) that Vedic *hiṃsā* is a cause of sin simply because it is *hiṃsā*, like worldly *hiṃsā*; for it is not the mere state of being *hiṃsā* that is the cause of sin, but rather being made the object of a prohibition. And it has already been stated that no such prohibition exists here.

However, some explain the word *mūla* as a synonym for *kāraṇa* (cause): the Veda is the root—that is, the foundational cause—of Dharma, both directly and indirectly. It is direct in injunctions such as, "One should study one's own Veda" (GDh 9.26) and "The learned man, upholding the Ṛgveda" (MDh 11.261); it is indirect by way of making known the essential nature of rituals such as the Agnihotra.

"And the tradition (smṛti) of those who know that. Memory is defined as a cognition whose object is a thing previously experienced. By the word "that" (tat), the Veda is referred to. Those who know it are "those who know that" (tadvidas). The recollection of those who know the meaning of the Veda—namely, "this should be done" and "this should not be done"—is also a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). Now, some say that tradition is not a means of valid knowledge. They argue that it merely restates an object of knowledge already apprehended by a prior means of valid knowledge and does not determine any additional fact.

True. For those who remember [the Smṛtis], the primary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that [matter] is the word and so forth [of Manu and others], not their own memory. For us, however, the Smṛti of Manu and others is indeed the means of valid cognition. Indeed, we do not understand the duty to perform the Aṣṭakā and other rites from any source other than that [Smṛti]. And such a memory on the part of Manu and others is determined from the statements composed by them, which have been handed down through a tradition of memory (*smṛtiparaṃparā*). From that memory, we conclude that this matter was experienced by Manu and others through a means of valid cognition, because they remember it. For the occurrence of memory is not possible for that which has not been experienced.

But surely, they might compose a work by merely imagining it, without having experienced it through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just as some poets tell a story by inventing a fictional event.

To this it is replied: This would indeed be so if there were no instruction regarding what ought to be done (*kartavyatopadeśa*) here. For an instruction regarding what ought to be done is for the purpose of performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). And those who conduct themselves with deliberate intelligence (*buddhipūrvavyavahārin*) do not deserve to perform [an action] based on something imagined according to their own whim. If it is argued that the accomplishment of performance occurs even through error (*bhrānti*), then while the error of a single person might exist, the notion that the entire world is in error—and that such error persists as long as *saṃsāra* lasts—is an extraordinary (*alaukika*) hypothesis. Furthermore, since the works of Manu and others are rooted in the Veda, there is no room for error or the like.

For this very reason, it is not accepted that Manu and others perceived the *dharmas* through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Perception is that cognition which arises from the contact of the sense organs with their objects. Now, contact of the sense organs with *dharma* is impossible, because *dharma* has the nature of something to be performed (*kartavyatā*). Furthermore, what is to be performed is not yet established; and contact pertains only to an object that is already established. Although inference and the other means of knowledge may convey an object that does not exist at the present time—for instance, one infers future rain by the movement of ants carrying their eggs—nevertheless, no understanding of "what is to be performed" can arise from them. Therefore, when postulating a cause corresponding to the recollection of "what is to be performed," the Veda alone is indicated. And that Veda, being inferred [to exist], was apprehended by Manu and others.

(1) Now, that branch in which these Smārta duties were contained has been lost. Furthermore, one must consider whether there was only a single branch or many; and among those, whether certain [rites] such as the Aṣṭakā belonged to a particular one—such is the inference that proceeds.

(2) Now, even today those recensions (*śākhā*) are indeed being studied; however, those *dharma* rules are scattered. In one recension there is the originative injunction (*utpatti*) for rites such as the *aṣṭakā*, in another the substance (*dravya*), in another the deity (*devatā*), and in another the mantra (*mantra*). Thus, for the sake of easy comprehension, Manu and others compiled these scattered elements by bringing together their constituent parts (*aṅga*).
(3) Furthermore, these *dharma* rules arise solely from the indicative marks (*liṅga*) found in mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
(4) Now, some consider that this duty to be performed is beginningless, having come down through an unbroken succession of tradition, and is thus eternal like the Veda.

(5) Or else, they argue that for Manu and others—as well as for people like ourselves—it was a performance based on the conviction of another, and thus its scriptural basis must be eternally inferred.
The authors of the Vivaraṇa investigate such various alternatives.

This, however, is the conclusion: this performance is Vedic, because it is understood that there is an interconnection (*vyatiṣaṅga*) between the Smārta rites and the Vedic injunctions, and because performers, having observed that [interconnection], perform them. And that interconnection has been demonstrated: in some cases a Vedic element is the primary rite while the Smārta is subsidiary; in some cases the reverse; in some cases it concerns origin (*utpatti*); in some cases qualification (*adhikāra*); and in some cases it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Thus, all Smārta rites are interconnected with Vedic ones. This has been determined by us in detail in the *Smṛtiviveka*.
Because the Smārta and Vaidika [traditions] are constantly intertwined with one another,
they are never separated, whether by way of their agents or their rituals.
If only those who perform what is prescribed by direct Vedic revelation were to act in that manner, then there would be a foundation in the Veda.
The primary cause of validity is acceptance by those who know the Veda;
thus it has been said that there is an inference [of validity] regarding the Śrutis on account of the identity of their author.

However, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for determining any specific [details], nor is there any purpose [for such a determination]. Furthermore, the loss (*utsāda*) [of the texts] is even possible; for even today, Vedic branches (*śākhā*) are seen to have very few students. Some maintain that from those [branches] which might have suffered loss, the authors of the Smṛtis extracted and compiled only the injunctions (*vidhi*), devoid of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). Āpastamba states: "The injunctions are declared in the Brāhmaṇas; their recensions (*pāṭha*) that have been lost are inferred from actual practice. (ĀpDh 1.4.10)

In this case, however, it is impossible to disregard this branch which possesses such great purpose—in which all the duties of the various castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*), both those prescribed by tradition (*smārta*) and those pertaining to the household (*gārhya*), are recorded—and it would entail the assumption of many unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*) for all students, such as its total disappearance.

On the other hand, the extraction of the practical application (*prayoga*) of scattered texts—which are dense with explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), difficult to understand due to their being either for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) or for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), yet whose meanings have been determined through logic by those who are diligent—is entirely appropriate.

But in this view, since both contradictions are based on direct perception and Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śrautatva*), there can be no sublation of the Smṛti through an option (*vikalpa*). And that [sublation] is not intended by the distinguished ones (*viśiṣṭānām*). Furthermore, the authors of the Smṛtis accepted sublation and the fact that [the Smṛti] is rooted in an inferable Vedic text (*anumeya-śruti-mūlatva*). To this effect Gautama says: "The teachers [hold] that there is only one stage of life (*aikāśramya*), because the householder’s state is directly enjoined" (GDh 3.35). For if those branches were directly perceived by Manu and others, what kind of expression would this be: "because the householder’s state is directly enjoined"? [Objection: But surely all stages of life (*āśrama*) are directly enjoined. [Response: This is merely Gautama’s own opinion taught under the guise of citing "the teachers," because he began with "There is an option of stages of life for him" (GDh 3.1) and concluded with this [statement].

(3) Furthermore, the status of mantras and *arthavādas* as authoritative sources of knowledge is not contradicted. Although *arthavādas* are intended for the praise of injunctions (*vidhi-uddeśa*) and do not themselves enjoin their own literal meaning, nevertheless, in some cases, their being subservient to another purpose is not possible until an injunction regarding their own subject matter is understood. For example, in passages such as "A thief of gold, a drinker of liquor... (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.10.9), their status as supplementary to the injunction concerning the five fires (*pañcāgni-vidhi*) is not possible until the prohibition of stealing gold and so forth is understood. The understanding that "one who studies this knowledge does not fall even if he practices the theft of gold or associates with such people, whereas otherwise he falls" is not contradictory.

Now, who has established this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "only the statement of an injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*) conveys an injunction (*vidhi*), and not an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)"? In the case of "These four fall" (*ete patanti*, ChU 5.10.9), there too a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is heard. If you argue that injunctive suffixes (*liṅ* etc. are absent [there], then in the case of the night-sacrifices as well, in the phrase "they stand firm" (*pratitiṣṭhanti*, cf. TāṇB 23.2.4), there is likewise no hearing of an injunctive suffix. If you then claim that in that case, because there is a requirement for a governing context (*adhikāra*) and a syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), an injunction is determined through the assumption of the fifth mood (*pañcamalakāra*) and so forth, then the same will apply here as well. Furthermore, there are many injunctions regarding substances and deities that are understood from explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). In those cases, since the explanatory passages are subordinate to a particular injunction, and since that injunction itself requires the substance, deity, and so on, the function of the explanatory passage is limited to providing the specific details; thus, the understanding of those specific details dependent upon the explanatory passage is not a fault. However, in the present case, because another unrelated injunction is sought, there arises the contingency of a syntactic split (*vākyabheda*); therefore, these [explanatory passages] cannot be subordinate to the original injunction. And in the absence of that subordination, the understanding of the prohibition based upon it would not occur. Consequently, they say that this is different from the case of "He places the smeared pebbles" (*aktāḥ śarkarā upadadhāti*, TB 3.12.5.12) and "Ghee is indeed brilliance" (*tejo vai ghṛtam*, AitB 8.20).

That is incorrect. Even though there is a difference in meaning, since this comprehension is rooted in syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), there is no possibility of the objection regarding a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Mantras are understood by their very nature to be illuminators of the performance (*prayoga-prakāśaka*); since that performance is not established from any other source, they postulate the object to be illuminated (*prakāśya*) in order to fulfill their function as illuminators. Furthermore, the illumination of the origin (*utpatti*) and the qualification (*adhikāra*) of the *Aṣṭakā* sacrifice is not possible for something non-existent; thus, mantras provide knowledge of the origin, qualification, application (*viniyoga*), and performance. In this way, injunctions based on the wording of mantras (*māntravarṇika-vidhi*) are also accepted, such as the injunction regarding the deity in the *Āghāra* offering. For it is accepted that Dharma has four feet (*catuṣpād dharmaḥ*). Among these, only a small portion is explicitly heard (*śruta*), while the cause for understanding the remainder of its parts is of the same nature [as the mantra], because the relationship is grasped within the injunction itself. In every respect, therefore, a connection with the Veda is possible.

Manu, having associated with many disciples who studied numerous branches [of the Veda] as well as other learned brahmins (*śrotriya*), heard those branches from them and composed a book. Having presented those [branches] as the root source, he established his book as authoritative. Thus, others, relying on his authority, have adopted the practice without making an effort to find the original root. And this is our inference.

Therefore, even though there is a conflict and both are equally based on direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*), sublation is logically established. When the performance is accomplished through one direct revelation, there is no further requirement for another revelation. This is just as, in the case of the *sāmidhenī* verses, the archetype is already occupied by the number fifteen (*pañcadaśya*); thus, it does not require the number seventeen (*sāptadaśya*), even though the latter is also directly revealed. For the denotative meaning is proximate, and it sublates the weaker cognition—which is understood only through the requirement of the denoted meaning—due to its remoteness. Moreover, this does not entail a loss of authority; it should be viewed exactly like the archetypal auxiliary elements that, when obtained in modified rites (*vikṛti*) through the rule of transfer (*codaka*), are sublated when they come into conflict with the modified elements.
(4) Where there is no interruption of the tradition, there is the attainment of the lineage; for in that case, no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been applied by anyone.

(5) Even the position that [the Veda] is eternally inferable does not differ significantly from the position of oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*). We have set out to examine the source of the recollections of Manu and others; if the Veda were for them also merely inferable—as it is for us—then they would not be "rememberers" (*smartāraḥ*). Furthermore, it is impossible for an object that has never been perceived by anyone to be inferable, because a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is impossible. In the case of actions and the like, there is indeed a perception of a relationship in a general sense. Alternatively, actions and so forth are determined through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), and here there is no such thing as "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*).

Therefore, Manu and others possess a connection to the Veda regarding this matter; however, it is not possible to determine that this is the *only* manner [of such a connection]. It is more appropriate to assume that the firm understanding of duty among those who know the Veda is rooted in the Veda itself, rather than being based on error or other causes; thus, an assumption of a cause consistent with that understanding is made. In this regard, since direct Vedic texts—such as mantras and arthavādas—are available as sources for what has been lost or scattered, their status as the basis [for the Smṛti] remains plausible. Furthermore, even an explicit injunction is sometimes seen to serve as a root source, such as: "One should not dwell with one who wears soiled clothes" (VaDh 12.5). And that [injunction] is recited both in the context of formal study and in the initiation ceremony. This has been stated by us only in brief; the full details, however, should be learned from the *Smṛtiviveka*.
Some branches have become extinct; this is not considered by me to be a valid position, for in this position many unobserved things would follow as consequences.
The position that those who are distracted [from meditative concentration] undergo a collection of births and so forth here and there is more plausible;
for this is generally what is observed.
Respected by many disciples, teachers, and other Vedic scholars,
he was capable of composing [the work] after hearing various Vedic recensions from this or that source.
At that time, having been born, our possession was based on what was seen;
today, our certainty also stands as it occurs according to the facts.
The mantras are indicators of the performance; their indication occurs by way of name. Without the origination of the qualification [to perform], there is no possibility of the performance.
The attainment of a specific deity in the substratum is based on the words of the mantra;
because the mantra is illuminative, that [attainment] is caused by its fulfillment.
When there is a transition from one established form into another form,
that does not lead to the destruction of its own nature, just as in the case of the qualification for the Viśvajit sacrifice.
When a ritual injunction has been established, it is appropriate to postulate meanings related to it;
however, if no basis for such an injunction is observed anywhere in the mantras or the arthavādas, [then such a postulation is not justified].
The Blessed One Pāṇini remembers that injunction (*vidhi*) is to be understood from the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers;
those words which denote established entities (*siddhavastu*) are not capable of expressing an injunction.
If a meaning were intended to be understood through a figurative description (*guṇavāda*) that is not primarily concerned with its own literal sense (*atatpara*),
how could that [figurative] meaning be considered true?
One should not split the sentence because the nights are expectant of something;
rather, it is appropriate that the completion of the sentence be understood through that specific [context].
Even when theft and other such acts are prohibited, the application of another injunction is certain;
consequently, there would be a split in the sentence (vākyabheda), and therefore the proposed [objection] is not equal.
All [mantras] are employed in the Vācastoma because of the scriptural injunction for the application of mantras;
there is no specific reason for the cognition of a mantra in the case of the Aṣṭakā and other such rites.
An indicative mark (liṅga) is not a means of application without a general connection;
nor is there any such connection for it without [the presence of] context (prakaraṇa) and the like.
On this point, some who maintain that [the Veda] is its source offer a rebuttal:
"They establish themselves in the three nights" occurs even though the optative suffixes and other such markers are non-existent.
The understanding of that meaning is intended by means of the fifth *lakāra*;
thus it would be in cases such as "they do not fall [into error] because they have not spoken like barbarians" (*na mlechitavai*).
Regarding the *vācaḥstoma*, the rule for the *ṛcs* is that all the *daśatayas* (the ten *maṇḍalas*) are used;
those [hymns] which were repeated within the tenth *maṇḍala* are excluded and recited externally.
It is said that the very designation (samākhyā) is what establishes the general relationship;
thus, each of the Gṛhya-mantras has its own specific designation corresponding to its respective ritual action.
The status of [the passage concerning] the thief of gold as a supplement to the knowledge of the five fires is established by the censure of the thief of gold;
for that statement regarding the thief of gold would not exist without the prohibition of such theft.
The understanding of its being a subordinate element (śeṣatva) follows from the sense;
however, the fact that it is not to be performed [independently] serves to strengthen that subordinacy and is not, on the contrary, in conflict with it.

Whether it be the position that [the self] is eternally inferable, or the succession of scriptural tradition, between these two there is nothing but a blind transmission; no difference whatsoever is observed.

This being the case, the statement by Gautama that the householder’s stage of life (*gārhasthya*) is "directly enjoined" (GDh 3.36) is intended with reference to the immediate operation of the word. That meaning which is understood immediately following the hearing [of the word] is "direct" (*pratyakṣa*). However, that which is to be understood through the consideration of the capacity of that [directly perceived] meaning once the meaning has been understood is not "direct," because its comprehension is delayed; thus, everything is logically consistent.

"And [the authority of] Smṛti and Śīla for those who know them. Smṛti and Śīla together are "Smṛti-śīle. They say that Śīla is the abandonment of passion (rāga) and hatred (dveṣa). And that is the root of Dharma, not as an indicator like the Veda and Smṛti, but rather by way of its production; for from the abandonment of passion and hatred, Dharma is produced. But has it not been stated that "Dharma is the means to the highest good" (śreyas-sādhana)? And the very nature of that [means] is the abandonment of passion and hatred. In that case, since there is no distinction [between the means and the end], why is it said that "Dharma is produced from the abandonment of passion and so forth"?

We have already stated that this word *dharma* is sometimes employed by the authors of the *Smṛtis* to refer to an action that constitutes the subject matter of an injunction or prohibition, and sometimes to a certain entity produced by the performance of that action which persists until the time of the fruition of the result. Regarding the existence of such an entity, the word itself is the sole authority. For if the sacrifice were to perish without producing such an entity, how could the result arise at a later time? It is precisely this entity that is intended here by the term *dharma*. Therefore, it is not at all unreasonable to say that its root is ethical conduct (*śīla*). All conventional usages are indeed based on this intention.
"Dharma alone is the true friend who follows one even unto death" (MDh 8.17).
Since a ritual action perishes immediately after its performance, how could it persist into another time?

To this, an objection is raised: Surely every matter enjoined by Śruti and Smṛti is the root of Dharma; since good conduct (*śīla*) is also included therein, its separate mention is redundant. Furthermore, it will be prescribed [later].
"One should apply oneself day and night to the conquest of the senses" (MDh 7.44);
"When this [mind] is conquered, these two groups of five become conquered" (MDh 2.92).
We shall explain that this very conquest of the mind is the renunciation of passion and hatred.

Some say: the separate instruction is for the sake of showing respect; for this [duty] is useful in the performance of all ritual acts and is also primary in itself, like the *agnihotra* and other rites. Furthermore, it is a duty for all social classes (*varṇa*) and a duty for all stages of life (*āśrama*). Therefore, it is stated here on this occasion of defining the common duties.

We, however, say this: *samādhi* is called *śīla*. For it is recited among the verbal roots as *śila samādhau* (DhP 523). And *samādhāna* (concentration) is a mental quality. That state of the mind which, by avoiding distraction toward other objects, is inclined toward the discernment of the meaning of the scripture—that is called *śīla*. This is a *dvandva* compound in the sense of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*). Therefore, what is intended is that memory (*smṛti*) and conduct (*śīla*), being mutually dependent, possess authority regarding *dharma*; it is not, as in the previous case, their status as producers [of knowledge]. This is what is meant: that memory which possesses concentration is authoritative, not mere memory. Consequently, even if one knows the meaning of the Veda, the remembrance of those who are not intent upon it is not rooted in *dharma*, because for those devoid of attention to the meaning of the scripture, error and the like are possible. The word *ca* ("and") is recited here. It should be seen as following the word *tadvidām* ("of those who know that"); however, it is read in this way due to metrical requirements. Furthermore, since there is no other previously mentioned item to be conjoined, this word has a conjunctive sense (*samuccaya*); it conjoins what was stated in the third quarter [of the verse], namely, "that of the virtuous" (*sādhūnām*).

Therefore, three qualifications are relied upon here: the tradition of those who are learned—having acquired knowledge from a teacher—and likewise of those devoted to its practice and devoted to its performance, is authoritative. It is remembered that all this was the case for Manu and others; otherwise, the acceptance of the treatises composed by them by the learned (*śiṣṭas*) would not be possible.
If this were so, it should have been stated quite plainly: "The words of Manu and others are the root of Dharma. What is the use of this definition?

True. This statement regarding the grounds for authority is intended for one who might somehow dispute its validity; it is an exposition of the reasons for authority well-known in the Nyāya-śāstra. Even today, whoever possesses these grounds for authority should have their words accepted as valid, just like Manu and others. And so it is in the case of the instruction on penance and other matters by the learned: "Only those of such a nature become authoritative as an assembly (*pariṣad*), for even a single best of the twice-born who knows the Veda may determine the Dharma" (MDh 12.113).

For this very reason, the enumeration of Smṛti-authors as "Manu, Viṣṇu, Yama, Aṅgiras" (YDh 1.4) is without foundation. For instance, Paiṭhīnasi, Baudhāyana, Pracetas, and others are remembered by the learned (*śiṣṭas*) in such a manner, yet they are not included in that enumeration. In every respect, the word of one whom the learned remember or speak of without contradiction as being endowed with such qualities and as having composed this [work], would be an authority regarding Dharma even though it is of human origin. This is the meaning of the rule: "And [the conduct] of those who know that [Dharma], in their Smṛti and Śīla."
