If someone at the present time were to compose a treatise endowed with such qualities and for such a reason as these, he would become an authority for future generations just like Manu and others. However, for contemporary people, there exists no cause for their conviction in that work other than what they themselves possess; therefore, understanding does not arise from his words alone. For as long as a modern author does not demonstrate his source, learned men do not accept his statement as authoritative. But once the source is shown and the text is established as authoritative, if at some later time it should somehow come to resemble the source of the *Aṣṭakā* and other such practices, then it is logical to infer its basis through the fact that its acceptance by the learned (*śiṣṭas*) would otherwise be inexplicable.

"And the conduct of the virtuous (*sādhūnām*). By the word *ca* ("and"), the phrase "of those who know the Veda" (*vedavidām*) is connected. Through these two terms, the status of being a refined person (*śiṣṭatvam*) is indicated. Whatever the conduct (*ācāra*) of the refined is, that too is a root of Dharma. Conduct means customary practice (*vyavahāra*) or performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). Where there are no scriptural or traditional (*smṛti*) statements, yet the refined perform [an act] with the consciousness that it is Dharma, that too must be understood as Vedic, just like the previous cases. For example: the tying of the marriage bracelet (*kaṅkaṇabandhana*) and other rites performed for the sake of auspiciousness during a wedding; the worship of famous trees, Yakṣas, crossroads, and so forth, by a girl on the day she is to be married, which varies according to region; likewise, the number of tonsures (*cūḍā*) and regional variations; the service rendered to guests, teachers, and others, consisting of pleasant and beneficial speech, salutation, rising from one's seat, and so on; and the recitation of the *Pṛśnisūkta* while holding grass in the hand, as when they offer fodder to the horse during the Aśvamedha sacrifice—such is conduct. This conduct also takes many forms due to differences in individual nature and the resulting health or ill-health of the mind; because of its infinite variety in every particular, it is impossible to record it all in a book. That which is observed to be very pleasing to one person at one time may become the opposite at another occasion. Thus, the attendance (*paryupāsana*) shown by a householder to a guest may be pleasing to one, who thinks, "He attends me like a servant," but to another it is otherwise, who thinks, "I cannot sit here at ease in his presence," and becomes repelled by that very attendance. In such cases, neither a general inference from the Veda nor a specific one is possible. However, in the case of the *Aṣṭakā* and other rites, there is a recollection of the entire procedure in a fixed and uniform manner; this is the distinction between Smṛti and Ācāra.

"And contentment of the self" is also [a source of Dharma]; the phrase "the root of Dharma" is understood to carry over, as is the qualification "of the virtuous who know the Veda. They say that its status as the root of Dharma is due solely to its authority (*prāmāṇya*). For when the mind of such persons is serene regarding an action to be performed, and no aversion arises, that is Dharma. But would it not follow that even an action which is strictly prohibited could be considered Dharma if the mind were serene toward it? And what doubt could there be regarding a prescribed act—that it is not Dharma? [No, for the mind of the wise is never serene toward what is prohibited.]

It is so. For such great-souled and wise persons, the clarity of mind possesses such great power that even what is non-dharma attains the nature of dharma, and dharma attains the nature of non-dharma—not so for those possessed of defects such as passion and hatred. Just as whatever substance enters the *rumā* salt-mine all becomes salt, so too by the sudden arising of mental satisfaction in one who knows the Veda, everything is rendered pure. Therefore, just as the taking up of the cup, though prohibited, is not a fault when performed according to the rule in the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, there is no optionality here as there is in the case of that taking up. For prohibitions are established as applying to other objects, excluding the domain of self-satisfaction.

Alternatively, their own self does not find satisfaction in unrighteousness; just as a mongoose bites only a medicinal herb that neutralizes poison and no other. Therefore it is said: "Whichever one the mongoose bites, that one is a poison-neutralizer. And here the venerable ones say: regarding those matters that admit of alternatives, whichever alternative the mind finds pleasing, that alternative should be adopted. And he will state [later] in the section on the purification of substances and penances: "One should perform austerity in that manner until it becomes a source of satisfaction" (MDh 11.232).

Alternatively, it is said that one who lacks faith due to atheism has no entitlement [to this path]. For the soul of an atheist is not satisfied even when performing Vedic rites; therefore, the action performed by him is indeed fruitless.

Alternatively, the clarity of disposition (*bhāva-prasāda*) regarding all actions is being taught: at the time of performance, one should abandon anger, delusion, grief, and so forth, and remain joyful. And for this reason, like ethical conduct (*śīla*), this [faith] is designated as the root of dharma because it is a prerequisite for everything. (2.6)
Whatever dharma has been proclaimed by Manu for anyone, all that is stated in the Veda, for it consists of all knowledge. (2.7)

He clarifies by this [verse] what was stated regarding the authority of Smṛti through its connection with those who know the Vedas: whatever dharma—whether the dharma of the castes (*varṇadharma*), the dharma of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*), or the dharma of the sacraments (*saṃskāradharma*)—exists in its general or particular forms for any caste such as the Brāhmaṇas and so forth, has been proclaimed by Manu; all of that is declared and established in the Veda. How this is so was stated in the preceding verse: "For he consists of all knowledge. The Veda is the cause or the source of all cognitions concerning supersensible objects (*adṛṣṭaviṣaya*). The suffix *mayaṭ* is applied here by superimposing the state of being a modification (*vikāratva*) upon knowledge, as if it were composed of all cognitions. For that which is a modification of something is said to "consist of" (*tanmaya*) or have that as its nature. And since the Veda is the cause of knowledge, it "consists of" knowledge. Furthermore, according to the Satkāryavāda view, the cause possesses the nature of the effect. Alternatively, the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied in the sense of "come from" (*āgata*) from the cause "all-knowledge," according to Pāṇini 4.3.81: *hetumanuṣyebhyaḥ*. (2.7)
But having examined all this in its entirety with the eye of knowledge, the wise man should indeed abide in his own duty (svadharma) by virtue of the authority of the scriptures. 2.8.

Having examined with the eye of knowledge—consisting of hearing and reflecting upon the fields of learning such as logic (*tarka*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), etymology (*nirukta*), and ritual inquiry (*mīmāṃsā*)—all that is to be known, whether created or uncreated, within the scope of the scriptures or within the scope of perception and so forth, or beyond the scope of perception and so forth; for the study of the scriptures is like an eye, because it shares the commonality of being a cause of knowledge. Just as form is known by means of the eye, so too is *dharma* known by means of the scripture; this is the commonality. Having thus examined and determined [the truth] through correct investigation, one should enter into *dharma* and practice *dharma* on the basis of the authority of revelation, that is, the authority of the Veda.

For when all the treatises have been correctly understood, the authority of the Veda alone remains established; this is not the case when they are not understood. For instance, by examining those treatises with great skill, one determines that there is no sound reasoning for their authority, whereas such exists for the Veda. The term "all" (*sarva*) is an adjective qualifying the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). The word "entire" (*nikhila*) is an adverbial modifier of the action "having examined" (*samavekṣya*). The meaning is as follows: having examined everything—that is, having demonstrated all possible arguments that might appear regarding the authority of other treatises or the lack of authority of the Veda from the perspective of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), and having refuted them with the reasons established in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) as defined by their specific characteristics—and having set forth the proofs for one's own position, the authority of the Veda stands firm. This is what is indicated by the word "entire. Thus, although the two words "entire" (*nikhila*) and "all" (*sarva*) are synonyms, they are not redundant because they refer to different aspects of the subject matter. The inclusion of the word "own" (*sva*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*); for that which is the duty (*dharma*) of one is indeed the non-duty (*adharma*) of another. (2.8)
For a person who practices the dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti attains fame in this world and supreme happiness after death. (2.9)

For one who, out of nihilism (*nāstikatā*), is deluded by the thought that Vedic rituals are fruitless and thus does not engage in their performance, the author—acting as a friend—shows visible results in order to induce such engagement. Let other results stand aside for now; however, by performing that action called *dharma* which is declared in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, one obtains fame, praise, honor, and good fortune in this world as long as one lives. Abiding on the righteous path, everyone honors him, thinking, "This man is highly meritorious. He becomes beloved to all. After death, in another body, he attains that happiness than which there is nothing higher. Generally, the qualification belongs to one who desires heaven (*svarga-kāma*), and since heaven is unsurpassed bliss, it is described here as "unsurpassed" (*anuttama*). Therefore, this [verse] is intended to mean that no one seeking a visible result alone would be motivated to engage in this very practice. (2.9)
The Śruti is to be understood as the Veda, and the Smṛti as the Dharmaśāstra;
these two are not to be questioned in any matter, for from them indeed has Dharma shone forth.

Is this recollection of the relationship between words and their meanings a treatise on nomenclature (*abhidhānakośa*), such as "Ātmabhūḥ, Parameṣṭhī," and so forth, rather than a treatise on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*), by which it would be said: "The Veda is to be known as Śruti, while the Dharmaśāstra is indeed Smṛti"?

It is said: In this context, the conduct of the virtuous (*sadācāra*) is neither *śruti* nor *smṛti*, because it lacks a formal composition; for it is well known that *smṛtis* consist of composed words. Therefore, [the author] establishes its status as *smṛti*: "That which teaches duty (*dharma*) as a task is a *dharmaśāstra*; where duty is taught—that is, where it is understood as something to be performed—that is *smṛti*. Whether there is a formal composition or not is irrelevant. From the conduct of the virtuous (*śiṣṭasamācāra*) as well, there arises the understanding of duty as something to be performed; that too is indeed *smṛti*. Consequently, wherever a *smṛti* is to be cited for a particular purpose, the conduct of the virtuous must also be accepted there.

If *dharmaśāstra* were simply *smṛti*, then since the Veda is also the foremost teaching of Dharma, it would follow that the Veda too is *smṛti*. To avoid this consequence, he says: "But the *śruti* is to be understood as the Veda. That in which the term "instruction on Dharma" is heard is *śruti*; and that in which it is remembered is *smṛti*. Since that [term] also exists in the case of traditional practice (*samācāra*), that too is indeed *smṛti*; for there is no authority in it unless it is based on an unremembered Vedic word. Alternatively, the mention of *śruti* is for the purpose of showing that *smṛti* is equal to the Veda.
Furthermore, what common function of the Śruti and Smṛti is obtained by another [means], namely, through customary practice (samācāra)?

It is said: those two, namely *śruti* and *smṛti*, are not to be subjected to critical inquiry (*amīmāṃsye*) regarding all matters. Even concerning all matters that are utterly inconceivable through means of knowledge pertaining to the perceptible world—such as how from the very same act characterized by violence there may be, in one case, prosperity and in another, sin; or how from drinking liquor there is hell, while from drinking *soma* there is purification of sin—in such cases, one must not engage in deliberation by way of advancing a thesis and its counter-thesis. *Mīmāṃsana* (critical inquiry) consists in raising doubts and conceiving alternative positions. For example: "If violence is a cause of sin because its essential nature is no different [from worldly violence], then Vedic violence ought likewise to be so; or if Vedic violence is a cause of prosperity, then worldly violence should also be so, since their form is identical. What is prohibited here is the stubborn adherence to a particular tenet (*siddhāntābhiniveśa*), which is the investigation of a matter whose nature has been understood from the Veda by means of fallacious reasons and unsound arguments based on faulty logic. It is not this kind of inquiry that is forbidden—namely, the inquiry into whether a certain point in the Veda is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) or the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). For the author will state later: [The text continues with the subsequent verse.]
"He who investigates by means of reasoning knows Dharma, and no other" (MDh 12.106).
But is this a prohibition against inquiry for the sake of some unseen result?

We say: no. For from those two [the Veda and the Self], Dharma indeed shone forth. By this, he declares the fallacious nature of the logical proofs (*tārkikapramāṇa*) of the dialecticians which seek to establish conclusions contrary to the meaning of the Veda. For such are their arguments: "Vedic injury is a cause of sin, because it is an act of injury, like worldly injury. In that case, the fact that injury is a cause of sin is not established by any other means of knowledge apart from scripture (*āgama*). Thus, as long as scripture has not been accepted as authoritative, there is no reason to establish that injury is a means to sin. And once the authority of scripture is accepted, a reason that contradicts it is not tenable, because that would result in the scripture losing its authority. Consequently, there is a mutual contradiction: first accepting it as authoritative, and later denying its authority. This position is self-contradictory, like saying, "My mother is barren"; and it is also in conflict with scripture.

Now it is said: Scripture (*āgama*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). How, then, can pointing out its contradiction serve as a refutation? Because of the defects of falsehood, internal contradiction, and tautology. For instance, regarding rituals such as the *kārīrī* sacrifice, which are performed with the desire for an immediate result, the attainment of that result does not necessarily follow immediately after the performance. If it is argued that the result will occur at a later time, it has been stated in this regard: "The *kārīrī* sacrifice was performed in autumn while the rice crops were drying up severely;
yet the rain falls in spring—the result of that [sacrifice] is the death of cattle. (70)

Even regarding rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, which have results to be experienced at another time, since the action perishes without leaving a trace (*niranvaya-vināśa*), the claim that its fruit will arise after a hundred years is comparable to the speech of an untrustworthy bard. Therefore, [the Veda] is false. There is also contradiction (*vyāghāta*): "The oblation should be offered after sunrise; there is a fault for one who offers before sunrise: 'Every morning, those who offer the Agnihotra before sunrise speak untruth'" (AitB 5.31). Likewise, it is said that the oblation should be offered before sunrise: "Just as one would give to a guest who has arrived unexpectedly, so is the offering made at that time" (TB 2.1.2.12). Thus, in one place the offering after sunrise is enjoined by censuring the offering before sunrise, while the opposite is enjoined elsewhere. In this case, which position should be adopted? There is thus indecision (*anadhyavasāya*). Furthermore, whatever rite such as the Agnihotra exists in one recensional branch (*śākhā*) is found in other branches as well; the accepted principle is that a single rite is recognized across all branches. Consequently, there is redundancy (*punarukta*).

In this regard, it is established by this very verse-quarter that such [a claim] is indeed false. For from the Veda, *dharma* alone—merely the state of being an obligation concerning sacrifices and the like—is manifested, shines forth, and is understood; however, a specific time for the production of the fruit is not [manifested], because no specific time is heard in the sentences constituting the *adhikāra* (entitlement) injunctions. From an injunction, one understands only that "the fruit comes to be"; the temporal limitation is not part of the injunction. Indeed, the divisions of time—past, future, and present—are related to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). And this fruit is not the fruit of the verbal root's meaning, but rather the fruit of the injunction (*vaidha*). For the fruit of the verbal root's meaning is accomplished at that very moment, such as the relinquishing of a substance (*dravya*) for the sake of a deity, the modification of the oblation (*havirvikāra*), and so forth. If someone is an executor of another's command, he is dispatched with the words, "Go, go to the village. Having set out to fulfill that command, he might sometimes receive the reward for his wages at the very beginning, sometimes in the middle, sometimes immediately after the object of the command has been completed, or on the next day, or at some other later time. Thus, the fruit of this scripture (*śāstra*) is of indefinite time. As for divine rain and the like, by their very nature, only proximity is understood, but not necessarily production on that very same day.

And just as there are obstacles to such a result in the world, so too in the Veda there is previously committed evil action (*duṣkṛta*) and the like. And the Veda itself shows this: "If it should not rain, one should dwell in that very same way. Regarding the *sarvasvāra* sacrifice, however, they dispute: "This is not the fruit of the sacrifice; this is a subsidiary injunction (*aṅga-smaraṇa*). The fruit of the sacrifice belongs to him who desires: 'May I go to the heavenly world free from disease.'"

As for the claim that there is no difference between worldly and Vedic violence (*hiṃsā*), the nature of that [Vedic violence] is indeed to be understood through scripture, not within the scope of perception and other means of knowledge; and in this regard, there is a distinction. Worldly violence is characterized by passion (*rāga*), whereas non-worldly violence is characterized by injunction (*vidhi*). Furthermore, the violence pertaining to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice is characterized by injunction; thus, there is a great difference. Therefore, there is nothing false in the Veda. The opponent will resolve the contradiction later with a verse itself. (2.10)

That twice-born man who, relying on the treatises of logic, would show contempt for these two roots [the Veda and the teacher], should be excluded by the virtuous as an atheist and a reviler of the Veda. (2.11)

In the absence of any cause for invalidity, if a twice-born person, relying on the science of logic (*hetu-śāstra*)—the science of logic being the treatises of the nihilists such as the Buddhists and Cārvākas, wherein it is proclaimed again and again that the Veda is unrighteousness (*adharmya*)—should show contempt for the *Śruti* and the *Smṛti*, and if someone should try to turn him away from forbidden acts by saying, "Do not do this; it is prohibited by the Veda," he should disregard that person and desire to act, saying: "What does it matter if it is prohibited in the Veda or in the *Smṛtis*? Indeed, there is no valid authority (*prāmāṇya*) in those two at all. Or he might reflect thus in his mind. If he is seen to be devoted to the treatises of logic, he should be excluded by virtuous and cultured men (*sādhu-śiṣṭa*) from various activities, such as officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the hospitable reception of guests. Since no specific action is mentioned, it is understood that he is to be excluded from those things worthy of the learned. For it is the ignorant person, whose self is improperly refined, who behaves in this way due to his mere scent of logicianism (*tārkika-gandhitā*). In these activities, however, only the learned are qualified. For this very reason, in the preceding verse, such inquiry is prohibited because it is performed with the intent of showing contempt for the Veda, and not because it is done out of a desire to know its specific meaning. He states the reason for this very purpose: "A nihilist (*nāstika*) is one who reviles the Veda. Therefore, one who might argue in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the Veda lacks authority would not necessarily be a nihilist. The mention of the reason in the prima facie position is solely for the sake of strengthening the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). As for the term "reviler of the Veda," the *Smṛti* was not explicitly mentioned [in the definition]; the intention is that since both are equally the subject under discussion, the mention of either one effectively includes both. (2.11)

But as for one who, not understanding this point, assumes that the word "Veda" refers only to its intended literal sense, and might conclude that the exclusion of a reviler of Smṛti is not prescribed here, whereas the exclusion of a reviler of the Veda alone is, the author says to him:
"The Veda, Smṛti, the conduct of the virtuous, and what is pleasing to oneself—these four, they say, are the direct indicators of Dharma. (2.12)

There is no distinction here. By the prohibition against reviling the Veda, the exclusion of one who reviles even Smṛti, established custom, and self-satisfaction is ordained by this [text]. For these too have their designation as Dharma based upon the Veda; therefore, one who reviles Smṛti and the rest is indeed a reviler of the Veda itself.
[Objection: Is there not no purpose served by these two verses? It should rather be stated thus:
"A twice-born man, by resorting to the treatises on logic, [rejects] the means of knowledge beginning with Śruti and ending with self-satisfaction..."
He who would revile [it] must be excluded by the virtuous on account of his nihilism.

It is said: The teachers do not consider the bulkiness of the text; rather, they strive to avoid the burden on the intellect. For when that burden exists, there is an incorrect understanding of the Dharma, and that destroys the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Even though they could have indicated both [the Veda and the Smṛti] together in a single mention, they might have raised the objection: "Only the mention of the Veda should be made, since all Dharma is Vedic. Therefore, for the sake of clarity, both are mentioned separately: the first verse is for those who prefer brevity, while the two verses are for others.

By the phrase "and what is pleasing to oneself," that which was previously mentioned as *ātmatuṣṭi* (self-satisfaction) is precisely what is being stated here. The inclusion of the word *sva* (one's own) is for the purpose of completing the meter. This is the direct definition, cause, and indicator of dharma, but it is not [dharma] itself as a perceptible object (*pratyakṣa*). As the Nirukta states: "those who have directly realized dharma" (Nirukta 1.20). The word *vidhā* signifies a variety or mode. Dharma has only one means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely that called the Veda; however, these others—Smṛti and so forth—are its subdivisions.

Others, however, explain this verse for the purpose of a summary, [stating] that the section on the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇaprakaraṇa*) is completed. A repetition indicates completion, just as in the Vedic auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*), where the double recitation "they stand near with the *saṃsthājapa*, they stand near" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 1.13.10) serves as such. Thus, the previously stated meaning remains in the mind as if condensed into a single whole. This is generally the method of authors of treatises; likewise, even the author of the Mahābhāṣya sometimes recites a *sūtra* or a *vārttika*, explains it, and then recites it again. (2.12)
For those who are unattached to wealth and desire, knowledge of Dharma is prescribed;
for those seeking to understand Dharma, the Śruti is the supreme authority. (2.13)

Wealth (*artha*) consists of property such as cattle, land, gold, and so forth. Attachment (*sakti*) to that is the performance of activities such as agriculture and service with the intent (*tātparya*) of acquiring and protecting it. Desire (*kāma*) is sexual union with women. Attachment to that is the constant indulgence in it, as well as in its accessories such as song and instrumental music. For men who are free from these [attachments], the knowledge of dharma—the awakening to dharma—is ordained; it is specifically established (*viśeṣeṇa dhīyate*), meaning it becomes firmly settled. This is the form of the root *dhī* in the sense of "placing" (*ādhāne*), according to Dhātupāṭha 1136.

But for what reason is there no knowledge of Dharma for those who are attached to that [worldly life], given that they too are able to know it according to the occasion—during times not incompatible with it, such as while eating, through hearing historical accounts, from the instruction of others, or by means of conventional practice? To this he says: "for those desiring to know Dharma. The Veda is the primary authority regarding Dharma, and it cannot be known by them; for it is extremely difficult to understand, requiring the study of the sciences of *nigama*, *nirukta*, grammar, logic, the Purāṇas, and Mīmāṃsā in order to comprehend its own meaning.

Furthermore, such a vast mass of literature cannot be mastered without the renunciation of all other activities. From customary practice (*samācāra*), historical accounts (*itihāsa*), and the like, only a few *dharma*s are understood; one does not grasp the performance of the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices complete with all their constituent parts (*aṅga*) as is possible from the Vedas and similar sources. Therefore it has been said: "The supreme authority is the revealed scripture (*śruti*). This, however, does not imply a deficiency in the authority of customary practice and the rest. As it has been stated:
"He who fears wealth as if it were a snake, sweet food as if it were poison, and women as if they were ogresses—he truly acquires knowledge. (MSSaṃ 4121)

Others, however, are called those who desire wealth and pleasure, seeking visible fruits. For those who are attached to these—desiring honor, fame, and the like, and whose purpose is merely the favor of the world due to their pursuit of visible results—neither the knowledge of Dharma nor the practice of Dharma is enjoined or taught.

That in which something is known is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*); here, it refers to performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). For when a duty (*dharma*) is being performed, it becomes more manifest than even at the time of its comprehension through the scriptures. Therefore, performance is called the knowledge of *dharma*. This is what is meant: although a visible purpose such as public esteem is obtained from the performance of *dharma*, one should nevertheless not engage in it for the sake of achieving that [purpose]. Rather, one should act on the grounds that it is enjoined by the scripture. If a visible result occurs while acting in this manner, let it be; it is not to be deliberated upon. And thus the *Śruti* restates the visible fruit of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*): "Fame and the ripening of the world," and "The world, being ripened, benefits him in four ways: through honor, through gifts, through invincibility, and through immunity from being slain," and so forth (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 11.5.7.1). There is also a verse on this point: *yaśasvī lokapaktiś ca dharmaṃ kuryād ato naraḥ | na tu lokopakārārthaṃ dṛṣṭatvāt tadupekṣyate ||* "Therefore, a man should perform *dharma* to become famous and to ripen the world; however, it is disregarded [as a motive] because it is merely a visible result. *Note: The provided text contains citations marked [86] and [87], which have been integrated into the narrative flow.*
Just as water sprinkled here for the sake of sugarcane also waters the grasses and the creepers,
so too a person walking upon the path of Dharma attains fame, desires, and wealth.

[Objection: But surely, whatever nature is known to belong to something does not deviate from that nature even when it is performed for another purpose; it certainly produces its own effect. For example, poison, even when drunk with the intention of taking medicine, still kills. Therefore, ritual acts prescribed by the scriptures, even when performed for the sake of visible results, will also produce invisible (transcendental) results. Why this resentment on your part, that one should not engage in such acts because they serve as a means of winning over the world? To this, he says: "For those desiring to know Dharma, the Veda is the authority regarding Dharma. By this, the following is stated: for those who desire objects consisting of visible fruits, no invisible result arises. Not only does no invisible result arise, but through the practice of what is prohibited, demerit (*adharma*) also arises. (2.13)
But where there is a conflict between two Vedic texts, both are traditionally held to be Dharma;
for both of them have been rightly declared as Dharma by the wise. (2.14)

The contradiction previously mentioned is now resolved: where there is a duality of scriptural injunctions—that is, a contradictory statement—such that one scripture declares "this is dharma" and another declares that very same thing "to be adharma," both of those dharmas are to be performed as alternatives.

For those two scriptural texts are of equal strength; in that case, it is impossible to distinguish which one is authoritative and which is not. Therefore, it has been stated that "when there is a conflict between two texts of equal strength regarding a single purpose, there is an option" (GDh 1.4), and thus both of them are indeed *dharma*. In that situation, their combination (*samuccaya*) follows; in this way, both become *dharma*, for otherwise only one would be so.

We say: no. Even when applied alternately, there is no contradiction in the application of the word "both. For this [word] does not refer exclusively to two things that are mutually dependent. Furthermore, an option (*vikalpa*) is logical. Just as in the case of the single rite called Agnihotra, for which three times have been prescribed—wherein the ritual action is primary and time is secondary—and since the three times cannot coexist in a single performance, it is not proper to repeat the performance merely out of regard for the time; nor should the primary act be repeated merely out of regard for its subsidiaries. Therefore, this is logical, according to the rule: "When there is a conflict between those of equal strength, there is an option" (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.4).
For both of these are indeed *dharmas*. [Objection: But what is the distinction between those two *dharmas*?

[Response: None at all. By the former [verse], his own view was presented; by the latter, he strengthens his own view through its agreement with the views of other teachers, showing that this very same point has been stated by other wise men as well. (2.14)
Whether the sun has risen, has not yet risen, or is at the juncture of dawn, the sacrifice is performed in every way; such is the Vedic revelation.

This is an illustration regarding the contradiction [of injunctions] shown immediately above [in section 89]. These three times for the *homa* have been prescribed by means of mutual censure; the meaning of the Vedic statements in this regard is as follows: "The sacrifice proceeds in every way. That is to say, the *homa* proceeds in all its forms—it must be performed in every manner. The censure of the *homa* performed after sunrise (*udita-homa*) is not intended to prohibit it, but rather to enjoin the *homa* performed before sunrise (*anudita-homa*). The same applies to the other cases as well. Thus, the following meaning is expressed: the rite must be performed in one or another of these times. Whichever time it is performed in, the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled therein. This Vedic revelation has such a purport; its intention lies in this sense, and not in the prohibition of that which is being censured.

*Yajña* means *homa*; here, that which is called the *agnihotra* is intended, since there is no absolute difference between *yāga* and *homa*. A *yāga* is the renunciation of one's own ownership over a substance with reference to a deity, [expressed as]: "This is not mine; this belongs to the deity. This essential nature is present in *homa* as well. However, this is the distinction: in *homa*, the additional element is the casting (*prakṣepa*) of the substance, specifically its offering (*āropaṇa*) into the fire and so forth. Therefore, the word *yajña* is used here to denote *homa*. For these times are prescribed in the Śruti for *homa*, not for *yāga* in general.

Furthermore, by the words "at sunrise" (*uditādi*) and so forth, the Vedic injunction (*śruti*) such as "one should sacrifice when the sun has risen" is indicated by a part [of its meaning]. The construction is as follows: this very Vedic injunction—"one should sacrifice at sunrise, one should not sacrifice at sunrise"—is intended for that purpose (i.e., the praise of the *jyotiṣṭoma*). By the word "when the night has passed" (*samayādhyuṣita*), the time of dawn is expressed by means of the whole [compound].

Others, however, say that these are two words. The word *samaya* signifies proximity and requires something proximate. Because of the proximity of the times when the sun has risen and when it has not yet risen, the time near them is the twilight period (*saṃdhyākāla*). *Adhyuṣitam* means the time at the end of night; the meaning is "when the night has dawned. This *smṛti* text is an imitation of Vedic sentences—reading thus in some *śruti*s and thus in others. Therefore, whether these are two words or one must be determined from those very [Vedic] sources.

Therefore, since there is an injunction for three times with respect to the single ritual act called *homa* by means of option (*vikalpa*), there is no contradiction. For a contradiction would exist in the case of an established entity (*siddharūpa*), because it is impossible for mutually contradictory forms to coexist therein; but this is not the case with that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Indeed, that which is to be accomplished is understood as being accomplished by this [means] and also by that [means]. In that regard, whence could there be a contradiction? And this very principle of option is the correct one for conflicting Smṛti texts. (2.15)

He for whom the ritual procedure beginning with the impregnation and ending with the cremation ground has been prescribed by means of mantras—only he should be known as qualified for this scripture, and no one else whatsoever. (2.16)

They recite: "This [Veda] is to be studied by a learned Brāhmaṇa" (MDh 1.103). This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Because the suffix *tavya* is seen there, someone might have the misconception that it is an injunction. To prevent the doubt that, if this were so, the study would be precluded for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, this verse demonstrates their eligibility. Furthermore, lest a Śūdra, acting according to his own desire, should proceed to study since there is no prohibition against him, the ancients explain this verse as being intended to prevent that as well.

The word *śāstra* here refers to the text of Manu. *Adhikāra* is the understanding: "This is to be performed by me. Now, it is not possible for a collection of words, which is by nature already established (*siddha-svabhāva*), to be understood as something to be performed; for an action cannot be understood as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) without depending on some substance (*dravya*). Therefore, it is understood that there is an entitlement (*adhikāra*) toward some action that has the *śāstra* as its object. In this regard, the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* are not perceived as the objects [of the *śāstra*]. This is because *bhū* and *as* have the sense of "becoming" (*bhavati-arthatvāt*). For if they were connected with *bhū* and *as*, the meaning would be understood as: "One should perform that which is the becoming and the existence of the *śāstra*. And it is impossible for one person to be the performer of the existence belonging to another. Nor is it possible in the sense of the root *kṛ* (to do), because words are eternal and sentences have been composed by others. Therefore, the action of studying (*adhyayana-kriyā*), which accompanies the *śāstra*, is what is perceived. Thus, the following meaning is stated: his entitlement is to the study of the *śāstra*. Just as it is with the study, so too it is with the hearing of its meaning.

Objection: Since the Mānava text has a beginning in time, how can it be said that the injunctions concerning its subject matter are rooted in the beginningless Veda? Response: It cannot be generally inferred that any sentences expounding the scriptures are not to be studied by a Śūdra. Those Vedic sentences, those explanatory sentences regarding their meaning, and even the words of commentators that correspond to them, are indeed eternal because they exist in an eternal stream (*pravāha*). However, the subject matter of the scripture is its practical application (*anuṣṭhāna*), and in that regard, all four social orders (*cāturvarṇya*) possess the qualification (*adhikāra*). Objection: If this were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a Śūdra would have the qualification for general duties (*sāmānyadharma*) where no specific agent is mentioned. Response: We shall explain in various places how this does not occur.

But how can there be eligibility for ritual action (*karmādhikāra*) when eligibility for study and comprehension is prohibited? For it is not possible for one who does not know the nature of the ritual to perform it, nor is comprehension of its meaning possible without study, and one who lacks knowledge is not eligible [for rituals]. True. However, even through the instruction of others, such knowledge is sufficiently established. A Śūdra who has taken refuge with a Brāhmaṇa, or one who is engaged in the work, will instruct him, saying, "Having done this, do that. Therefore, the study and comprehension of the Śūdra are not prompted by the performance of ritual; like women, his performance is accomplished through the conviction of another, just as for women, the husband’s own knowledge serves their purpose incidentally, and the scriptural injunctions regarding ritual do not prompt their acquisition of knowledge. Only those men for whom there is the injunction "One's own Veda must be studied" have the conviction of themselves as the cause for performing the rites—and that applies only to the three higher castes. Even for them, study and comprehension are not prompted by the desire to know the meaning, but rather by two injunctions: the injunction to act as a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*) and the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayanavidhi*).

*Niṣeka* is the impregnation (*garbhādhāna*). That collection of sacraments (*saṃskārakalāpa*) which has that as its beginning is called *niṣekādi*. And for some, the impregnation is prescribed with the mantra, "May Viṣṇu prepare the womb" (*viṣṇur yoniṃ kalpayatu*, RV 10.184.1), during the first approach after marriage; for others, it occurs at every menstrual cycle until conception. That which has the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) as its end is called *śmaśānānta*. By the word *śmaśāna*, the place where the remains of the dead are deposited is denoted. And by association, this term indicates the post-mortem sacrament (*parācīṣṭi*), for that [rite] possesses mantras, whereas the physical site does not. By this [term], the twice-born (*dvijāti*) are indicated, for their sacraments are accompanied by mantras. The expression "of the twice-born" was not explicitly stated; such is the diverse composition of the verses of this Svāyambhuva Manu.

The connection is not that "the procedure (vidhi) is stated by means of mantras," for mantras do not state a procedure. Rather, they are reminders of the enjoined action at the stage of its performance, not enjoiners of it. Therefore, it should be explained thus: "this procedure belongs to those [rites] which are joined with mantras, i.e., which possess mantras."

The phrase "of no one else" is a restatement, because [the practice] is restricted to the twice-born. Alternatively, someone might think that this [practice] is prescribed as a mandatory duty for the twice-born, but for Śūdras it is neither enjoined nor prohibited; it is for the purpose of removing such a doubt that this has been stated. (2.16)
The region between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī, that land created by the gods is called Brahmāvarta. (2.17)

The authorities on Dharma have been stated; and in case of conflict, an option has been declared; and the qualified persons have been mentioned in general. Now, those regions are described within which Dharma becomes fit for performance by virtue of suitability. There is a river named Sarasvatī and another called Dṛṣadvatī. The region that lies between these two rivers, in their midst, the learned call and designate by the name "Brahmāvarta. The mention of the gods is for the purpose of praising the limits of the boundary; for it was created by the gods, and therefore it is more purifying than all other regions. (2.17)

Whatever custom has been handed down through traditional succession in that region for the social classes (varṇas) and the intermediate castes (antarālas), that is called the eternal practice (sadācāra).

Now, regarding the authority of the practice (*ācāra*) that exists in this particular region: is it accepted that being learned (*vidvattā*) and being refined (*śiṣṭatā*) are the qualifying conditions (*upādhi*)? Or is the mere condition of the region itself the authority for those who are unlearned and unrefined? What follows from this? If these are not required, then the two qualifications stated in the verse, "And the practice of the virtuous" (MDh 2.6), would be purposeless; for the status of being the root of Dharma cannot be established for the practice of the non-virtuous, since their connection with the Veda is impossible. On the other hand, if they are required, then the connection with a specific region provides no assistance; for it cannot be said that the practice of the refined (*śiṣṭa*) is lacking in authority even in another region.

It is replied: this designation is general. It has been stated that "in this region, the presence of cultured people (*śiṣṭas*) occurs by way of general prevalence; whatever the custom is in that region, that is right conduct (*sadācāra*).
Others, however, say that this is for the purpose of prohibiting regional customs, such as marrying the daughter of a maternal uncle in other regions.
That is incorrect, because it was stated without any qualification:
One should determine that which is not inconsistent with the customs of the region, the family, and the caste. (MDh 8.46)

And that [practice] is contradicted by the rule: "Beyond the seventh degree from paternal relatives... and beyond the fifth degree from maternal relatives" (GDh 4.3, 5). Even in this region, practices such as eating together with one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*) are by no means accepted as being in accordance with *dharma*. Furthermore, there is no possibility of the authority of a practice that contradicts *smṛti*, because it is remote from the *śruti*. From practice (*ācāra*), *smṛti* must be inferred; from *smṛti*, the *śruti*. But *smṛti* leads to the inference of a *śruti* that is immediately proximate. Moreover, such practices arise from the perception of a specific motive: they married a beautiful daughter of their maternal uncle out of fear of the king, so that there might be no punishment for illicit intercourse with a maiden (*kanyāgamana*).

Others, however, being ignorant, have grasped the literal meaning of the verse, "By that path his fathers have gone" (MDh 4.178), and accepted it as a matter of dharma. Furthermore, although the penance has been heard in the text, "One should not marry these three for the sake of a wife" (MDh 11.173), there is a cause for delusion, namely the thought: "Any woman other than these three is not prohibited. We shall explain how this is not its true meaning. Moreover, there is no authority for Smṛti or custom when they are based on perceptible motives. As the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda has said:

A Smṛti that is contradictory, contested, based on perceptible objects, and has a perceptible cause cannot have the Śruti as its source; and so too is this [Smṛti] which refers to a possible Śruti. Therefore, these passages praising specific regions—such as "the twice-born should resort to these countries" (MDh 2.24)—are merely explanatory statements (arthavādas) intended to glorify those regions as supplements to that injunction.

*Pāraṃparya* is simply *paraṃparā*. A lineage (*paraṃparā*) is a stream consisting of such a form as: from one [person] to another, from that one to yet another, and from that one to yet another. *Krama* is the non-interruption of that; "come from that" means arrived from that. "Mixed castes" (*saṃkīrṇayoni*) refers to the intermediate ones. [The compound refers to] those social classes (*varṇas*) together with those [intermediate ones]. (2.18)
Kurukṣetra, the Matsyas, the Pañcālas, and the Śūrasenakas—
this is indeed the land of the Brahmarṣis, which follows immediately after Brahmāvarta.

These are names of regions. Kurukṣetra and Samantapañcaka are well known; the Kurus met their destruction there. The etymological derivation is: "Perform good deeds quickly (*kuru vā sukṛtam kṣipram*), for here there will be protection. Words such as *matsya* and others ending in the plural number denote regions. *Brahmarṣideśa* is a collective designation. *Brahmāvarta* is a region created by the gods. Since *brahmarṣis* are slightly inferior to the gods, this region is inferior to *Brahmāvarta* because of its connection with the *brahmarṣis*. Thus it is said: it is *anantra* to *Brahmāvarta*, meaning slightly different. The particle *nañ* has the sense of "slight," just as in the instruction, "One suffering from illness should drink barley-gruel that is *anuṣṇā*" (not hot), which they explain as "slightly warm. The word *antara* denotes difference, as in the expression, "there is a great difference between women, men, and water" (*nārī-puruṣa-toyānām anataram mahad antaram*). 2.19.
From the presence of a twice-born man born in this region, all men on earth should learn their respective duties. (2.20)

In these regions, such as Kurukṣetra and others, they should learn—that is, seek to understand—their respective conduct and customs from the presence of the twice-born Brāhmaṇas born therein. This has been explained by the rule: "In that region" (MDh 2.18). || 2.20 ||
The region situated between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains,
extending eastward from Vinaśana and westward from Prayāga, is proclaimed as Madhyadeśa.

In the northern direction is the Himavat mountain; in the southern direction is the Vindhya. Vinaśana is the place where the Sarasvatī disappears. Prayāga is the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā. Taking these regions as boundaries, one should know that the intermediate region is called Madhyadeśa. It is called Madhyadeśa because it is neither too elevated nor too low, and not because it is situated at the center of the earth. (2.21)
From the eastern ocean to the western ocean, the wise know that the region between those two mountains is Āryāvarta. (2.22)

The region situated between the eastern ocean and the western ocean, as well as the intermediate space between those two mountains—the Himavat and the Vindhya—taught in the preceding verse, is called Āryāvarta by the wise and the learned. The Āryas dwell there, arising again and again; even though Mlecchas may repeatedly invade it, they do not remain there for long. The prefix *ā* here denotes a limit (*maryādā*), not an inclusive extension (*abhividhi*). Therefore, the islands of the oceans are not part of Āryāvarta. These four boundaries have been established for the regions: the eastern ocean in the east, the western ocean in the west, and the Himavat and Vindhya in the north and south respectively. Since these two [mountains] are taken as boundaries, they themselves do not possess the status of being Āryāvarta. Thus, having raised the objection that there would be no residence [of Āryas] there, he says this [verse 2.22].
That land where the black antelope roams by its own nature should be known as a land fit for sacrifice; beyond that is the land of the Mlecchas. 2.23.

Where a black-and-white, black-and-yellow, or black-spotted *kṛṣṇasāraṅga* deer roams and dwells—where its birth and origin occur naturally in that region, and not where it has been brought from another land for reasons such as being prized or as a gift, and resides there for only a short time—that region is to be understood as *yajñiya*, fit for sacrifice. Therefore, beyond the range of the black deer lies another land, the *mleccha* country. The *mlecchas* are well known; they are those excluded from the four caste classes (*cāturvarṇya*), born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*), and ineligible [for Vedic rites], such as the Medas, Andhras, Śabaras, Pulindas, and others.

Nor is the location of this place enjoined as the locus for the sacrifice, as in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice on level ground," because of the use of the present tense in the word *carati*. For it is not possible to perform the sacrifice at the very same moment one has begun to move; for the place is the locus of the sacrifice by way of supporting the liquids and other substances that depend upon the factors of action (*kāraka*), such as the agent who performs its means. And it is impossible for two corporeal entities to exist in the same place at the same time. Nor is it proper to resort to indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding time, since indirect indication is improper in a primary injunction (*vidhi*). As it was stated in the section concerning the winnowing basket (*śūrpa-adhikaraṇa*): "For this is said to be 'being done' [in the present]. (Śabara-bhāṣya 1.2.26).

But surely, the contained (*ādheya*) need not necessarily pervade its entire locus (*ādhāra*), such that the fulfillment of the meaning of the locus would require the pervasion of the whole locus, as in the case of "oil in sesame seeds" (*tileṣu tailam*, ŚveU 1.15). What then? Even by a contained object that is connected to only one part, the status of being a locus for the whole is established, as in "he sits on the palace" (*prāsāde āste*) or "he stands upon the chariot" (*ratham adhitiṣṭhati*; cf. Pāṇini 1.4.45). For in this way, since the region consisting of a collection of villages and cities, bounded by rivers, mountains, and so forth, is the subject under discussion, one who moves even in a single part—such as a mountain or a forest—makes the whole his locus. Therefore, this is not a fault; for two corporeal things, a single [shared] location is not possible.

It is said: there is no injunction here stating that “one must sacrifice” (*yaṣṭavyam*). An injunctive suffix is heard after the root *jñā* (“to know”), not after *yaj* (“to sacrifice”). What is heard there regarding the sacrifice is its fitness (*arhatā*), in the sense that “this region is fit for sacrifice. And that fitness of the sacrifice is possible even in the absence of an injunction; for in these regions, the sacrificial implements—such as *darbha* grass, *palāśa* leaves, and *khadira* wood—are generally found. Furthermore, those entitled to perform the rites (*adhikāriṇaḥ*)—namely, the members of the three higher castes who have mastered the three Vedas—are seen only in those very regions. Therefore, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the fitness for sacrifice based on these facts. Even the gerundive suffix in the word “to be known” (*jñeyaḥ*) has its injunctive force superimposed upon it; like the passage “one should offer with wild sesame gruel” (*jartilayavāgvā juhuyāt*), it is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) within an injunction.

As for what was said, "But beyond this is the land of the Mlecchas," this too is merely a general restatement. For in these lands, Mlecchas generally reside; however, the Mlecchas are not defined by their connection to this land, because they are well-known by themselves, just like the castes of Brāhmaṇas and others. Now, if this term "land of the Mlecchas" were applied by way of its meaning (i.e., as a descriptive label), then if the Mlecchas should somehow invade even the land of Brahmāvarta and establish their residence there, that very place would become a land of the Mlecchas. Likewise, if some king of Kṣatriya or other caste, being of virtuous conduct, should defeat the Mlecchas, settle the four castes there, and establish the Mlecchas as outcastes (Caṇḍālas) just as in Āryāvarta, that land too would be fit for sacrifice. For the earth is not defiled in itself; rather, it becomes defiled through contact, like [ground] contaminated by impure substances. Therefore, even outside the aforementioned lands, provided all other requirements are met, one must certainly perform sacrifices even in a land where the black antelope does not roam. Thus, the statement "that is to be known as the land fit for sacrifice, but beyond this is the land of the Mlecchas" is a restatement serving as a supplement to the subsequent injunction. (2.23)
The twice-born should diligently seek refuge in these countries;
however, a Śūdra, distressed for a livelihood, may dwell in any place whatsoever. (2.24)

He now states the rule for the purpose of which the enumeration of the different names of regions was given: "The twice-born, even if born in another region, should resort to these regions beginning with Brahmāvarta. Abandoning the land of one's birth, one should make an effort to take refuge in a region such as Brahmāvarta.

On this point, some say that this injunction regarding residence in these specific regions has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Even though it is possible to have the entitlement (*adhikāra*) [to perform rites] in other countries, one must nevertheless dwell in these particular regions. In that case, since the entitlement would have to be inferred, either this injunction for dwelling in these regions is to be understood as a means of purification, like bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) such as the Gaṅgā—just as certain waters are more purifying, so too certain portions of the earth are purifying, as stated in the Purāṇas—or else heaven is attained through the mere act of residing there independently, as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice.

In this regard, both of these two positions are untenable. If a location not previously established were being enjoined, then entitlement (*adhikāra*) might indeed be postulated. Regarding that, it is considered: which position is logical? However, by the method already stated, for those who are entitled to perform rites both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*), this very location is already established as possible for performance. For it is not possible to perform the entirety of the ritual duties outside of this location. To illustrate: first, in places such as Kashmir in the Himalayas, those afflicted by cold are not entitled to perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) outdoors, nor is the study of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) possible according to the rules, since it is prescribed that one must "go out from the village toward the east or the north. Furthermore, during the winter and dewy seasons, daily bathing in rivers and the like is not possible.

And this very point is indicated by the expression "the twice-born" (*dvijātayaḥ*). No region whatsoever becomes a land of barbarians (*mlecchadeśa*) by its own nature merely through the absence of contact with barbarians. Otherwise, if one were to become a barbarian simply by contact with that region, how could one possess the status of a twice-born?
Now, it might be argued: "Barbarism does not arise from mere travel, but rather from residing [there]; and that [residence] is what is prohibited by this [text]."

And that is not so; for in this context, "resorting to" (*saṃśraya*) is what is heard. And for one who is already in another country, that [resorting] would mean a connection with another country through the abandonment of the former. It is not the case that one who has already resorted [to a place] resorts [to it] again. Otherwise, he would have said simply: "Having abandoned these countries, one should not dwell elsewhere. Now, if resorting were already established, then stating that [rule] would be for the purpose of excluding others, which would constitute an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*). And such a specification entails three faults. Furthermore, there would be the abandonment of the directly stated meaning (*śrutārthahāni*), namely: "One should not abandon these countries. Since the directly stated meaning is possible, a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not appropriate. For this very reason, there is no recourse to the notion of "having been previously [so]. Therefore, this is an indicative mark (*liṅga*): it is not that men become barbarians (*mleccha*) by virtue of their connection to a country; rather, it is by virtue of their connection to men that a country becomes a barbarian country.

Since service to the twice-born is prescribed for the Śūdra, residence in the same region as them would always be required; however, for one who cannot subsist there, residence in another country is permitted. When, due to having a large family or an inability to perform service, the twice-born person upon whom he depends should support him, then he may reside in another country where the acquisition of wealth is possible. Even there, he should not dwell in a land abounding in Mlecchas, but rather in a land suitable for sacrifice (*yājñiya*); for if he were surrounded by Mlecchas, it would be impossible to avoid contact through activities such as traveling, sitting, and eating, which would lead to the risk of his becoming like them.

"Emaciated by livelihood" means afflicted by the lack of livelihood. "Livelihood" (vṛtti) refers to wealth sufficient for the maintenance of oneself and one's family. The emaciation resulting from its absence is expressed here as being related to that [livelihood], just as in the expression "famine caused by the rains," where a famine caused by the absence of rain is designated as being "caused by the rains. By saying "in this or that [circumstance]," he indicates there is no fixed restriction. || 2.24 ||
This origin of dharma has been proclaimed to you in brief, as well as the source of all this; now learn the duties of the social classes.

The summary of the entire meaning of the text has been stated for the purpose of avoiding forgetfulness. "Yoni" means the cause. "In brief" means in a condensed manner. And "origination" (*saṃbhava*) refers to a reflection upon the subject matter of the first chapter. Regarding the phrase "of all this," he points to the creation of the world as if it were perceived directly by the intellect. "Duties of the castes" (*varṇadharma*) are those duties to be performed by the castes; "learn them"—this is the specific instruction, namely, "in detail."

Regarding this, the authors of the *Smṛtivivaraṇa* elaborate that dharma is of five kinds: the dharma of caste (*varṇadharma*), the dharma of life-stage (*āśramadharma*), the dharma of both caste and life-stage (*varṇāśramadharma*), occasional dharma (*naimittika*), and dharma based on specific qualities (*guṇadharma*). Among these, *varṇadharma* is that which proceeds by depending solely on birth (*jāti*) and does not rely on distinctions of age, life-stage, and so forth. For example: "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed"; "Liquor must not be drunk by a Brāhmaṇa. This dharma applies to one who possesses the mere birth [of a Brāhmaṇa] until his final breath. *Āśramadharma* is that where birth alone is not required, but rather the undertaking of a specific life-stage (*āśrama*) is relied upon. For example: "For a student (*brahmacārin*), there is the kindling of the sacred fire and the practice of begging for alms" (GDh 2.8). *Varṇāśramadharma* depends on both [birth and stage]. For example: "The bowstring is the girdle of a Kṣatriya" (MDh 2.42), and so forth. Its illustration is the wearing of this [girdle] neither in another life-stage nor by another caste. However, its initial acquisition is the dharma of initiation (*upanayana*), not the dharma of a life-stage; and since initiation is for the sake of entering a life-stage, it is not itself the dharma of a life-stage. *Naimittika* refers to occasional matters such as the purification of liquids and the like. *Guṇadharma* is that which rests upon a specific quality (*guṇa*); for example: "And he is to be avoided by the six [castes]" (GDh 8.12), and so forth. These dharmas arise from the quality of great learning (*bāhuśrutya*). Likewise, there are those dharmas belonging to an anointed Kṣatriya.

Thus, it is shown that by the mention of "color" (*varṇa*), everything is included; however, the internal subdivisions remain established from that very [mention]. There are also properties of non-colors (*avarṇa*) that depend solely on being a person (*puruṣatva*); these too would have to be expressed as distinct [categories]. In this way, other subdivisions may also be inferred. Furthermore, the mention of "color" here is for the sake of illustration, not for the purpose of excluding those produced internally (*nāntaraprabhava*). For this proposition is merely a restatement of what was previously asserted. (2.25)

For the twice-born, the purifying refinement of the body, beginning with the rite of impregnation (*niṣeka*), must be performed through meritorious Vedic rituals; it leads to purification both in this world and after death. (2.26)

The application of mantras refers to Vedic rituals; here, "Vedas" is intended to mean the mantras. Those utterances belonging to them are what is meant by that term. Consequently, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *adhyātma*. Alternatively, the word "Vedic" (*vaidika*) is used figuratively because it is rooted in the Vedas. By the word "rituals" (*karma*), the ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is understood. Thus, there is a valid distinction between the goal and the means: the goal is the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) beginning with *niṣeka*, while the means are the rituals consisting of the performance of the procedure, of which the primary element is the utterance of the mantra.

*Niṣeka* is the depositing of semen in the womb. It is the first of the series of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) to be described hereafter, ending with the initiation (*upanayana*). The singular number in the term "bodily purification" (*śarīrasaṃskāra*) refers to the collection as a whole. By the word *saṃskāra*, that which brings about the body endowed with its qualities is expressed; therein, *niṣeka* is the producer [of the body], while the others are the causes of specific characteristics.

He says this very thing with the word "purifying" (*pāvana*). It is called "purifying" because it purifies—that is, it removes impurity. Regarding the phrase "both after death and here," since one who has been consecrated is entitled to perform all rites—whether those with visible results or those with invisible results, such as the *Kārīrī* sacrifice or the *Jyotiṣṭoma*—it states that [the sacraments] are beneficial to both worlds. "By means of merits" means by means of auspicious and propitious things; the distinction between the meanings of the words "meritorious" (*puṇya*) and "purifying" (*pāvana*) is that the former brings about good fortune while the latter dispels misfortune. The term "twice-born" (*dvijamanām*) is for the purpose of excluding the *Śūdras*. This is a designation of those to be consecrated, and by figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the members of the three higher castes are understood, for at that time they are not yet "twice-born. (2.26)

By means of the fire-oblations performed at conception, the birth-rite, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle, the sins derived from seed and from the womb are wiped away for the twice-born. (2.27)

The purpose of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) has been stated: the purification of the body is both sanctifying and meritorious. In this regard, its sanctifying nature is explained as the removal of defects from that which is defiled.

To address the doubt as to how the body itself can be impure, he says: "The sin pertaining to the seed and the womb. That which arises from the seed or has the seed as its cause is "pertaining to the seed" (*baijika*). The same applies to that which pertains to the womb (*gārbhika*). "Sin" (*enaḥ*) refers to an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) cause of suffering. Because these two—the seed and the womb—are the instrumental causes of that [sin], it is here stated that [the body] possesses only a state of impurity. Semen and blood constitute the seed of the person, and they are inherently impure. The womb, too, is indeed defiled by the transmission of defects. Therefore, the impurity caused by those two is wiped away—that is, removed—from the person by means of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).

Now, he points them out by mentioning some by name and others by means of specific characteristics of the rite to be performed (*saṃskāra*). "By the *gārbha* oblations": these are performed when a woman has conceived. Alternatively, they are called *gārbha* because they have the embryo as their purpose, being intended for the sake of securing the embryo; in this context, the woman is merely the instrument (*dvāramātra*), while the embryo is the actual motive. Therefore, because they are prompted by that [embryo], the oblations for the sake of that [embryo]—namely, *puṃsavana*, *sīmantonnayana*, and *garbhādhāna*—are included. The word "oblation" (*homa*) is used figuratively to indicate the ritual action in general, for the *garbhādhāna* itself is not an oblation. The form of the ladle, the deity, and so forth for these rituals is to be understood from the *Gṛhya-smṛtis*. "Just as by the *gārbha* oblations," so too by the rite called *jātakarma* (birth-rite). And likewise by the *cauḍa* (tonsure rite); it is called *cauḍa* because it is for the sake of the *cūḍā* (the top-knot). The *mauñjīnibandhana* is the initiation (*upanayana*); for in that rite, a girdle made of *muñja* grass is tied. Thus, by that term, the initiation rite is indicated. *Nibandhana* simply means "tying"; the prefix *ni-* is for metrical completion. The names of the rites beginning with *jātakarma*, formed as a copulative compound (*dvandva*), are indicated here as instruments (*karaṇavibhakti*) for the cleansing (*enopamārjana*).

Every *saṃskāra* (purificatory rite) imparts some specific quality—whether perceptible (*dṛṣṭa*) or imperceptible (*adṛṣṭa*)—to that which is to be refined (*saṃskārya*), provided that the object has already served its purpose as a subordinate element in another action, or is intended to serve such a purpose in the future. For example, in the injunction "One threshes the rice grains" (*vrīhīn avahanti*, ĀpŚ 1.21.7), the removal of the husks and chaff is the perceptible quality imparted to those grains that are about to accomplish the sacrifice, according to the rule "One should sacrifice with rice grains" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*, ŚB 11.3.1.3). In the case of "Having removed the garland from the head, one places it in a clean spot," an imperceptible quality is imparted to the garland because of the restrictive disposal (*pratipatti-niyama*) of what has been used and is now disheveled. In this context, these purificatory rites are prescribed for the sake of the body's purity. However, no removal of odor is observed in the body resulting from these rites, as is seen when the body is cleansed by contact with earth and water. Therefore, this purity should be understood as an imperceptible quality, similar to the purity resulting from the time of birth and other such events. Purified by this purification, one becomes qualified for rites prescribed by the *Śruti* and the *Smṛti*, just as clarified butter (*ājya*) purified by mantras is required for a burnt offering (*homa*). But in worldly matters, purity depends solely on the physical cleansing of the substance, as in the case of clarified butter used for eating. Indeed, the touchability of a child is established merely by the rule "The limbs are purified by water" (MDh 5.108); thus it is said: "There is no impurity resulting from touching him" (GDh 2.3).

But how, then, can these have the status of being for the sake of ritual action (*karmārthatva*)? It is logical that the act of purifying (*utpavana*) is for the sake of the clarified butter (*ājya*), because its application is determined by the context (*prakaraṇa*). However, these [rites] are external and are not heard of in the context of any specific ritual action. Therefore, their status as being for the sake of ritual action through the medium of the person (*puruṣa*) is difficult to maintain. Furthermore, if there is no utility in a purposeful effect, a mere refinement (*saṃskāra*) cannot be brought about in its own right. If that were the case, its character as a refinement would be lost, and it would instead become a primary ritual act (*pradhānakarma*). Consequently, the scriptural usage of the accusative case in such passages as "the refinement of the body is to be performed" (*kāryaḥ śarīrasaṃskāraḥ*) and "when a son is born, before the touching by others" (*kumāre jāte purānyair ālambhāt*, ĀśG 1.13.1) would be contradicted; there would be a disruption of the application (*viniyogabhaṅga*), as in the case of "he offers the *śatru* oblations," and one would be forced to assume a separate qualification (*adhikāra*), leading to many other inconsistencies.

It is said in reply: We do not define the characteristic of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) as being for the sake of that [the primary act] based on the authority of direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth; rather, we define it as being a source of assistance (*upakārakatva*). And this quality of assistance is possible even in the absence of being an auxiliary, as in the case of the injunction for the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna-vidhi*) and the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*). For in these cases, the means of proof such as direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth do not exist. As for the Āhavanīya fire and others, they are already employed [in rituals] by such rules as "one offers oblations in the Āhavanīya. Furthermore, because their essential nature is non-worldly (*alaukika*), their accomplishment is achieved solely through the injunction for the establishment of the fires, according to the rule: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fires in spring" (TB 1.1.2.6). Therefore, the establishment of the fires is utilized in the sacrifices by way of producing the Āhavanīya and other fires. Yet it is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) [to the sacrifice itself]. The injunction for Vedic study also assists the sacrifices by way of bringing about the comprehension of the meaning [of the texts]. In the same way, these purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) function as follows: the injunction for study applies to one who has been consecrated by these rites; marriage applies to one who has accomplished the purpose of the injunction for study; the establishment of the fires applies to one who has performed marriage; and eligibility [for sacrifices] applies to one who has established the fires. Thus, there is a utility for external personal purificatory rites in accomplishing the effects of the [Vedic] rites.

In every instance, beginning from the *niṣeka* (conception), the father holds the authority. Thus, the mantra for the *jātakarman* (birth-rite) states: "Thou art indeed my very self, named son" (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 14.9.4.26). For it is enjoined that he must both procreate offspring and provide instruction to them: "Having discharged the three debts... (*Manusmṛti* 6.35); and "Therefore, they say a son who has been instructed wins the world" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.5.17). Instruction consists in the communication of one's own authority, and we shall explain that this occurs through the teaching of the Veda, culminating in the comprehension of its meaning. For this very reason, the sacraments (*saṃskāras*) benefit both: in the injunction regarding the production of offspring, they benefit the father; and in the rites to be accomplished by means of the consecrated boy, they benefit the youth himself. Therefore, the authority belongs to the father, or in his absence, to one who occupies his place. Accordingly, it is said: "But those who have not been consecrated should be consecrated by their brothers who have already been consecrated" (*Yājñavalkya Smṛti* 2.128). || 2.27 ||
He now shows, by way of illustration, those actions in which the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are beneficial for the young student:

"By Vedic study, by vows, by burnt offerings, by the triple knowledge, by sacrifice, by the procreation of sons, by the great sacrifices, and by other sacrifices, this body is made fit for union with Brahman. (2.28)

The act of recitation (*adhyayanakriyā*) is intended here by the word *svādhyāya*. This is its specification of the object (*viṣayanirdeśa*), namely, "by means of the three Vedas" (*traividyena*). Even though there is an intervention [of words], the relationship is based on meaning (*arthalakṣaṇa*), according to the maxim: "that which has a meaningful connection with something [is connected to it]. For this very reason, even though they are in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the relationship between object and subject is established through a change of case-ending (*vibhaktivipariṇāmena*); the meaning is "by means of the study of the three Vedas. The term *traividyam* refers to the three Vedas themselves; the formation of the word follows the pattern of *cāturvarṇya* and similar terms. Alternatively, "by means of *svādhyāya*" refers to the study of the Veda, while "by means of *traividyena*" refers to the comprehension of its meaning. "By means of vows" (*vrataiḥ*) refers to those such as the *Sāvitra*, performed by the religious student (*brahmacārin*). "By means of oblations" (*homaiḥ*) refers to those performed at the time of the instruction in the vows. Or else, the kindling of the fire with fuel-sticks (*samit*) by the student in the evening and morning is called "oblation" (*homa*) because of the commonality of its connection with the locus of the fire (*agnyādhāra*). Now, one might ask: is the placing of fuel-sticks not an oblation, such that it is said to be so "on account of a commonality of connection"? They say it is not, because sacrifice (*yāga*) and oblation (*homa*) must be accomplished by means of edible substances (*adanīyadravya*). How then [is it an oblation]?
One should, unwearied, offer oblations with those [verses] into the fire both in the evening and in the morning. (MDh 2.186)

Thus it has been said. By means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the placing of fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*) is expressed by the word "oblation" (*homa*). Just as a substance being offered is cast into the fire, so too are the fuel-sticks intended for the purpose of kindling. Therefore, on the basis of this commonality, the act of kindling itself is called an oblation. For in the originative injunction (*utpatti-vākya*), it is heard: "One should place a fuel-stick"; and regarding the statement, "One should offer with them into the fire," we shall explain later that this mention of "the fire" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for another purpose. And there is no fault of secondary indication in a restatement.

However, this is logical: that sacrifice (*yāga*) and oblation (*homa*) are accomplished by means of sacrificial materials (*medhya-dravya*) alone. This being the case, many injunctions (*codanā*) become meaningful, such as: "He casts the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *sūktavāka* mantra" (ĀpŚ 3.6.6). For in that instance, they call the *prastara* the material and the verb "to cast" (*harati*) a sacrifice (*yajati*). Thus, by virtue of the scriptural statement, it is indeed such a sacrifice. Furthermore, for some, even *darbha* grass is edible. How then regarding the *śākala-homa*? If it is argued that there too the originative injunction is "He places the wood-shavings (*śakala*) on the fire," then what would be the status of the *graha-yajña*? One should offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*) to each of the *grahas*, such as those of the *arka* and others. Therefore, wherever the word "one should offer" (*juhuyāt*) occurs and a connection with a deity is heard even in the originative sentence regarding wood and the like, that too is indeed a *homa*.

By sacrifice and by the propitiation of the divine sages; this, first of all, is the collection of duties for one who has been initiated during his period of student life (*brahmacarya*). Now follow the duties of the householder: by means of sons through the rite for procreating offspring; by the five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*), beginning with the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*); and by Vedic sacrifices (*śrauta*) such as the *jyotiṣṭoma*.

Now, if these ritual acts had some other purpose, then external purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) intended for the production of fitness for those [acts] would be meaningful. Therefore, he says: "This body is made *brāhmī*. *Brahman* is the Supreme Self, the causal Person; this "body" (*tanu*) belonging to Him—that is, His physical form—is made by all these ritual acts prescribed in the Śrutis and Smṛtis.
