One should not give that to anyone; since this [prohibition] alone establishes the rule for the vows of a *snātaka*, the specific prohibition regarding Śūdras will be explained in that very context. Although the fourth case-ending (*caturthī*) would have been expected, the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the purpose of prohibiting a mere relationship [of ownership]. Even for those who do not know, "This was given to us," food should not be prepared for their eating, such as for dogs, cats, and so forth. For here the sense of "giving" (*dadāti*) is not complete; there is only the cessation of the giver's ownership, but no acquisition of ownership by another.

The word *antarā* signifies the middle. There are two times for eating: evening and morning. One should not eat at any other time than those. Alternatively, the word *antarā* signifies an interval (*vyavadhāna*). Having ceased the activity of eating, one should not eat again that very same food previously taken in the vessel after intervening with another action. However, a specific rule is recited in another *Smṛti*: "interrupted by rising and sipping water" (cf. GDh 17.19). Some, however, explain *antara* as a break. It is heard in the *Śruti*: "Holding the vessel with the left hand and taking a portion with the right, he offers it into the mouth, which is his sacrificial fire. In that context, [the interruption] is that which follows the support of the vessel with the left hand.

One should not eat excessively—that is, one should not consume food beyond the proper measure. This is intended to illustrate the causes of ill health, such as heavy, incompatible, and other [unwholesome] foods. From the instruction on causes and from the *Āyurveda*, the nature of excessive intake should be understood. One should eat only so much that the food consumed does not fill the stomach and digests properly. There are three parts of the stomach: one and a half parts for food, half a part for drink, and one part for the movement of the bodily humors (*doṣas*). Otherwise, there is ill health.

And one should not go anywhere while still impure from food remnants; therefore, having removed the remnants and attained purity, one should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) in that very same place. 2.56.
Excessive eating is detrimental to health, detrimental to longevity, and detrimental to heaven; it is meritless and despised by the world; therefore, one should avoid it. (2.57)

He explains the scriptural basis for the prohibition against overeating: [209] ill health is the onset of disease; suffering from fever, abdominal ailments, and the like; the loss of life through cholera and similar illnesses is what constitutes a lack of longevity. Because it violates the protection of the body as enjoined by the rule, "One should protect oneself from all things" (GDh 9.34), it is non-heavenly (*asvargya*). The attainment of hell follows from the absence of heaven. It is unmeritorious (*apuṇya*) and causes misfortune. It is loathed by the world and censured for being gluttonous. For these reasons, one should avoid overeating; one should not do it. (2.57)
A Brahmin should always perform his ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma tīrtha;
he may use either the Kāya or the Traidaśika tīrtha, but never the Pitrya.

By the word *tīrtha*, a sacred place for water is denoted. It is called *tīrtha* because it stands (*tiṣṭhati*) for the purpose of crossing over (*tāraṇa*) and for liberation from sin (*pāpapramocana*). In some instances, however, *tīrtha* refers to a path for descending into water—something by which one crosses over (*taranti anena*). Here, however, it refers to a specific part of the palm that holds water. Or, the use of the word *tīrtha* may be by way of praise (*stuti*), for water does not reside there permanently. Therefore, one should touch it (*upaspṛśet*) or sip water (*ācāmet*). The phrase "with the *brāhma*" is also solely for the sake of praise; [it means] "Brahmā is its deity. For water cannot be the deity of a *tīrtha*, since it is not of the nature of a sacrifice (*ayāgarūpa*) and lacks mantras. Having superimposed the nature of a sacrifice upon it through certain attributes such as being a cause of purification, the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) expressing "deity" is applied. This applies both at all times for the sake of purity and as a constituent part of ritual acts. What is Prajāpati? He is its deity, thus it is *kāya*. Likewise, "the thirty gods (*tridaśa*) are its deity," thus it is *traidaśika*. When the suffix *ṇi* (forming *devatā*) is added to the word *tridaśa*, the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of the base itself. And the status of being a deity is as explained before. One should sip water with these *tīrthas*. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" (*vipra*) is not intended to be restrictive (*avivakṣita*), because the author will later state specific rules for Kṣatriyas and others. Furthermore, a specific injunction is not appropriate unless there is a general application already established, as in the passage beginning, "But the king [should sip] with [water] reaching the throat" (MDh 2.62). One should never use the *pitrya* [tīrtha], which has the ancestors as its deity. Even when the *brāhma* and other *tīrthas* become unfit due to boils, pustules, or similar conditions.

But surely, the *pitrya* [tīrtha] is not obtained simply because it is not enjoined? There is a doubt here: in order to make known the *pitṛtīrtha*, one must necessarily state "the *pitrya* is below those two," yet no specific function for it is indicated here. Since there is an expectancy for a function, a connection with that function might be suspected due to its being the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*). Now, however, since there is a prohibition, the understanding of the function comes from the designation (*samākhyā*) "pitrya" itself: the ancestral rites, such as the water-libation (*udakatarpaṇa*), are to be performed with this *tīrtha*. In this way, the praise becomes consistent. Furthermore, since the *brāhma* and other [tīrthas] are enjoined by direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*), it is appropriate to mention this [the *pitrya*] in order to remove the doubt that might arise regarding their absence. (2.58)
They declare that the *brāhma* tīrtha is at the base of the thumb;
the *kāya* tīrtha is at the base of the fingers; the *daiva* tīrtha is at their tips; and the *pitrya* tīrtha is below those two. (2.59)

The base of the thumb is its lower part; the palm-region there is the *brāhma* (Brahmanic) *tīrtha*. He says the palm is the interior of the hand. The *brāhma* [tīrtha] is within the hand, facing oneself, ending at the great line (*mahārekhā*). Above the staff-line (*daṇḍarekhā*) at the base of the fingers is the *kāya* (Kāya) [tīrtha]. At the tips of the fingers is the *daiva* (Divine) [tīrtha]. Although the word "fingers" (*aṅguli*) is subordinate, it is connected to the word "tips" (*agra*) because of their mutual dependence. The *pitrya* (Pitṛ-related) [tīrtha] is below those two. Here too, the word "fingers," though secondary, is connected with the thumb. And the finger intended here is the index finger (*pradeśinī*). The space between those two is the *pitrya*. This is explained thus on the strength of the authority of other Smṛtis and the consensus of the learned, since a literal connection is impossible. As Śaṅkha says: "The *brāhma* *tīrtha* is below the thumb and before the tip-line; between the index finger and the thumb is the *pitrya*; before the first joint of the little finger and the palm is the *kāya*; and the tips of the fingers are the *daivika*. (2.59)
One should first sip water three times, then wipe the mouth twice;
one should touch the cavities with water, as well as the self and the head. (2.60)

One should sip water three times through one of the prescribed *tīrtha*s (parts of the hand), causing the water to enter the stomach through the mouth. Then, following that consumption of water, one should wipe the two lips twice by repeated application. Here, "wiping" (*pramārjana*) refers to the removal of the particles of water adhering to the lips with the wet hand. Why "with the hand"? Because of established custom (*samācāra*) or because the context concerns the *tīrtha*s. Furthermore, the phrase "only with water through the *tīrtha*" heard later in the text is drawn back to this point as well. And since wiping serves a visible purpose, the word "mouth" (*mukha*) here refers to its constituent parts as previously described. One should touch the cavities (*khāni*), which are the orifices, with water held in the hand; touching itself is what is meant by "upasparśana. Since the mouth is the subject under discussion, this rule for touching applies specifically to the primary cavities. Gautama also says: "And one should touch the cavities belonging to the head" (GDh 1.36). By the word "self" (*ātmānam*), he indicates either the heart or the navel. For it is stated in the Upaniṣads: "One should behold the self within the heart. Therefore, this touching of the heart pertains to the pervasive self, the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*); for there can be no possibility of touching that which is formless. It is recorded in some Smṛtis: "One should touch the navel" (ĀśŚ 1.13.1); therefore, we consider the navel to be intended. "Head" (*śiras*) is well known. And because the Smṛtis have a single purpose, rules such as "having washed the hands up to the wrists" (GDh 1.36) are also obtained here. Likewise, not making noise is the restraint of speech, and the sprinkling of the feet is mentioned. In the Mahābhārata, the washing of the feet is also shown. (2.60)

One who knows the Dharma and desires purity should always sip water that is neither hot nor frothy through the proper part [of the hand], in a secluded place, facing either the east or the north. (2.61)

The word *uṣṇa* (hot) is intended to indicate boiled water; for it is stated thus: "with unboiled waters. In this way, water heated by summer heat or naturally hot water is not prohibited. The mention of *phena* (foam) is also for the purpose of indicating bubbles (*budbuda*); and it is recited: "devoid of foam and bubbles" (YDh 1.20). The phrase "by the *tīrtha*, the knower of Dharma" is merely for the sake of completing the meter. *Śaucepsuḥ* means desiring to obtain purity; that is, one who desires purification. One does not become pure otherwise. "Always"—not only in the context of eating, but rather also in purifications involving semen, feces, urine, and so forth. Because water is the object in the act of consuming, the instrumental case is used; this rule applies not only to water being consumed, but also to water serving as an instrument, such as in sprinkling the feet and so on. We, however, say that even in consumption, water is indeed the instrument, for sipping (*ācamana*) is not a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of those [waters]. In a secluded and pure place; for a secluded spot, being uncrowded by people, is generally pure.

"Facing northeast" (*prāgudaṅmukhaḥ*): the word *mukha* is connected with each [direction]. Thus it has been stated by Gautama: "Facing east or facing north" (GDh 1.35). The analysis (*vigraha*) should be made thus: "one whose face is toward the northeast. This is not a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing a *dvandva*, but rather a *bahuvrīhi* alone. If it were a *dvandva*-containing compound, there would have to be the suffix *-a* for the collective (*samāhāra*). Nor is it a *dvandva* in the sense of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), for it is impossible to face two directions simultaneously. In that case, it would follow that one part of the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) must be performed facing east and another part facing north; yet the sipping is not a single partial act. Furthermore, the meaning of direction (*dig-artha*) cannot be taken up [as a subordinate element] such that the two [directions] could be connected in mutual dependence. Nor is the term *prāgudak* well-known as a designation for the "invincible" (*aparājita*) direction—like *dakṣiṇapūrva* and so on—by which it would be understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound of directions. Therefore, this is not a *bahuvrīhi* containing another type of function; hence, there is an option (*vikalpa*). And it has been cited in another *smṛti*: "One should begin the purification facing east or facing north" (GDh 1.35). Just as in the expression "the six-day sacrifice having the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* *sāmans*," the *Bṛhat* occurs on some days and the *Rathantara* on others, but both *sāmans* do not exist together in a single day. 2.61.
The sipping of water with the [appropriate] part of the hand has been described; however, its measure has not been stated. Therefore, he says this in order to determine it:
"A Brahmin is purified by water reaching the heart, a Kshatriya by water reaching the throat, a Vaishya by water that is merely swallowed, and a Shudra by water touched at the extremity. (2.62)

*Hṛdgāḥ* means those that go to or reach the heart. The suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *gam* according to Pāṇini 3.2.101 (*anyeṣv api dṛśyate*). The substitution of *hṛd* for *hṛdaya* occurs by splitting the rule Pāṇini 6.3.50 (*hṛdayasya hṛd*) into two separate rules. It becomes purified, attains purity, and its impurity is removed. *Āpaḥ* refers to water measuring slightly less than a *culuka* (a handful). With those waters reaching the throat—that is, pervading only as far as the throat—the *bhūmipaḥ*, or Kṣatriya, is meant. Sovereignty over the earth is ordained for the Kṣatriya; thus, by this well-known function, the Kṣatriya caste is indicated. If the intention were merely to express sovereignty, he would have spoken of it specifically among the duties of a king (*rājadharma*). A Vaiśya [is purified] by waters that have been *prāśitāḥ*, meaning they have been introduced into the mouth. Even if they do not reach the throat, they are causes of purification for a Vaiśya. A Śūdra [is purified] by waters that are *spṛṣṭāḥ*, "at the end" (*antaḥ*). The suffix *tasi* is used here in the sense of the third case (instrumental), according to the rule for words beginning with *ādi*. This word *anta* has the sense of "nearness," as in "he went to the edge of the water" (*udakāntam*), which is understood to mean "near the water. It also has the sense of a "part," as in "the edge of a garment" (*vastrāntaḥ*) or "the hem of a cloth" (*vasanāntaḥ*); in both cases, it requires another related term, such as "near what? or "a part of what? Here, it is understood that "by the end" refers to the specific parts where sipping is prescribed for the other castes, namely the *tīrthas* (the parts of the hand) and the tongue and lips. However, the sense of "nearness" is not possible here, because the act of sipping being enjoined cannot be accomplished by mere proximity. Even in the case of touching, there is a form of "sipping," for when something is touched by the tongue and lips, the tasting of its flavor is inevitable. In this context, a quantity slightly less than that for a Vaiśya is intended: up to the root of the tongue for a Vaiśya, and up to the tip of the tongue for a Śūdra. Because water is liquid, the crossing of these limits is unavoidable; however, if it actually reaches those points, there is impurity. All this division of *tīrthas* applies to the touching of the right hand, due to the natural propriety of the hand and because the practice of right-handedness is ordained as a duty of man. It is for this very purpose that this is stated regarding this limit. (2.62)
When the right hand is raised, the twice-born is called *upavītī*;
when the left is raised, he is *prācīnāvītī*; and when it hangs from the neck, he is *nivītī*. (2.63)

But surely, objects established by worldly convention are also relied upon in the *Dharmaśāstra*. [Reply: The statements of Manu and others are not intended for the purpose of defining the technical meanings of words, unlike the *Abhidhānakāṇḍa* of grammar or traditional lexicons (*smṛti*). We have already stated that if they define a meaning that is not very well-known, how can they be subject to reproach? Furthermore, there is another specific purpose here: it is so that when the sequence of sipping water (*ācamana*) is being taught, items such as the upper garment (*upasaṃvyāna*) may be understood as ancillaries (*aṅga*) to that sipping. Even though wearing the sacred thread (*upavīta*) is always required—whether for the sake of a religious vow (*vrata*) or as a duty for the person (*puruṣārtha*)—nevertheless, if one performs the sipping of water without it, the act remains incomplete. In the absence of this statement, there would be a deficiency in the vow and a fault on the part of the person. On the other hand, if one performs the sipping without the sacred thread, it is equivalent to not having performed it at all; furthermore, there would be the fault of consuming water while impure.

But how is it that the *upavīta* alone is a constituent part of the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), given that other things are also prescribed here, such as the *prācīnāvīta*? It is said in reply: the *prācīnāvīta* is enjoined by its own specific term for the ancestral rite (*pitrya-karman*); since its purpose is already fulfilled there, it cannot be treated as an optional alternative to the *upavīta*, whose purpose remains unfulfilled. The *nivīta* likewise has its purpose in the practice of sorcery (*abhicāra*). Even though there is no specific application for the *nivīta* in this context, nevertheless, because the various *smṛtis* share a common purpose, its application elsewhere still serves to give it relevance here as well. The mention of "taking hold of the hands" is intended to indicate the arms, for in common usage one is called *upavītī* when the arms are raised. We shall explain later that the *upavīta* is to be worn at all times. One is not *upavītī* merely by raising the hand; rather, one is *prācīnāvītī* when the left arm is raised. This is a compound name. The non-compound form is used for the sake of the meter. Regarding "hanging on the neck": "hanging on the neck" (*kaṇṭhe sajjana*) means attachment or placing [the cloth]. When either of the two arms is raised, whether it be the cloth or the thread, then one becomes *nivītī*. (2.63)
Having cast the girdle, the skin, the staff, the sacrificial thread, and the water-pot into the water when they are worn out, he should take others with the appropriate mantras. (2.64)

The discarding of those that have been damaged in water and the taking up of others is prescribed here. The sequence of discarding and taking up is exactly as heard in the text. Furthermore, because of this re-employment, these [vessels] do not merely constitute an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). For if they were an ancillary part of it, their use would necessarily terminate with the conclusion of that rite. What then? They are to be maintained for as long as one's period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) lasts.

Now, is it not the case that at the very time of initiation (*upanayana*), prior to the completion of the ritual action, there can be no disposal (*pratipatti*) of those [sacrificial implements] destroyed by divine or human impediment? And since they must be taken up again for the sake of completing the performance—just as in the case of the potsherd (*kapāla*)—it is on this basis of their being taken up again that the necessity of their preservation (*dhāraṇa*) is inferred.

It is said: First, the taking up of the staff is enjoined, as is the binding of the girdle. Among these, the placement of the sacred thread (*sūtra*) must necessarily be performed as an integral part (*aṅga*) of the initiation (*upanayana*). Once that is done, the purpose of the scripture has been fulfilled. What does it matter afterwards whether those items are lost or not? Furthermore, in the case of the loss of an accessory (*aṅga*), a specific disposal (*pratipatti*) serves to assist the ritual act. No specific function for them is prescribed such that their formal acquisition at a particular time would be required for its accomplishment. Since the function has not yet been performed, the re-acquisition prompted by that function is said to be established by necessity. Therefore, because of the injunction regarding disposal and the statement regarding acquisition, wearing [the items] is an accessory (*aṅga*), but it does not terminate with the performance of the rite. For, since they are mentioned on the same footing as the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), which continues after the initiation, their persistence thereafter is understood. And that [persistence] is an accessory of the vow (*vrata*). Thus, the girdle and the other items serve a dual purpose: they are for the sake of the initiation due to the context (*prakaraṇa*), and once the initiation is completed, they persist for as long as the state of studentship (*brahmacarya*) lasts, as seen from the texts. The water-pot, moreover, must be used for the purpose of carrying water precisely because of this injunction regarding disposal; otherwise, the disposal would be contingent, occurring only when the water-pot was present.

In that context, since "carrying a staff" is understood as "one should go for alms while carrying a staff," it follows by sequence that this is merely a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the practice of begging. Due to established custom (*samācāra*), this applies even when one wanders for purposes other than begging. However, it does not mean that one must always hold the staff in the palm of the hand while standing, sitting, sleeping, eating, and so forth. Accordingly, he will prescribe the *brahmāñjali* (the cupped-hands gesture) for Vedic study. By the phrase "with mantras," he reiterates the taking [of the staff] according to the ritual procedure for initiation (*upanayana*). And in that [procedure], there is a mantra for the girdle (*mekhalā*), but none for the staff. (2.64)
The tonsure ceremony (keśānta) is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya it is in the twenty-second, and for a Vaiśya two years after that. (2.65)

The sacrament called *keśānta* (the tonsure) must be performed for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year from conception. Regarding the precise definition of its nature, the *Gṛhya-sūtra* alone is the authority. "In the twenty-second plus two years" means in that twenty-second year with two added; or rather, "time" alone is the referent of the compound. Thus, it means at a time two years beyond the twenty-second year. For a Vaiśya [it is performed] as follows: the word "two" (*dvi*) refers specifically to the years, for those [years] are the subject under discussion. (2.65)
This entire sequence of rites for women must be performed without omission, for the sake of purifying the body, at the proper time and in the proper order. (2.66)

This sequence (*āvṛt*) for women is to be performed entirely without mantras. Beginning from the *jātakarman* (birth-rite), this is the sequence of the sacraments (*saṃskāras*), meaning the entire collection of rites along with their specific procedures. He states that the purpose [of these rites] for women—as well as for men—is for the sake of sanctification (*saṃskāra*) and for the purification of the body. "At the proper time": without transgressing the time at which each specific rite is prescribed. The compound *yathākālam* is an *avyayībhāva* formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.7 (*yathāsādṛśye*), signifying non-deviation from the object; the same should be understood regarding the order (*krama*). Since this sequence has been ordained as being devoid of mantras alone, there is no possibility of its occurring out of the proper time or order; therefore, the prohibition is a restatement (*nityānuvāda*) intended merely to complete the meter. This much is intended to be expressed: "And these [rites] for women are without mantras. (2.66)

Since the preceding statement regarding the prohibition of mantras might lead one to conclude that the marriage ceremony (*upanayana*) for women is likewise to be performed without mantras—just like the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) and others—it is commenced here to preclude that:
"The ritual of marriage is declared to be the Vedic sacrament (*saṃskāra*) for women.
Service to the husband is their residence with the teacher; the household duties are their tending of the sacred fires. (67)

The Vedic sacrament known as *upanayana*, which is for the purpose of receiving the Vedas, is for women the rite of marriage (*vaivāhika-vidhi*). That which occurs in marriage, pertains to marriage, or is accomplished by marriage is [the sacrament]. Therefore, because marriage is ordained in the place of *upanayana*, there is a statement regarding its substitution for that [sacrament] in the case of marriage. And its cessation [occurs] if marriage performs the function of that [sacrament].

Ah! The study of the Vedas has been completed, and the observance of vows has been accomplished; let there be no more of that which is called *upanayana* (initiation). This [following rule] sets aside both of those: "service to the husband is her residence with the teacher. Since she serves, attends upon, and honors her husband, that itself constitutes her residence with the teacher. Study is to be performed while residing with a teacher, but since she has no residence with a teacher, how can there be study? The "household purpose" refers to domestic duties such as cooking, managing the household goods, and supervision—those which will be described in the ninth chapter: "And in the accumulation of wealth, her... (MDh 9.11), and so forth. That same fuel-offering (*samid-ādhāna*) which the religious student (*brahmacārin*) performs morning and evening is her domestic duty. And by the term "fire-rite," the entire collection of restraints and observances belonging to the religious student is implied.

And this has been stated regarding marriage being the equivalent of the initiation (*upanayana*): just as for a man, from the time of his initiation onwards, there exist Vedic, Smṛti-based, and customary injunctions, whereas prior to that there is freedom of action, speech, and diet; so too for women, there is freedom of action prior to marriage, and thereafter they possess the entitlement to perform Vedic and Smṛti-based rites.

Alternatively, the construction of the words is as follows: for women, marriage itself is the Vedic sacrament that constitutes the *upanayana*. Even though it is not a formal *upanayana*, marriage is figuratively designated as such. What is the similarity between marriage and the *upanayana* on account of which it receives that designation? To this, he says: "service to the husband," and so forth. (2.67)
Conclusion of the Section: This rite of initiation for the twice-born has been declared; it is meritorious and manifests their true birth. Now, learn of the application of ritual action. (2.68)

This concludes the section on initiation (*upanayana*). Whatever has been stated here is all for the purpose of initiation. [Objection: But would this not also apply to the tonsure (*keśānta*)? [Reply: No, because its performance is prescribed at its own specific time before the initiation has taken place. Even that which is recited within a particular context may have a different purpose due to a direct scriptural statement (*vākya*); thus, the tonsure is desired by some even for one who has returned home from his studies (*samāvṛtta*).

That which pertains to the initiation (*upanayana*) is *aupanāyanika*. The lengthening of the final vowel of the second member [of the compound] is as explained previously. "Manifestation of birth" (*utpattivyañjaka*): birth is the production from one's mother and father; that which makes this manifest, reveals it, and brings about its state of being endowed with qualities is the "manifestor of birth. Even though born, one who has not been initiated is equal to one unborn because of the absence of entitlement (*adhikāra*). Therefore, this rule is the "manifestor of birth. The word "meritorious" (*puṇya*) has already had its meaning explained. Now, listen to that which is about to be declared: the ritual action by which the initiated person has a connection—that is, an entitlement—and whatever must be performed by him once he is initiated. (2.68)
Having initiated his pupil, the teacher should first instruct him in purification,
as well as in proper conduct, the fire-ritual, and the twilight devotions.

He should teach and train [the student] in purity from the beginning. By the expression "from the beginning," it is not intended that the instruction in purity must precede [the rules on] conduct (*ācāra*) and the rest. Rather, these [topics] have no fixed sequence relative to one another; however, he will state later that the instruction regarding the observances (*vrata*) follows immediately after the initiation (*upanayana*), and the study of the Veda follows once the Vedic observances have been prescribed. Therefore, since the kindling of the fire and the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) involve the recitation of mantras, the recitation of those mantras—which would otherwise not be applicable before the instruction on observances—is here enjoined. Purity (*śauca*), moreover, has no fixed time; thus, it must necessarily be taught on that very day. The same applies to conduct (*ācāra*). Consequently, this expression "from the beginning" is for the sake of emphasis, and does not enjoin that purity must be the first thing taught. Purity consists of the rules beginning with "one [application of earth] on the penis" and ending with the sipping of water (*ācamana*) (MDh 5.136–145). Conduct (*ācāra*) consists of rising to meet teachers and others, offering them seats, saluting them, and so forth. The fire-rite (*agnikārya*) is the act of establishing the sacred fire, namely the kindling of fuel-sticks (*samit*). Twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) is the meditation upon the nature of the Sun during the twilight; or alternatively, it refers to the rule "the morning twilight" (YDh 1.101) and so forth. This is the duty regarding the observances (*vrata-dharma*). (2.69)
Now he states the rules for Vedic study:

"But one who is about to study, having sipped water according to the scriptures, facing north, with hands joined in the *brahmāñjali* gesture, wearing light clothing, and with senses subdued, is to be taught. (2.70)

This *lṛṭ* suffix should be understood as referring to what is about to happen. That is to say, one who is about to engage in study, about to begin study, or who desires to study. He should be taught facing north. However, according to Gautama (GDh 1.54), the pupil may face east and the teacher west. "Having sipped water according to the scriptures" (*ācānta*) recalls the previously mentioned rule for sipping water (*ācamana*). "By whom the *brahmāñjali* has been made"—because [the word] belongs to the class beginning with *āhitāgni*, the past participle ending is placed at the end of the compound. Alternatively, the reading is *brahmāñjalikṛt*. "Wearing light clothing" (*laghuvāsas*) means wearing washed clothing; by washing, the garments become light. Thus, through lightness, the purity of the clothing is indicated. Or rather, if he were wearing thick clothing such as wool, he might not feel a blow when struck during a distraction of mind, and consequently, he would not be fit to recite. Furthermore, if the clothing were removed, the teacher would experience distress; and if the body were uncovered, the child, being struck with a rope or similar object, would experience great pain. Therefore, wearing light clothing serves a visible purpose. "One by whom both sets of senses have been conquered and restrained" is *jitendriya*. It is meant that he should not look here and there, he should not hear anything whatsoever, and he should remain attentive to his study. (2.70)
At the beginning and at the end of the recitation of the Veda, one should always clasp the feet of the teacher;
having joined the palms together, one should study, for that is known as the *brahmāñjali*.

Although this word *brahman* has many meanings, here it is understood as denoting the Veda because the context concerns the commencement of study (*adhyayana*). The locative case here is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta-saptamī*). And precisely because of the context of study, the action of studying that subject is intended; this is its commencement, the first recitation by a person. In this regard, the mention of the "feet" (*pāda*) refers to the feet of the teacher. However, the commencement spoken of here does not refer to the initial syllables of the Veda—namely, "agnim īḷe" (RV 1.1.1), "iṣe tvā" (TS 1.1.1.1), and "agna āyāhi" (SV 1.1)—for it is not possible for those [syllables] to function as a cause, since they are eternal. A cause must be something occasional (*kādācitka*). Therefore, what is meant is this: one who is about to begin the study of the Veda should perform the clasping of the teacher's feet; having done so, he should then pronounce the syllables of his own recitation. But once the act of study has already commenced, he should not clasp the feet again.

But surely, the commencement is the first moment of action, and that is the cause (*nimitta*). And it is logical for something that exists to be a cause, just as living is [the cause for the *āśauca* period]. In this regard, even a past event such as the burning of a house is a cause; in those cases, it is heard [in the scriptures] in exactly that way. Therefore, the simultaneous performance (*sahaprayoga*) of Vedic study and the clasping of the teacher’s feet is indeed appropriate.

It is said: the resolve to teach is called the "commencement," not the first moment of the action. At the very moment the teacher says, "Recite! (*adhīṣva*), the student resolves upon it. Immediately thereafter follows the clasping of the feet. This is the pleasing of the mind of the teacher who has set out to provide assistance. Just as in the world someone honors with words one who has set out to help them, saying, "Indeed, you have liberated us from this evil!"; so too is this request for instruction wordless: "I have approached for the sake of study. For the teacher is not to be importuned by saying, "Teach me!"; rather, he must simply be approached for the purpose of making himself understood that the time for study has arrived. Therefore, for one who has performed the approach, there is the utterance of the syllables of the Veda. Moreover, it is prescribed that one should study with the hands joined together; in that case, the student engaged in recitation would violate the rule regarding the clasping of the feet.

*Avasānam* (conclusion) means completion, the cessation of study. Although the word *brahma* is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) at the beginning [of the compound], nevertheless, because the conclusion requires something to refer back to (*sāpekṣatva*) and because it is proximate, its connection is understood with the word *brahma* itself, as no other term is heard in the text. The inclusion of the word *sat* (always) is so that this rule may apply to both the commencement and the conclusion of the daily practice; otherwise, it would apply only to that primary commencement which immediately follows the instruction on the vows (*vratādeśa*). Furthermore, just as the *Anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice, though enjoined at the start of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, occurs only at the commencement of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* performance that follows the fire-consecration (*adhāna*), and not at the commencement of every monthly performance; so too, from morning until the daily lesson is finished—provided the extent is merely two chapters—the act of studying remains one single whole. Even if there is some interruption in the middle, once one resumes, it no longer possesses the designation of a "commencement," and thus the ritual of prostrating at the teacher's feet (*pādopasādana*) is not performed again. And it is recited in another Smṛti: "The clasping of the teacher's feet takes place every day in the morning."

Having joined, brought together, and closely pressed the two hands against one another, it should be studied. That well-known arrangement of the hands known as the *kacchapa* (tortoise) should be performed in that manner; for that is indeed the *brahmāñjali*. This is an explanation of the meaning of the term. 2.71.
The clasping of the teacher's feet should be performed with crossed hands:
the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand. (2.72)

The salutation (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) of the teacher mentioned in the preceding verse should be performed with crossed hands. But what kind of crossing of the hands should be done? To this he says: the left foot is to be touched—that is, contact is to be made—with the left hand; however, one should not remain pressing [the foot] for a long time. And this crossing occurs when the two hands simultaneously move to each other’s directions. Standing in front and facing the teacher, the salutation must be performed. In that case, the left [hand] is led to the right path, and the right [hand] to the left; thus the left foot is touched by the left hand, and the right [foot] by the right [hand]. This is the crossing of the hands.

Others, however, read the text as "vinyastapāṇinā. Since the act of placing [the hands] is already established by the mere fact of touching, one should not touch with only the tips of the fingers out of fear of being burned—like touching an iron ball heated by fire—but rather both hands should be placed or set down. They explain that squeezing, which causes pain, is forbidden. (2.72)
But when the pupil is about to begin his studies, the teacher, always free from sloth, should say, "Recite, sir! and he should conclude with, "May there be a pause. (2.73)

The words beginning with *adhyeṣyamāṇam* have been explained previously. This is an injunction for the teacher (*guru*). When the teacher desires to teach the student (*māṇavaka*), he should then address him, saying, "Recite, sir! The teacher must not be troubled by one who has not been so addressed, [saying], "Teach me the *anuvāka*. And it has been said: "And when summoned, he should study" (YDh 1.27). Having uttered the word "Let there be a pause" (*virāmo 'stu*), he should cease—that is, he should stop. Who? The teacher himself, because of the nominative case ending. Alternatively, he should cease when dismissed by the teacher, and not according to his own will. And thus this is explained: "When the teacher says, 'Let there be a pause,' then the religious student (*brahmacārī*) should cease."

Others, however, maintain that this rite pertains to the mere student and the teacher at the time of their passing away. Accordingly, another *smṛti* states: "Having recited his private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), at the time of cessation, one should touch the earth with the forefinger and say 'Svasti' among the *yajus* hymns; 'Vispaṣṭam' among the *sāman* chants; 'Virāmaḥ' among the *ṛc* verses; and 'Āramaḥ' among the *atharvan* hymns."

*Atandrita* means free from laziness (*analasa*). *Tandrā* is sloth; because of its presence, a person is said to be *tandrita*. Having abandoned sloth, one is *atandrita*. This is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Here, *tandrā* does not mean fatigue. Nor should this doubt be raised: "This rule applies to one who is *atandrita*, while for one who is lazy, there is another. (2.73)
One should always place the *praṇava* at the beginning and at the end of the *brahman*.
What is not preceded by *oṃ* flows away, and what is not followed by it falls apart. (2.74)

Here too, according to the principle previously stated, one should place the *praṇava* at the beginning and at the end of the Veda; this should be understood as referring to the act of study pertaining to the Veda. The word *praṇava* denotes the syllable *oṃ*. And so he will say later: "That which is not preceded by *oṃ* flows away. The inclusion of the term "always" (*sarvadā*) is intended so that this may be a rule applying solely to the injunction for study; otherwise, due to the context, it would apply only to the student (*brahmacārin*) for the purpose of learning. This being the case, it becomes established for all instances: for the purpose of non-forgetting, and for householders and others who, according to the rule, "should study their own portion of scripture every day. Furthermore, he will enjoin its use in the recitation during the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā-japa*) and so forth by his own words: "This syllable and this [verse]" (MDh 2.78). Nor is this a rule of the Veda in general such that it would apply whenever one begins the utterance of any Vedic sentence whatsoever. Therefore, there is no *praṇava* at the commencement of *homa*-mantras, *japa*, scriptural recitations (*śāstrānuvacana*), *yājyā* verses, and the like, nor in other instances of uttering Vedic sentences merely for the sake of illustration. Thus it is settled: the inclusion of the term "always" is for the purpose of being a rule for the injunction of study within the specific context of one's own portion of scripture. As for the fact that the employment of the *praṇava* serves to mark the commencement of daily [study], that is established simply by the continued application of the mention of the regular time.

The explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for this is: "That which is not preceded by *oṃ* flows away. At the beginning, at the start, the Veda that is not preceded by *oṃ*—that is, not consecrated (*saṃskṛta*) by the word *oṃ*—flows away. The compound is *sādhana-kṛtā* (consecrated by the means). Alternatively, *oṃkṛta* refers to that Veda in which the syllable *oṃ* has been uttered; the inversion [of the word order] is due to its inclusion in the *sukhādi* group. And "afterwards" means at the conclusion. By the word *ca* ("and"), the phrase "not preceded by *oṃ*" is connected [to both]. Through both terms, "it flows away" and "it perishes," the fruitlessness of the study is established. Furthermore, it is an explanatory praise of censure (*nindārthavāda*), meaning that whatever ritual action the studied Veda might be employed for becomes fruitless. Just as when milk or the like, poured out for cooking, spills and leaks here and there because the vessel is cracked before the cooking is complete, that is called "flowing away" (*sravati*). When it has reached the state of being cooked, formed into a solid mass, and fit for consumption, its destruction is called "perishing" (*viśaraṇam*). (2.74)
Seated upon grass-blades pointing eastward, purified by means of purifiers,
and cleansed by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), he then becomes worthy of the syllable Om.

The word *kūla* signifies the tips of *darbha* grass. "Sitting around them" (*paryupāsīna*) means seated upon those *darbha* blades with their points directed eastward. According to Pāṇini 1.4.46, *adhi-śīṅ-sthā-sām*, the status of being an object (*karman*) arises from the elision of the prefix *ā* in the root *ās* (as in *ā-ās-ām*). Here too, in the compound *pari-upa-ā-āsīna*, it should be understood that the prefix *ā* is joined [to the root]. The words *pari* and *upa* are devoid of meaning [in this context].

"Purified by *darbha* grasses" means rendered pure (*śucitva*). However, mantras such as the *aghamarṣaṇa* are not denoted here by the word "purifier" (*pavitra*), because the religious student (*brahmacārin*) has not yet studied them at that time. Nor do *darbha* grasses become instruments of purification merely by their own existence while performing no action. With regard to an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*), contact with the breath (*prāṇopasparśana*) is understood from another *smṛti*; for Gautama says: "Contact with the breath by means of *darbha* grasses, and sitting on [grass] blades pointing eastward" (GDh 1.48, 50).

Purified by three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*): the *prāṇa* is the air that moves through the mouth and nose; its *āyāma* is its restraint, its retention within the body, and the prevention of its exit to the outside. Regarding the duration of this retention, a measurement is handed down in another Smṛti, as well as the recollection of the mantra: "One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Śiras, joined with each *praṇava*, three times while the breath is restrained; that is called a *prāṇāyāma*" (cf. VaDh 25.13).

The venerable Vasiṣṭha has also taught the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*). Since no other limit is prescribed, the cessation occurs precisely at the end of the mantra; and because all the Smṛtis have a single purpose when there is no contradiction, the practice here is likewise exactly so.

But surely, in this way, there would be a circular dependency (*itaretarāśraya*): the *oṃkāra* should not be performed until the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) has been accomplished, yet breath-control does not take place without the *oṃkāra*. This is not a fault. When it says "one should recite three times," what is intended regarding the breath-controls is the mental recollection of the *oṃkāra* through a mental operation; for indeed, the utterance of sound is not possible for one whose breath is restrained. Although some forms of recitation (*japa*) are accomplished by means of vocal activity, in the case of the study of one's own sacred texts (*svādhyāya-adhyayana*), however, actual pronunciation is intended. This is because the act of studying is of such a nature; for this verbal root [√adhi-i] refers to a vocal action, and sound, which is perceivable by the ear, is not grasped by the mind alone.

And this is not a property of the syllable *oṃ* such that it would follow [as a requirement] even when it is uttered in other contexts. For it has been stated: "It should be performed at the beginning of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). If it were indeed a property of the syllable *oṃ*, then it would follow in common worldly sentences such as "we say *om*," and so forth. However, Gautama has recited: "The three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāmas*) consist of fifteen *mātrās*" (GDh 1.49). By the word *mātrā*, the duration of an unmodified vowel such as *ā* is expressed. In that case, because of the contradiction, the time mentioned in other Smṛtis does not apply; nor is there the recollection of a mantra there, for there are breath-restraints even without the syllable *oṃ*. Thus, the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) does not arise. Therefore, the ellipsis is "one ought to perform the *oṃkāra*. When this entire compound is used conventionally (*rūḍhi*) to denote the *praṇava*, it refers to the *praṇava*. But when *kāra* means "the act of making" (*karaṇa*), then *oṃkāra* is the utterance (*uccāraṇa*) of "oṃ"; in that case, there is no dependence on another word. Having stated the obligation by means of the word *praṇava*, he here restates it with the word *oṃkāram*; therefore, these two have the same meaning. And thus it has been shown. (2.75)
Prajāpati milked forth from the three Vedas the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*, as well as the words *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*. (2.76)

This is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the preceding injunction. Regarding the *oṃkāra*, which consists of a collection of three syllables, he states the etymological derivation of each one: from the three Vedas—that is, from the three collections of sacred knowledge—he "milked out" or extracted it, just as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is extracted from curd. Not only the three syllables, but also this other [formula], namely *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. (2.76)
From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out foot by foot that [first] quarter of this Sāvitrī verse beginning with "tat. (2.77)

This explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the origin of the *gāyatrī* verse beginning with "That excellent splendor of Savitṛ" (RV 3.62.10) is intended for its injunction. In the preceding verse, the injunction for the *vyāhṛtis* is likewise derived from the explanatory passage alone. The sequence, however, is understood from the order of recitation. And he will say:
"Reciting this syllable and this [gāyatrī] preceded by the *vyāhṛtis*" (MDh 2.78).

"He milked out," that is, he extracted [the verse]. Although the word *tat* could be understood by way of its representative portion (*pratīka*) as "that of Savitṛ we choose" (RV 3.82.1), it is not [to be taken] as consisting of three feet; rather, it must be accepted as having exactly three feet, for the Sāvitrī consists of three feet. There are also other Prajāpatis such as Kaśyapa and others; therefore, he specifies [this one] as "Parameṣṭhin," meaning Hiraṇyagarbha, for he is established in the highest station characterized by non-return. This is said for the sake of showing the extreme reverence due to the Sāvitrī: that this [verse] was indeed directly extracted from the Vedas by the foremost Prajāpati himself. (2.77)
A Brahmin who knows the Veda, by muttering this syllable and this [Gāyatrī] preceded by the Vyāhṛtis at the two twilights, becomes endowed with the merit of the Veda. (2.78)

Even though it occurs within the context of the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), this is an injunction for the twilight recitation (*saṃdhyā-japa*) because it forms a single syntactical unit. In that regard, there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *gāyatrī*, while there is an injunction for what was previously unestablished (*aprāpta-vidhi*) concerning the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*.

Regarding this, someone says: This is not an injunction for the twilight ritual (*saṃdhyā-vidhi*), because it is not the subject under discussion (*aprakaraṇāt*). For if it were an injunction, it would apply to the religious student (*brahmacārin*), since he is the one under discussion; yet it cannot apply to him. For here it says "one who knows the Veda" (*vedavit*); and a person who has just been initiated does not possess the status of knowing the Veda. Moreover, a fruit is heard here: "he is joined with the merit of the Veda" (*vedapuṇyena yujyate*). The injunction for the obligatory twilight worship (*nitya-saṃdhyopāsana*) is not for the sake of a fruit. Nor do we know what this fruit called "merit of the Veda" is, by which this recitation (*japa*) is said to be joined. If, first of all, the merit intended is that which results from the study of the Veda, and the "joining with the merit of the Veda" is intended as its attainment—then, regarding the injunction for private Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) which is the subject at hand, there is no fruit other than the comprehension of the meaning, because no such [other] fruit is mentioned in scripture and because the comprehension of meaning is already perceived. Furthermore, the injunction for householders and others, "One should study the Veda every day," is also purely obligatory (*nitya*). As for the mention of a fruit therein—"milk, curds, ghee, honey"—that is merely a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*). Therefore, this is not an injunction. For if it were an injunction, all of this [the fruit, etc. would have to be intended as significant. But when this is a commendatory statement, then the word "reciting" (*japan*) refers to the study (*adhyayana*) which is the subject at hand, and the phrase "by the merit of the Veda" is also interpreted in some way or another.

To this it is replied: It has already been stated that the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside by the syntactical connection (*vākya*). Precisely because the terms "knower of the Veda" (*vedavit*) and "twilight" (*saṃdhyā*) do not connect with the subject matter at hand, this injunction applies elsewhere. The extent of the injunction is simply: "One should recite these three during the two twilights. The term "knower of the Veda" will be treated as a restatement (*anuvāda*). If it is argued that while being a knower of the Veda is possible for householders and others, it is not possible for a student (*brahmacārin*), we reply: what does his impossibility matter? For if it is a restatement of what is already established, then all those belonging to the various stages of life (*āśrama*) have the entitlement (*adhikāra*). Indeed, if the term "knower of the Veda" were a qualification of the agent, the student would have no entitlement. But how can this be a restatement? Because it would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Since the injunction regarding the twilight prayers is already established, the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*—which are not otherwise established—are what must be enjoined therein. In that case, if another element, namely "the knower of the Veda," were also enjoined, there would be a split of the sentence; for when a ritual action is already established, it is impossible to enjoin multiple things simultaneously. However, a restatement of the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis* is not possible [in this context].

Therefore, this is the meaning of the sentence here: regarding what was stated—that one should mutter the Sāvitrī at the two twilights—there is this further qualification: one should mutter it preceded by the Praṇava and the Vyāhṛtis. And the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is intended merely as an illustration.

As for what was said—that a fruit is heard here, yet this injunction regarding the *saṃdhyā* is obligatory—what contradiction is there? There will simply be a desire for that very quality within the obligatory rite; from that [rite] which has the *praṇava* and *vyāhṛtis* as its qualities, this fruit arises. Just as cattle are the fruit of the *agnihotra* when it is accompanied by the fetching of the *godohana* vessel, by the force of the statement: "One desiring cattle should fetch [water] with the *godohana*. And this was stated for the student, but this is not an optional (*kāmya*) injunction. For in another *smṛti*, this injunction is clearly stated as being indeed obligatory:
"One should recite the Gāyatrī together with its head, preceded by the Vyāhṛtis" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.23).
You yourself have already stated that the understanding of the fruits [of these rites] has been explained.

This is indeed the meaning of the phrase "by the merit of the Veda. Whatever merit is declared in the Veda regarding the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), by that [merit] one becomes joined with this triad while reciting it, and not merely with the *gāyatrī* alone. And "merit" (*puṇya*) is dharma; because the *smṛtis* are rooted in the Veda, even that which is stated in the *smṛtis* is designated as "the merit of the Veda"—that is, the merit belonging to the Veda (*vedapuṇya*). Furthermore, what is the merit of the Veda? It is that which is propounded by it. Although that which arises from the Veda being recited can also be said to belong to it, nevertheless, because of its unique nature, it is more appropriate to designate only that which is propounded, and not that which is produced. Sacrifices and the like produce dharma, but the Veda alone is its propounder.

As for those who claim that the final quarter [of the verse] has the following force: namely, that regarding what was stated, "One should constantly recite [the Veda]," they mean that by merely performing the triple recitation (*trikajapa*) at the junctions of the day (*saṃdhyā*), one fulfills the requirement; this too is incorrect. If that were the case, it would constitute an option (*vikalpa*) with respect to that injunction. And in that situation, there would be an occasional sublation (*pākṣika-bādha*) of the status of constant recitation. Furthermore, when non-sublation is possible, one should not accept sublation. The phrase "this syllable" (*etad akṣaram*) is a reference to the *oṃ* sound.

But is it not the case that this [mantra] consists of neither one syllable nor two or three? It is said: by the word *akṣara*, both the vowel alone and the conjunction of consonants are meant. Here, however, the designation refers to such [a unit] as is under discussion. And this [mantra] is the Sāvitrī, beginning with "That excellent splendor of Savitṛ. It is "preceded by the *vyāhṛtis*," meaning that which has the *vyāhṛtis* at its beginning. Only the three *vyāhṛtis* under discussion are understood here, because this [term] refers to what is under discussion, and not the seven ending with *satya*. (2.78)
But by practicing this triad externally a thousand times, a twice-born man is freed from even great sin within a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin. (2.79)

“Outside” (*bahiḥ*) refers to an unenclosed place; by this, the following is meant: in the forest outside of villages and towns, on riverbanks, and so forth. Having practiced—that is, having repeated [the mantra]—one thousand times. Now, one might object: since repetition is already conveyed by the suffix *-kṛtvasuc* (in *sahasra-kṛtvaḥ*), its mention again by the word “having practiced” (*abhyasya*) constitutes redundancy. This is not a fault, because of the relationship between the general and the particular. By the word “having practiced,” practice in general is stated; when there is a need for a specific detail, the phrase “one thousand times” is used. Furthermore, the understanding of both [general and specific] does not arise from the suffix *-kṛtvasuc* alone, because that suffix requires a specific action [to which it is attached]. Indeed, when it is said, “Devadatta [came] five times during the day,” the meaning of the sentence is not completed until it is stated what he did, such as “he ate.”

But surely, by the word "practicing" (*abhyasya*), no specific action is mentioned? True; however, it is understood that one should practice *japa*, which is the subject under discussion. "Repetition" (*āvṛtti*) means service performed again and again. "Even from great sin": great sin includes such things as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). One is liberated even from that; how much more so from minor offenses (*upapātaka*)? The particle *api* here expresses possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), not conjunction (*samuccaya*). Conjunction is understood when distinct items are presented, as in: "Devadatta has authority here, and Yajñadatta too. Here, however, there is no such indication.

From which secondary sins (*upapātaka*), then, is this liberation said to occur? Secondary sins include the killing of cows and so forth. For each such sin, there are prescribed expiations (*prāyaścitta*) along with their secret rites. Furthermore, regarding those [sins] one may not know whether they were committed—though they have not been mentioned as avoidable—one realizes they must have occurred by the very nature of things; for these too, the obligatory rites such as the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*) are the means of removal. If this [recitation of the *Gāyatrī*] were itself the expiation, then it would have been stated right there [in that context], as in: "One of restricted diet should indeed recite the *Saṃhitā* of the Veda three times" (MDh 11.76). Moreover, if this were the expiation, the entire section on expiations would be rendered useless. For who, unless cursed by fate, would abandon a purification achievable through mere recitation and instead resolve upon *kṛcchra* penances that destroy both body and life? And it has been said:
If one were to find honey on an arka tree, why would he go to the mountain?
When a desired object is attained, what wise person would exert effort [to seek it elsewhere]?
Likewise:
"For a wise man does not buy what can be obtained for a single paṇa with ten paṇas.

Nor is there any reason—such as a state of being incomplete when separated—that would establish syntactical unity with the preceding [injunction], whereby this could be stated as an explanatory passage (arthavāda) serving as a supplement to it.

To this it is replied: This is indeed a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*). This ritual application is solely for the purpose of liberation from sin. As for what was said—that "an option is not established when the rules are unequal"—in this case, the option will apply specifically to the expiation consisting of recitation (*japa-prāyaścitta*). The removal of all sins by means of the *aghamarṣaṇa* and other rites has been stated; therefore, there is an option with respect to this [present rite]. For in the case of the *aghamarṣaṇa*, a three-day fast is prescribed, whereas here one becomes purified through a monthly performance even while eating. Thus, one is not measured by a penance so vastly different [from others] that there would be a disparity in the rules.

Alternatively, this is the purification of previously committed sin when a divine affliction has been indicated by the unfavorable position of the planets and so forth; from that [sin], there is liberation. "Sin" (ena) refers to what is undesirable; one is liberated from that, meaning one is no longer connected with its fruit.

Like the outer skin: just as a snake becomes free from its worn-out skin, by this it is demonstrated that there is a destruction of sin without remainder. As for the evil deeds performed in the past, indicated by skin diseases and the like—for which many expiations (*prāyaścitta*) are prescribed in other Smṛtis—we shall point them out specifically within the section on expiations. With this very intention it was said:
"For those who mutter prayers and offer oblations, no downfall is seen" (MDh 4.146). || 2.79 ||
Deprived of this Ṛgvedic verse and his own timely ritual action, one born of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya lineage incurs reproach among the virtuous. (2.80)

One who is separated from this *Sāvitrī*, having neglected the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and abandoned his private Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*), incurs reproach—that is, censure—among the virtuous and distinguished. What kind of reproach does he incur? To this, the author says: "And by his own action at the proper time. Regarding "time," when the period prescribed by the rule "until the sixteenth year" (MDh 2.38) has passed without [initiation], one is censured. Thus, even if initiated, one who is unfit for the commencement of Vedic study and is devoid of the *Sāvitrī* becomes a *vrātya* (an outcast). That which is the common "own action" for all three [classes] is indicated here; and that is indeed the initiation (*upanayana*). In this way, the word "time" is meaningful. If the intention were merely to refer to one's own duties such as Vedic study, it would have been sufficient to say simply "by his own action. The word *yoni* is a synonym for birth and conveys the sense of caste (*jāti*). The meaning is: "belonging to the caste of a Brāhmaṇa and so forth. This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) intended for the penance of a *vrātya*. (2.80)
The three imperishable great utterances preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*, together with the three-footed *Sāvitrī*, should be known as the mouth of Brahman. (2.81)

Those [mantras] which have the syllable *oṃ* at their beginning are called *oṃkārapūrvikāḥ*. The *mahāvyāhṛtis*—which are the very subject under discussion—are the words *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*; they are designated as such because they are imperishable (*avyayāḥ*), meaning indestructible. This is stated because the fruit [of their recitation] endures for a long time; otherwise, the qualification "all these words are eternal" would be redundant. The three-footed *sāvitrī*, namely "That of Savitṛ," is the mouth of Brahman. It is designated as the "mouth" because it is the first; therefore, this is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the fact that this [verse] should be studied at the commencement [of study]. Alternatively, "mouth" means a door or a means; it says precisely this: that by means of this [verse], the attainment of Brahman occurs. (2.81)
He who studies this day after day for three years without weariness reaches the supreme Brahman, becoming like the wind and possessing the form of space.

He becomes all-pervading and omnipresent like space; he becomes one whose form is space and whose nature is space. However, "form" here does not mean a physical body, because space has no body. Now, what is this Brahman of which it is said that [the self] attains its form? It is the Supreme Self, whose nature is bliss, from whom these individual souls (kṣetrajñas) emerge, like waves from a mass of water tossed by the force of the wind. Just as those waves become of the same nature as that [water] when it is in a state of perfect calm, so too do these selves become of that same nature. Furthermore, all of this will be explained specifically in the twelfth chapter. This study of the Gāyatrī is enjoined, not as a mere recitation (*japa*), nor is there a count of repetitions. From the expression "without sloth," it is understood that it should be performed many times; for if it were performed only once, there would be no possibility of suspecting sloth. This rule is intended for one who seeks liberation. (2.82)
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the supreme austerity; there is nothing higher than the Sāvitrī; and truth excels silence. 2.83.

The syllable *oṃ* is the single syllable (*ekākṣara*). It is the supreme Brahman, because it is the means for attaining Brahman. Regarding the [Yoga Sūtra] 1.28: "The repetition of that [syllable] and meditation on its meaning," by means of that [repetition], the attainment of Brahman is thus described. *Oṃ* is the designation for Brahman. For thus they say: "The *praṇava* is its designator" (YSū 1.27). Why is it "supreme" (*param*)? Because it is superior to other meditations on Brahman, such as "One should meditate on food as Brahman" (TU 2.2.1) or "The sun is Brahman; this is the instruction" (ChU 3.19.1). The meditation on the *oṃkāra* is superior to these meditations, because its attainment is stated to occur through mere study, and because the Word itself is heard to be Brahman: "He who is proficient in the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) attains the Supreme Brahman" (MaitU 6.22). For every object does not transcend verbal usage, and *oṃkāra* is the root of all speech. Thus says the Śruti: "Just as all leaves are pierced by a pin, so all speech is pierced by *oṃkāra*. *Oṃkāra* alone is all this" (ChU 2.23.3). "Piercing" (*saṃtardana*) means following after or becoming the substratum. But how is all speech pierced by *oṃkāra*? First, it has been stated that Vedic speech is preceded by *oṃkāra*. As for worldly speech, there is the statement of Āpastamba: "Sentences should begin with that" (ĀpDh 1.13.9). This has been explained differently in the *Upadeśasāhasrī-bhāṣya*, but it is not shown here as it is not useful for the present context. The word *prāṇāyāma* refers to the restraint of breath accompanied by a specific procedure, like the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*). It is the "highest austerity" (*paraṃ tapaḥ*) compared to the *Cāndrāyaṇa* and other penances. What, then, is its excellence? It is devotion (*bhakti*). There is no knowledge of mantras higher than the *Sāvitrī*. The word "of these" (*eṣām*) is used for praise. Truth (*satya*) is superior to silence (*mauna*). "Silence" is said to be the restraint of speech. And whatever fruit results from that, something greater than that is obtained from speaking the truth. In truthful speech, the purpose of the injunction is likewise fulfilled; whereas in silence, there is merely the performance of the prohibition against falsehood. This verse is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). (2.83)
All Vedic rites of oblation and sacrifice flow away;
but the Imperishable is to be known as the Imperishable, as Brahman, and as Prajāpati.

Whatever Vedic *homas* there may be, such as the *agnihotra* and others, and whatever *yajñas* there may be, such as the *jyotiṣṭoma* and others—all of these are perishable; they do not become eternal. Or rather, their fruit "flows away," meaning it quickly perishes. But this imperishable (*akṣara*)—known by the name *oṃkāra*—is to be understood as the imperishable, having inexhaustible fruit. For one who has become Brahman, there is no further return to *saṃsāra*. Therefore, because its fruit is inexhaustible, it is called "imperishable" (*akṣara*). One instance of the word *akṣara* is the term being designated (*uddeśya*), while the second is a derivative (*yaugika*) word based on its etymological function. And that very thing is Brahman; and Prajāpati is indeed the *oṃkāra*. This is a praise. The mention of the verbal roots *juhoti* and *yajati* refers to the *yajña* and *homa* rites which are the objects to be accomplished through those actions. The plural number is used in view of the individual instances. Alternatively, this is a reference to the meanings of the verbal roots themselves in the forms *juhoti* and *yajati*. The "actions" (*kriyāḥ*) are those distinct from them, such as giving (*dāna*) and so forth. This is a *dvandva* compound: both *juhoti-yajati* and the "actions. Because of their importance, *homa* and *yajña* are mentioned separately.

Regarding this, some maintain that the praise of the syllable *oṃ* mentioned here is intended for the purpose of prescribing its recitation (*japa*) even when it stands alone. However, it is not merely a supplementary detail (*śeṣa*) to the rule under discussion, because there is no subsequent reference back to it. In the case of the Vaiśvānara sacrifice, the qualities such as being "eightfold" are connected to the same single sentence through the recurring term "Vaiśvānara," as seen in: "In that it is on eight potsherds, he purifies him with the *gāyatrī* and with spiritual luster; in that it is on nine potsherds, he bestows brilliance upon him by means of the *trivṛt*. Since a connection to a single sentence is possible throughout by depending on the word "Vaiśvānara," there is no possibility of a separate injunction (*vidhyantara*) by assuming a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). In this case, however, in the statement "the syllable is to be known," there is no dependence on what precedes it, nor is there a subsequent reference back to the *sāvitrī* and so forth. Therefore, since the meaning of the sentence is completed solely by its own constituent words, it cannot be a supplement to anything else. In the phrase "is to be known" (*jñeyam*), the suffix *-tavya* functions as an injunctive. And because of its connection with the word "Brahman," it is to be known as having the nature of Brahman—that is, it is to be meditated upon (*upāsya*) and contemplated (*bhāvanīya*). When that is being contemplated, what is called "mental recitation" (*mānasa-japa*) is thereby accomplished. (2.84)
The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is ten times superior to the ritual sacrifice (vidhiyajña);
the whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is a hundredfold more effective, and the mental recitation (mānasa) is declared to be a thousandfold.

The *vidhiyajña* (ritual sacrifice) is that which is the object of an injunction (*vidhi*), such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices. That action which is enjoined by the command "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) and is performed through external activity with the completion of all its constituent parts, including the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and so forth—that is what is called the *vidhiyajña* here. Recitation (*japa*), however, is not a sacrifice; it is called a sacrifice only figuratively by way of praise. Therefore, it is not a *vidhiyajña*. It is distinguished—that is, superior, excellent—as a sacrifice by ten qualities compared to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and others. By this, the great fruitfulness of recitation is expressed: whatever fruit is obtained from a sacrifice, that very same [fruit], but in greater measure, is obtained from recitation. And it is not logical that recitation should have a greater fruit than the Vedic sacrifices (*śrauta-yāga*). For if that were the case, who would undertake sacrifices that consist in the depletion of body and wealth? Therefore, this is merely a praise, like the statement: "By the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one obtains all desires. Its meaning is this much: that very same fruit, such as heaven and so forth, is obtained, but—unlike in the world—it is due to a specific intensity of effort. Because the sacrifice itself is not specified, there is a distinction in the magnitude of the fruit: whatever fruit belongs to whichever sacrifice—whether heaven, a village, sons, cattle, or the like—that is obtained from the recitation of that [mantra]. Recitation done in a whisper (*upāṃśu*) is a hundredfold, when another person does not hear it even if standing nearby. A thousandfold is the "thousandfold" (*sāhasra*) mental [recitation], which is contemplated by the mere operation of the mind. These qualities, such as being whispered and so on, apply to the entire scope of recitation, because they are separated from the context of the previously mentioned [sacrifices] by the word "who has studied" (*yo 'dhīta*). Therefore, these qualities apply everywhere to recitation used for expiation (*prāyaścitta*), for pacification (*śāntika*), or for prosperity (*ābhyudayika*). "Sāhasra" means "that which has a thousand"; since qualities are the subject under discussion, the existence of a thousandfold quality is understood. The word "quality" (*guṇa*) here denotes a part, and the abundance of the fruit is understood through their connection. (2.85)

The four types of cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), together with the ritual sacrifices (vidhiyajña), all of them are not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña). || 2.86 ||

The *mahāyajñas* are called *pākayajñas*; excluding the *brahmayajña*, there are four such sacrifices. These are described as *vidhiyajñas*; "endowed with" (*samanvitāḥ*) means accompanied by them. They do not merit even a sixteenth part—*kalām* means a portion or a sixteenth part; they are not equal to even a sixteenth fraction. Alternatively, the root *arh* is used in the sense of attainment or in the context of bargaining for a price. By adding the suffix *tip* to the word *arha*, the form *arhanti* is produced. (2.86)
A Brahmin shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt about this.
Whether he performs other rites or does not perform them, he is called a Brahmin who is a friend to all (maitra). (2.87)

One may attain perfection—whether it be the acquisition of desired fruits or the realization of Brahman—through recitation alone (*japya*). One should not harbor doubt in this regard, such as: "How can that which is to be obtained through great exertions like the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and through meditative realizations (*bhāvanā*) be accomplished by recitation? It is indeed accomplished.

One might perform other rites, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others, which are impermanent; or rather, one should not perform even those, because a Brāhmaṇa is said to be "maitra" (friendly). "Maitra" means simply "friend. A Brāhmaṇa must be one who delights in friendliness toward all living beings. And how can there be friendliness in the injury of an animal during the Agniṣomīya sacrifice? This is merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), and not a prohibition of the ritual acts involving animals, since it is understood as a supplement to what precedes it, and because those acts are prescribed by direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*). Thus ends the rule regarding the recitation of prayers. (2.88)
A wise man should exert effort in restraining the senses as they roam among alluring objects, just as a charioteer restrains his horses. 2.88.

"One should apply effort toward the restraint of the senses"—this much is the meaning of the scripture; the remainder is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) up to the injunction for the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*). Restraint (*saṃyama*) consists of avoiding engagement with prohibited objects, and even with respect to those not prohibited, it is the avoidance of excessive attachment. Among these, the avoidance of the prohibited is established by those very prohibitions themselves. This collection of verses is intended to prohibit excessive attachment even to those things that are not prohibited. This is precisely what [the author] says: "For those wandering among objects," that is, for those who proceed independently, acting according to the inherent power of things. "Among captivators": objects are called "captivators" because they carry away, attract, make one their own, and bring a person under their control; these are the objects said to be "mind-stealing. In this context, "wandering" means moving about in various and specific ways. If the senses did not move specifically, then even if objects were not captivators, what could they do? Or, let the senses be unrestrained; if objects were rejectable, then the self would still be easy to restrain for a person. But since both are culpable, effort must be applied, for these [senses] are indeed difficult to control.

Just as a driver, the controller of horses yoked to a chariot, exerts effort in restraining and regulating them—which by their very nature are prone to wandering—so that they do not, against his will, carry him along a wrong path but instead submit to his authority, even so must the sense-faculties be brought under control. 2.88.
I shall correctly explain, in due order and as they truly are, those eleven faculties which the wise of old have declared. (2.89)

This enumeration of numbers is to be understood through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is not the primary subject matter of this treatise; however, it is explained here out of friendliness. The ancient sages have already spoken of these [categories]; I shall describe them hereafter by name and by function. The mention of "succession" (*ānupūrvyam*) implies orderliness. By the use of the word "ancient" (*pūrva*), it is shown that this systematic arrangement was not merely devised by logicians (*tārkika*), but was indeed established by the teachers of old as well. Those who do not know this are ridiculed by the world as being "unacquainted with the scriptures" (*nāgamika*); therefore, this must be understood. Well-known categories and those already explained previously [are now concluded]. (2.89)
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth; the anus, the generative organ, the hands and feet, and speech is recorded as the tenth. (2.90)

The ear and the other [senses] are well known. Because of the distinction between their physical bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there is a dual number for "the eyes" (*cakṣuṣī*); elsewhere, because the capacity residing therein is unitary, there is a singular number. The *upastha* is that which emits semen in a male and that which holds the *rajas* in a female. Since these two are mentioned as a copulative compound (*dvandva*) and are parts of a living being, they take a singular form according to Pāṇini 2.4.2. *Vāk* refers to the palate and so forth; it denotes a part of the body that manifests sound. This is a designation by name. (2.90)
Of these, the five organs of cognition, beginning with the ear, are enumerated in their proper order; and the five organs of action, beginning with the anus, are likewise declared. (2.91)

Now, he states their function for the purpose of determining their essential nature. For these are not themselves perceptible. The "cognitive faculties" (*buddhīndriyāṇi*) are the instruments that produce cognition; the genitive case is used here to express the relationship between the effect and the instrument.
