"The ear and so forth, in their proper order. One should not understand the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) as signifying a class; rather, "in their proper order" means sequentially. Since sequence depends upon a specific arrangement, the established order mentioned in the preceding verse is adopted here. The "action faculties" (*karmendriyāṇi*): here, "action" is intended to mean that which consists of movement. (2.91)
The eleventh, the mind, should be known as being of a dual nature by virtue of its own quality;
when it is conquered, these two groups of five become conquered.

The mind is the eleventh among the sense organs; its own specific quality is volition (*saṃkalpa*). By means of that, both [types of action], whether auspicious or inauspicious, are willed. Alternatively, because it is the root of volition in the engagement of the sense organs of cognition and the organs of action with their respective objects, it is said to be of a dual nature. When this [mind] is conquered, these two groups—the group of the sense organs of cognition and the group of the organs of action—each consisting of five as previously specified, become conquered. This is the exposition of the principles (*tattva*). (2.92)
Through attachment to the senses, one undoubtedly incurs fault; but by fully restraining them, one attains perfection. (2.93)

"Prasaṅga" means being intent upon that [practice]. By means of that as a cause, one encounters—that is, reaches—both seen and unseen faults; there is no doubt here, for this is certain. Having restrained those senses, one then attains "siddhi," which is the acquisition of the intended object—the complete fruit of performing the rites prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis. || 2.93 ||
Desire is never quenched by the enjoyment of the objects of desire;
like a fire fed with clarified butter, it only increases all the more. (2.94)

Let alone the longing for sense-objects, which is not undertaken because of the teachings of the scriptures; rather, even the visible pleasure resulting from cessation [of desire] occurs. For instance, even when sense-objects are being enjoyed, they produce an even greater greed. Even for one who has eaten his fill, who is satisfied, and who has reached the point of extreme satiation, there arises a longing in the heart: "How might I be able to eat something else? Yet, due to incapacity, one does not proceed to do so. Therefore, this cessation cannot be achieved through enjoyment; never is desire—the longing for objects that are desired and longed for—appeased or turned back by their enjoyment or service. On the contrary, it increases further and more, like fire with its black trail [smoke] fed by sacrificial butter (*havīs*).
And desire is of the nature of suffering; for one who has not experienced its flavor, desire does not arise. This is the enumeration of reality. And it has been said:
"Whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women there are upon the earth—all that is not enough for even one person. Having realized this, one should attain tranquility. (2.94)
Between one who might obtain all these things and one who might renounce them entirely, the renunciation of all desires is superior to their attainment. (2.95)

Relying upon the previously stated reason as its basis, this concluding verse is recited: "When desire increases through indulgence, therefore, he who is a seeker of desires might attain all these objects of desire, serving like a youthful lord of many realms; whereas he who renounces them and does not touch even the slightest bit of them is like a child devoted to his vow. Of those two, he who is the renouncer is superior—he excels, being pre-eminently the best—than he who is the attainer and enjoyer. This is directly perceived by oneself. (2.95)
These senses, corrupted by sense-objects, cannot be restrained by abstinence as effectively as they can be constantly restrained by knowledge. (2.96)

If this is so, then one might conclude that dwelling in the forest alone is required, for there the objects of the senses are not present; and since they are not present, they will not be indulged in. To address this, he says: "The senses are not to be restrained by non-indulgence. [Otherwise,] one would be devoid of happiness. Yet they also remember: "One should not let the forenoon, midday, or afternoon pass fruitlessly, but should devote them to dharma, artha, and kāma according to one's ability" (GDh 9.46). Furthermore, the maintenance of the body does not occur through non-indulgence; rather, what is being stated here is the prohibition of craving (*garddha*). And that craving, even while indulgence exists, is removed by knowledge—namely, by the knowledge of the defects inherent in sense-objects as taught in the scriptures such as, "The body has bones for its pillars and is bound together by sinews" (MDh 6.76), and by one's own direct experience of their loathsomeness in their ultimate maturation (*vipāka*). Does the desire cease gradually through the cultivation of detachment (*vairāgya*) by contemplating the initial defects of the very fruits of maturation? It cannot be abandoned all at once. Rather, "constantly" (*nityaśaḥ*) means at all times. This qualifies "knowledge. "Corrupted" (*praduṣṭāni*) means set in motion; because they are defective, those very things set in motion are called "corrupted. This suffix *śas* is employed in various places by great sages such as Vyāsa and others, as in the expressions *nityaśaḥ*, *anupūrvaśaḥ*, *sarvaśaḥ*, and *pūrvaśaḥ*. One must make an effort to establish its correctness. In that regard, under the rule for the suffix *śas*, it is recited: "*ekavacanāc ca vīpsāyām*" (Pāṇini 5.4.43). There, the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*) must somehow be indicated. Others, however, describe *śas* as a form derived from the root *sthā* with the suffix *kvip*. This is an adverbial neuter. The meaning is: "by means of knowledge that is constantly established. (2.96)
The Vedas, renunciation, sacrifices, observances, and austerities never lead to success for one whose disposition is corrupted. (2.97)

This is the very rule in this matter: the Vedas refer to their study, recitation (*japa*), and so forth; "renunciation" (*tyāga*) refers to giving (*dāna*) by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Alternatively, it refers to the avoidance [of even those things not expressly forbidden], such as the eating of honey and meat, according to the rule: "The abstention from even what is not prohibited yields fruit" (MDh 5.56). "One whose disposition (*bhāva*)—that is, whose mind (*citta*)—is utterly corrupted does not attain success (*siddhi*); that is, the means for accomplishing the fruit do not become effective at any time whatsoever. Therefore, at the time of performance, one must not have a mind directed toward desired objects and the like. It might then be asked: can the mind be fixed upon the ritual action by setting aside all other mental fluctuations? Indeed, the abandonment of thoughts regarding sense-objects during rituals is prescribed by this statement as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the rites. In its absence, the ritual would be fruitless. For this is the defect of disposition (*bhāvadoṣa*): when one has engaged in the performance of a rite, to abandon devotion to it and fix the mind on vices. (2.97)
That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled,
neither rejoices nor desponds, should be known as one who has conquered his senses.

Having heard the sound of flutes, songs, and the like, or having heard such words as “You are Bṛhaspati,” he does not rejoice. Having heard harsh, rough, and abusive speech, he does not languish; he does not experience mental distress. *Glāniḥ* means exhaustion or weariness. Having touched garments such as those made of *rāṅkava* wool or *kauśeya* silk, as well as the *kutapa* blanket made of goat hair, he experiences them with equanimity. Likewise, he remains the same whether beholding well-dressed young women and actors, or seeing an enemy. He eats equally whether it be food with much ghee and *ṣaṣṭika* rice, or *kodrava* grain. He smells equally whether it be *devadāru* oil or camphor and the like. One should act in such a way that one is not touched by purely mental pleasures or pains. In this manner, his senses become conquered—not merely through non-activity. This much extent of self-restraint (*saṃyama*) is to be resorted to. (2.98)
But surely, a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) must avoid association with women with great effort; why then is the acceptance of prepared alms-food prohibited? To this he says:
"But if even one among all the senses leaks, through that his wisdom flows away, like water from the foot of a leather water-skin. (2.99)

The genitive case is used here in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*). If even one single sense-organ leaks—that is, if it functions independently in its own object and is not restrained—then his wisdom (*prajñā*) and fortitude leak away, as does [the stability of] the other senses' objects. A leather bag (*dṛti*) is a vessel made of the skin of goats and the like for carrying water and such things. Even if its other parts are closed, if water flows out from a single foot, the whole thing becomes empty. Fortitude is that which is accumulated through the practice of knowledge, or perhaps right knowledge itself. For one whose mind is absorbed in the objects due to greed for them, the meanings accessible through reasoning and scripture do not appear correctly in reality. (2.99)
Having brought the collection of senses under control and likewise restrained the mind,
one should accomplish all goals through yoga without wasting the body.

He concludes: Even though the mind (*manas*) is indeed a sense-organ (*indriya*), it is mentioned separately because of its predominance. "Village" (*grāma*) means a collection. Having brought the senses under control, one should likewise bring the mind under control; one should accomplish—that is, bring to completion—all goals achievable through rites prescribed by the *Śrutis* and *Smṛtis*. One should do so "without emaciating the body," that is, without afflicting it. "By means of yoga" means by means of proper method (*yukti*). For someone of a delicate constitution, affliction may arise suddenly from practices such as sitting on a hard seat or wearing a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*). To address this, the following is said: those for whom food has been well-habituated and well-prepared, and whose beds and so forth have been soft, should not abandon these suddenly; rather, they should be gradually made into a habit, and the opposite [of what is harmful] should be done. "Yoga" is said to be gradual engagement. And in that context, the connection is with the phrase "having brought [them] under control by means of yoga. Alternatively, the word "yogataḥ" should be construed with "in their proper place" (*yathāsthānam*). One should not cause the body to fall away from what is appropriate; one should not abruptly discard that which is suitable for the body. Or, "yoga" refers to intent (*tātparya*). The suffix *-tasi* is used in the sense of the third case. One should protect the body with intent. (2.100)
One should stand reciting the Sāvitrī during the morning twilight until the sun appears; but during the evening twilight, one should always remain seated until the stars are clearly visible. (2.101)

The morning twilight (*pūrva-saṃdhyā*) occurs when the sun is directly in front; the evening twilight (*paścima-saṃdhyā*) occurs at the setting of the sun. One should remain standing during that time, reciting the *Sāvitrī*. Having risen from one's seat, one should remain in one place, refraining from movement. The *Sāvitrī* has already been mentioned as "That excellent splendor of Savitṛ" (*tat savitur vareṇyam*). For there are indeed restatements of it. The rule regarding the syllable *Oṃ* and so forth is set forth in the verse for the purpose of the twilight recitation: "This syllable and this [verse]" (MDh 2.78). Regarding the phrase "until the sight of the sun," it means until the divine Sun is seen. This is the specific instruction concerning both the recitation and the posture.

Now, what is the use of a ritual injunction? The twilight (*saṃdhyā*) ceases at the very rising of the sun. For indeed, this is the twilight when darkness has not entirely vanished nor has light reached its fullness. And it is said:
"That time when there is light in the sky and darkness on the earth is designated as the *sāvitra* [twilight]."

It is also stated in the *Nirukta*: "In the enumeration of sacrificial animals, it is known that 'the lower part belongs to Sūrya. On account of what similarity? Because [the lower part] is red below and black below" (*Nir* 12.13). Furthermore, upon the rising of the sun, darkness is dispelled from all sides. And the *saṃdhyā* (twilight) consists in the non-cessation of both characteristics: the characteristic of night and the characteristic of day. This accusative case in the word *saṃdhyām* is used in the sense of continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). By this, it is meant that one should remain for as long as the time of *saṃdhyā* lasts; beyond that, independence is established.

Some say that this accusative case is not used here for absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). Rather, according to the Vārttikakāra’s rule, “Time [and distance] becomes designated as the object (*karman*) of intransitive verbs,” the accusative is applied here by the rule *karmaṇi dvitīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.2). As for the rule *kālādhvanor atyantasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.5), its scope is where a word expressing an action is not employed—for example, *krośaṃ kuṭilā nadī* (“the river is winding for the distance of a *krośa*”) or *sarvarātraṃ kalyāṇī* (“she is auspicious throughout the night”). And where there is a transitive verbal root—as in *māsam adhīyate* (“he studies for a month”)—that is its domain. But here, in the injunction *saṃdhyāṃ tiṣṭhet* (“one should stand during the twilight”), the root *sthā* is intransitive. Therefore, the mention of the rule is intended to ensure that the standing and sitting are performed throughout the entire duration of the twilight. The time of commencement, however, is not explicitly stated here, because it is already provided by the word *saṃdhyā* itself. For the very beginning of the twilight period is the same as the beginning of its prescribed ritual. Indeed, the twilight period is not as long as the time of the full moon and so forth; if one were to delay, it would be difficult to perceive, owing to its extreme subtlety, like the rising and falling of the ends of two balance scales. The end of the night and the beginning of the day have no perceptible sequence. The blessed Sun moves with extreme speed; just as astronomers maintain that his transition from one zodiacal sign (*rāśi*) to another occurs in a mere moment (*truṭi*) once he has finished one sign, so too do sunrise and sunset mark the beginning and end of the day. Before sunrise it is night; once the sun has risen, it is day. According to this, there is no separate twilight, since the end of the night occurs precisely with the rising of the sun. For this very reason, the performance of the rite takes place in the vicinity of sunrise and sunset. When the sun and the stars are clearly visible, the rite ceases; thus, he who performs the worship for this duration necessarily fulfills the injunction at the primary time. And for this reason, what is intended here by “twilight” is the period pertaining to the sun (*sāvitra*), not the calculation of the astronomical sciences. That has been explained previously.

If this is so, then for those for whom this alone is the time for the *agnihotra*, it would follow that there is an absence of the twilight (*saṃdhyā*) ritual. What is the point of this objection? It is entirely appropriate that a Smārta rite be superseded by a Śrauta one. Furthermore, there is no contradiction here; for the oblation can be offered both while standing and while sitting. But surely, at the two twilights, not only standing and sitting are prescribed, but also the recitation of the triple formula (*trikajapa*). And how could one, while reciting the *Sāvitrī*, utter the mantra for the oblation?

Let there be a sublation of the *japa* (recitation). First, regarding the principal act (*pradhāna*), standing and sitting are not contradictory; however, by the maxim "when a subordinate element (*guṇa*) is omitted, the primary remains" (PMS 10.2.62), a sublation of the *japa* is appropriate because it is a subordinate element. Furthermore, the status of those two [standing and sitting] as the principal is established by their direct connection with the injunction through the words "he should stand" and "he should sit. The *japa*, however, is subordinate, since the verbal root *jap* ends in a present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), which indicates that it serves as a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*). Moreover, the connection with the qualification for the rite pertains only to standing and sitting, as seen in the passages: "He who does not stand during the morning... and "Standing, he removes the sin of the night" (MDh 1.103, 102).

As for what has been stated by someone else: "In this context, standing (*tiṣṭhati*) is the subordinate element (*guṇa*), while the act of recitation (*japakarma*) is the primary element; for it is from that [recitation] that we have heard the fruit [arise],"—to that it is replied: This is not an injunction for one who desires a specific result. Why, then, would there be a mention of a fruit? As for the misconception regarding the statement concerning the *praṇava* and so forth—that "one is joined with the merit of the Veda" (MDh 2.78)—which is thought to be a restatement of a fruit, that has already been resolved in that very place. Therefore, standing and sitting are the primary elements.

Alternatively, those who maintain the *agnihotra* may recite the *Sāvitrī* once or repeat it three times; by that much, there is no lapse in the time for the *agnihotra*. Regarding the statement, "Having eaten in the evening, he is released," the *agnihotra* is not thereby obstructed. The word "eating" (*aśnan*) denotes a long duration of time. By that much, the purpose of the twilight ritual (*saṃdhyā*) is fulfilled. For the limit of the sight of the sun is merely a subordinate element (*aṅga*). For those who offer the *agnihotra* after sunrise, the offering of the *agnihotra* occurs only after they have performed the twilight ritual.

Gautama, however, states: "Until the stars appear, because the light [of the sun] is visible" (GDh 2.11). This is the meaning of the sūtra: this much time is called *saṃdhyā* (the twilight period); it is not a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the ritual injunction. In that regard, there is no repetition of the rite during this entire duration. Just as in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice on the full moon day" (ŚB 11.1.3.6), there is no repetition of the ritual action merely by following the time, so too with the statements "the morning *saṃdhyā* is with the stars" and "the evening *saṃdhyā* is with the sun. That too is a definition of the time; here, this much time is designated by the word *saṃdhyā*. Within that, the *saṃdhyā* rite is to be performed. If, within this time denoted by the word *saṃdhyā*, one performs standing, sitting, and recitation (*japa*) for even a single *muhūrta*—that is, for three or four units of time—the purpose of the injunction is indeed fulfilled. For here, unlike the rule of Manu, a pervasion of the entire duration is not heard in scripture. In every respect, the *agnihotra* and the *saṃdhyā* rites, though having the same time, can both be performed.

The word *sadā* (always) expresses permanence. It refers to the remainder of both twilights. *Āsīta* means sitting; it denotes a state of remaining seated rather than standing upright; one should be seated. *Ṛkṣa* means a constellation. *Ā tadvibhāvanāt*—the letter *ā* here is to be connected with *ārkadarśanāt* (until the appearance of the sun). The word *samyak* (properly) is an adjective qualifying both "appearance" (*darśana*) and "manifestation" (*vibhāvana*). When the sun has its orb fully complete, and the constellations are radiant, endowed with their own luster, and not overwhelmed by the brilliance of the sun. 2.101.

Standing while reciting prayers during the morning twilight, one removes the sin committed at night; sitting during the evening twilight, however, one destroys the impurity created by the day. (2.102)

The subject matter here is stated as follows: *enaḥ* is the fault (*doṣa*) born from the practice of what is prohibited; he removes (*vyapohati*), that is, dispels it. *Naiśam* means occurring at night, i.e., committed during the night. In this way, *mala* (impurity) has the same meaning as the word *enas*.

Nor is this expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for every [sin] committed by day or by night; for if that were the case, the specific expiations taught, such as the *kṛcchra*, would be rendered useless. As it is said: "If one should find honey on a *arka* tree, why should one go to the mountain?"

Thus, according to common worldly discourse. What then? That minor offense which is unpracticed, committed unintentionally, unavoidable, for which no specific expiation has been prescribed, and which passes away—such as the subtle killing of living beings by one who is asleep through the movement of hands or the turning over of the bed; the scratching of the private parts (which is prohibited by the rule that one should not touch them "without cause"); and the impurity resulting from the flow of saliva and so forth while an existing state of impurity caused by something done at another time persists, such as the practice of what is forbidden. It is with this very intention that the following was said:
"One who is devoid of the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) should always be known as impure.

Nor does this entail the consequence of [the rule] being non-permanent, because such a defect is never absent [in one who neglects it]. Furthermore, for one walking on a path during the day, there is the occurrence of fixing one's gaze upon the face of another's wife; when the agitation of the mind produced by that is manifested, there is angry and indecent speech. These two [acts] remove the merit of the twilight rites. (2.102)
But he who neither remains at the morning twilight nor performs worship at the evening twilight is to be excluded from all duties of the twice-born, like a Śūdra. (2.103)

By stating that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) for its non-performance, he establishes its obligatory (*nitya*) nature: "He who does not stand during the morning *saṃdhyā* and does not remain seated during the evening [saṃdhyā] should be known as equal to a Śūdra; he is to be excluded from and barred from all duties of the twice-born, such as the offering of hospitality and other marks of respect. Therefore, the *saṃdhyā* must be performed regularly in order to avoid being equated with a Śūdra. This is the statement of qualification (*adhikāra-vākya*). And here, standing and sitting are prescribed specifically for the recitation (*japa*). That which is connected to the qualification is primary; everything else related to it is a subsidiary (*aṅga*). (2.103)
Restrained and established in the daily rule, he should go to the forest and, with a concentrated mind, recite the Sāvitrī near water.
This is another rule for Vedic study; because it is not heard in the same context, it is distinct from the previous one which was for the purpose of memorization.

"A desolate region outside the village" refers to the forest (*araṇya*). Having gone there and reached a place near water, such as a river or a pond; or, in the absence of such, even at a place where water is contained in vessels like a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and so forth—"restrained" means pure and diligent; "composed" means having abandoned mental distraction—he should recite the *Sāvitrī*, even if he is unable to do so due to some pressing business involving many hymns, sections, or chapters. "Abiding by the daily rule" (*naityaka*): *naityaka* means that which is indeed obligatory (*nitya*). One whose wisdom is thus established understands, "This rule is obligatory. Furthermore, the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi*) for the purpose of learning is the archetype (*prakṛti*); this [present rule] is its modification (*vikāra*), and therefore it assumes its properties. Consequently, the rules such as "the syllable *praṇava* for the Veda" and "with the tips of the grass blades pointing eastward" (MDh 1.74, 75) apply here as well.

Others, however, explain that *vidhi* means injunction, method, manner, procedure (*itikartavyatā*), and so forth. In the case of the daily recitation of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*), which must necessarily be performed by a lifelong student (*nitya-brahmacārin*), he relies upon that procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the injunction. Furthermore, the obligatory nature (*nityatva*) of this injunction is to be understood from such scriptural statements as: "For that is remembered as the perpetual sacrifice of Brahman" (*brahmasatraṃ hi tat smṛtam*, MDh 2.106).

The first explanation alone appears to be the most appropriate. For the word *vidhi* is not commonly known as denoting a "manner" (*prakāra*). Moreover, if by the term *naityaka* the rule for the religious student (*brahmacārin*) were intended, then in the verse "In the case of the *naityaka*, there is no suspension of study" (MDh 2.106), that same [student] would have to be designated by the word *naityaka*; consequently, the prohibition of the suspension of study would apply only to him. || 104 ||

Furthermore, there is no prohibition regarding the study of the Vedas' auxiliary sciences (vedopakaraṇa), nor regarding the daily recitation of one's own Veda (svādhyāya), nor indeed regarding the mantras for the burnt-oblation (homa). (2.105)

The *upakaraṇa* (auxiliary sciences) are said to be the *vedāṅgas*, such as the *kalpasūtras* and *niruktas*. When these are being studied, there is no restriction (*anurodha*) or requirement regarding days unfit for study (*anadhyāya*). Indeed, even on days unfit for study, and in the case of *homa* mantras, those unfit days are not to be observed as prohibitions; one should study even on days unfit for study. Alternatively, the reading is *na nirodhaḥ*: there is no cessation of study on days unfit for study.

Even though the rule of non-study during forbidden days (*anadhyāya*) is a property of the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), and the injunction for study has the *svādhyāya* as its object, and the *svādhyāya* is the Veda—whereas the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) are not denoted by the word "Veda"—nevertheless, because they are interspersed with Vedic sentences, the notion that they are the Veda might arise; therefore, it is stated for the sake of clarity. Or rather, this is an illustration: just as there is no period of non-study regarding the Vedic auxiliaries, so too there is none regarding the Veda itself.

Regarding the mantras for the *agnihotra* oblation, or those used in other *sāvitra* and propitiatory (*śānti*) oblations—this is mentioned by way of illustration—the recitation of Vedic sentences that constitute the constituent parts of a ritual, such as the mantras for constant recitation (*japa*) and the directions (*praiṣa*), is governed by the rule of non-study during forbidden periods (*anadhyāya*), which is prompted by the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*). One who, thinking thus, concludes that there should be no recitation of mantras for oblations and the like on the fourteenth day and other such days, is corrected by this matter established by logic and restated here: the sequence of non-study during forbidden periods is prompted by the injunction for the study of one's own Veda; it is not a property of the Veda itself. Therefore, there is no period of non-study regarding mantras that are constituent parts of a ritual. This refers to the obligatory rule for the study of one's own Veda (*naityaka svādhyāya*), which is enjoined for members of all stages of life (*āśrama*) by the preceding statement. (2.105)
In the daily obligatory rite there is no suspension of study, for that is remembered as the "Brahma-sacrifice.
It is meritorious, offered with the oblation of the Veda, and consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ*-call even during times when study is otherwise suspended. (2.106)

This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) supplementary to the preceding rule. For this reason, there is no suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) for the daily recitation (*naityaka*), because that is remembered as the "Brahma-weapon" (*brahmāstra*). Just as a sacrificial session (*satra*)—such as the sacrificial session of a thousand years and so forth—is constantly in progress and never interrupted, so too is this [daily study]. The "Brahma-sattra" is that which is accomplished through the study of the Veda; and because it is a *satra*, it must never be interrupted. For if it were interrupted, its status as a *satra* would not exist.

Now he applies the nature of a *sattra* sacrifice through the device of metaphorical description (*rūpaka*). The Veda is the recitation; the oblation offered is another *sattra*, wherein the oblation of Soma is poured. The root *hu-* (to offer) is used here in the sense of non-cessation, because verbal roots have multiple meanings. By the word *brahma*, the act of recitation pertaining to it is indicated. The compound "the Veda-recitation as an oblation" (*brahmādhyayanam āhutiḥ*) is formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.56, *upamitam vyāghrādibhiḥ*. That recitation which takes place on forbidden days (*anadhyāya*) is "consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ*-call. Just as at the end of a *yājyā* verse the continuity is maintained by the *vaṣaṭ*-call, so too the recitation on forbidden days such as the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight stands in the place of the *vaṣaṭ*-call. By the word *vaṣaṭ*, the word *vauṣaṭ* is indicated. That which is performed or joined with that is "prepared" (*saṃskṛta*). The compound is formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.32, *sādhanaṃ kṛtā*. (2.106)
For him who, being self-restrained and pure, studies the Veda according to the prescribed rule for a year, this [sacrifice] constantly yields milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey. (2.107)

This is a supplement to the injunction under discussion (*prakṛtavidhiśeṣa*). And that [injunction] has been established as obligatory (*nitya*). In the case of an obligatory act, the mention of a fruit is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Furthermore, there is no injunctive suffix (*vidhivibhakti*) present here, by which—according to the principle "But when one thing serves two purposes, there is a distinct connection" (*ekasya tūbhayatve saṃyogaḥ pṛthaktvam*, PMS 4.3.5)—milk and the like could serve as the cause for a separate qualification (*adhikārāntarahetu*). Since an obligatory qualification has already been obtained, the principle of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice (*rātrisatranyāya*) does not apply either, whereby milk and the rest might be postulated as having no other fruit. Therefore, this is simply an explanatory praise; its basis is the restatement of the flowing forth of milk and so on, because one who studies [the Veda] obtains cows through social prestige, acceptance of gifts, and the like.

He who studies the Veda through his private recitation (*svādhyāya*) for a year—that is, for one full year—according to the rule by sitting on a seat of *prākkūla* grass, being self-controlled with restrained senses and pure through bathing and other rites; for that person, this *svādhyāya* constantly flows, streams, and bestows its fruit as long as he lives. This is *svādhyāya*. [The text continues: "milk, curd," and so forth.

Others, however, believe that *dharma*, *artha*, *kāma*, and *mokṣa* are denoted by the words "milk" (*payas*) and so forth: milk is *dharma* because of its common quality of purity; curd is *artha* because it is a cause of nourishment; ghee is *kāma* because of its common quality of unctuousness; and honey is *mokṣa* because of the unity of all flavors. Whatever human goal there may be, all of it is attained in just one year through the study of the Veda—how much more so in a longer period! Since these words such as "milk" are merely explanatory (*arthavāda*), one should not insist on their literal meaning. (2.107)

Having undergone the initiation ceremony, a twice-born man shall, until his formal return home, maintain the sacred fire, practice begging for alms, sleep on the ground, and perform what is beneficial for his teacher. (2.108)

Kindling the fire with fuel-sticks every morning and evening is *agnīndhana*. Not ascending a bedstead means sleeping on the ground; it does not mean sleeping exclusively on a bare patch of earth (*sthaṇḍila*). Service characterized by fetching water-jars and other items for the benefit of the teacher is *śuśrūṣā*. That which consists of performing services beneficial to him, however, lasts for as long as one lives. All this must be performed until the completion of the period of studentship, ending with the ritual bath (*snāna*) that marks the departure from the teacher’s household, because this is for the purpose of fulfilling the injunction to study one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi*). Since the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) and its specific duties persist until the acquisition [of the Veda] and cease upon its completion, their cessation is already established.

The repetition of the fire, fuel, and so forth is for the purpose of enjoining those same practices for subsequent stages of life (*āśrama*) that belong to a category of duties distinct from and transcending the former; as Gautama states: "And this is not in conflict with the subsequent [stages]" (GDh 3.9). Now, why is it not the case that these [duties] last only as long as the state of studentship (*brahmacarya*), while others may even cease before that? Another Smṛti has been shown on this point: the rule is that restrictive observances (*niyama*) follow the principal [stage], provided there is a logical possibility for doing so.
In the expression "gurave hitam" ("beneficial for the teacher"), the dative case is appropriate by virtue of its connection with the word *hita* [according to Pāṇini 2.1.36]. 2.108.

The son of a teacher, one who is obedient, a giver of knowledge, righteous, pure, trustworthy, capable, a provider of wealth, virtuous, and one's own kinsman—these ten are to be taught according to the Dharma. (2.109)

It will be stated [in MDh 4.233]: "Of all gifts, the gift of the Veda (*brahmadāna*) is preeminent. In that context, this verse is intended to define the characteristics of a worthy recipient (*pātra*) for whom knowledge should be given. Following the discussion on the duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*), this rule concerning teaching is now declared.

The son of the teacher (*ācārya*). Service consists of attendance, performing household tasks according to one's ability, and massaging the body. A giver of knowledge is one who teaches some text unknown to the teacher—whether it concerns wealth, pleasure, the arts, or dharma—that has somehow been learned by the student. This teaching occurs through the formal regulation of learning (*vidyāviniyama*). One who is righteous (*dhārmika*) is primarily devoted to the performance of rites such as the *agnihotra*. One who is pure (*śuci*) is purified by earth and water, and is pure in his purpose. The three terms "righteous," "pure," and "virtuous" (*sādhu*) are a tautology, like the expression "cattle and oxen. A trusted person (*āpta*) is a close friend, relative, or the like. One who is capable (*śakta*) is competent in grasping and retaining [the material]. A giver of wealth (*arthada*). One's own son who has been initiated (*upanīta*). The former [categories] refers to those who may be taught even if they have been initiated by another.

But is it not said that this is the *dharmatā* (the nature of things), such that by being taught these [sciences], one becomes a *dharma*? And since the teacher benefits [the pupil] through what is seen, why then is there an assumption of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*)? Who has said that it is an "assumption"? What is the assumption regarding what is heard? For it is heard directly that by teaching these ten, one becomes a *dharma*. But the Teacher says: "The established rule of the *Dharmaśāstra* is being stated. By being taught these, there is no transgression of *dharma*; however, when one who bestows wealth is taught, there is no *dharma* characterized by the giving of knowledge. (2.109)
One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks in an improper manner;
for even though he knows, a wise man should behave like one who is dull-witted in this world. (2.110)

If a syllable has been lost or recited out of tune by one who is studying but not yet a formal disciple (*anupasanna*), then, unless asked, he should not say: "This was lost by you; it should be recited thus. However, it must be told even to a disciple who does not ask. Even if he asks, it should still not be told if he asks improperly. Asking with humility—saying, "I have a doubt regarding this matter; you should instruct me"—is a question in accordance with the proper conduct of a disciple. Otherwise, even though he knows, he should behave in the world like one who is dull-witted or mute; he should act like one ignorant and remain silent.

This prohibition against removing doubts without being asked pertains to the subject matter of the treatise (*śāstra*). In legal practice (*vyavahāra*), however, he will say: "Whether appointed or unappointed, one who knows the law (*dharmajña*) ought to speak. Others, however, maintain that this applies without distinction. (2.110)
He who speaks according to what is not the Dharma, and he who asks according to what is not the Dharma—one of these two perishes or incurs enmity. (2.111)

He states the fault incurred by violating this prohibition: "If one who is questioned improperly or asked in an unjust manner says, 'This was taught for the purpose of study,' and he who asks it—both of them die before their time. Or, if one of them is the transgressor, he alone dies. If one does not speak when questioned improperly, then the questioner alone dies; but if he does speak in reply, then both die. By showing the fault in questioning improperly through this [verse], the proper method of questioning is established for the questioner; otherwise, he incurs hatred or becomes an object of hatred in the world. (2.111)
Where neither dharma nor wealth exist, nor even a corresponding desire to serve, there knowledge should not be sown, just as a fertile seed is not sown in saline soil. (2.112)

What was stated in the verse, “Ten persons should be taught according to the law” (MDh 2.109), is a brief restatement of that very point by way of another method, not a statement of a new subject, because it is a reference back to what has been previously introduced. The word *artha* should be understood as indicating mere benefit (*upakāra*), since teaching through the exchange of knowledge was already mentioned previously. Such [benefit] is appropriate for the act of teaching: great for a great [person], and small for a small one. In this context, *vidyā* (knowledge) is so called because by means of it every object (*artha*) is known; thus, *vidyā* consists of both the recitation of the text and the comprehension of its meaning. One who provides no benefit should not be taught, nor should an exposition of the meaning be made for him.

A saline plot of land is called *ūṣara*, in which, despite being entirely intact, a seed does not sprout due to defects in the soil. Excellent and superior grain, such as rice and the like, is sown with plows and other implements. In this same way, knowledge, when sown in a [suitable] field, yields great fruit. And it should not be thought that teaching for the sake of taking wealth constitutes wages (*bhṛti*). For in that case, there is no engagement preceded by a negotiation regarding the measure of the fee, such as: "If you give me this much, then I will teach you this. This is the nature of wages. It is not, however, [considered such] merely by the slightest scent of a benefit in the form of wealth.

As for the statement that one should not previously provide any service to the teacher, this is not a prohibition against prior assistance; rather, it means that when one is about to perform the ritual bath (snāna), having been so commanded, one must accomplish the teacher’s purpose to the best of one's ability. This prohibition is merely a supplement to that [injunction], not an independent sentence. [2.112]
A knower of Brahman should, if necessary, die together with his knowledge;
even in the midst of terrible calamity, he must never sow it in barren soil.

The word *sama* means "together with. It is fitting for a proponent of Brahman (*brahmavādin*), a student of the Vedas, to die while his own body is worn out by [the practice] that has not been imparted; it is not, however, [fitting] to impart it to an unworthy recipient.

By this it is known that teaching must necessarily be performed by one who has studied the Veda, not merely for the sake of livelihood; nor is its entitlement restricted solely to one desiring a specific fruit, as is the case with the giving of water and other gifts. Thus says the Śruti: "He who, having studied the knowledge, does not speak to one who seeks it, would be a destroyer of his duty; he should open the door to the highest good. One should teach; this is a great source of glory, which the seers call the supreme authority of speech. Upon this yoga all this is established; those who know thus become immortal. By the phrase "he would be a destroyer of his duty," the Śruti itself—by reiterating the fault in not teaching—makes known the necessity of performing it.

*Īriṇe*: where the three aforementioned purposes are absent. For even in a terrible and painful calamity—where "painful" refers to the absence of the disciples mentioned—this [obligation] holds true provided that it is something which must necessarily be performed. For if it were a compulsory (*nitya*) duty, then in the absence of the primary [disciple], the cessation of teaching would follow through the adoption of a substitute disciple, just as [the performance of a sacrifice continues] with *nīvāra* grass in the absence of *vrīhi* rice. Therefore, in this state, there is simply a cessation of the qualification for teaching, just as the honoring of guests ceases when there is no guest possessing the aforementioned characteristics. By the term "should sow," teaching is expressed metaphorically through the nature of a seed; for a seed sown in a field indeed yields abundant fruit, and knowledge is likewise.

Others, however, explain that this refers to a calamity caused by the lack of wealth: even for one who is utterly destitute, it is better to die than to sow in barren soil. [They argue that] even when such a means of livelihood exists—namely, teaching—one does not transgress the injunction: "One should protect oneself from everything" (GDh 9.34). This is incorrect; for the word *iriṇa* (barren soil) is a restatement of what was previously mentioned, and thus the giver of wealth is certainly not a barren soil. Furthermore, if he is not even a giver of wealth, how could his engagement in that activity during a time of distress be possible, such that it would need to be prohibited? (2.113)
Knowledge approached a Brahmin and said: "I am your treasure; protect me.
Do not give me to one who is envious, so that I may remain most powerful. (2.114)

This too is merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). Knowledge, having assumed a corporeal form, approached a certain teacher and said: "I am your treasure (*śevadhi*); protect me. [The teacher asked: "What is your protection? [Knowledge replied: "Do not give me to one who is envious, one who reviles, or one who censures; do not teach me to a censor. In this way, I shall become most powerful for you, performing your task with excellence. *Vīrya* refers to an extraordinary capacity for the accomplishment of a task. As for the reading "śevadhiṣṭe 'smi," where the substitution of *ṣ* has been applied, it is an imitation of a Vedic usage. (2.114)
But speak to that Brahmin alone whom you know to be pure, self-restrained, and a celibate student—a guardian of the treasure who is ever vigilant. 2.115

"To whatever disciple you may know to be pure, self-controlled, intent on effort, and a celibate practitioner—to him speak me. For he who guards and protects a treasure is one who, being vigilant, does not become negligent nor stumble, because of his devotion to that [task]. From this explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), it is understood that [this teaching] is to be given to all disciples who possess these qualities, such as those who are capable and who bestow the goal they have attained. (2.115)
He who acquires the Veda from one who is reciting it without permission is guilty of stealing the Veda and falls into hell. (2.116)

When one who is studying for the sake of practice explains the Veda to another person, and while he is thus teaching, someone else approaches him and acquires that Veda—which is as if it were new—or dispels his doubts, this fault is said to belong to that [second person]. Until permission is granted—[the student saying], "Just as these people are studying from you, so may I also study; please deign to grant me permission"—he should not learn. Otherwise, that study of the Veda is like theft. That student, being joined with this Veda-thief, reaches hell, which is a place of great torment.

The ablative case in *adhīyānāt* is used according to Pāṇini 1.4.29, *ākhyātopayoge* ("in the sense of acquisition from a teacher"). Alternatively, because a departure (*apāya*) is implied, it is as if the Brahman departs from the student; or, with the elision of the suffix *-lyap*, it refers to the object: having heard [the teaching] from one who is studying, he acquires it, that is, he learns it. || 2.116 ||
Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge, one should first pay homage to the person from whom that knowledge was received. 2.117
The incidental discussion has been concluded; the procedure for salutation is now commenced.

"Lokika" (worldly) refers to worldly existence, the training in worldly conduct, or alternatively, knowledge of the arts of singing and instrumental music, or knowledge of the treatises on the subjects of the arts by Vātsyāyana and Viśākhila. "Vaidika" (Vedic) refers to that which is enjoined by rule, concerning the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the Smṛtis. "Ādhyātmika-vidyā" (spiritual science) is the science of the Upaniṣads regarding the Self (*ātman*). Or, by metaphorical application (*upacāra*), it may refer to the body. One should first salute that person who is the teacher from whom one learns this knowledge. At the first meeting, the act of addressing someone face-to-face with a word—used for the purpose of offering a blessing—in the form that will be described hereafter, is the meaning of the verb *abhivādayati*. "First" (*pūrva*) means initially. By this, he is to be addressed; one need not wait for his speech [in response], for at that time one would become the one returning the salutation (*pratyabhivādayitṛ*). If it is argued that the word "first" is redundant because the sense is already established by the verb *abhivādayet* alone—since, upon examining the meanings of the root and the prefix, one understands merely "speaking toward [someone]"—that is not so. For when this word is present, this specific meaning is obtained. Through the consideration of the root and prefix, one understands merely the act of speaking toward someone; this indeed occurs even when one has been addressed by another. As for those who explain the verse as "first [one should salute] one's own parents and teachers," that is to be disregarded, as it is irrelevant to the context. (2.117)

A Brahmin who is well-restrained is better, even if his essence consists only of the Sāvitrī mantra, than one who is unrestrained, even if he knows the three Vedas, eats all kinds of food, and sells all kinds of goods. (2.118)

This is a praise of the rules of conduct beginning with salutation. One whose essence and primary focus is the *Sāvitrī* alone is described as such; that is, one who studies only the *Sāvitrī*. A Brahmin is better and superior if he is well-restrained—that is, if his self is governed by the scriptures—even if he is unrestrained, even if he knows the three Vedas and the scriptures. A "glutton" (*sarvāśī*) eats everything, including what is censured by worldly custom, even if it is not explicitly forbidden. Likewise, a "seller of all things" (*sarvavikrayī*). The mention of eating and selling is for the purpose of illustration, implying other prohibited acts as well.

This is what is meant: just as one is censured for abandoning other established rules, so too is one censured for abandoning the practice of rising [to greet]. Now, as for the phrase "the Brahmin is better" (*varaḥ vipraḥ*), since it ought to be "the Brahmin is the better one" (*varo vipraḥ*), some say that because a specific term is mentioned following a general introduction, the meaning is: "this is better; what is that? That a Brahmin is well-restrained. Others, however, say that the word *vara* has an inherent gender (*āviṣṭaliṅga*) and exists even in the neuter gender. (2.118)
One should not occupy a bed or seat already used by a superior;
rather, while remaining on one's own bed or seat, one should rise to meet him and offer salutation. (2.119)

The compound *śayyā cāsanaṃ ca* ("bed and seat") is a singular dvandva according to Pāṇini 2.4.6, *jātir aprāṇinām*. One should not occupy that [place] with a superior (*śreyas*), such as one who is more learned or a teacher; that is, one should not sit together with them. Does this apply to every case? No, he says: provided it is "used" (*adhyācarite*), meaning prepared for the purpose of being a bed or a seat. However, there is no fault in the case of a stone slab or similar object. Furthermore, he will state later, "One should sit together with the teacher" (MDh 2.204), and this [present verse] is a restatement of that very point.

Others explain it as "frequented" or "inhabited. One should not enter there even at a later time, not merely because of the prohibition against sitting together; for that [prohibition] is already established by what will be stated later. Furthermore, when a prescriptive rule is possible, a mere restatement (anuvāda) is not appropriate.

In this regard, some explain the distinction based on customary practice (*ācāra*). That which is known to belong exclusively to the teacher by way of being his bed or his seat—where the teacher sleeps or sits—there the disciple should not sit, whether in the teacher's presence or out of sight. However, where these actions have somehow been performed by the teacher, there is no prohibition provided the teacher is not present. It is precisely such conduct that is called "customary practice" (*adhyācarita*), and not merely that which is occupied through the relationship of owner and property.

If a superior person approaches while one is seated on a bed or a seat, then one must rise from there and offer a salutation. As for the rule "one seated on a vehicle or a seat" (MDh 2.202), that refers to descending when directed by a guru; its meaning is that one who is on the ground must simply abandon the bed or seat. However, this rising to meet a superior who is not a guru is possible only for one who remains seated on a seat. 2.119.
For the vital breaths of a young man indeed ascend when an elder approaches;
he recovers them again by rising to meet him and by saluting him. 2.120.

This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) concerning the former [rule]. When an elder (*sthavira*), one of advanced age, approaches or arrives, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)—the causes of life, the internal winds—of the youth (*yuvan*), the young man, move upward from the mouth and exit externally. Having abandoned the function of the downward breath (*apāna*), they intend to effect the cessation of life. By the salutation performed upon rising to meet him, they become capable of securing the stability of life as before; he regains his state and returns to life. (2.120)
For one who is habitually respectful and constantly attends upon the elders, four things increase: life-span, virtue, fame, and strength. (2.121)

He is one who addresses everyone first and is habituated to greeting others as is appropriate; this does not mean merely the utterance of the word of greeting. By the word "habit" (*śīla*), the absence of regard for personal gain is expressed. He constantly attends upon his elders with pleasant speech and the like, and he gratifies them with service according to his ability. For him, four things increase: long life; dharma, which is the tree bearing fruits such as heaven in the hereafter; and fame and strength, as previously mentioned. This explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) also serves as a cause for understanding the rewards [of such conduct]. (2.121)
After the salutation, a Brahmin greeting one who is superior should announce his own name, saying, "I am so-and-so by name. (2.122)

When another person is addressed by the word *ayam* (this one), and is either invoked for a blessing or questioned regarding their welfare, that constitutes a salutation (*abhivāda*). Following this salutation—that is, immediately after the word expressing the salutation—one should utter the word *imam* (this one), saying: "I am so-and-so by name. Here, the pronoun *asau* (that one) indicates every particular [person]. This use of such words is for the purpose of making [the other person] face oneself, [meaning]: "You are being saluted by me; you are being made to face me for the sake of a blessing. Then, having understood the request, the other person begins to perform the return-salutation (*pratyabhivāda*), such as by bestowing a blessing.

Furthermore, when a pronoun denoting a general sense is employed, this is not what is expressed: "By me, with this name, you are being saluted. Therefore, failing to understand the request for instruction, toward whom would one direct a blessing? Moreover, it is heard [in the scriptures] that "one should proclaim one's own name. In that case, when someone says, "I am Devadatta by name," the salutation is understood. Otherwise, because of the lack of purpose for the word *asau* (that one), there would be no determination of its meaning.

The authors of Sūtras also employ conventions according to other Smṛtis. For example, Pāṇini uses terms such as *dvitīyā* in the rule: “*karmaṇi dvitīyā*” (Pāṇ. 2.3.2). Here too, [the word] *asau* is used. It is also stipulated in the *Yajñasūtra*: “One should transfer one’s own name. If this is so, since the matter is already established by the phrase “one’s own name,” the addition of “this name” (*asau nāma*) would be redundant. It is for the purpose of employing the word *nāma*. How? [It is used in the formula]: “One should proclaim one’s own name: ‘I am named so-and-so. By means of this form, one indicates: “I am this person. Because they have the same meaning, authorities consider them to be optional alternatives.

In these two verses [354], the form of the salutation formula is established as follows: "I salute you, O sir, I who am named Devadatta. By the subsequent verse, the word "O sir" (bhoḥ) will be prescribed. Because of the mention of "one who is superior," there is also salutation for those who are equal or inferior; however, this specific manner is not applicable to them, because it pertains specifically to one who is superior. 2.122.
To those who do not understand the meaning of his name, a wise man should say "I am he," and the same applies to all women. (2.123)

This [rule] is intended to preclude the salutation of those who, despite being superior in wealth and other such matters, might otherwise be saluted according to rule even though they are ignorant. Whatever ignorant persons do not understand the salutation—that is, the formal utterance of a name for the purpose of greeting—because they are unacquainted with grammar (*avaidya-vyākaraṇa*) and do not comprehend the refined language (*saṃskṛta*), a wise man should salute them as well as women. These people do not grasp the refined language when it is spoken; in that case, omitting the specific portion of the rule regarding the mention of one's own name, he should say only this much: "I salute you" (*abhivādaye 'ham*). If they still do not understand even that, they should be saluted even in common, vernacular speech (*apabhraṃśa*); it is for this reason that the term "wise man" (*prājña*) is used. Having recognized their lack of comprehension, the wise man should adapt his mode of greeting rather than adhering strictly to the formal instruction. Women are to be treated in exactly the same way. The inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) implies that this applies even to the wives of teachers (*guru-patnī*) who are proficient in the use of refined language.

Others, however, explain that one who is well-known by a nickname, such as Vanamālīvarṇa, does not have his father-given name well-known; since that which is well-known is not [his formal] name, he should announce his own name. Others, moreover, describe those who do not know how to respond to a greeting (*pratyabhivāda*). According to the rule *pratyabhivāde ’śūdre* (Pāṇini 8.2.83), a protracted vowel (*pluta*) is prescribed at the end of the name. To those who do not know this, one should simply say "I am [so-and-so]. This was demonstrated by the author of the Mahābhāṣya in the context of presenting the purposes of grammar (*vyākaraṇaprayojana*).
"Those who are ignorant and do not know the protracted [pronunciation] of the name in returning a greeting—
among them, however, one may, after returning from a journey, speak as one would to women, according to one's desire.
On account of the force of other *smṛti* texts, they say that this word "greeting" (*abhivāda*) actually refers here to the "returning of a greeting" (*pratyabhivāda*).

If this were not explained in this way, then the statement "he is not to be saluted by a learned man" would be taken as a total prohibition of salutation in every respect; in that case, it would contradict another Smṛti text which says, "I shall say, 'This am I'. However, when it is explained in this manner, that prohibition is understood as being based on praise rather than as an injunction, since it is interpreted in accordance with this specific purpose. (2.123)
In greeting, one should utter the word "bhoḥ" at the end of one's own name;
for the sages have declared that the nature of the word "bhoḥ" is the very essence of names. (2.124)

One should utter the word *bhoḥ* at the end of one's own name. The inclusion of the word "one's own" (*sva*) is for the purpose of excluding the name of the person being saluted. The remainder is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). It is not only at the end of the syllables of the name, but rather after those [syllables], with the words "I am. For here, the particle *iti* is used to restrict the application; it must be employed in this very manner. Furthermore, in an ill-taught usage such as "Devadatta, O, I," because the comprehension is delayed, the presence [of the speaker] would occur only after a long time, which would obstruct the performance of the task. In a case where the connection is interrupted by a delay, someone might simply fail to pay attention.

*Svarūpabhāvaḥ* means the existence (*sattā*) of its own form. Alternatively, it occurs in the place of the forms of those names that are to be addressed; therefore, there is the cessation of their specific names. The word *bhāva* may function as either an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*) or an agentive noun (*kartṛsādhana*). Or, the term *svarūpabhāve* should be read with a locative ending. Regarding *bho-bhāva*: the becoming (*bhavana*) or the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the word *bhoḥ* is the essential nature of those names. Just as someone is addressed by taking up a name, such as "Devadatta, listen!", so too the word *bhoḥ*, ending in the vocative case, is remembered by the sages as being used for the very purpose of addressing. (2.124)
When greeting a Brahmin, one should say, "May you be long-lived, O gentle one.
Furthermore, at the end of his name, the vowel *a* should be pronounced with the preceding syllable as a protracted (*pluta*) vowel.

When a salutation has been performed, the one who returns the salutation—the father, in this case—should be addressed with the words, "May you be long-lived, O gentle one" (*āyuṣmān bhava saumya*). The particle *iti* indicates a manner; it serves to include such expressions as "May you be long-lived," "May you have a long life," "May you live for a long time," and so forth, which are well-established in the traditional conduct of the learned.

The vowel *a* at the end of the name of the person being greeted in return must be pronounced as a *pluta* (protracted). "Pluta" is the technical term for a vowel of three morae (*mātrā*). The mention of the letter *a* is intended to indicate vowels such as *i* and others as well. Furthermore, "being at the end" should be understood in relation to the preceding vowel (*ac*). Thus, even for a name ending in a consonant, it applies to the final vowel. This is a qualification of the vowel *a* that is about to become protracted, specifically referring to the preceding syllable. Here, "syllable" (*akṣara*) refers to a consonant; thus, the vowel joined with the preceding [consonant] is so described. What is meant is this: the vowel *a* that is not adventitious (i.e., not added) should be made protracted; rather, only that very vowel which already exists within the name itself should be lengthened.

All this explanation is based on the authority of the venerable Pāṇini’s traditional teaching (*smṛti*). Regarding the application of words and their meanings, the venerable Pāṇini possesses a greater degree of authoritative validity than Manu and others. Thus, in the rule *pratyabhivāde ’śūdre* (Pāṇini 8.2.83), he prescribes the protracted vowel (*pluti*) for the final syllable (*ṭi*). By the term *ṭi*, that which begins with the final vowel is denoted.

The mention of the *vipra* (Brahmin) is not intended to be restrictive; this same rule applies to Kṣatriyas and others as well, for the practice according to other Smṛtis is established in this very way, and there is no other rule for them. An example here is: "āyuṣmān devadatta3. For one ending in a consonant: "āyuṣmān edhi somaśarman3. (2.125)
A Brahmin who does not know how to return a greeting is not to be greeted by a learned man; he is just like a Śūdra. (2.126)

The statement that "one who does not know how to return a greeting should be addressed thus" is redundant regarding the greeting itself; it does not cohere [with the context]. It is not so. The construction should be understood as: "the return greeting should correspond to the greeting. For one who performs a greeting by uttering their own name, a protracted vowel (*pluti*) must be applied at the end of that name. However, for one who greets saying simply "I, sir" (*ahaṃ bho*), there is neither the utterance of a name nor the protracted vowel.

The phrase "not to be saluted" is a prohibition against the utterance of the words of salutation. Salutation must be performed according to the prescribed rule; one should not say "I, O sir," and so forth, because that has already been shown previously. This very point is understood from the example "as in the case of a Śūdra. For even a Śūdra who is advanced in age is intended to be saluted and addressed first. The word "viduṣā" (by the learned man) is for the purpose of completing the meter. 2.126.
Upon meeting a Brāhmaṇa, one should ask about his welfare; a Kṣatriya, about his freedom from illness; a Vaiśya, about his prosperity; and a Śūdra, about his health. 2.127.

When a greeting has been offered and returned, and a friendly rapport has been established, this restriction of words based on the distinction of caste is intended for a question arising from a desire to know. This restriction of caste applies to those who are to be questioned, not to the questioners themselves. Furthermore, because these terms do not have entirely different meanings, this rule of their specific form is prescribed. The words *ārogya* (health) and *anāmaya* (freedom from disease) have the same meaning; likewise, the words *kṣema* (security) and *kuśala* (well-being) are not absolutely distinct. Although the word *kuśala* denotes proficiency, it is used here in the sense of the non-departure of things associated with [the self], such as the body. These must necessarily be employed. There is no prohibition against using others as well, according to one's intuition and with a desire to know the specific details, as is shown in a certain chapter of the *Mahābhārata*.

Some argue that because of the expression "having come together here," this question does not concern elders and the like, but rather concerns only those of equal age; for approaching an elder is prescribed by rule, whereas coming together by chance is not. However, since there is indeed a "coming together" even in the act of formal "approaching," this argument is trivial. (2.127)
One who knows the Dharma should address an initiated person by name only if he is younger; otherwise, he should address him using the honorifics "bhoḥ" or "bhavat" placed before his name. (2.128)

At the time of returning a greeting, and on other occasions, one who is initiated (*dīkṣita*) in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices—from the initiation rite (*dīkṣaṇīyā*) until the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*)—must not be addressed by name; his personal name must not be uttered. By the word "even" (*api*), it is inferred that there is a prohibition against mentioning the name of an elder (*jyeṣṭha*) who has not been initiated. Thus says Gautama: "One should mention the name and lineage of a teacher preceded by [a term of] respect" (GDh 2.23). "Māna" means honor; the name should be taken preceded by that: for example, "The Lord Janārdana Miśra."

How, then, should one who has been initiated (dīkṣita) conduct conversation for the sake of business? [It should be] preceded by "bhoḥ" and "bhavat. Having employed the word "bhoḥ" first, one should address this initiated person using derivative terms such as "initiated" (dīkṣita) or "sacrificer" (yajamāna). However, the mention of his name preceded by the word "bhoḥ" is not permitted.

Regarding the statement that the word *bhoḥ* or *bhavat* precedes the address, when this is said, they explain the rule because these two words cannot be used together in a single sentence. When one is engaged in conversation with him, he should be addressed using the vocative case ending with the word *bhoḥ*. However, when one describes his qualities in his absence, one should employ the forms: "Thus was done by His Honor the Dīkṣita," or "His Honor does thus. Furthermore, since only the nominal stem *bhavat* is mentioned, it should be used ending in whatever case-ending it may take. (2.128)
But toward a woman who is the wife of another and not related by birth, he should address her as "Madam," "O blessed one," or "Sister. (2.129)

When conversation with a woman occurs for a specific purpose, it should be conducted in this manner: a woman who is another's wife should be addressed as "Lady" (*bhavati subhage*) or "Sister" (*bhavati bhagini*). This word *bhavat* ends in a feminine suffix and has its vowel shortened in the vocative case. In the phrase *bhavatīti*, the particle *iti* indicates that the actual form of the word—characterized by the reversal of its constituent parts—is intended to convey the meaning to the other person; thus, in the cases of "Lady" and "Sister," it refers to the specific forms of those words. Since the context concerns speaking, it is established that the actual phonetic form of the words is what is being prescribed. Furthermore, in the case of a teacher, she should be addressed with such terms as "Mother," "Illustrious One" (*yaśasvinī*), or "Long-lived One" (*āyuṣmatī*) when she is younger than one’s daughter. Because the text specifies "wife," this rule does not apply to an unmarried girl. Nor does it apply to a woman unrelated by birth—that is, one who has not attained kinship through either the maternal or paternal line, such as the daughter of a maternal uncle and so forth; for regarding them, he will state a different rule: "Women related by blood or marriage... (MDh 2.132).

But surely that very point has already been established; since this general rule finds its application elsewhere, what is the use of the phrase "and what is unrelated"? One need not strive to point out such redundancy here, for this is a work composed in verse. (2.129)
Upon rising to greet maternal uncles, paternal uncles, fathers-in-law, officiating priests, and teachers who are younger than himself, he should say, "I am so-and-so. (2.130)

Because of the plural designation in the word *gurūn*, it is not only the specific teacher mentioned here who is intended; rather, like the term in Gautama’s Dharma-sūtra (GDh 6.20), it is a general term referring to those superior in wealth and so forth. One should address them—those younger than oneself, such as a sister's son (*bhāgineya*)—who are of lower age relative to one's own years, by announcing one's own name with the formula, "I am so-and-so. The use of the word *aham* ("I") for that purpose is permitted. This should be done when they have arrived and one has risen to meet them. In the act of salutation, however, the use of the word *bhoḥ* is forbidden. And it is stated in Gautama’s work: "Those who have risen [to meet one] are to be saluted. (2.130)
A mother’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, a mother-in-law, and a father’s sister are to be honored like the wife of one’s guru; they are equal to the wife of a guru. (2.131)

And these women are to be honored like the wife of one’s guru by rising to meet them, saluting them, offering them a seat, and so forth. Although this is already established by the phrase "like the wife of the guru," the specific mention of the word "equal" (*samāḥ*) permits that other duties toward the guru’s wife—such as obeying her commands and the like—may also occasionally be performed. Otherwise, because of the context, the term "to be honored" would refer only to the matter of salutation. Furthermore, women of advanced age are prescribed [as objects of respect] in the Smṛtis; for even those who are younger, this same rule for salutation applies. (2.131)
The wife of one's brother of the same caste may be saluted every day;
however, upon returning from a journey, the wives of kinsmen and relatives must be saluted. (2.132)

The phrase "of the elder brother" is to be understood [as applying here]. "To be clasped by the feet" means to be saluted by touching the feet. "Of the same caste" (savarṇā) means belonging to the same social class. However, for women of the Kṣatriya and other castes, the duty regarding female relatives and connections applies even to the wives of one's brothers. Regarding "female relatives and connections after returning from travel": "after returning from travel" means having returned from a journey abroad; for it is not possible for one who is away on a journey to perform the clasping of feet. "Relatives" (jñātayaḥ) are those on the father’s side, such as paternal uncles and so forth; "connections" (saṃbandhinaḥ) are those on the mother’s side, such as fathers-in-law and so forth. It refers to the women of those who are elders among them. Since the clasping of feet is a form of honor, those who are younger do not deserve such honor. (2.132)
Toward his father’s sister and toward his mother’s elder sister, he should maintain the same conduct as toward his mother; yet the mother is more venerable than they. (2.133)

Regarding the sister of one's father and the sister of one's mother, as well as toward one's own elder sister, the same conduct prescribed for a mother is extended by analogy. Now, an objection may be raised: has this duty not already been stated for the mother’s sister and the father’s sister in the verse, "The mother’s sister, the maternal uncle’s wife... (MDh 2.131)? To this it is replied: in that case, it was said "as toward the wife of a guru"; here, however, it is said "the conduct is like that toward a mother. This is not a distinction; for the conduct toward the wife of a guru and toward a mother is indeed equal.

Some say that the statement, "the mother is more venerable than they," is reiterated in order to express the greater venerability of the father over both sisters and the mother; for when the mother gives an order and the sisters and others do not, then the mother's command is to be carried out, not theirs. Nor should it be argued that this [point] is already established by the text, "The mother excels in venerability" (MDh 2.145), because that [passage] is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

Others, however, maintain that there is a difference in conduct toward the wife of one's guru and toward one's mother. For the wife of the guru, the previous injunctions and so forth are mandatory; for the mother, however, because of her affection due to childhood, there may even be a different treatment [of respect]. Regarding the maternal aunt and the paternal aunt, the rule is established based on both [the general principle and the specific exception]: in childhood, the fondling is exactly the same as for one’s own sister; but for one whose childhood has passed, they are to be honored like the wife of the guru. Nor is this point established by the present verse alone; for if there were not two distinct statements, then by the mere phrase "conduct as toward a mother," only the cessation of the salutation (which is the subject of the context) would be understood. (2.133)
Furthermore, the application of the principle of affection is extended as follows:

[366] Friendship among citizens is based on a ten-year difference in age; for those who possess the arts, it is based on a five-year difference; for Vedic scholars, it is based on a three-year difference; and among those of the same lineage, it exists even with a very small difference in age. 2.134.

It was stated previously: "For the vital breaths depart from a youth when old age approaches" (MDh 2.120). In that regard, after how many years does one become old? For in common worldly usage, the designation "old man" is applied upon the graying of the hair; this [verse] is intended to define that.

Friendship with fellow citizens is said to exist even when there is a difference of ten years from birth. Therefore, one who is more than ten years older becomes an elder (*jyeṣṭha*), yet he should be treated like a friend. As it is said: "O sir" or "friend. One is an elder after ten years. *Ākhyā* means "designation. It refers to a friendship for which ten years constitute the designation. This is a three-word *bahuvrīhi* compound. There is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "years" and "friendship" because the years serve as the cause for that designation; this is because the distinction between the cause and the effect is not intended to be emphasized here. Such is the meaning contained within the compound: one who is born earlier remains merely a friend until [the lapse of] ten years.

The "citizens" (paurāḥ) are those belonging to the city; the mention of the "city" is for the sake of illustration, as this same rule applies even to village-dwellers. Whosoever reside in a single village, provided there exists some cause for mutual proximity between them, they are friends (*sakhāyaḥ*).

However, among those who possess some craft such as sculpture, singing, or instrumental music, he who is more than five years senior is a friend; beyond that, he is a superior (*jyeṣṭhaḥ*). Among those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyāṇām*), friendship lasts for three years.

Even by a short period of time, among those of one's own birth and of the same lineage, he who is senior for even a few days is the elder (*jyeṣṭha*). But how much is this "short period"? It is not a year; for having specified "prior by three years," what is described as "by a short [time]" is understood to be less than that. Furthermore, because of the use of the singular number, it is not two years, nor is it a single year, since the qualification "by a short [time]" would be inappropriate [if it were a full year]. For the object denoted by the word "year" has a determined measure, and that which is deficient by even a single day and night does not possess the status of a "year. Therefore, the term "by a short [time]" refers to time in general. And its specific distinction is that it is less than a year. Moreover, the word *api* (even) should be understood in the sense of *eva* (only/just). Friendship [is established] by a short time alone, whereas seniority exists only through a long time. And this should be understood to apply to those of equal qualities and of the same caste. By this, the worldly definition of "elderly"—which is relative and dependent on others—is set aside.

Others, however, explain it thus: "By this, seniority (*sthaviratva*) is not indicated; rather, it is friendship (*sakhitva*) alone. If one were to abandon what was heard [in the scriptures], there would be a definition of seniority such as: 'Up to this time one is a friend, but beyond that, one is an elder'. And this is the meaning of the verse: those who dwell in the same city for ten years are friends. The sixty-four arts are acquired through association with those who know them over five years. Furthermore, among those living together even for a short time in their own birthplace, there is only friendship. Therefore, everyone is a companion (*vayasya*) by virtue of age; what else could it be? And this is the defining characteristic when there is equality of age.

This is correct; however, it contradicts the following verse. For in that [verse], the priority belongs to the caste (*jāti*), not to age (*vayas*). And if seniority were said to be determined by this much time, then even the potential seniority of those of different castes would not be precluded—this is logical. Furthermore, the earlier commentators accept only the first interpretation. (2.134)
One should recognize a ten-year-old Brahmin and a hundred-year-old king as father and son; yet, of the two, the Brahmin is the father.

One who has been born for ten years is "ten-year-old," which refers to the time that delimits him; the Brāhmaṇa delimited by that time is what is meant by "learned" (śruta). Neither his high or low status, nor his emaciation and so forth, can be measured by time; rather, it is some action of his [that serves as the mark]. And that [action] is the very act of sustaining life, which is eternally inherent from birth onwards. Thus, regarding the phrase "one hundred years": these two, father and son, are to be understood. When these two are compared, the Brāhmaṇa is the father.
