The meaning of the section is that even a Kṣatriya who is long-advanced in age must rise and salute a Brāhmaṇa, however few his years may be. 2.135.
Wealth, kinship, age, ritual action, and learning as the fifth—these are the grounds for respect; each subsequent one is weightier than the preceding. (2.136)

The superiority of birth as a cause for honor has been stated: one of superior birth is to be honored by one of inferior birth. Now, the relative strength and weakness of those factors—such as salutation—that serve as causes for honoring among those of equal birth are being discussed. In this context, age is mentioned again for the sake of determining its relative strength and weakness. Here, connection with wealth and so forth is everywhere a cause for honor; namely, the possession of wealth, the possession of kinsmen, and the status of being an object of respect. This is the meaning here: it is not merely the distinction of kinship—such as being a paternal uncle or maternal uncle—that is the cause of respect; rather, one who possesses many kinsmen is respected as "one honored by his kin. It should be understood that age is "excellent" [only] in such a sense. And it is generally in this very sense that this term is employed.
"A son, even when he has reached maturity, must always be instructed by his father.

And as long as age remains a cause for honor, it has already been stated: "that which is called ten years" (MDh 2.134). Ritual action (*karman*) refers to the performance of *śrauta* and *smārta* rites. Knowledge (*vidyā*) is the understanding of the meaning of the Vedas, together with their auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and their ancillaries (*upakaraṇa*).

[Objection: But surely it is said, "The learned man sacrifices; the learned man officiates at a sacrifice. Since one who lacks knowledge has no entitlement to perform ritual actions, how can rituals be a cause for merit (*māna*) without knowledge? [Reply: This is not a fault. What is intended here is excellence (*apakarṣa*). Knowledge that possesses excellence is the cause of merit. Even for one with very little knowledge, the performance of rites is possible. To whatever extent one knows, to that extent one is entitled. The status of knowledge as a cause for entitlement is not based on a scriptural injunction (*vācanika*), but rather is characterized by capability (*sāmarthya*). For how could an ignorant person, who does not know the nature of the ritual and whose conduct is like that of an animal, be entitled [to perform it]? Indeed, such a person might be able to perform recitation (*japa*) and austerity (*tapas*) after hearing a few sentences from the *Smṛtis*. However, for rituals such as the *Agnihotra*, understanding the Vedic sentences is helpful. Even there, to whatever extent one knows, to that extent one is entitled. He who understands the meaning of the *Agnihotra* passages is entitled to that [rite]; knowledge of other sacrifices (*kratu*) is not helpful in that regard.

Now it is said: "The entire Veda is to be mastered" (MDh 2.165). This injunction regarding the whole Veda extends up to its full comprehension. In that case, since the comprehension of the entire Veda is required, how can there be this possibility of understanding only a portion, such that it is said: "He who knows the meaning of the *agnihotra* passage, even if he does not know the meaning of other passages, is qualified [to perform the rite]"? To this it is replied: First of all, the study of at least one recensional branch (*śākhā*) must necessarily be performed. In that regard, he by whom one branch has been studied and its meaning determined is qualified [for the rite], even though the meaning of other branches has not been determined.

But surely, the meaning of the scripture is one and the same everywhere; even if there is a difference in the sequence of words and syllables, the nature of the scripture itself remains undivided. Furthermore, comprehension arises through the mastery of word-meanings and logical principles (*nyāya*). Neither word-meanings nor logical principles differ from branch to branch. Therefore, by whatever reason the meaning of one branch is determined, that same reason applies to another branch as well; it does not require a different method of mastery. Thus, if one branch is understood, all branches are indeed understood.

True. There should be no difference between those rites such as the *agnihotra* that are taught in one [branch of the Veda] (*śākhā*) and those being taught in another branch. However, certain rites are not taught at all in some branches. For example, in the *Āśvalāyana-śākhā* of the Rigveda (*bāhvṛca*), the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the sorcery rites such as the *śyena*, and others like the *somayāga*, *vājapeya*, and *bṛhaspatisava* are not mentioned. In that case, one is qualified for those rites such as the *agnihotra* and *jyotiṣṭoma* which depend on that particular branch. But how could a student of that branch know the rites prescribed in another branch, since that branch has not been studied or heard? Nor are these *somayāgas* obligatory (*nitya*), such that one would seek out another branch to understand them out of fear of the sin (*pratyavāya*) incurred by non-performance. As for the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), even though it is not recited there, there is the injunction regarding the *āhavanīya* fire: "Bring forth the *āhavanīya*" (*uddharāhavanīyam*). Not understanding its purpose from common worldly usage, one asks, "What is this *āhavanīya* for whose consecration [is required]? and thus seeks out another branch. Then, one thoroughly examines the entire section on the consecration (*ādhānaprakaraṇa*) as it is read in that other branch. Similarly, having heard the scriptural statement, "Having sacrificed with the *āmāvāsya* oblation or the *paurṇamāsa*," one likewise searches for another branch to determine what the form of these two rites is. In the same way, regarding any other optional (*kāmya*) or obligatory (*nitya*) rite to be performed, if any collection of subsidiaries (*aṅgajāta*)—whether pertaining to the Adhvaryu or the Udgātṛ—is not mentioned therein, one seeks out another branch to fully understand it. However, there is no possibility of knowing a rite to be performed that is taught in a different branch [if one only knows one's own]. But for one who studies many branches and is intent on their meaning, all of this is directly perceived. Thus, the performance of rites is possible even without such specialized knowledge; or rather, performance is possible even with only a slight proficiency.

But for one whose knowledge is stainless and whose fields of knowledge are to be explained, that knowledge is a ground for veneration. The suffix *īyasun* in the word *garīyaḥ* is used here to express a comparative degree between two things. One who knows the fourteen fields of knowledge is honored by virtue of that knowledge alone, even if they are otherwise disqualified due to being lame, blind, destitute, or the like.

Regarding their conflict, he states the relative strength and weakness: "Whatever is subsequent is more weighty. If one person possesses wealth and another has many kinsmen, the one with kinsmen is to be honored over the one with wealth; for that which is subsequent is more important than that which precedes it. Likewise, the age of a kinsman is more significant than the aforementioned wealth; this is established as being superior even to that. Therefore, Gautama’s statement is justified: "But sacred learning is more important than all [the others], because it is the root of dharma" (GDh 6.21–22).

Regarding the word *garīyaḥ*: how can there be a suffix expressing excellence (*prakarṣa*) when the preceding [element] lacks heaviness? For if two things are heavy, then the upper garment (*uttarīya*) possesses a greater heaviness; however, in that case, there is no such thing relative to the preceding one in the case of wealth (*vitta*). If this is argued, [the answer is: when heaviness is intended in general with respect to the aggregate, it is appropriate to use the suffix *-īyasun* when one wishes to express the excellence of the other. *Mānaḥ* means honor; its *sthāna* is the cause. Or, in the reading *mānyasthānāni*, it should be understood as containing an implied abstract sense (*bhāvārtha*). Thus, *mānyatvasthānāni* means the causes of being honored. (2.136)

It has been stated that superiority belongs to the later [caste] when there is a connection with each single quality individually. Now, however, where two earlier qualities belong to one person and a single later quality belongs to another, how is it determined? To this he says:

"Among the five [qualities], wherever three exist within the [three] castes, and they are both numerous and possessed of qualities—he is worthy of honor therein, even if he be a Śūdra who has reached the tenth stage. (2.137)

Among these five grounds for respect (*mānasthāna*), that one which possesses more, many, or numerous [grounds], but not all, is the one to be respected. In that case, the status of being "other" (*paratva*) should not be overly emphasized. For example, one person has wealth and kinsmen (two grounds), while another is advanced in age (one ground). Here, the former [grounds] are the subordinates. Even if they are numerous, if they are not superior, and if one person possesses a single, extremely excellent [ground], then there is equality; the status of being "other" does not constitute a subordination. This is because the greater [number] fulfills its purpose only in relation to the single [excellent ground]. However, if the [grounds] are numerous, virtuous, and extremely excellent, then even if there is equality in number with the others—such that the former and the latter are equal in count—there is no relationship of subordination and subordinator based on priority. Rather, there is simply equality.

But surely, since it is stated that "he who possesses qualities is worthy of honor" in this context, it would be more logical for the preceding rule—even if it has an equal number [of syllables]—to be the sublater. This is not so; for when the qualities are equal, this [present rule] achieves its purpose. Just as when one person is learned and another is also learned, the one whose learning is superior in quality is praised; so it is in all cases.

Regarding the three castes—the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya—if these qualities are more numerous and more excellent in a Kṣatriya, then even a Brāhmaṇa of inferior qualities, though superior by birth, must honor that Kṣatriya. Likewise, a Vaiśya is to be honored by a Kṣatriya. In this manner, even a Śūdra is to be honored by all three twice-born castes when he has reached the tenth stage. The "tenth stage" refers to the final state; it is an indication of extreme old age. Thus, wealth and kinship are not grounds for a Śūdra’s honor toward members of the three higher castes, because of the mention of the "tenth stage. However, ritual action and sacred knowledge are simply not possible for him, as he lacks the qualification for them.

The word *bhūyāṃsi* expresses mere excess (*ādhikyamātra*), not the specific number "many" (*bahutvasaṃkhyā*). By this, even the state of having two objects as the referent is established; for there is no evidence that this word *bahu* denotes number alone. Furthermore, this is the word *bhūyas*, not *bahu*, and its usage is seen in various places to signify excess. In the phrases "And here the rebuttal is more [extensive]" (*bhūyāṃś cātra parihāraḥ*) and "I shall be joined with greater success" (*bhūyasābhyudayena yokṣye*), even the plurality of the suffixal meaning (*pratyayārtha*) is not intended. For this plural form is used according to Pāṇini 1.2.58, *jātyākhyāyām*. If it were intended, a single person possessing excellence would not be the cause for the honor; consequently, the previously understood [rule] would be contradicted. Moreover, in the passage "A Śūdra also [is honored] at the tenth [year]," by stating that age alone in its excellence is the cause for honor, he demonstrates the lack of intention [to limit it to many]. And the traditional practice (*samācāra*) is exactly thus. (2.137)
Way must be yielded to one who holds a wheel, to one in his tenth decade of life, to the sick, to one burdened with a load, to a woman, to a *snātaka*, to a king, and to a bridegroom. (2.138)

This other mode of worship is stated as incidental: [one should give way to] a charioteer, a rider of a chariot, or one mounted on a vehicle such as a cart. His path should be yielded. That portion of ground by which a village or another region is reached is called a track or a path (*panthā*). If a charioteer should approach from behind or from the front, then the pedestrian should step aside from that part of the path which would obstruct his passage. A person in their tenth decade is one whose age is fully matured. A sick person is one excessively afflicted by disease. A burden-carrier is one who has taken up heavy goods such as grain; he too, being unable to pass [easily], is to be favored. A woman [is to be given way to] simply by virtue of her being female, regardless of her caste, qualities, or relationship to a husband. And by "king" (*rājā*) here, the lord of a realm is intended, not merely a member of the Kṣatriya caste. For it will be said later in the conclusion: "by the term *pārthiva*"; a *pārthiva* is the lord of the earth (*pṛthivyā īśvaraḥ*).

But surely, since the word *rājan* is heard at the beginning, it is appropriate that the word *pārthiva* occurring in another part of the sentence refers to that very same person; for the word *rājan* is known to denote the Kṣatriya caste. Since it appears at the beginning and its meaning has not yet been contradicted, it must be taken in its primary sense. However, in the passage concerning "power" (*bala*) and so forth, because the application of the word *pārthiva* is possible through the duty of protecting the earth—which is prescribed for the Kṣatriya caste and depends upon that [status]—it is improper to interpret it as referring to another caste.

To this it is replied: Respect is indeed heard of here, in the statement, "The *snātaka* is entitled to honor from the king. In that regard, the fact that the *snātaka* is to be honored by anyone belonging to the Kṣatriya caste is already established by the rule, "A ten-year-old Brāhmaṇa... (MDh 2.135). For it has been stated there that the word *bhūmipa* (lord of the earth) is intended as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the Kṣatriya caste in general. And because the royal caste is thus indicated, this duty is understood to apply even to a Kṣatriya who is a lord of subjects.

The groom has set out for the wedding; the way must be yielded to them. The meaning of "giving" (dadati) here is merely relinquishment, and relinquishment consists in moving away from the path. For this very reason, the dative case has not been employed. (2.138)
Among those gathered together, the Snātaka and the king are to be honored;
and between the royal Snātaka and the king, the Snātaka receives honor from the monarch.

Among those who have assembled and gathered together in one place, the *snātaka* and the king are to be honored by means of the aforementioned path of giving (*dāna*). The king is "one who receives honor from the king" (*nṛpamānabhāk*), meaning he partakes in or obtains honor from the presence of the king; this is an instance of the genitive case used for specification (*nirdhāraṇe*, Pāṇini 2.3.41). As for the chariot and the other items, however, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between them, and that depends upon one's capacity (*śakti*). (2.139)
But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the Kalpas and the secret doctrines (Upanishads), him they call an Ācārya. (2.140)

This [work] is commenced for the purpose of defining the meaning of words such as "ācārya" and others, for their usage in the world is figurative (sopacāra). Furthermore, this [meaning] has not been defined by the traditional authorities (smartṛ) such as the teacher Pāṇini and others regarding the relationship between word and meaning. And this traditional recollection (*smṛti*) of the meaning of the term "ācārya" is rooted in worldly usage (*vyavahāra*), not in the Veda, like the *smṛtis* of Pāṇini and others. For here no duty (*kartavya*) is enjoined; rather, the meaning is established in the form of a fact—namely, "this is the meaning of this word"—and is not something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Having brought [the student] near—that is, having performed the *upanayana*—he who teaches the Veda, causes it to be grasped, is the *ācārya*. Here, "grasping" (*grahaṇa*) means the memorization of the sequence of sentences independently of any other learner. The word "kalpa" is intended to indicate all the auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*). "Rahasya" refers to the *Upaniṣads*. Although these too are already included by the term "Veda," they nevertheless have a second designation, namely "Vedāntas. Considering that the word "anta" (end) signifies proximity, one might think, "These are not the Vedas. To dispel that doubt, the term "Rahasya" is employed.

Others, however, describe the secret meaning (*rahasya*) as the meaning of the Vedas (*vedārtha*). Therefore, the status of an *ācārya* is not accomplished by the mere grasping of the [Vedic] form itself, but rather through that accompanied by its exposition. Accordingly, it is stated in the *Abhidhānakośa*: "He who explains the meanings of the mantras is called an *ācārya*" (MBh 14. App. 4: 2528). The mention of "mantra" is intended to indicate Vedic sentences in general.

And according to this interpretation, the comprehension of the meaning would also be prompted by the injunction for making someone a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), not merely the recitation alone. Consequently, everyone would be compelled to perform the entire rule of Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*). Even if the performance is prompted by another, the student’s own purpose regarding the rule of Vedic study would still be accomplished. However, when the teacher does not proceed because the injunction for making someone a teacher is optional (*kāmya*), then the performance of the purpose of the rule of Vedic study would not occur. Thus, the rule of Vedic study would become a compulsory (*nitya*) one. Furthermore, the word *rahasya* is not well-known as denoting the meaning of the Vedas. Therefore, the purpose of including the term *rahasya* is indeed as previously stated. Or, it is mentioned separately because of its importance. As for the statement, “and he explains the meanings of the mantras,” this is simply a non-remembrance (*asmṛti*), since there is no evidence that the word *mantra* is intended as an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, the prompting force of this injunction is directed toward the recitation. Hence, once the student has acquired the form of the Veda, the injunction for making someone a teacher is fulfilled. (2.140)
But he who teaches a portion of the Veda, or even the Vedāṅgas, for the sake of his livelihood, is called an Upādhyāya. (2.141)

A portion of the Veda, whether it be the *mantra* or the *brāhmaṇa*, or even the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) alone excluding the Veda—whosoever teaches these, as well as the entire Veda, for the sake of livelihood or subsistence, and not by virtue of the injunction regarding the office of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), he is an *upādhyāya* (sub-teacher), not an *ācārya*. He who teaches the entire Veda to one who has been initiated (*upanīta*) by another is not an *ācārya*. Likewise, he who, though having initiated a student, does not teach him the entire Veda, is also not an *ācārya*.

If this is so, since the term "partial instruction" (*ekadeśagrahaṇa*) was used in the definition of an *upādhyāya*, while the term "initiation" (*upanayana*) was used in the definition of an *ācārya*, what then is the definition of one who does not initiate [a pupil] but teaches the entire Veda? He is neither an *ācārya* nor an *upādhyāya*. Nor is any other name for him heard in the scriptures. It is said: by the verse, "Of whatever sacred learning, whether little or much... (MDh 2.149), he is designated a *guru*; he is inferior to an *ācārya* and superior even to an *upādhyāya*. Furthermore, the two particles (*api... punaḥ*) are for the purpose of completing the meter. (2.141)
That Brahmin who performs the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony according to the rules, and supports [the child] with food, is called the Guru. (2.142)

This instruction regarding the status of the father as a guru is based on the act of *niṣeka*. *Niṣeka* means the emission of semen; it is the first among those rites. By the inclusion of the word "first," all the purificatory sacraments (*saṃskāras*) are understood. He who performs these, and he who supports and nourishes him with food—[the reading] "and him" (*caivam enam*) is also found; however, the meaning remains the same, since support is logically established through food alone. The reference to a different object is "this boy" (*enam kumāram*).

But surely this is a case of subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*). And yet, there has been no prior mention here of the boy. It is not so; for whom else would the *niṣeka* and other rites be performed? Even by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), the designation [of "teacher"] occurs, not merely from the explicit statement itself. He who performs those rites—thus, lacking these two qualities, one is merely a biological progenitor and not a teacher. Nor should it be thought that in the absence of the status of teacher he is not to be honored; he is the very first to be honored. And so the Blessed Vyāsa said:
"The master is the progenitor of the body, the doer of what is pleasing, the giver of life, and the teacher."
"And the father is the visible deity who instructs in what is beneficial.
The mention of the "brahmin" is for the sake of illustration. (2.142)

He who, being chosen by someone, performs for him the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the cooked sacrifices (pākayajñas), and the soma-sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others—he is called his officiating priest (ṛtvij) in this world. (2.143)

The rite that produces the fires, such as the *āhavanīya* and others, is called *agnyādheya*. It is enjoined thus: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fires in the spring" (*TB* 1.1.2.6). The *pākayajñas* are the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other such sacrifices; the *makhas*, beginning with the *agniṣṭoma*, are Soma sacrifices. The word *makha* is a synonym for *kratu* (sacrifice). He who performs these rites for someone is called that person's *ṛtvij* (officiating priest). The words "of whom" (*yasya*) and "for him" (*tasya*) indicate a relationship. He is called the *ṛtvij* only of that person for whom he performs these rites, not of anyone else. All these terms, beginning with *ācārya*, are relative terms. "Appointed" (*vṛtaḥ*) means requested and having performed the formal selection according to scriptural injunction. Because the context concerns those worthy of honor, the designation *ṛtvij* is taught here; for there is no occasion for officiating priests among the duties of a student (*brahmacārin*). This definition is stated in the sense that he is to be honored like an *ācārya* and the others. (2.143)
He who truly fills both ears with the Veda is to be known as mother and father; one should never act with malice toward him. (2.144)

He who covers both ears with the *brahman*—that is, by teaching the Veda—he should be known as mother and father. This is not an injunction that the teacher is to be designated by the words "mother" and "father"; for the words "father" and "mother" have well-established meanings, namely: the progenitor is the father, and the one who gives birth is the mother. These terms are used figuratively for the purpose of praising the teacher, just as one might say, "The Vāhīka is an ox. In the world, mother and father are renowned as the ultimate benefactors; they produce what is beneficial, nourish [the child] with food and other necessities, and act for the welfare of their son even at the cost of their own bodies. Therefore, because of his great helpfulness, the *upādhyāya* (teacher) is praised through them. He who assists in knowledge is superior to all other benefactors. This is an adverbial modifier meaning "truthfully": one should not bear malice toward that [teacher] by means of the *brahman*—that is, the truth, consisting of the syllables, accents, and phonemes, without error. "Malice" (*droha*) is doing harm or showing contempt toward him. One should never bear malice, even after the study of the texts has been completed and thereafter. And so says the author of the *Nirukta*: [397] "One should not bear malice toward that [teacher] by means of the *brahman*... "Malice" is injury or disregard toward him. One should never bear malice, even when the grasping of the text has been accomplished and at subsequent times. Thus says the author of the *Nirukta*: [398]...
Those Brahmins who, having been taught by their gurus, do not respect them in word, thought, or deed—
meaning they do not honor them but rather treat them with contempt— are just like those [already mentioned].
Disciples are not to be fed by the Guru;
they do not serve for his enjoyment.
In the same way, that sacred learning does not benefit them.

There is an alternative reading, *ātṛṇatti*, meaning "it pierces"; by this metaphor, it is said that [learning] merely perforates the ears. As it is said: "That man is considered to have unpierced ears for whom the sacred learning has not entered the range of his hearing. This prohibition against malice applies to all teachers—whether they be *ācāryas*, *upādhyāyas*, or *gurus*—even toward one who has been pierced [by learning]. (2.144)
An Ācārya is ten times more venerable than an Upādhyāya; a father is a hundred times more venerable than an Ācārya; but a mother exceeds a thousand fathers in respect. (2.145)

The prescription of the preceding as superior follows the order of praise: "The teacher is more excellent than the sub-teacher, the father than him, and the mother even than him. The mention of the numbers ten and so forth is merely for the sake of praise; what is intended is the progressive superiority of each subsequent person over each preceding one. For this very reason, there is the statement: "A thousandfold [is the debt] to the father."

"He exceeds ten preceptors (*upādhyāya*). He is superior to ten preceptors. But how is the accusative case used here? The word *ati* is a *karmapravacanīya*. Having transcended [the number] preceptor after preceptor, he "exceeds" them; that is, he is endowed with an excellence of respect. Alternatively, *atireka* means "surplus" (*ādhikya*); the verbal root is used in the sense of overcoming (*abhibhava*) caused by that surplus. He overcomes the preceptors through an excess of respect. As for the form *atiricyate*, the accusative is not contradictory when used in the sense of the agent-as-object (*karmakartṛ*), because of the inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahulam*) in the rule: "In the case of the roots *duh* and *pac*, when they are transitive, the agent-as-object is frequently [expressed by the accusative]" (Pāṇini Vārttika 14 on 3.1.87).

But will it not be stated immediately thereafter that "the father who imparts the Veda is more venerable," while here the superiority of the father over the teacher is asserted? This would be a mutual contradiction. This is not a fault. Here, the teacher (*ācārya*) is intended in the sense of a mere reciter according to the etymological view (*nairuktadarśana*), being so designated merely by virtue of performing the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and instructing in proper conduct (*ācāra*): "the teacher is one who causes [the pupil] to grasp the conduct. Furthermore, there is no rule that linguistic usage must proceed solely with technical designations established within one's own system. For the word *guru* is defined here as referring to the father, yet it is employed in various places to refer to the teacher as well. Therefore, this superiority of the father is stated in comparison to a teacher who provides only slight assistance, performs only the initiation (*upanayana*), and teaches proper conduct without providing formal instruction in the Veda.
And when this sequence is intended, among these [four], the mother is to be saluted first, then the father, then the teacher (ācārya), and then the sub-teacher (upādhyāya). || 2.145 ||

When the principal teacher and the father who performs the sacraments are both present, what is the order of precedence? To this he says: "Between the progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is more venerable; for the birth from the Veda is eternal for a Brahmin, both after death and in this world. (2.146)

The progenitor who gives birth and the giver of the Veda who teaches—both of these are fathers. Of these two fathers, the one who gives the Veda is the more venerable father. Therefore, when the biological father and the teacher are present together, the teacher is to be saluted first.

In this context, he states an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) that serves as a reason: "For [this] is the birth from Brahman. Birth for the purpose of acquiring the Veda is "birth from Brahman" (*brahmajanma*). This is a compound according to the *śākapārthiva* class (cf. Pāṇini Vār 8 on 2.1.69). In this compound, the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) constitutes the birth from Brahman. Alternatively, the acquisition of the Veda itself is the birth. That [birth] is eternal and constant for the Brāhmaṇa; it is beneficial after death and beneficial in this world as well. (2.146)
One should understand that the birth which occurs when his mother and father produce him together through desire is merely his physical origin within the womb. (2.147)

These two verses are an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). When the mother and father produce and generate this child, they do so in private, driven by mutual desire and under the sway of passion; one should understand that to be his "origination" (*saṃbhūti*). The origination and birth of that child consists in his being born within the womb of the mother and acquiring his major and minor limbs. Furthermore, those entities whose nature it is to originate perish in that very same way. Therefore, what is the use of that origination for which destruction follows immediately? (2.147)
But that birth which the teacher, having mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to rule with the Sāvitrī—this is true, and it is free from old age and death. (2.148)

But that birth of his which comes from the teacher is indestructible; for since the attainment of heaven and liberation results from the performance of rituals once the Veda has been acquired and its meaning understood—and since all of this is rooted in the teacher—he is the most excellent.

That birth which he produces—that second birth called initiation (*upanayana*)—which brings about the praise of birth as being "true," "undecaying," and "immortal" through the recitation following the *Sāvitrī*: although these words have essentially the same meaning, they are employed here with the intention of expressing the excellence of qualities of this birth known as initiation over the birth from a mother. For old age and death do not occur for a birth as they do for living beings; however, its indestructibility could be established by a single word alone, yet that is not what is being expressed. The construction of the words is as follows: the teacher, who has mastered the Vedas, produces that birth according to rule through the *Sāvitrī*—the word *sāvitrī* here signifying the entire complex of elements constituting initiation—and that [birth] is superior. "Birth" (*jāti*) means birth (*janma*). (2.148)
One should know that person as a teacher in this world by virtue of that service of learning, whoever assists one with their learning, whether it be little or much. (2.149)

The meaning is that whichever teacher benefits a student by means of sacred learning—whether it be little or much, this being an adverbial modifier—one should know even such a teacher as a guru who has benefited him with only a small amount of learning.

This construction, however, is superior: "Of that learning (*śruta*) which stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—whether it concerns the Veda, the Vedāṅgas, or other sciences such as logic and the arts—the small or great [benefit] which it provides" is the ellipsis to be supplied. That which is learning and that which is its service constitute "service to learning" (*śrutopakriyā*); by means of that act of service, because it is the cause thereof, the learning is designated as "service"—this is the coreferentiality. In that regard, the conduct toward a teacher must be observed, or rather, the designation [of the science] as such is recorded there, just like the word "teacher" (*ācārya*) and so forth. (2.149)
One who performs the rites of a Brāhmaṇic birth and is a teacher of his own duty becomes, according to dharma, the father of an elder even if he is a mere child. (2.150)

The birth for the purpose of grasping the Veda is the "Brahmic" birth; the one who performs this is the initiator (*upanetṛ*). He is the instructor and teacher of one's own duty through the exposition of the meaning of the Vedas. Such a person, though a child, becomes the father of an elder or senior Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, even the elder must behave toward him as toward a father.

But how can a younger man initiate an elder? For initiation is prescribed for the eighth year; and as long as one has not studied and mastered the Veda, he is not qualified for the injunction regarding the office of a teacher. If this is so, then in this context initiation is not the "Brāhma-birth" (the second birth), but rather the acquisition of the *svādhyāya* (Vedic study). The performer of that [acquisition] is the instructor. He becomes a father by instructing and explaining the meaning of the Veda, which is his own duty (*svadharma*). According to the law (*dharmataḥ*), the duties of a father must be performed toward him. By the phrase "according to the law," it means that fatherhood exists there on account of the law. And those duties pertaining to a father are not already established for the instructor and the expounder. Therefore, it is enjoined: "One should behave toward a Kṣatriya as toward a Brāhmaṇa. (2.150)
The child Kavi, the son of Aṅgiras, taught his fathers;
having encompassed them with his wisdom, he said to them, "O little sons! (2.151)

This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) known as *parakṛti*, serving as a commendatory supplement to the rule for conduct toward one's father mentioned previously. A young child named Kavi, the son of Aṅgiras, taught those who were older than himself—his paternal uncles, maternal uncles, their sons, and others—who were equal to his father. On occasions requiring formal address, he called out to them, "O little sons, come here! Having embraced them with knowledge—that is, having accepted them and made them his disciples. (2.151)
Filled with indignation, they questioned the gods regarding that matter;
and the gods, having assembled, said to them, "The child has spoken what is right for you."

Addressed with the invocation "O little sons," which was equivalent to calling them "father" and so forth, they were provoked to anger and filled with wrath; they questioned the gods regarding that matter—the use of the word "sons"—asking, "Why are we being addressed thus by this boy? Is this appropriate? Being thus questioned, all those gods held a consultation, and having assembled and reached a consensus, they spoke to the ancestors of Kavi, saying, "What the child has said to you is right and fitting. (2.152)
The ignorant one is indeed a child; he who imparts the sacred hymns is the father.
For they call the ignorant one a "child," but the giver of the hymns, a "father. (2.153)

One does not become a child merely by being young in years; rather, even an old man is a child if he is ignorant and foolish. The term "giver of mantras" (*mantrada*) is an illustration; he who gives, teaches, and explains the mantras—that is, the Vedas—is the father. The word *vai* indicates another traditional source (*āgama*). This tradition of the gods is indeed ancient. Likewise, the phrase "thus they say" (*āhuḥ*) indicates a historical tradition (*aitihya*); our predecessors also said that an ignorant and foolish person is a "child. The term "father" refers to the giver of mantras. The use of the particle *iti* indicates that the preceding words refer to their own literal form, since they are heard following it. By the word "child" (*bāla*), one is designated simply as an ignorant person; therefore, there is no accusative case ending after the word "child. This passage from the *Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa* concerning childhood has been described here in substance by the author of the Smṛti. (2.153)
Neither by years, nor by gray hair, nor by wealth, nor by kinsmen did the seers establish dharma; he among us who is learned in the Vedas is great. 2.154.

This is a praise of the teacher. The word *hāyana* is a synonym for a year. One does not become great, venerable, or mature in age merely by many years; nor by grey hair—meaning that the hair of the head, beard, and body has turned white; nor by great wealth; nor by kinsmen. These aforementioned grounds for respect are attained [only when combined]. One does not become great by these taken together, but rather by learning alone. For this is what the seers (*ṛṣi*) established. A seer is so called because of his vision (*darśanāt*). Those who have seen the entire meaning of the Vedas and reached a firm conclusion established this as the law (*dharma*). He who is *anūcāna*—one who has performed the "reciting after" (*anuvacana*), that is, the teaching of the Veda along with all its auxiliary limbs—he is our "great one," our most excellent. The root *kṛ* here functions in the sense of establishing, not in the sense of producing something previously non-existent. (2.154)
The seniority of Brahmins is by knowledge, that of Kṣatriyas by valor, that of Vaiśyas by grain and wealth, and that of Śūdras alone by birth. (2.155)

This too is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda). That which was stated—that knowledge alone is superior to wealth and the other factors combined—is precisely what is being pointed out here in detail.

The seniority of Brahmins is by knowledge, not by wealth and such; that of Kṣatriyas is by valor—valor being skill in the use of weapons and firmness of breath; and that of Vaiśyas is by grain and wealth. Because "grain" is mentioned separately, the word "wealth" (*dhana*) here refers to gold and the like, as in the expression "Brahmins and wandering mendicants. A Vaiśya who possesses much wealth is the senior one. The suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the third case, according to the rule "from *ādi* etc. [Pāṇini 5.4.44]; it signifies the instrumental case, as in "by reason of" (*hetau tṛtīyā*, Pāṇini 2.3.23). || 2.155 ||
One does not become old simply because one's head is gray; rather, the gods know him as an elder who, even if young, is devoted to study. 2.156

One is not called "venerable" (vṛddha) merely because his head is gray with white hair, nor because the hairs upon his head have turned white. How then? Even one who is young and in the prime of life, if he has studied [the Vedas], him the gods know and call "venerable. This is praise, for the gods are indeed the knowers of all. (2.156)
Just as an elephant made of wood, just as a deer made of leather, so too is a Brahmin who has not studied; these three merely bear the name. 2.157.

This is a praise of study and the student. Just as a wooden elephant made from timber with an axe and other tools is fruitless—it does not perform the work of an elephant for kings, such as the slaying of enemies—so too a Brāhmaṇa who does not study is like wood; he has no qualification for anything. A leather deer, or any other animal made of leather, is likewise fruitless; it does not perform the work of hunting and so forth. These three bear only their names, but not their actual purpose. (2.157)
As a eunuch is fruitless with women, as a cow is fruitless with a bull, and as a gift given to an ignorant man is fruitless, so is a Brahmin who knows not the Rigveda fruitless. 2.158

A eunuch, a hermaphrodite, or one incapable of sexual intercourse with women is fruitless among women, just as a cow is fruitless with a female cow; even so, a Brahmin who is ignorant of the Rigveda and does not study it is fruitless. (2.158)

The seven or eight verses that have passed were for the purpose of praising the student and the teacher. Now, however, the mind of a disciple who lacks faith yet persists in his studies becomes distracted.
One who desires righteousness (*dharma*) should instruct living beings toward their welfare through non-violence alone, and should employ speech that is both sweet and gentle. (2.159)

When anger arises in a teacher, the excessive resorting to beating, harsh speech, and the like—which would otherwise be justified—is here prohibited. For the sake of the welfare (*śreya*) of living beings—meaning one's wife, sons, slaves, pupils, and uterine brothers—one must provide instruction through non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), that is, without beating them. By the inclusion of the term "living beings" (*bhūta*), it is not to be understood as applying solely to the pupil. *Śreya* refers to the attainment of visible and invisible fruits; for that purpose, instruction is to be given. This may consist of oral advice not contained in a formal text, or the teaching and explanation of a scripture. What is prohibited here is excessive beating and shouting as far as possible. However, slight beating is indeed permitted, as stated in the rule: "with a rope or a split bamboo cane" (MDh 8.299). How then should they be established on the path? "Speech alone should be sweet and preceded by conciliation. One should use pleasant and gentle speech, not in a loud, arrogant, or harsh tone like a crow. Even when being affectionate, one might say: "Study, my dear son; do not let your mind be fixed elsewhere. Having completed this lesson quickly with faith, you shall immediately play with your bright-eyed peers. But for one who does not apply such faith, the aforementioned rule applies: "with a split bamboo cane. They should be urged—that is, spoken to—by one desiring merit (*dharma*). In this way, the duty of teaching becomes preeminent. (2.159)
He whose speech and mind are pure and always properly guarded indeed attains the entire fruit taught in the Vedānta.

When there is a cause for agitation, whether from the teacher or another, if his speech and mind do not become turbid but remain pure; and even when turbidity has arisen, if they are properly guarded such that there is no resolve to harm others nor any undertaking of action intended to cause them pain—this is the proper guarding of speech and mind. The inclusion of the word "always" (*sarvadā*) is for the sake of establishing this as a duty for every person, not merely for the teacher at the time of teaching. "He indeed attains everything. The term *vedāntāḥ* means the established conclusions (*siddhāntāḥ*) of the Vedas. The word *siddha* is elided just as the word *atyanta* is elided in the rule *siddhe śabdārthasaṃbandhe* (Pāṇini’s Vārttika on Pāṇ. I.1.1). It refers to the conclusion accepted by those who know the Vedas regarding Vedic sentences—that for this ritual act, this is the result. He attains all of that fruit. By speaking thus, this statement declares that the restraint of speech and mind is both a duty of the person and a duty within the sacrifices. For if it were not a duty of the person alone, then in the absence of a deficiency in the sacrifice, why would one who is unrestrained in speech and mind not attain the full fruit, such that it is said: "The self-restrained one attains everything"?

Others, however, explain the Vedāntas as the *Rahasyabrāhmaṇas*. According to them, whatever fruit is accepted for the obligatory (*nitya*) rites and for the fruitless restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), that fruit—characterized by the attainment of Brahman—one attains in its entirety. But how can it be that the obligatory rites have the attainment of Brahman as their purpose? There is the view of some that this is so. Alternatively, the "end" (*anta*) of the Veda is the completion of its study; therefore, one attains that fruit which results from the injunction regarding the status of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*). However, if explained in this way, [the passage] would merely have the injunction regarding teaching as its purpose. (2.160)

One should not be a wounder of others even when afflicted, nor should one have a mind intent on deeds that harm others; one should not utter that speech by which another is agitated, for such speech does not lead to the higher worlds. (2.161)

This is another duty pertaining solely to the purpose of human life (*puruṣārtha*): one should not speak words that are "wound-inflicters" (*aruṃtuda*), meaning words that strike the vital points (*marman*) and cause pain, or words of abuse that produce extreme agitation. Even when afflicted or oppressed by another, one should not speak such unpleasant things. Likewise, one should not perform actions intended for malice toward others (*paradroha*)—that is, for the sake of harming them—or harbor the intent (*dhī*) for such an end. Alternatively, one should not even direct the mind (*buddhi*) toward the act of malice itself. Furthermore, one should not utter speech—even if employed in jest—by which another person is agitated; nor should one utter even a single part of such speech, since from a mere fragment, through the context of the matter and so forth, the indication of another (hostile) meaning may be perceived. For such speech is "unworldly" (*alokyā*), meaning it is an obstacle to attaining the heavenly worlds and the like. (2.161)
A Brahmin should always tremble at honor as if it were poison;
he should always long for dishonor as if it were nectar. (2.162)

When begging for alms, whether at the house of a celibate student or from a teacher who teaches for a livelihood, one should not allow the mind to be disturbed by the absence of honor; rather, one should recoil from honor itself and should not value what is given out of reverence. One should always desire and long for contempt and disdain as if they were nectar. By attributing to the verb *ākāṅkṣ* the sense of the root *adhi-i* (to study), because of the commonality of longing (*utkaṇṭhā*), the genitive case is employed according to Pāṇini 2.3.52.

"But surely, that which is not honored is unfit to be eaten" (MDh 4.214). True; this is for the purpose of prohibiting mental agitation. However, it does not mean that such food is declared fit to be eaten. One should remain equanimous toward both honor and dishonor, and one should certainly not seek out dishonor. For a religious student (*brahmacārin*), however, even an insulted gift of alms is permissible. Moreover, this is not a formal acceptance (*pratigraha*), so it would not fall within the scope of the rule: "He who accepts what is honored... (MDh 4.236). || 2.162 ||
For he who is held in low esteem sleeps in peace and wakes in peace;
he moves through this world in ease, while the scorner perishes. 2.163

This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for the preceding injunction, intended to demonstrate its fruit: he who is not disturbed by insults sleeps in peace; otherwise, being consumed by hatred, he finds no sleep whatsoever. Even when awake, being preoccupied with thoughts of that [insulter], he finds no happiness. Having risen from his bed, he moves about his duties with ease. But he who is the perpetrator of the insult perishes through that very sin. (2.163)
By this sequential method, the twice-born man, his self purified, should gradually accumulate the austerity conducive to the attainment of Brahman while dwelling with his teacher.

A twice-born man, whose self has been refined (*saṃskṛtātman*) by this sequential application (*kramayoga*), should accumulate austerity (*tapas*). By the phrase "beginning with 'one who is about to study'" (*adhyeṣyamāṇa*, MDh 2.70), that which was prescribed as the duty of a student (*brahmacārin*) is referred to here by the word "by this" (*anena*, MDh 2.164). Through this collection of injunctions practiced in their proper sequence, one should accumulate—that is, gradually and without haste, both acquire and increase—austerity characterized by the refinement of the self (*ātmasaṃskāra*) consisting in stainlessness (*niṣkalmaṣatva*). Just as stainlessness is achieved through austerities such as the *Cāndrāyaṇa* and others, so too is it achieved through this collection of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) for the purpose of grasping the Veda. Therefore, he should accumulate it; that is, he should acquire and augment it slowly and without haste. "Sequence" (*krama*) means the proper order: having done this, this must be done, beginning with "preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*" (*oṃkārapūrvikāḥ*), and so forth. "Application" (*yoga*) refers to the connection of the performance with that sequence. "For the sake of attaining the Brahman" (*brahmaṇa ādhigamikam*) means for the purpose of attainment. Attainment (*adhigama*) consists of both the study and the comprehension [of the Veda]. (2.164)
The entire Veda, together with its secret portions, must be mastered by the twice-born through various specific austerities and vows prescribed by rule. (2.165)

By means of various and manifold specific austerities, such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, and by fasting for one meal a day or eating only at every fourth meal-time, he should emaciate his body. Furthermore, through vows such as the *upaniṣads* and the *mahānāmnikas*, which are prescribed by rule and taught in the *gṛhya-smṛtis*, the entire Veda is to be mastered.

As for those who say that the word *tapas* used in the previous verse refers to the duties of a student (*brahmacārin*), and that here too those same specific forms of austerity are intended, they do not think correctly; for these are already included by the word *vrata* itself. Indeed, according to the scriptures, *vrata* denotes a restrictive observance (*niyama*). Furthermore, because the word *vrata* is a general term, its inclusion of the *mahānāmnikā* and other such observances is established. Therefore, what is intended here are austerities such as fasting and the like.

In this context, some maintain that the singular number in the word *veda* is intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*). Although, due to the use of the suffix *-tavya*, the Veda appears to be the primary object (*pradhāna*) by virtue of its application as the thing to be refined (*saṃskārya*), nevertheless, both according to the injunction (*vidhi*) and in reality, it is subordinate (*guṇabhāva*) with respect to the comprehension of meaning. When subordination is intended, the student’s activity regarding the Veda—which extends up to the comprehension of meaning—is determined by a consideration of the function of the injunction. For the meaning of the injunction here is: "One should effect the comprehension of meaning by means of the studied Veda. Otherwise, its status as the object to be refined would not be established. Indeed, everything is refined when it is subordinate to another purpose. And the visible purpose of the Veda once studied is the production of knowledge of its own meaning; otherwise, even if its primacy were heard in the text, it would have to be abandoned, as in the case of the injunction "He offers groats" (*saktūñ juhoti*). Furthermore, the verbal root itself has the sense of comprehension. For "attaining" (*adhigamana*) is said to be knowledge (*jñāna*); it is recorded in the Smṛti that "all roots meaning motion mean knowledge. Moreover, the grasping of the Veda's own form was already enjoined previously by such rules as "one should study having joined the hands together" (MDh 2.71). This [present rule] establishes that very [grasping of the form] as extending up to the grasping of the meaning. It is precisely considering this intention [of significance] that the study of multiple Vedas—which was not otherwise required—is re-enjoined by the rule "having studied the Vedas" (MDh 3.2). Even though the study of multiple Vedas exists [elsewhere], where would the intention of singularity be useful? Very well, it is indeed useful. If only a single Śākhā were studied, the requirement of the injunction "one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied" would be fulfilled. Study of multiple Vedas, however, occurs by choice. If it were not impelled by an injunction, what madman would trouble himself with a tooth-cup? There certainly is another injunction here, namely "having studied the Vedas," and that applies to one who desires a fruit. And the fruit is heaven. Or, if something else—such as streams of clarified butter—is mentioned in the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) of this injunction, then that alone must be the result. For the injunction for the religious student (*brahmacārin*) concerns the comprehension of meaning and has a visible purpose, since comprehension is seen to be useful for the performance of rituals, and only the learned person is entitled to perform rituals. The study of each individual Veda, on the other hand, is for the sake of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) alone. Otherwise, since the injunction regarding one's own Veda would be fulfilled by the study of a single Veda, the statement "having studied the Vedas" and so forth would be entirely meaningless if there were no injunction for Dharma.

It is argued: How can this position be consistent, given that there is this single injunction, "The Veda is to be studied"? If it is not assumed to have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) because it is an injunction for a preparatory act (*saṃskāra-vidhi*) and because it serves the performance of visible rites, then the same applies to the study of multiple Vedas; for that same principle exists there as well. Furthermore, there would be a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*): in some cases, like the injunction for the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), there would be a connection with obligatory and optional rites by way of comprehension, while in other cases, it would be directly for the sake of a result.

Now, if it is thought that "having studied the Vedas" (*vedān adhītya*) is a separate injunction (*vidhyantara*), not prompted by the injunction to become a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), and that therefore only one who desires its fruit is qualified for this [study], that is incorrect. This is not a separate injunction. Rather, since there is no intention to specify a number (*saṃkhyāvivakṣā*) regarding the study of the Veda under the very injunction at hand, it restricts the three-fold study—five, six, or seven branches—to the extent permitted by one's capacity. Furthermore, the injunction "one should study" (*adhīyīta*) is not heard here; rather, the injunction here is "one should dwell in the householder stage of life" (*gṛhasthāśramam āvaset*).

Furthermore, that which was stated regarding the intended significance of the number is utterly irrelevant. For the intentionality of a number arises from its application (*viniyoga*), not from its mere presentation. And that application prescribes study for the sake of the Veda itself (*svādhyāya*). The predominance perceived through the two accusative endings does not disappear by virtue of the meaning being subordinate. If it were accepted in this way, then even in the case of "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), the singularity would be intended; for even though it is the predominant factor, it indeed possesses the status of an instrument (*sādhana*) with respect to the cleansing. However, that [instrumental status] is not expressed by the word. Just as in "He offers with the cups" (*grahair juhoti*), the cups have a subordinate status even with respect to the oblation. Therefore, the predominance of the Vedic text (*svādhyāya*) follows from both its direct expression and its application; and since it is predominant, the singularity is not intended.

Well then, if the purpose of the injunction for Vedic study were fulfilled by the mastery of even a single Veda, one must state the purpose of studying multiple Vedas; we shall explain this in the third [book].

Now, if this injunction extends until the final comprehension [of the meaning], then even after the Veda has been memorized in its own form, as long as the comprehension of the meaning has not arisen, the performance of restraints and observances such as the avoidance of honey and meat would remain unceased during that interval. What is the fault in that? It is a contradiction with the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). For the learned, even while listening to the meaning of the Veda they have studied, do not refrain from honey, meat, and so forth.

This is not a fault. For there is another Smṛti text: "Having studied the Veda, one should bathe" (Baudhāyana Gṛhyasūtra 2.5.6). In that context, the word "having studied" (*adhītya*) refers merely to the recitation of the text. And the phrase "one should bathe" (*snāyāt*) indicates the cessation of the restraints and observances that are ancillary to the injunction for private Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) at its proper time. Just as honey and meat are prohibited, so too is bathing. Thus, while bathing is permitted therein, by association (*sāhacarya*), it also permits honey, meat, and the like, because they belong to the same context. However, sexual intercourse with women is prohibited by another text: "One whose student-life (*brahmacarya*) is unviolated" (Manu Dharmaśāstra 3.2). And even upon the transgression of that, nothing is lost regarding the comprehension of the meaning of the injunction for private Vedic study; for in that state, sexual intercourse is not an ancillary part of that injunction, since all restraints and observances terminate with the formal grasping of the Veda. This prohibition, however, pertains to the person's own welfare (*puruṣārtha*). Therefore, if a violation occurs somehow, the penance for an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of chastity) applies. For the emission of semen while established in a vow (*vratastha*) is a dereliction; and one established in a vow is not eligible for this penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) such as the Cāndrāyaṇa.

Furthermore, what is the reason for taking the phrase "he should bathe" as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)? It is said in reply: First of all, this "bathing" does not consist of the washing of the body with water, because that would entail the consequence of it having an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Moreover, since the observances (*niyama*) of the religious student (*brahmacārin*) require a terminal point (*avadhi*), and since this [injunction] is logically established as a rule providing that required meaning by serving as the limit, there is no need for another limit for them. For those observances exist for the sake of the injunction regarding Vedic study (*svādhyāya*); therefore, their cessation itself is their limit. And their cessation occurs through the cessation of the object. Study is its object, and its cessation is directly perceived.

True, provided that its scope were restricted solely to what is heard (the Vedic text). However, even that which is not heard—the comprehension of the meaning (*arthādhigama*) which is the result—also becomes its object, because otherwise the injunction would be inexplicable as a rite of purification (*saṃskāravidhi*). For if it were restricted to the hearing and recitation of the text, its status as an injunction would be contradicted. For the nature of an injunction is to impel one toward the performance of its own purpose (*svārtha*), and its own purpose consists of the *kārya* (the end), the *karaṇa* (the instrument), and the *itikartavyatā* (the procedure). And there is nothing else besides the meaning of the injunction itself. The *kārya* is not the object (*viṣaya*), because they are expressed by a single word. In the term *adhīyīta*, the verbal root-meaning (such as "reciting") qualifies the sense of the abstract action (*bhāvārtha*). The observance of restraints and duties (*yama-niyama*) constitutes the *itikartavyatā*. In that case, the possibility of this injunction impelling one toward its own purpose does not exist; for the fulfillment of the impulsion of all injunctions occurs only through the mediation of the performance of their objects. And the performance of the object of this [injunction] is already established by the force of another injunction: namely, the injunction of the teacher, "Having initiated the pupil, he should teach him the Veda" (MDh 2.140). Since the teaching cannot be accomplished without the recitation, the teacher impels the boy toward the recitation in order to fulfill his own injunction. Furthermore, since no performance is possible for one who has not been impelled by the teacher himself once he has understood [the duty], the fact that the boy is impelled by the teacher's injunction must necessarily be accepted. When it is thus impelled, the performance is established; therefore, the injunction serves no purpose for the boy regarding the recitation of the *svādhyāya*. Consequently, since it is impossible for it to be an impeller (*prayoktṛ*), what kind of injunctive form can this injunction have? Since the destruction of its essential nature (*svarūpa*) would follow, one seeks that mode by which its status as an impeller may be obtained. In this regard, it is certain that this is a rite of purification (*saṃskāravidhi*), and a rite of purification is never fruitless. For when there is recitation, some kind of connection with the meaning is observed, and that is useful for the performance of all those ritual acts. Therefore, the injunction is understood from the necessity of producing an understanding connected to the subject matter of the heard recitation. And although, by the very nature of things, understanding arises immediately upon grasping the sentence, it is not yet of a determinate form. Thus, in the aspect by which certainty is attained, the injunction possesses the power of impulsion. Certainty arises through deliberation (*vicāra*) by way of the removal of doubt and other such obstacles. Nor is deliberation obtained from any other source—not from the teacher’s injunction, because that is fulfilled by the mere act of recitation; nor is it prompted by a visible result, for what could a person not achieve without deliberation that would cause them to exert themselves?

If it is argued that even the act of inquiry might occur by chance, as in the case of one desiring a village and so forth, then, because human desire is unrestricted, someone might not inquire at all; or, if they were to inquire, it might not be immediately following the study. Therefore, since this portion [of the process] is not otherwise established, and because the scope of an injunction (*vidhi*) consists of that which is unestablished, the operation of the injunction exists here. Consequently, since the study itself is obtained from another source, and since the comprehension connected to it arises through the very nature of things in an indeterminate form—such comprehension having no purposeful utility anywhere even when present, as its function as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) is already fulfilled once it exists—and since only determinate knowledge is useful for the performance of fruitful rituals, and since such determination is achievable only through inquiry, and since inquiry must necessarily be performed at a fixed time, this injunction stands as one whose final aim is inquiry, in order to ensure its performance.

Therefore, there arises an expectation regarding the restrictive rules (*niyama*): does the limit [of study] conclude with the mere recitation of what is heard (*śruta*), or does it conclude with the investigation of the meaning for the sake of generating a certain understanding that is implied [by the injunction]? Thus, in response to this expectation, the limit is provided by the rule: "Having studied the Veda, one should bathe. In that context, since there is no distinction between the subject matter at hand and the requirement [for a limit], a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is appropriate.

Now, why is it said that there is "understanding without hearing," when it is indeed heard [in the text]: "it is to be mastered" (MDh 2.165)? In the Veda and in other Smṛtis, it is likewise read: "one studies the Veda" and "one's own portion of the Veda is to be studied. Since this [text] is a Smṛti of Manu, its meaning is identical because it is rooted in that same Smṛti. This term "mastery" (*adhigama*) intends understanding as implied; or else, mastery is simply the grasping of the form [of the text]. However, the fact that it culminates in understanding is obtained by that very same logic. Nor is it inconsistent that one injunction has a certain part of its subject matter prompted by the injunction regarding the teacher, while another part of that same subject matter has that very [teacher] as its prompter—there is no such disparity. What is untenable here? Nothing, because it is understood precisely as having the [text's] meaning as its object.

As for what was stated—that "the study of multiple Vedas is appropriate for the sake of transcendental merit"—we shall provide the refutation of that in the context of the passage beginning with "thirty-six years" (MDh 3.1).

The word *veda* denotes a branch (*śākhā*) consisting of a collection of sentences from both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas. Since the word *veda* is observed to be used even for a sentence that is merely a part of it, the word *kṛtsna* (entire) is employed to eliminate that doubt. Even if the study were not yet complete when one sentence had been studied—because other sentences would also be denotable by the term *veda*, and because [the study] is a purificatory act (*saṃskārakarman*) like the [soma-]cup offerings (*graha*)—nevertheless, the inclusion of the word *kṛtsna* is for the sake of clarity.

Others, however, explain the word *kṛtsna* (entire) as referring to the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*). For the word *veda* denotes a collection of sentences of a specified extent; in that case, even if it were deficient by a single *ṛc*, the *svādhyāya* would not have been studied. Therefore, the word *kṛtsna* is intended to include the study of the auxiliary sciences. Accordingly, another *smṛti* states: "The Veda with its six auxiliaries is to be studied by a Brāhmaṇa as a duty without [any specific] motive."

Is it not the case that here it is understood that "whatever is the Veda, that is the whole"? And the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) are not denotable by the word "Veda. Therefore, how could there be association with the auxiliaries? As for that Smṛti rule, "The Veda with its six auxiliaries is to be studied," there the auxiliaries are included by their own specific term. But here, since the word "whole" (*kṛtsna*) functions as a qualifier of the Veda, how could the auxiliaries possibly be grasped [as part of it]?

It is said: "One's own Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) is to be performed"—this is the very root of this Smṛti rule. And that [study] is established as extending up to comprehension (*avabodha*). Since comprehension is not possible without the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), the inclusion of the auxiliaries is established by implication. Therefore, the knowledge of *Nigama*, *Nirukta*, *Vyākaraṇa*, and *Mīmāṃsā* is also necessitated by the injunction. Having thus accepted the inclusion of the auxiliaries for the sake of this purpose, the word "entire" (*kṛtsna*) is appropriately used in its indicative sense. In this regard, just as the hands, feet, and so forth are called the "limbs" (*aṅga*) of a person because they constitute his body, the *Nirukta* and other sciences do not constitute the body of the Veda in that same way. Nevertheless, they are called "limbs" of the Veda figuratively. For indeed, without them, the Veda is not capable of conveying its own meaning; therefore, there is here a metaphorical superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of limbs upon them. Thus, the word "entire" is justified through the superimposed status of being the Veda.
"With its secret" (*sarahasya*): "secret" (*rahasya*) refers to the Upaniṣads. Although they possess the status of being Veda, they are mentioned separately because of their preeminence. (2.165)
A best of the twice-born who wishes to perform austerity should always practice the Veda;
for the study of the Veda is declared here to be the supreme austerity for a Brahmin. (2.166)

The repetition (*abhyāsa*) for the purpose of recitation, which is already established as a subsidiary element of the primary rite (*prakṛtaśeṣatayā*), is restated here for the sake of praise; it is not, however, a separate injunction (*vidhyantara*). The word *sadā* (always) refers specifically to the time of recitation. The word *tapas* (austerity) refers to scriptural practices such as the restriction of food that produce bodily affliction. Here, however, by means of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it denotes the purification of the self (*ātmasaṃskāra*) produced thereby, as well as the capacity [to grant] boons or curses. In this context, the verbal root *taps-* is used in the sense of the heat that is a constituent part of the acquisition [of merit]. Since the status of the object as the agent (*karmakartṛtva*) is not intended to be expressed, the *parasmaipada* ending is employed. The second half-verse, which functions as a reason, is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). For Vedic study is indeed a certain kind of preeminent austerity; therefore, Vedic study—which is superior to that—is praised by superimposing upon it the fruitfulness equal to that [austerity]. (2.166)
Truly, that twice-born man performs the highest austerity even to his very fingertips,
who, though wearing a garland, studies his own Veda daily to the best of his ability.

This is another explanatory restatement (*arthavādānuvāda*) regarding the rule for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*) found in the *Vājasaneyaka-Brāhmaṇa*. The connection is with the words “even unto the tips of the nails” (*ā nakhāgrebhya eva*). The particle *ha* indicates traditional report (*aitihya*). Since the excellence of austerity (*tapas*) is already understood from the word *parama*, the mention of the “tips of the nails” expresses the excellence even of that which is already excellent. Even the lifeless tips of the nails are pervaded by this austerity. For ordinary austerities such as the *kṛcchra* penance do not yield complete results because they do not pervade the tips of the nails; this [study], however, pervades them as well—this is the praise. Regarding the form *tapyate*: in the rule “*tapas tapaḥ karmakasyaiva*” (Pāṇini 3.1.88), the suffix *yaṅ* and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) are applied. “Even he who is garlanded”: one who possesses a garland (*sragvī*) is a person wearing a wreath of flowers. By this, the author shows the abandonment of the restrictive rules of a student (*brahmacārin*). Even having abandoned the duties of a student, if one studies the Veda daily, according to one's ability—even if only a small amount—one is joined with the highest human goal (*puruṣārtha*). This is a mere eulogy; it does not mean that study is permitted upon the abandonment of the restrictive rules. (2.167)
The twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in other matters, quickly falls to the status of a Śūdra while still alive, along with his descendants. (2.168)

For those for whom the word *kṛtsna* (entirety) is intended to include the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), since the study of these might otherwise occur in an indefinite order, the sequence is now regulated: first the Veda is to be studied, and thereafter the auxiliaries. However, for those for whom the word is used to preclude the suspicion that the Veda itself might be incomplete, the study of the Veda alone is obtained as occurring after the *traividyavrata*. It is not permitted to study the auxiliaries until the Veda has been mastered.

That twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, exerts excessive effort and application toward another treatise, or toward the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*), or toward the texts of the science of logic (*tarka-śāstra*), attains the status of a *śūdra* even while still alive—quickly, that is, immediately—and along with his lineage, meaning together with his progeny of sons, grandsons, and so forth. Since it is impossible to prohibit the exertion itself, once that [Vedic study] is completed, other branches of knowledge may be studied as occasion demands. The statement regarding the attainment of *śūdra*-hood is an expression of extreme censure. Because of the mention of "the twice-born," this rule of sequence applies to one who has been initiated (*upanīta*). Prior to initiation, the study of the auxiliary sciences such as phonetics (*śikṣā*) and grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), provided they are not mixed with Vedic sentences, is not prohibited.

But surely, the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) are implied by the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), and the student performs that injunction under the direction of a teacher. Before initiation (*upanayana*), since a teacher does not exist, how could there be the possibility of studying the auxiliaries? This is not a fault. According to the text, "Therefore, they say a son who has been instructed is worthy of the world" (BĀU 1.5.17), he who is to be consecrated by the father shall teach him grammar and the other sciences before his initiation. (2.168)

The entitlement of the twice-born (dvijāti) to various [sacrificial] acts has been heard [in the scriptures]. Regarding this, as with terms such as "teacher" (ācārya) and so forth, he speaks in order to define its meaning because of the [need for] friendship:
"The first birth of the twice-born occurs before the mother; the second at the tying of the girdle (mauñjibandhana);
the third at the initiation for sacrifice (yajñadīkṣā), according to the injunction of the Śruti. (2.169)

The first birth of a man is from his mother; the second is at the binding of the girdle of muñja grass, that is, at the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). The short vowel [in *mauñjibandhane*] is according to Pāṇini 6.3.63: *ṅyāpor bahulam*. The third is at the consecration (*dīkṣā*) for sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma. Consecration is also heard of in scripture as a form of birth: "The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) make him a fetus again when they consecrate him" (*Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* 1.3). These three births of the twice-born are enjoined by the Śruti.

But if this is so, would it not follow that there are three births? Let it be so. For the designation "twice-born" (*dvija*) is based upon the *upanayana* ceremony; and the entitlement to perform rites prescribed by the Vedas (*śrauta*), the Smṛtis (*smārta*), and conventional custom (*sāmayika-ācārika*) is contingent upon that designation. The mention of a first and third birth is for the purpose of praising the second birth; for that is the best of all births. Indeed, one who has not been initiated (*adīkṣita*) is not entitled to sacrifice at all, whereas one who has not undergone the *upanayana* is not entitled to anything whatsoever.

Others, however, because of the commonality of being "first," consider the *ādhāna* (the ritual installation of the sacred fires) to be the initiation for sacrifice (*yajñadīkṣā*). For that too there is the possibility of birth, as it is said: "He who has not installed the fires is truly unborn. (2.169)
In that regard, his birth as a Brahmin, which is marked by the tying of the girdle of muñja grass, is said to have the Sāvitrī as its mother and the teacher as its father. (2.170)

Among these three births, that which is the "Vedic birth" (*brahmajanman*)—marked by the investiture with the sacred thread (*mauñjībandhana*) and characterized by the binding of the girdle (*mekhalā*)—is as follows: therein, the *Sāvitrī* is his mother, for it is through her being recited that this birth is accomplished. By this, he shows that the recitation of the *Sāvitrī* is the primary element in the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), since the boy is brought into proximity [to the teacher] for that purpose. The father is the teacher (*ācārya*). Birth is something to be brought about by both mother and father; therefore, by way of a metaphorical figure (*rūpakabhaṅgī*), the teacher and the *Sāvitrī* are there called "mother and father. (2.170)

It has been stated that [the boy] is marked by the binding of the girdle of muñja grass. In that regard, because of the fastening of the cord, the teacher might be honored like a father; for that purpose, it is said:
"They declare the teacher to be a father because of the imparting of the Veda;
for no ritual duty whatsoever is applicable to him prior to the binding of the muñja girdle. (2.171)

They designate the teacher as "father" because of the imparting of the Veda; this is due to teaching the entire Veda, not merely from the recitation of the *Sāvitrī* which is a constituent part of the initiation (*upanayana*). "Imparting" means the production of the student's capacity for the utterance of the syllables of the Veda. If this were so, then as long as fatherhood has not been attained by the teacher, the student would not undergo his second birth. And, having not yet attained the status of the twice-born, he would be free to act as he pleases, just as before the initiation. Therefore, it is said: "For prior to the tying of the girdle of muñja grass, no rite—whether based on the Śruti, the Smṛti, or established custom—that serves an unseen purpose, is applied to this student; nor is he entitled to perform them. Immediately after the initiation, he is entitled to all the duties of a twice-born man.

But surely, because he lacks knowledge at that stage, how could he be entitled [to perform the rites]? It is for this very reason it was said: "The pupil and the sacrificer [are both dependent] upon the teacher" (MDh 8.317). He must be instructed by the teacher. As it has been stated: "And he should instruct him in the rules of purification and conduct" (YDh 1.15). And as Gautama says: "The observance begins with the initiation ceremony" (GDh 2.6). However, the duty of the teacher extends until the completion of the Veda. 2.171
He shall not pronounce the Veda except when offering the *svadhā* libation;
for he is equal to a Śūdra as long as he is not born to the Veda. (2.172)

The phrase "until the tying of the girdle of muñja grass" is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Alternatively, the determination of the limit is established by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating "as long as he is not born into the Veda. *Brahman* here means the Veda; one should not utter that.
