This is the instruction for the father: just as he would protect [the child] from drinking intoxicants and the like, so too [he must protect him] from the utterance of the syllables of the Veda.

Some, however, describe this very prohibition against the utterance of *brahma* as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the study of auxiliary sciences such as grammar prior to initiation (*upanayana*). They explain the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) as follows: "He should not be made to speak by his father"; however, there is no fault in a child reciting some indistinct Vedic sentences on his own. This, however, is not correct. For it is read in another Smṛti: "One should not utter *brahma*" (GDh 2.5). Furthermore, it is heard in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) that "he is indeed equal to a Śūdra. This means it is stated that just as a Śūdra incurs sin, so too does this [uninitiated person].

By the word *svadhā*, the food prepared for the ancestors is meant here; or rather, the ancestral rite (*paitrya-karman*) itself is denoted by the word *svadhā*. That mantra by which [the offering] is poured out, abandoned, or delivered is called *svadhā-ninayana*, such as "May the ancestors be purified" (*śundhantāṃ pitaraḥ*, Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.6.14), and so forth. Apart from that, no other mantra should be recited. From this very [text], it is understood that the offering of water, the *nava-śrāddha*, and other rites for the father must be performed even by one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*). However, regarding the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* and similar rites, there is no entitlement because of the absence of sacred fire (*agnimattva*). This will be explained in the section on the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka*; we shall establish this point more precisely in the third book. (2.172)

For one who has undergone the initiation ceremony (upanayana), the instruction in the observances (vratādeśana) is prescribed, as well as the formal acquisition of the Veda (brahmagrahaṇa), in due order according to the rules. (173)

By the statement, "Having initiated the pupil... (MDh 2.69), the sequence of purification, conduct, and study has been declared. Therefore, one should recite [the texts] in that very order. Since study would follow immediately after initiation, this [next section] is commenced to establish a different sequence.

For one who has been initiated (*upanīta*), the vow of the three Vedas (*traividyā*) and so forth must be performed. Following that, [the injunction] "The Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied" [applies]. For the student (*brahmacārin*) for whom the initiation has been performed, the instruction regarding the vows (*vratādeśana*) is both prescribed and carried out by the teachers. It is prescribed in this manner on the basis of the scriptures (*śāstra*). Therefore, this very desire (*eṣaṇā*) is established as something that ought to be done. Consequently, the statement that "the grasping of the Veda (*brahman*) occurs in this sequence according to rule" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to complete the verse. (2.173)
Whatever skin, thread, girdle, staff, and garment have been prescribed for him, those same items are also required during his religious observances.

The authors of the Gṛhyasūtras have taught those rites that bear the name of *vrata*: "One who desires to grasp a Veda or some portion thereof [should perform this]. This practice of *vrata* is the entire collection of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*). In that regard, the rules that apply at the commencement of another *vrata* upon the completion of a previous one, as well as those at the initiation (*upanayana*), are the same for the instructions on the *vrata*. Now, what is the disposal of those items previously acquired? They are to be cast into water. But has it not already been stated regarding those previously acquired? What is the disposal of those that have perished? Upon their destruction, their function is performed by means of the scriptures, and they cease to exist because other [materials] are taken up. As for the skin prescribed for a particular student—for example, "the skin of a black antelope for a Brāhmaṇa, the skin of a Ruru deer for a Kṣatriya" (cf. MDh 2.41)—the same should be understood to apply to the staff and other such items. Since the subject under discussion is the *vrata*, the word *vrata* here refers to the instruction on the *vrata* (*vratādeśa*). (2.174)
A student living with his teacher must observe these rules, fully restraining the collection of his senses for the sake of increasing his own ascetic merit. (2.175)

This verse is intended to proclaim the importance of the collection of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) that will be described hereafter by treating them as a separate section. Thus, what was previously stated must certainly be performed; however, this [present practice] is even more significant than that, yielding a great fruit when it is carried out.

The mention of the *brahmacārin* is for the purpose of connecting [this section] as a distinct topic (*prakaraṇāntara*), lest there be a suspicion that these are not its specific duties. If this were merely a duty of the *brahmacārin*, why then is it stated as a separate topic? Because these [duties] are superior to the previous ones and share common characteristics, they are designated as a "separate topic" despite this degree of difference. The remaining words are restated merely for the sake of completing the verse.

He should serve—that is, he should practice—these [qualities] which are about to be described; they are indicated by the pronoun "these" (*imān*) because they are present in the mind. "Dwelling with the teacher" means residing in the proximity of the teacher for the purpose of studying knowledge, thereby expressing constant attendance. "Having fully restrained the collection of senses" means according to the path previously mentioned. This is for the sake of increasing austerity—that is, for the sake of the self-purification (*ātmasaṃskāra*) produced by the performance of the injunctions for study. (2.175)
He now states those rules which were previously promised:
"Having bathed daily and being pure, one should perform the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors, as well as the worship of the deities and the placing of fuel on the sacred fire. (2.176)

Having bathed daily and become pure—that is, having removed impurity through bathing—one should perform the libations (*tarpaṇa*) for the gods, sages, and ancestors. However, if one is not [already] pure, then one must certainly bathe. Because bathing is taught here as a cause of purification by the mention of the term "pure," it is not to be performed as a mandatory observance (*vrata*) like that of a *snātaka*. For this very reason, bathing is prohibited in another *smṛti* text. That prohibition refers to bathing with clay characterized by grooming. Gautama, however, has prescribed bathing in this manner: "He floats in the waters like a staff" (cf. ĀpDh 1.2.30). The removal of dirt by scrubbing with the hands and so forth must not be done. In the absence of contact with impure substances and the like, that dirt which arises from sweat or is innate to the contact of dust with the garment does not constitute impurity; for that is of a fixed nature. And thus the *Brāhmaṇa* shows that the wearing of such dirt is indeed a means of dharma: "What indeed is dirt? What is the antelope skin? What are the beard-hairs? What is austerity? (AitB 7.13).

How, then, is it understood that bathing has the purpose of purification? It is not the case that one who has bathed and one who is pure—both being thus qualified—are enjoined for the rites of the gods. This is because there is no impurity in one who has already bathed; furthermore, since bathing is prescribed for one who has already performed purification, sipping water (*ācamana*), and so forth—as in the rule, "Having bathed and sipped water, he should sip water again" (VaDh 3.38)—when such a degree of purity is understood to be intended by the term "pure," then bathing itself, which was already applicable when its occasion arose, is stated once more. Moreover, this other Smṛti text serves to prohibit [bathing] even when the occasion of impurity is absent. Thus, in the rule, "Having studied the Veda, he should bathe" (BauG 2.5.6), it will serve as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) once the injunction for Vedic study has been completed.

One should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the gods, sages, and ancestors. This is understood to be exactly like the offering of water (*udakadāna*) prescribed among the duties of a householder, because of its association with the word *tarpaṇa*. As it is said: "Whatever one satisfies with water" (MDh 3.283), and likewise, "he satisfies the deities" (ĀśG 3.4.1); thus the authors of the *Gṛhyasūtras* have declared this rite to be accomplished by means of water. Furthermore, this is known as "water-libation" (*udakatarpaṇa*). Those deities recited by the authors of the *Gṛhyasūtras* are Agni, Prajāpati, Brahmā, and so forth. And their "satisfying" (*tarpaṇa*) does not mean the production of satiety; rather, it is the casting of handfuls of water intended for them. Therefore, this is said to be a sacrifice (*yāga*) having water as its substance. For otherwise, they would not possess the status of a deity; for it is recorded in tradition that a deity is the recipient of a sacrifice, not the agent of satisfaction.

For this is the defining characteristic of a deity: deities are recipients of hymns (*sūkta*) and recipients of oblations (*havis*). In this context, they partake of the hymn by virtue of being its object of praise, and they partake of the oblation by virtue of being its recipient. Furthermore, the act of offering water is figuratively described as making them recipients for the purpose of their satisfaction. A gift to a teacher or similar person is understood through the ownership [of the object] directed toward that person, such as a cow or other property; likewise, a deity is also a recipient. Because of this commonality of being a recipient, it is said that "they are satisfied. If this [offering of water] were for the sake of satisfying the deity, then the water-libation (*udakatarpaṇa*) would be a purificatory rite (*saṃskārakarma*). However, it is not possible for deities to be objects of purification, for they have never been used [for a purpose], nor will they ever be used. Nor is it possible for something whose function has not been performed or will not be performed to be an object of purification.

The sages (*ṛṣi*) are those who are the ancestral seers (*ārṣeya*) of a particular lineage; for example, among the Parāśaras, they are Vasiṣṭha, Śakti, and Pāraśarya. However, the authors of the *Gṛhya-sūtras* have specified that the sages who are the "seers of the mantras" (*mantradṛś*) are to be offered libations, namely Madhucchandas, Gṛtsamada, Viśvāmitra, and so forth. Since the word "sage" (*ṛṣi*) is used without qualification, both types of sages would seem to be included. Nevertheless, because the *Gṛhya-smṛti* is a specific (specialized) tradition, it is proper to accept only those [sages] mentioned therein.

The ancestors are those who have passed away before, namely the fathers and grandfathers, as well as the *sapiṇḍas* and the *samānodakas*. The "satisfying of the ancestors" (*pitṛtarpaṇa*) is simply the act of libation itself. This will be explained explicitly in the section on the rules for the *śrāddha* ceremony.

Regarding the worship of deities (*devatābhyarcanam*): On this point, some ancient authorities have reflected as follows: "What indeed are these so-called 'deities' for whom this worship is prescribed? If they are those depicted in paintings or manuscripts—four-armed, holding a thunderbolt in hand, and so forth—as worldly people refer to them, then the designation 'deity' applied to them is merely figurative (*gauṇa*). Alternatively, if they are those understood from Vedic injunctions (*codanā*) and mantra-texts related to hymns (*sūkta*) and oblations (*havis*), such as Agni, Agni-Soma, Mitra-Varuṇa, Indra, and Viṣṇu, as recorded by those who know the relationship between words and their meanings; even so, their status as deities would consist solely in their connection to those ritual acts, not in their connection to any external object. Furthermore, a deity belongs only to that specific oblation for which she is enjoined. For instance, in the rule 'the eight-potherd cake is for Agni' (*āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālaḥ*), Agni is the deity for the *puroḍāśa* cake, but not for a *caru* offering to Sūrya. And this is their conclusion: since a primary sense is impossible, it is logical to accept the figurative one, especially because of established practice (*samācāra*). Therefore, this injunction for worship applies only to images. As for the true nature of this matter, we shall explain it under the verse beginning 'as in the case of a vow, [one should act] toward the deity of the gods' (MDh 2.189)."
The placing of fuel means the throwing of small pieces of wood into the fire every morning and evening. (2.176)
He should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, savory flavors, women, all fermented acids, and indeed the harming of living beings. (2.177)

*Madhu* refers to honey from bees (*sāragha*). As for *mādhvīka*, because it is an intoxicant (*madya*), it is prohibited even before the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) by the rule: "A Brāhmaṇa should always avoid intoxicants" (cf. GDh 2.20). *Māṃsa* includes even meat that has been consecrated (*prokṣita*) and so forth. By the word *gandha*, substances such as camphor and aloe-wood (*aguru*)—which possess an excellence of fragrance—are prohibited through a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on their relationship [to the sense of smell]. What is prohibited is the enjoyment of these, such as by using them as unguents; however, the fragrance itself, which comes from its own source, cannot be prevented. Even in that case, there is no prohibition against [the scent] occurring spontaneously; yet, if one seeks enjoyment through incense of aloe-wood and the like, there is indeed a fault. Therefore, when one is employed by a teacher to cut down a sandalwood tree or similar wood, there is no fault in smelling its fragrance arising from the very nature of the object. Because of its association with garlands (*mālya*), such a fragrance is understood here. However, there is no prohibition regarding fragrances that are not of this kind—that is, those which do not intoxicate the heart, such as the scent of *kuṣṭha*, ghee, or putrid wood. *Mālya* is a flower strung together. *Rasa*s are the sweet, sour, and other tastes.

But surely, since that which is devoid of flavor cannot be eaten, the very function of life would cease? True; what is prohibited here are substances such as molasses and the like when they possess an excessive degree of flavor. Furthermore, there is a prohibition even against those [substances] contained within other materials used for seasoning. Alternatively, this is a prohibition against attachment to food that has been prepared and is extremely flavorful. As it has been said: "He who fears wealth as he would a serpent, sweet food as he would poison, and women as he would ogresses—he attains true knowledge. (MSSaṃ 4121)

Others, however, maintain that [the prohibition applies to] the erotic and other sentiments (*śṛṅgārādi*). They hold that nourishment by the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) should not be produced through the viewing of dramas and the like, or through the hearing of poetry. But the view of others is this: just as sugarcane, *āmalaka* fruit, and so forth possess a juice (*rasa*) in the form of internal liquid like water, the prohibition applies to that which has been squeezed out and separated, but not to that which remains within it. And this is incorrect; for the word *rasa* is not commonly known as a synonym for liquid. Furthermore, only that which is fit to end in consumption is prohibited for that thing. Thus, there is a prohibition regarding the eating of honey and meat, but not regarding their being seen or touched. In the case of perfumes and garlands as well, the taking of them with the intent of adorning the body is prohibited, but not their grasping by the hand or otherwise in any way. Likewise, women [are prohibited] in connection with sexual intercourse. It is precisely because of such a suspicion that he will prohibit looking at and touching them. And thus says Gautama: "Looking at and touching women when there is a suspicion of sexual intercourse" (GDh 2.16).

"Sour things" (*śuktāni*) are those that have acquired a sour taste either through mere fermentation or through contact with other substances. Since they are already established as being prohibited by virtue of their nature as twice-born (*dvijāti*) duties, the repetition [of the term] is for the purpose of including "figurative" (*gauṇa*) sour things. By this, harsh and rough words are also prohibited. As Gautama stated, "sour words" (*GDh 2.19*), this inclusion of "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of revealing this very meaning. Having referred back to those things sour in taste, "all" is prescribed; thus, the inclusion of the figurative sense is established.

However, those who explain it thus—that by the word *śukta* (sour) there is a prohibition of taste, and by the word *sarva* (all) there is a prohibition of non-mental utterances—should be asked this: why is the inclusion of the word "all" not for the purpose of prohibiting those things whose [specific] meanings have already been prohibited? For if that were the case, it would follow that curds and the like, when they have turned sour, would also be prohibited. But if, having relied upon their actual occurrence, the prohibition is explained as having its meaning already established, then there is no fault whatsoever.

Since the killing of living beings such as mosquitoes and flies might occur through negligence, this prohibition is reiterated for the sake of careful avoidance. Alternatively, it serves to establish itself as an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). For there is not only a transgression of a prohibition intended for human welfare (*puruṣārtha*) in the case of violence, but also a transgression of the purpose of the injunction for Vedic study. If it is asked, "Why is this not likewise assumed for sour gruel (*śukta*) and other such things?"—the answer is that in those cases there is scope [for the prohibition] elsewhere; and when another alternative exists, it is more weighty to avoid the futility of a single, uniform subject matter. (2.177)
Anointing the body, applying collyrium to the eyes, wearing shoes, carrying an umbrella, as well as desire, anger, greed, dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments; 2.178.

*Abhyaṅga* (anointing) is the rubbing of the head and body with unctuous substances such as clarified butter or oil; *añjana* (collyrium) is for the eyes. The mention of the eyes is merely for the sake of completing the meter. Furthermore, the prohibition regarding these two applies to them when intended as bodily ornaments, not when used for medicinal purposes, as they are mentioned in conjunction with perfumes, garlands, and the like. *Upānahau* refers to leather sandals, not shoes alone. The carrying of an umbrella is prohibited whether by one's own hand or by the hand of another. *Kāma* is passion; the prohibition of sexual desire (*manmatha*) is already established by the prohibition of women. *Krodha* is anger; *lobha* is delusion. *Ahaṃkāra* and *mamakāra* are mental states. *Nartana* (dancing) is the movement of limbs for the delight of common people, as well as the application of dramatic gestures (*abhinaya*) as seen in the works of Bharata and others. *Gīta* (singing) is the demonstration of musical notes such as *ṣaḍja*. *Vādana* (instrumental music) is the production of pitched sounds with instruments such as the lute or flute, as well as the striking of drums such as the *paṇava* and *mṛdaṅga* in accordance with rhythmic measures (*tāla*). (2.178)
Gambling, idle gossip, slander, as well as falsehood; gazing at and touching women, and the harming of others. (2.179)

Gambling is playing with dice. Betting on animals such as cocks and the like is prohibited because the word *dyūta* (gambling) is a general term. "Dispute with people" refers to verbal quarrels over worldly matters without cause, or the seeking of news regarding local events, or questioning them. "Slander" is the speaking of others' faults out of malice. "Falsehood" is when something seen or heard in one way is stated otherwise. The accusative case is used here due to the connection with the phrase "he should avoid in all cases. And [he should avoid] looking at and touching women. "Looking" is the examination of the arrangement of their limbs, thinking, "This limb of hers is beautiful, this is not. "Touching" is embracing. These two are prohibited even for a child, lest there be suspicion of sexual intercourse. "Harming another" means doing injury; it is the persistent obstruction of someone in the accomplishment of a certain goal. When asked about the acquisition of a maiden or similar matters, one should not state that even an unsuitable person is unsuitable; rather, one should remain silent, because of the prohibition against falsehood. (2.179)
One should always sleep alone and never let semen be spilled;
for by spilling semen out of desire, one destroys his own vow. 2.180.

One should always sleep alone and never spill one's semen, even in a non-vaginal opening; [the inclusion of "even in a vaginal opening" is established by the general prohibition against women]. Regarding this, there is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*): "For by spilling it out of desire. Here, "desire" (*kāma*) means intention. By spilling—that is, discharging—semen through manual manipulation or sexual intercourse in a non-vaginal opening, one destroys and ruins one's own vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). (2.180)

If a twice-born student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should involuntarily emit semen during sleep, he shall bathe, worship the sun, and then mutter three times the verse beginning with "punar mām. (2.181)

The penance for an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow) due to lust [is prescribed elsewhere]; however, regarding this [penance], he says it is for when it is done unintentionally (*akāmāt*). The mention of "sleep" is not intended to be significant; rather, "unintentionally" is itself the cause. For indeed, there can be no occurrence of desire (*kāma*) in sleep. Therefore, even if semen should somehow flow out while one is not asleep—just like a discharge of sweat or blood—even in that case, this same penance applies. Having unintentionally emitted semen, one should perform this penance and mutter the verse beginning with "punar mām" (AVŚ 7.67.1). 2.181.
He should fetch a water-pot, flowers, cow dung, earth, and kuśa grass—as much as required—and he should go out for alms every day. (2.182)

He should fetch water-jars and so forth for as much as is necessary to accomplish the purpose of his teacher. This is mentioned by way of illustration; he should also perform whatever other household tasks are appropriate and not censurable. This verse is intended to show that he must not be made to perform censurable acts—such as cleaning up after [the teacher] or clearing away leftovers—except when the teacher himself does so. For service toward the teacher has been enjoined in general terms. The analysis of the compound is: "as much as is the purpose (artha) of these."

He should go for alms every day. Here, "alms" (*bhaikṣa*) refers to cooked food that is extremely small in quantity, sufficient only for sustenance. This is understood from the use of the word "food" (*anna*) in the prohibition, "One should not eat the food of a single person" (MDh 2.188). Furthermore, because of the grammatical coordination in the rule, "Having collected alms and having offered them [to his teacher], he should eat" (cf. MDh 2.51), it is understood to be cooked food. For if dry grain were begged, how could there be eating of it? Moreover, if food were collected and then cooked in the teacher's house, it would have the nature of being raw material (*prakṛti*) for alms, rather than being alms itself. It is by common usage that such [cooked food] alone is called "alms. "Every day" (*ahar-ahaḥ*). Now, one might object: since it is already established by the rule, "He should subsist constantly on alms" (MDh 2.188), does this not already imply going for alms every day? The inclusion of the word "constantly" (*nitya*) is for the purpose of prescribing the mode of subsistence. Otherwise, one might subsist even on stale food provided it is mixed with fats like ghee; to prevent this, the following is stated: having begged every day, one must eat. One must not, however, eat on a subsequent day something that was begged on a previous day after it has been kept overnight, even if it is mixed with some fat, as a counter-exception. (2.182)
He states those from whom alms are to be obtained:
"A student, being self-restrained, should daily collect alms from the houses of those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifices, who are praiseworthy in their own duties. (2.183)

From the houses of those who are not deficient in their knowledge of the Vedas and are endowed with the study of the Vedas, and who, being eligible, are performers of sacrifices—not deficient or excluded, meaning they are possessed of them—and who are praiseworthy in their own duties; or, alternatively, those who are "praiseworthy in their own duties" refers to those who are content with their own proper occupation and do not subsist on livelihoods such as usury; from the houses of these, one should collect alms by begging and take them, being self-controlled and pure. The word "daily" (*anvaham*) is a restatement. (2.183)
One should not beg for alms from the family of the guru, nor from the families of one's kinsmen or relatives.
However, if houses of others are unavailable, one should avoid each preceding [house] in preference for the next.

Even though he possesses these qualities, he should not beg for alms at the house of his teacher. First, from the family—that is, the lineage; nor even from those who are the teacher’s paternal uncles and so forth. From "kinsmen" (*jñātayaḥ*) means from the family of those on the father's side who are fellow students; and from "relatives" (*bandhuṣu*), meaning those on the mother's side such as maternal uncles and so forth. One should not construe it thus: "from the teacher's kinsmen and so forth," because they are already included by the word "family" (*kula*) itself in the phrase "the teacher's family. From where, then, should he beg? From other houses besides these. If there is no acquisition—that is, if it is impossible [to find food] in other houses; or if the entire village is pervaded by the teacher's kinsmen and relatives and there are no others at all; or if there are others but they do not give food—then one may beg even in these houses. In the absence of others, he should first beg from a relative; in the absence of that, from a kinsman; in the absence of that, from the teacher's family. (2.184)
Or, if those previously mentioned are unavailable, he may wander through the entire village, restraining his speech and remaining pure, while avoiding those who have been accused of crimes. (2.185)

In the absence of those previously mentioned who are not lacking in Vedic study and sacrifices, he may wander for the sake of subsistence through the entire village, disregarding the distinctions between social classes (*varṇa*), provided he avoids only those who are accused—that is, those notorious for having committed sins—even if their current offenses are not visible. Thus says Gautama: "He may wander for alms among all classes, excluding those who are accused or outcastes" (GDh 2.35). Restraining his speech, he shall not utter any words other than the request for alms until he has obtained them. (2.185)
Having brought fuel from afar, he should place it in the open air;
and evening and morning, he should unwearyingly offer oblations into the fire with that fuel. (2.186)

The mention of "far away" (*dūragrahaṇam*) is intended to indicate a place that is not possessed by anyone. It is said that the forest is far from the village, and there is no ownership of anything there. For if the meaning of "far" were not indicated, the sense of the scripture would be unsettled as to how far [the wood] must be. *Āhṛtya* means having brought; *saṃnidadhyāt* means one should place it. *Vihāyasi* means above the house. Indeed, placing [the wood] in the supportless atmosphere is not possible. One should offer oblations with those [sticks] in the evening and in the morning. As for the bringing [of the wood], it may be done at that time or at another time according to one's wish. They say that placing it in the atmosphere is for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Others, however, say that wood being brought at present becomes damp from a tree; therefore, it should be understood that it is to be placed above the house or on something else such as a wall. 2.186.
If, while not being ill, he fails to go out for alms and fails to kindle the sacred fire for seven nights, he shall perform the penance of an *avakīrṇin*. (2.187)

Without performing [the rites of] maintaining the sacred fire, gathering fuel, and begging for alms continuously for seven nights—that is, for seven days—one who is not ill, being healthy, shall perform the expiation known as the *avakīrṇi-vrata*, whose nature will be described in the eleventh chapter (MDh 11.117). This is for the purpose of proclaiming the gravity of the offense; however, this is not itself the expiation in this case. For in another Smṛti, a different, minor expiation is prescribed here: "An oblation of clarified butter to Savitṛ, or [recitation] of the *retasyā* verses" (cf. GDh 23.20). Furthermore, there is an indicative mark here: if this were the actual expiation, then it would have been listed as the occasion [for the rite] in the section on the expiation for an *avakīrṇin*, just like sexual intercourse with a woman.

However, those who explain that both of these must necessarily be performed for seven nights, and that there is a fault in failing to do so, whereas after the seven nights have been completed there is no fault in not performing them thereafter, and that those seven days are taken from the beginning, starting from the initiation (*upanayana*)—this is incorrect, because it contradicts the rule, "One should perform [them] until the return home" (MDh 2.108), and because it contradicts the immediately following verse. || 2.187 ||
One who observes the vow should always subsist on alms; he should not eat food from a single source. For one who observes the vow, subsistence on alms is declared to be equal to fasting. (2.188)

But is it not already established by scripture that "he should go for alms day after day" (MDh 2.182)? For in this way, the practice of begging for alms serves a visible purpose. And it has been stated: "Having offered it to his teacher, he should eat" (MDh 2.51). Moreover, that eating is not a consecration of the alms such that it would serve as a means of livelihood. Some say: [this rule] is restated in order to declare that one who observes the vow must not eat food from a single source.

This too is incorrect, because the eating of food from a single person is already prohibited by the word *bhaikṣa* itself. *Bhaikṣa* is defined as a collection (*samūha*) of alms; therefore, how could there be any possibility of eating the food of one person? All of this is restated for the purpose of permitting [the consumption of food] for ancestral rites (*pitrya*). One should maintain oneself through *bhaikṣa*; that is, one should sustain oneself by eating alms-food. One should ensure the maintenance of life, but one should not eat food belonging to a single person, nor should one consume the food of a single alms-offering.

Furthermore, one should not entertain this doubt: "One should not eat food belonging to a single owner, but rather that which belongs to many owners who are undivided brothers. *Ekānnāda* means one who eats *ekānna*—that is, the food of one person or the food of a single individual. *Vratī* refers to a celibate student (*brahmacārī*). This word is understood from the context itself; the term *vrati* is included merely for the sake of completing the verse. Here follows an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*): it is traditionally taught that the subsistence of a celibate student by means of alms alone—the maintenance of the body—is equal in merit to fasting. (2.188)
In a rite dedicated to the gods, he may eat like one observing a vow; in a rite for the ancestors, he may eat like a seer (ṛṣi).
If invited, he may eat at his pleasure; his vow is not thereby violated. (2.189)

This is an exception (*apavāda*) regarding the instruction on living by begging (*bhikṣāvṛtti*) under specific circumstances. When a *devadaivatyam*—a meal for Brahmins performed in honor of the gods—is being prepared, or when a *pitryam*—a rite for the ancestors—is being performed, one who has been invited and requested may eat food from a single person at will; however, he must not beg for it himself. Furthermore, that [eating] is "like a vow" (*vratavat*), meaning it is not contrary to his vows and is devoid of honey and meat. The two words *vratavat* and *ṛṣivat* express one and the same meaning; they do not establish a distinction between village and forest life based on different rituals. The double mention is merely for the sake of the meter. If "ṛṣi" were taken to mean a forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*), then the eating of meat would also be permitted for a religious student (*brahmacārin*), since for such a person there is the rule: "He may even consume meat from a deer" (*GDh* 3.31). A *devadaivatyam* is that which has the gods as its deities (*devatā*). This feeding of Brahmins is prescribed in divine rites such as the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, and others, as well as in rites like the *āgrahāyaṇī*, where it is stated: "Having fed the Brahmins, he should cause them to recite benedictions. In this context, this is the permission granted.

Others, however, consider that the feeding of Brahmins which is performed on the seventh lunar day and so forth, dedicated to deities such as Āditya, constitutes a rite for a deity (*devadaivatyam*). That is incorrect. For there is no connection with a deity in the act of eating, since eating is not a means of sacrifice (*ayāgasādhana*). Nor is a deity merely the object of dedication; otherwise, it would follow that in the cases "he gives a cow to his teacher" and "he sweeps the house," the teacher and the house would also be deities. For the act of eating has a direct connection with the eater. Āditya, however, is neither a grammatical participant (*kāraka*) nor an object of dedication like a house, nor is the meal intended for him. Indeed, the accusative case indicates that the meal is for the sake of the eater, not for the sake of Āditya. Furthermore, this has never been stated anywhere: "One should feed Brahmins dedicated to Āditya and others."

If it is argued that the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is to be inferred from established practice (*samācāra*), we say no, because such a practice has an observable basis. Indeed, there is a basis: the external *smṛtis*. In that case, the meaning of the scriptural injunction would be "one should gratify the deities by feeding Brāhmaṇas. But this meaning cannot be so inferred. For the purpose of the scripture does not consist primarily in the gratification of the deities; rather, it consists primarily in the performance of the enjoined act (*vidhyartha*). Furthermore, in this enjoined act, there is no connection with the deities intended—such as Āditya and others—either through the medium of the object (*viṣaya*) or through the medium of the qualification (*adhikāra*). It is not a contingent occasion (*nimitta*) like the breaking [of a sacrificial vessel], nor is it something desired as being connected to oneself (*svasaṃbandhitayā*) like cattle and the like, because they are not of a nature that can be enjoyed. If it is argued that the satisfaction residing in them is what is desired, even that requires another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for its own establishment. And no such means exists. For the satisfaction of Āditya and the others is not established through perception or other means in the way that cattle and the like are, such that it could be linked to an injunction for a sacrifice performed by another for the sake of that which is desired.

But as for the idea that "my master will cause [me] to sacrifice so that he may obtain his own desired fruit"—this too must be disregarded due to a lack of evidence. Furthermore, an injunction (*vidhi*) is not the authority regarding this matter. For an injunction enjoins a person by connecting itself to a known qualification of the performer; it does not, however, make known the existence of that which is being desired. Rather, the injunction measures out its authority by establishing that the object of desire—already known through other means of knowledge—is a qualification of the performer, related to the performer, and to be accomplished through the performance.

Now, this sacrifice is the [primary] act, and its consumption is the disposal (*pratipatti*). Let it be so, provided there is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). First of all, it cannot be established that the consumption is directly connected to the deity; however, a connection mediated by the sacrifice is not precluded. Furthermore, one does not engage in this with the thought of a sacrifice; rather, [one thinks], "When the Brahmins have been fed, the deity is pleased. Therefore, the deity is neither the factor (*kāraka*) of the consumption nor a qualifier of that factor. Consequently, there is no connection [of the deity] as the object (*viṣaya*). Nor is there the status of being the intended recipient (*uddeśyatva*) for Āditya and others. For one is intended as the recipient in the act of feeding only when food is given to them, and that [food] is given to the Brahmins. Moreover, being merely the intended recipient does not constitute being a deity, because it would follow [absurdly] that the house and the teacher in such cases as "he gives a cow to the teacher" and "he sweeps the house" would also be deities.

But then, how can there be the feeding of Brahmins at a rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*)? For even there, the ancestors would not be the deities; nor does the *homa* have the status of being "for the ancestors," because other deities are heard [in the injunctions]. Since the satisfaction of the ancestors—unlike the satisfaction of Āditya and others—is not established by any other means of knowledge, it cannot be the objective (*sādhya*) related to the injunction.

On this point they say: the gratification of the ancestors (*pitṛprīti*) is indeed established here. Because the selves (*ātman*) are imperishable, the ancestors are established; and for them, a connection with a body is brought about through their *karmas*. For the offering of food (*tadbhojana*) is the primary element here. Indeed, its fruit is heard in scripture: "By feeding [the ancestors], one obtains abundant fruit" (cf. MDh 3.119). And that fruit belongs to the ancestors, insofar as there may be their satisfaction (*tṛpti*). This satisfaction is merely pleasure (*prītimātra*); it does not arise characterized by satiety (*sauhitya*), which is the fruit of the act of eating as it occurs for human beings. There is some form of pleasure for the ancestors resulting from their own *karma*, produced when they have been reborn in a particular birth. This verbal root expresses mere pleasure, whereas satiety is a specific state; that [satiety] is to be understood through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*).

And it should not be objected here: "The son is the agent; how then can the fruit accrue to the agent when [the rites] are performed for the ancestors? For those who know the principles of logic do not say that these Vedic rituals bestow their fruit upon another.

For in this matter, the fathers themselves are the qualified agents (*adhikārin*) and the performers (*kartṛ*). By the very act of procreating offspring, all this has been accomplished by the fathers. It was for this purpose alone that he [the son] was produced, with the thought: "He will provide benefit, both seen and unseen. Consequently, just as in the *Sarvasvāra* sacrifice, due to the absence [of the sacrificer], the deceased exercises agency through the command, "O Brāhmaṇas, complete my sacrifice," regarding the subsequent ritual members (*aṅga*), so too should it be understood here. This much is the distinction: there, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)—who seek their livelihood and are hired for wages—are the performers, being impelled by another qualification; but here, the son is impelled solely by that [procreative] injunction. Just as the father, impelled by the injunction of procreation, has the qualification for the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) performed for the sake of the son because that injunction extends up to the final instruction (*anuśāsana*), so too does the son have the qualification for the *śrāddha* and other rites for the sake of the father. Likewise, while the father is alive, [the son must perform the rite] when the parents are old, according to the rule: "But when mother and father are old" (added verse to MDh 11.5); and the same applies even when he has passed away.

Furthermore, this entitlement is not optional like that of the Vaiśvānara sacrifice. As it is said: "Upon the birth of a son, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. He who, when a son is born, performs this sacrifice, becomes purified, radiant, an eater of food, and endowed with sensory power" (TS 2.2.5.3). Thus, the father's entitlement to the Vaiśvānara rite for the sake of obtaining results such as a son is not mandatory, unlike the *cūḍā* and other rites. In this case, however, because of the rule "the ancestral rite (*pitrya*) must be performed until death" (MDh 3.269), it is a lifelong obligation.

The claim that the Vedic fruit does not accrue to the performer is otherwise refined as follows: Just as the fruit characterized by possessing a son distinguished by the Vaiśvānara rite belongs to the father alone—and thus the fruit does not go to one who is not the performer—so too here, that fruit which is the father’s joy belongs to the son alone. In both ways, the fact that the fruit accrues to the father as the performer is not contradicted; for since such a fruit is desired precisely through the procreation of offspring, there is no occurrence of an undesired fruit even for the ancestors.
If the ancestors are not the deities in the *śrāddha*, how then is there this patronymic suffix (*taddhita*) in the term "this is a rite for the ancestors" (*pitrya*)?

We say: "Because of the commonality of being the intended recipient (*uddeśyatva*). [In the case of the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*,] the ancestors are instructed thus: "This feeding of Brahmins is for your benefit. However, in the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the ancestors themselves are the deities (*devatā*). They do not consider the ancestors to be the deities in the *śrāddha*. Rather, that the Brahmins are fed is like the offering (*avadāna*) of clarified butter, sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), and so forth, into the fire during a *homa*. Such is this [feeding]. And thus, the Brahmins attain the status of ancestors. Therefore, at the time of serving the food, the ancestors alone are the intended recipients, with the thought: "This is for you, not for me. The Brahmins, however, occupy the position of the *āhavanīya* fire. The only difference is that while in the *āhavanīya* the oblation is cast [into it], in the case of the Brahmins it is placed near them, and they take it up by themselves.

Nor can it be said that "the *śrāddha* is not a sacrifice (*yāga*), because the *svāhākāra* is not for the sake of a deity therein," since we observe [the use of *svāhākāra*] in rites such as the *sviṣṭakṛt*. Therefore, even though it is a sacrifice, the *śrāddha* rite will have the ancestors (*pitṛs*) as its purpose. This will not contradict the fact that the ancestors possess the status of deities (*devatātva*) and are the recipients of the fruit. We shall explain in the third [chapter] something related to this that has not yet been mentioned.
Consequently, it is established that the Sun and other [deities] are not the deities in the feeding of Brahmins.

But is this definition not also too narrow? For we observe the conventional usage of the term *devatā* even in the absence of a connection with sacrifice, as in the cases: "the worship of the deities" (*devatānāṃ ca pūjanam*) and "one should approach the deities" (*daivatāny abhigacchet*). Neither worship nor approaching by means of walking toward them is possible in relation to deities. This is not a fault. Where there is an injunction regarding a deity, there this rule for worship will apply—whether in the case of the Vaiśvadeva deities or those connected with the Agnihotra and other rites.

But even so, this is not tenable. For it is not possible for a deity to be an object of worship, because that would entail the loss of its essential nature (*svarūpa*). If it were the object of the act of worship, it would become the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) of the sacrifice. As it has been said: "Nothing happens to [the agent] in respect to another action. For a *kāraka* is a capacity (*śakti*), and that capacity differs with each action. Since it is understood through its effects, its differentiation is logical only as far as the effects extend. Therefore, what is a recipient remains precisely a recipient; it does not incur the status of being an object (*karman*). How then is it that in the case of "Give to the cook," the agent of the root *pac* (to cook) becomes the recipient of the root *dā* (to give)? Or as in: "With his limbs wounded by arrows, he went along helplessly while being gazed upon by the side-glances of his beloved"? The resolution to this has already been stated: because the distinction between the capacity and the possessor of the capacity is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), the expression "having eaten, he goes" (*vrajati bhuktvā*) is established. Therefore, if this [passage] concerns the object of worship, there is no attainment of a deity; if the deities are Āditya and others, there is no injunction for worship. For when a deity is already established, worship is not enjoined with reference to it. Indeed, the word "deity" is not a general term for Āditya and others, in the way that the word "cow" applies to the Śāgaleya and other breeds.

To this it is replied: It is true that the Sun and others are not deities by their very nature; this is a relative term (*saṃbandhiśabda*). The meaning of "deity" is to be understood solely from the injunction (*vidhi*), according to the principle: "That for which an oblation is prescribed is its deity. It has already been stated that the same Agni is not the deity in a rite other than the Āgneya. However, a rule of worship cannot occur without an object of worship, and deities are heard of in scripture as objects of worship. In that regard, if worship is possible in its primary sense toward the deity, then sacrifice itself must be understood as worship. Since that [sacrifice] requires components, and in the absence of an explicit mention of substance and deity, this [text] is to be understood as a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of prescribing the forenoon time. Thus, it is effectively stated that "rites dedicated to the deities (*daivata*) should be performed in the forenoon."

Why is it said that no deity is heard [in the text], given that the word "deity" (*devatā*) does not appear explicitly? This word "deity" is not a general term; rather, this is a prescription for worship directed toward those whose status as deities is observed elsewhere. Therefore, Agni, Āditya, Rudra, Indra, Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, and so forth, are to be worshipped. And for the sake of worship, there is the offering of incense, lamps, garlands, food-oblations, and the like. Among these, Agni has a direct connection [to the ritual]. As for Āditya, because he resides at a distance, one offers substances such as perfumes by designating him while in a pure place. Since the actual forms of Indra and the others are imperceptible, the procedure is carried out by designating them through their names, Indra and so on. Although worship primarily consists in the object being worshipped, nevertheless, when those being worshipped are subordinate to some other purpose, it is understood that the act of worship itself is what must be performed. For if the substance were primary, it could not be the subject of an injunction. As stated: "Those [actions] are of two kinds, being either subordinate or primary" (PMS 2.1.6), and "But those by which a substance is intended to be prepared... (PMS 2.1.7).

But it is logical [that this is for the sake of the worshipper], as in the case of hymns of praise and the like. Just as a hymn of praise is not for the sake of the object praised, so too this worship is not for the sake of the object worshipped. If it is argued that there is no mention of the roots *stu* (to praise) or *saṃs* (to honor), it has been stated here that the accusative case is used because it is observed in the case of groats (*saktu*). Likewise, in the injunction, "One should circumambulate clay, a cow, and a deity from left to right," the practice of moving to the right is prescribed. Ritual acts for the gods must be performed with the right hand. For it is not possible for a deity—unlike clay and the like—to occupy a position by way of the right path, because a deity is formless.

Thus, regarding the injunction "one should approach the deities": since it is impossible to reach the vicinity of the deities through the activity of walking on foot, and because the root *gam* signifies "knowledge," how does this "approaching" (*abhigamana*) differ from "recollection"? The meaning is that one should approach the deities; at the time of the ritual, one should meditate upon them with the mind and avoid mental distraction, which is known as agitation. In this way, this Smṛti rule possesses a verifiable source: "One should meditate with the mind upon whichever deity the oblation has been taken for."

But surely this too is already established by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for its being the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*). There is no fault here, because confusion and agitation are possible. In the same way, common usages such as "the property of the gods," "the cattle of the gods," and "the wealth of the gods" are to be understood as referring to cattle and other items that have been set aside for the sake of those [gods].

In matters concerning punishment (*daṇḍādhikāra*), however, they maintain that the legal dealings regarding deities apply only to their images (*pratikṛti*). Otherwise, there would be a violation of the established order. Since images—which are the assumed forms of deities—are related to them through an assumed relationship of owner and owned, it is precisely these that constitute "deity-property" (*devadravya*) in such passages as: "The property of deities, Brahmins, and kings should be known as the most excellent" (NSm 14.15). For deities do not possess a relationship of owner and owned; since the primary meaning is impossible, only a figurative meaning is to be accepted.

What, then, is the secondary (gauṇa) meaning here? For in all cases, the comprehension of a secondary meaning arises from the connection with common qualities, as in examples such as "The boy is fire," where one perceives those qualities in the white boy. And those qualities are to be determined through perception and other means of knowledge. But in this case, since the referent of the deity is to be understood only through its function (*kārya*), and because its specific nature is not understood from its function, how can there be a determination of common qualities in the images?

To this it is replied: because such forms are heard in the mantras and arthavādas, and because those [passages] are explained as figurative praise (guṇavāda), those who—failing to perceive their basis—grasp the literal meaning and thus establish that identity in Indra and others, perceive a similarity in the images; therefore, figurative usage (gauṇatā) is entirely appropriate.

As for those who claim that the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas for the Viśvedevas at the *śrāddha* itself constitutes the rite dedicated to the gods (*daivadevatya*), for them this repeated mention is purposeless; because it is an ancillary part of the ancestral rite (*pitrya*), it is already included by the term "ancestral. Furthermore, since the word is a general term, how can a specific meaning be understood? If you argue it is due to association (*sāhacarya*), then this would only hold if it were not already included by the word "ancestral. Even the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*) applies only when there is a distinction in the scope of the objects involved. (2.189)
This duty has been taught by the wise as belonging solely to the Brāhmaṇa;
however, for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, this duty is not prescribed in such a manner. (2.190)

This practice of eating only once a day and so forth, which has been prescribed, was taught by wise and learned men to the Brāhmaṇa alone after they had obtained it from the Veda; however, they do not approve of this for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya. For them, there is never a time when food other than that obtained through begging is permitted.

But surely, only Brāhmaṇas have the entitlement to eat at a *śrāddha*. Because of the statement, "Those best of the twice-born who are to be fed there, and those who are to be avoided... to the most worthy Brāhmaṇa" (MDh 3.124 [114]), only a Brāhmaṇa has the entitlement to receive gifts. In that case, why is there this prohibition regarding Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas? Furthermore, this is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) and not an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*). And prohibitions depend upon a prior possibility of occurrence.

It is said: For Brahmins who have already eaten, the disposal of the remaining food is prescribed by the rule: "One should provide for one's kinsmen" (MDh 3.264). In that context, there is no regard for caste; whoever is one's kinsman, he is the one to be fed. Furthermore, in that instance, Kṣatriyas and others are not connected as recipients, but rather as kinsmen. Therefore, this verse is a prohibition of that which would otherwise be applicable. 2.190.
Whether constantly urged by his teacher or even without being urged, he should apply himself to his studies and to the welfare of his teacher. (2.191)

Even if not urged by his teacher, he should apply himself with effort to his studies, even if not assigned [a specific task]. But has it not been said that "one should study when summoned"? How, then, can application be enjoined for one who has not been urged? This is stated for the sake of further qualities for one who has already mastered a portion of the Veda; in that case, the teacher's formal command need not be awaited. Likewise, whatever is beneficial to the teacher—such as fetching the water-pot and so forth, or massaging him when he is fatigued—that too must be performed even without being assigned. (2.191)
Restraining his body, speech, organs of perception, and mind, he should stand with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the face of his teacher. (2.192)

Having arrived from somewhere, he should remain looking at the face of his teacher and not sit down. Restraining his body, he should not move his feet or hands, nor laugh; he should not say anything useless. He should control his faculties of perception (*buddhīndriyāṇi*). Whatever is of a marvelous nature in the presence of the teacher, he should not contemplate that again and again. This applies to the ears and other senses as well. As for the restraint of the eyes, it is accomplished simply by looking at the teacher’s face. He should also restrain the mind; he should mentally avoid conceptualizations concerning the scriptures and undertakings such as household chores or the filling of store-rooms. As for the statement, "He should exert effort in self-restraint" (MDh 2.88), that prohibition is intended to prevent attachment. Even if the sense organs are not otherwise forbidden, one should not allow them even the slightest range of activity in the presence of the teacher. With palms joined, he should keep his hands in the *kapota* gesture, held upward. (2.192)
He should always have his right hand raised, be of pleasant conduct, and well-restrained;
and when told, "Be seated," he should sit facing the teacher. (2.193)

The hand must be withdrawn not only from the *sūtra*, but also from the garment. The inclusion of the word "always" (*nitya*) indicates that this withdrawal of the hand is required not only when standing, nor only at the time of study, but rather at other times as well. One should maintain good conduct (*sādhvācāra*), meaning one's behavior, speech, and so forth, should be virtuous and irreproachable. Because of the inclusion of the word "always," one must not engage in vulgar speech and the like even in the absence of the teacher. Being "well-restrained" (*susaṃvṛta*) means having the self controlled through speech, mind, and eyes; one should avoid even the slightest fault. A person who acts according to their own whims is called "unrestrained" (*anāvṛta*) in the world; the opposite of that is "well-restrained."
Others, however, hold that one should remain with the body covered by a garment in the presence of the teacher; one should not remove the upper cloth.

One should remain thus. But when the teacher says, "Sit," or by means of this word, or by a movement of the eyebrows and so forth—for the purpose of conveying an injunction, and the conveying of an injunction is not solely the operation of words—then one should sit, that is, one should take a seat. Facing him, that is, directly opposite him. (2.193)
In the presence of the teacher, he should always have inferior food, clothing, and attire;
he should rise before him and go to rest after him. (2.194)

In the presence of his teacher, he should eat inferior and scant food. "Scantiness" may refer to quantity in some cases and to preparation in others. If he has obtained from alms such prepared food as clarified butter, curds, milk, or condiments, then, provided that the teacher has not eaten such food at that same time while dining together with him; or if such food was not prepared in the teacher's house, then he must not consume it. However, if the teacher also has such food, then a reduction [in his own portion] must be made. As for clothing, if the teacher’s is made of wool, then the student must not wear cotton or similar materials. This applies also to dress, ornaments, decorations, and the like; these too must be inferior. This is because one must always remain beyond [the bounds of] celibacy (*brahmacarya*); for this very reason, the mention of "dress" is made, as ornamentation is not desired for a celibate student. He should rise first from his bed at the end of the night, or having perceived the occasion for rising from his seat, he should rise before the teacher. Finally, afterwards, at the time of sleep, when the teacher has fallen asleep, he should lie down—that is, take recourse to his bed—or sit upon his seat. (2.194)
One should not engage in responding or conversing while lying down, nor while sitting, nor while eating, nor while standing, nor with one's face turned away. (2.195)

"Pratiśravaṇa" (responding) is the act of listening to the words of a teacher or his relatives when one is being summoned or appointed to a task. "Saṃbhāṣā" (conversation) is the exchange of speech with the teacher. These two refer to responding and conversing. One should not perform these while lying down with one's limbs cast upon one's own bed; nor while sitting seated on a seat; nor while eating; nor while standing—remaining motionless in one place, standing upright; nor while turned away; that is, one should not do so by turning one's back toward the direction in which the teacher is seen. (2.195)

Standing, one should attend to one who is seated; approaching, one should attend to one who is standing; going forward to meet, one should attend to one who is coming toward oneself; and running after, one should attend to one who is running. (2.196)

How then? When the teacher gives an order while seated, [the pupil], standing up from his seat, should respond and converse. But when the teacher is standing, [the pupil] should go toward him. When the teacher commands while standing, then [the pupil], going toward him, should take several steps forward facing him. When [the teacher] is approaching—that is, coming—he should go out to meet him, having gone toward him directly; for *prati* signifies "facing. When [the teacher] is running—that is, moving with speed—he should run after him. Or likewise when he is staying behind. (2.196)
Facing one who has turned away, approaching the presence of one who is at a distance, bowing down before one who is lying down, and likewise standing by the side of one who is giving orders. (2.197)

Likewise, when the teacher has his back turned, the disciple should sit facing him. If the teacher turns around and somehow remains standing while sending him away, the disciple should go in that direction, turn to face him, and perform what was previously prescribed. Having approached—that is, having come near and reached—the presence of one who is either seated or lying down, he should bow down, becoming humble by bending his limbs. Even for one standing nearby, he must first bow down, as was previously stated regarding "approaching. (2.197)
In the presence of his teacher, his bed and seat should always be low;
within the range of the teacher's vision, he should not sit as he pleases. (2.198)

One should sit on a low seat, not a high one; "low" is relative to the teacher's bed and other such items. Because of the inclusion of the word "constantly," this applies even after the period of student life (*brahmacarya*). Furthermore, within the range of the teacher's vision—wherever the teacher can see—one should not sit as one pleases, such as by stretching out one's feet or lounging with the limbs at ease. The mention of "seat" is intended to indicate bodily movements in general; one should not engage in arbitrary movements. (2.198)
One should not utter his name alone, even in his absence;
nor should one imitate his gait, speech, or gestures. (2.199)

One should not utter or pronounce the name of this guru alone, even in his absence, without such honorific titles as *upādhyāya*, *ācārya*, or *bhaṭṭa*. Nor should one imitate him—that is, one should not act like him in a theatrical manner—as in: "In this way our guru walks away"; or in speech, such as [imitating] his speed, whether fast, slow, or moderate; or in gesture, such as "he eats in this way," "he ties his turban in this way," "he turns around in this way," and so forth. This prohibition against imitation is intended to prevent mockery. (2.199)
Wherever censure or even slander of the guru takes place, there one should cover one's ears or depart for another place. (2.200)

In whatever place, upon encountering wicked people, there occurs the censuring of the teacher—namely, the recounting of his actual faults, his disparagement, or the attribution of faults that do not exist—one should cover one's ears with the fingers or other means and block them; or else, one should depart from that place to another. 2.200.
From speaking ill of others one becomes a donkey; indeed, a slanderer becomes a dog.
One who consumes another's property becomes a worm; a miser becomes an insect. (2.201)

This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) supplementary to the preceding prohibition; therefore, it should be explained as follows: "Upon hearing slander, one becomes a donkey. Here, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used either with the sense of cause (*hetau*)—with the elision of the suffix *lyap*—or in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*): "having heard slander. A "reviler" (*nindaka*) is one who hears slanders; he is called a reviler by figurative extension (*upacāra*). Likewise, a "butcher" (*avaghātaka*) is one who performs the ritual preparation [of the victim]. Since hearing is already prohibited, the prohibition of performing [it] directly is established by implication. A "consumer" (*paribhoktā*) is one who lives off his teacher through deceitful means. An "envious person" (*matsarī*) cannot endure the prosperity or advancement of his teacher and burns within. Since these two [categories of persons] have not been previously mentioned, this is an original injunction (*apūrvo vidhiḥ*). Regarding the forms *parivāda* and *parīvāda*, the lengthening or shortening of the vowel occurs according to Pāṇini 6.3.122: *ghañy amanuṣye bahulam*. (2.201)

One should not salute him while standing at a distance, nor when angry, nor in the presence of a woman; likewise, if one is seated in a vehicle or on a seat, one should descend before saluting him. 2.202.

In this context, the offering of perfumes, garlands, and so forth by means of sending another person is prohibited. Agency (*kartṛtva*) is equal whether an act is performed by oneself or caused to be done by another, because the status of being an agent is traditionally recognized even for the instigator (*prayojaka*). Since this understanding might lead one to think that worship through another’s mouth is permissible, this prohibition is stated. There is no fault in the case of incapacity for one staying in another village; for we observe such usage as: "The teacher is going to another village; you should pay him homage," or "He has gone, so you should go and pay him homage. "One should not [pay homage] when angry. Since anger toward the Guru is impossible, even if anger arises from some other cause, the instruction is given to abandon it at the time of worship so that the mind may become serene. Others read the word as *kruddham* (accusative singular). "Not in the presence" means not near a woman who is a lustful object. Because the entire range of service is dedicated to the propitiation of the Guru, anything that might be feared to cause mental distress is prohibited. Therefore, it is explained as "by a woman. "Vehicle" refers to a cart and the like; "seat" refers to a stool, a couch, and so forth. Having descended from or stepped down from those, one should pay homage.

In the verse *śayyāsanasthaḥ* (MDh 2.119), rising from the seat was already mentioned; by this [present rule], descending is prescribed. For one who has not descended, rising from a couch or a seat is possible; however, descending is not possible for one who has not risen. Therefore, since this [rule] alone establishes the point, the mention of the "seat" (*āsana*) in the phrase *śayyāsanasthaḥ* is redundant.

It is not purposeless. If the pupil is facing away and perceives that the teacher has arrived from the direction behind him, he should rise while still seated, turning around in haste to face him; he should not, however, rise and then turn around. For in that case, the act of rising would intervene between him and the teacher’s presence, and the teacher might become angry. Furthermore, if the pupil rises while facing away, the teacher might think: "He did not rise for me; his rising was caused by some other circumstance. Therefore, the mention of "seated" is meaningful in both instances. (2.202)
One should not sit with one's teacher to the wind or downwind;
nor should one say anything at all within earshot of the teacher that he would not wish to hear. (2.203)

When the wind comes from the direction where the teacher is situated toward the place of the disciple, or from the place of the disciple toward the place of the teacher, these are respectively "against the wind" (*prativāta*) and "with the wind" (*anuvāta*). One should not sit with the teacher in either of these two positions—one against the wind and the other with the wind—but rather one should position oneself so as to be in a crosswind relative to the teacher. In a place where there is no hearing (*asaṃśrava*), one should not mention anything at all regarding the teacher, whether it concerns him or others. Where the teacher does not hear clearly, but perceives through the movement of the lips and so forth that the disciple is conversing with someone about something, one should not mention that. (2.203)
One may sit together with one's teacher on a vehicle drawn by oxen, horses, or camels, on a palace, on a stone slab, on mats, or on a rock, a wooden plank, or a boat. (2.204)

The word *yāna* (vehicle) is connected with each [term]. That which is stated as a vehicle by means of cows, horses, and camels is "the vehicle of cows, horses, and camels" (*go’śvoṣṭrayāna*). Just as in the case of *dadhighaṭa* ("a jar of curds") and so forth, there is an elision of the word *yukta* ("yoked to") in the compound. However, in the case of mere riding on the back of a horse and so forth, there is no [prohibition against] mounting. If the word *yāna* were understood as independent, then permission might indeed apply; however, from established custom (*samācāra*), occasional permission is observed. Regarding a palace (*prāsāda*), sitting together is established on the ground level of the upper rooms and so forth, just like the ground level of ordinary houses. A *prastara* is a mat (*āstara*) strewn with grass such as *darbha*. A *kaṭa*, however, is well known as being made of reeds (*śara*), *vīraṇa* grass, and so forth. A *śilā* is a stone on a mountain peak or elsewhere. A *phalaka* is a wooden seat, such as a plank or the like. A *nau* is a boat for crossing or floating upon water. By this, it is established that [the prohibition applies] even to boats and the like. (2.204)
When the teacher’s teacher is present, one should behave toward him as toward one's own teacher;
nor, unless permitted by his teacher, should he salute his own teachers. (2.205)

The conduct toward the teacher has been explained; now it is extended by analogy to other cases. Because this entire subject matter pertains to the duties of Vedic study (*adhyayana-dharma*), the term "teacher" (*guru*) here should be understood as the *ācārya*. When his own teacher is present, he must behave toward him as toward the [primary] teacher. The word "present" does not mean that he should go to that person's house for the purpose of salutation and so forth. While residing in the teacher’s house, he must not go to salute his own teachers—such as his mother and father—without being sent or permitted by the [primary] teacher. However, when his own teachers happen to come while he is staying in the teacher’s house, he need not wait for the teacher’s permission to salute them. Why is this? Because his mother and father possess absolute reverence. Furthermore, for one who proceeds to salute paternal uncles, maternal uncles, and others, there is no obstacle whatsoever to the practice of conduct toward the teacher; indeed, all this effort is solely for the sake of propitiating [the primary teacher]. Regarding the order of salutation when the mother, father, and teacher are encountered together, it has been stated: "The mother is the greatest of all. Between the father and the *ācārya*, however, there is an option (*vikalpa*). Since the reverence of the *ācārya* is ordained through the attribution of the status of "father," therefore the father is superior. And since it is said, "The father who imparts the Veda is more venerable" (MDh 2.146), therefore the *ācārya* is [superior]. Thus, this is an option. (2.205)

One should always behave toward one's teachers of knowledge in this very same way as toward one's own parents—even toward those who forbid one from unrighteousness and those who instruct one in what is beneficial. (2.206)

This is also an extended application (*atideśa*). Other than the *ācārya*, those such as the *upādhyāya* are teachers of knowledge (*vidyāguru*). Toward them, one must behave in exactly the same manner, through the duties prescribed in such passages as "the body itself... (MDh 2.192). Toward one's own kin, such as elder brothers, paternal uncles, and so forth, the constant conduct is that of a teacher. However, for teachers of knowledge other than the *ācārya*, this applies only until the acquisition of knowledge is complete. Even toward peers who forbid one from unrighteousness (*adharma*) or improper acts, such as adultery and the like; for even a friend or similar person may wish to perform an improper act due to excessive intimacy, and [one should say to him]: "A friend should turn one away from improper acts, even by seizing the hair" (MBh 5.91.11). Toward such a person, even if they are of equal or inferior age, one must behave as toward a teacher. And toward those who instruct in what is beneficial in the form of a rule, even if not in a formal treatise; or alternatively, those of noble birth (*abhijana*) who are instructors of what is beneficial are so called. (2.206)
One should always behave toward those who are superior as one does toward one's own guru—toward the guru’s son, toward the teacher, and likewise toward the guru’s own kinsmen. (2.207)

"Superiors" (*śreyāṃsaḥ*) are those who possess excellence in wealth, age, learning, and so forth, relative to oneself. Toward them, one should always practice the conduct due to a teacher (*guruvat*), such as salutation, rising to meet them, and so on, as far as possible. Many words with already understood meanings are employed here; their use is not faulty because of the requirements of the meter (*vṛtta*). One need only have said "toward superiors" (*śreyaḥsu*); "as toward a teacher" (*guruvat*) is implied, and "conduct" (*vṛttim*) and so forth are already established by context. All of this is to be inferred for oneself throughout this entire treatise.

"Likewise toward the teacher’s son and the *ācārya*. By the mention of the *ācārya*, the status of a teacher (*adhyāpaka*) is indicated. If the teacher is absent and his son teaches for a few days, then one should behave toward him as toward the teacher. There is an alternative reading: "toward the teacher’s sons and the *āryas*. The word *ārya* here denotes a virtuous Brāhmaṇa by birth, as seen in the usage: "An *ārya* is superior even to a Śūdra. Furthermore, this rule of conduct is not prescribed for every teacher’s son. [The text continues: "And likewise toward the teacher’s own kinsmen. The inclusion of the word "own" is for the sake of those belonging to the teacher’s lineage. In this context, the mere fact of being related to the teacher’s lineage is the cause; neither age nor learning is taken into account. (2.207)
Whether he is of equal age, a young child, or a pupil, the son of a teacher who teaches during a sacrificial rite deserves honor just like his father. (2.208)

For those who do not read the inclusion of the word "teacher" (*ācārya*) in the previous rule as being for the purpose of qualifying the son of the teacher, [the following applies]: when the one who teaches is virtuous and of the same caste, the conduct due to all teachers would have applied; by this specific qualification, it is restricted. A son of the teacher deserves honor and worship like a teacher while he is teaching, but not when he is not teaching.

But surely, since the conduct toward a teacher is occasioned by the reception of knowledge, such conduct would already apply to the teacher’s son when he too teaches, just as it does to the teacher himself; and since this is established even for one who is younger based on the example of the *Śaiśava-Brāhmaṇa*, the phrase "whether he be a child or of equal age" need not have been stated for that purpose either.

True. This mode of livelihood is prescribed even for one who teaches the Veda or a portion of the Veda but is not an *ācārya*. However, this person is not a primary recipient (*grāhaka*); he merely teaches for a few days or for a single part of the day. Therefore, since he is neither an *ācārya* nor an *upādhyāya*, this rule is prescribed for one to whom [the standard rules] would otherwise not apply. From this very statement, it is understood that for another teacher—such as one whose mantras are broken—the full duty toward a guru is not to be performed.
And for those who read the word *ācārya* in the preceding [verse], this is restated for the sake of what follows; he will say, "and the removal [of bodily hair]" (MDh 2.209).

Or [he is to be honored] like a disciple in the performance of a sacrifice. The mention of "the performance of a sacrifice" is for the sake of illustration. In some subsidiary part (*aṅga*)—that is, in a certain portion of the Veda, whether in the section of mantras (*mantrabhāga*) or in some portion of the Brāhmaṇas—he is to be honored like a teacher (*guru*), provided he is the son of one's teacher. Therefore, it has been stated that if one learns some branch of knowledge (*vidyā*) from him in this manner, one must behave toward him as toward a teacher; such is the purpose of this introductory statement, as it is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

As for those who explain: "By the word 'teaching' (adhyāpayan), the capacity to teach is indicated; if he is capable of teaching, let him teach, or let him not teach; if he has mastered the Veda, he is to be regarded like a guru"—for them, this literal interpretation is indeed true. However, the suffix *śatṛ* has the sense of a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), according to Pāṇini 3.2.126: "The suffix *śatṛ* [is used] after a verb in the sense of a characteristic or a cause. And here, a specific action is heard: "He deserves honor like a guru. (2.208)
One should not perform the massaging of the limbs, the bathing, or the eating of the leftovers for the teacher's son, nor should one perform the washing of his feet. (2.209)

One should not perform the rubbing or massaging of one who has been anointed [with oil]. This refers to the son of the teacher (*guruputra*). Also, the washing—that is, the rinsing—of the feet. From this very prohibition, it is understood that even though not explicitly stated, these acts must be performed for the teacher himself. However, when the son of the teacher himself becomes the "teacher" by virtue of being the one who imparts the entire Veda, then there exists for his own sake the eating of leftovers and so forth; that is not prohibited by this rule. This prohibition applies to what is extended by analogy (*ātideśika*), not to what is directly enjoined (*aupadeśika*). (2.209)
The wives of one's gurus who belong to the same caste (varṇa) should be honored like the gurus themselves;
those of a different caste, however, should be honored by rising from one's seat and by salutation. (2.210)
