The wives of the guru are the guru’s consorts. Those who are of the same *varṇa* (caste) are of the same class; they are to be honored like the guru himself by carrying out his commands and so forth. However, those of a different *varṇa* are to be honored merely by rising from one's seat and saluting. By the use of the plural number, the sense of "and so forth" (*ādi*) is included here. Consequently, [the rules regarding] doing what is pleasant and beneficial, following [the guru's] movements, and not imitating [his] speech, and so on, are also extended [to the wives]. (2.210)
Anointing, bathing, massaging the limbs, and the dressing of the hair—these should not be performed by the wife of one's teacher. (2.211)

Anointing (*abhyañjana*) is the smearing of the hair and body with ghee, oil, and the like. Rubbing (*udvartana*) is the massaging of the limbs. Because it shares the same purpose, washing the feet is also included. In every respect, any practice whatsoever that is accomplished through contact with the body is prohibited. And he will state the reason: "This is the nature of women" (MDh 2.213). Furthermore, the grooming of the hair refers to the fashioning of its arrangement and so forth, as well as the parting of the hairline with saffron, vermilion, and other substances. This is mentioned by way of illustration; therefore, the grooming of the body, such as the application of sandalwood paste, is also forbidden. (2.211)
But the wife of one's guru, if she is young, should not be saluted by touching her feet here by a man who has completed twenty years of age and understands virtues and faults.

"By one who has completed twenty years" means by a youth. For a child up to sixteen years of age, there is no offense. One for whom twenty years are complete is described in this way. This time-period is intended as an indicator of the emergence of youth. Therefore, it says: "by one who discerns virtues and faults. By "virtues and faults," the pleasure and pain arising from desire are intended; or, regarding women, they refer to the characteristics of a beautiful form versus an ugly form, or to steadfastness and fickleness. In every respect, the number twenty is not strictly binding. (2.212)
This is the very nature of women: the corruption of men in this world.
Therefore, the wise do not become negligent toward young women for the sake of their own welfare. (2.213)

This is the nature of women: that they cause men to fall from their fortitude. Indeed, through association, women may lead men away from their vows. For this reason, and for this cause, [the wise] do not become negligent; they avoid women from afar. Negligence consists in such acts as touching them. This is the inherent nature of things: that a young woman, when touched, produces a mental agitation caused by desire. In that regard, even mere mental agitation is forbidden—let alone any other passionate engagement in vulgar acts. [Such are] women, *pramadāḥ*. (2.213)
For in this world, women are capable of leading astray both the ignorant man and even the wise man who has fallen under the sway of desire and anger. (2.214)

Nor should it be thought: "He who has long restrained his senses commits an extremely grave sin even by looking upon the wife of a guru with a wicked intent; however, for one who knows this, there is no fault in touching her feet and so forth. For both he who recognizes such faults and he who recognizes none at all are equal regarding women. This is because, in this matter, learning is of no avail. Women are capable of leading—meaning of bringing—one who follows the sway of desire and anger onto every wrong path, an improper course that is contrary to the world and the scriptures. The meaning is: he who becomes bound by desire and anger.

This is intended to indicate specific exceptions. With the exception of those who are extremely young, those who are extremely old, and those who have attained the excellence of yoga—by whom the human qualities of *saṃsāra* have been severed without remainder—there is no person whatsoever who is not drawn by women, just as iron is drawn by a magnet. Nor does this imply that women possess sovereign power here; rather, it is due to the very nature of things that the minds of men are agitated upon seeing young women, especially in the case of celibates. (2.214)
One should not sit in seclusion with one's mother, sister, or daughter;
for the powerful collection of the senses drags away even a wise man. (2.215)

Therefore, one should not sit in a secluded place, such as a deserted or empty house; nor should one, without restraint, engage in touching the limbs or similar acts. For the aggregate of the sense-faculties is exceedingly restless; it drags away, carries off, and renders dependent even a wise man whose self is restrained by the scriptures. (2.215)
However, on this earth, a young man should duly perform a salutation to the wives of his elders who are themselves young, saying, "I am so-and-so. (2.216)

The word *kāmam* indicates a lack of preference. This is connected with what follows: "Having returned from a journey, [he should perform] the grasping of the feet" (MDh 2.217). However, the salutation by touching the feet on the ground is indeed desired. This rule applies when a young man [meets] young women, that is, between two youths. If, however, the student (*brahmacārī*) is a child or the wife of the teacher is elderly, then the clasping of the feet is not prohibited. "I am so-and-so" is a restatement of the rule previously mentioned. "According to rule" means with hands placed separately. (2.216)
Having returned from a journey abroad, one should clasp the feet of the teacher’s wives every day and offer salutations, remembering the dharma of the virtuous. (2.217)

Upon returning from a journey, one should grasp the feet according to the rule, "the left with the left" (MDh 2.72). This salutation on the ground should be performed every day, day after day, while recollecting that this is the duty and the conduct of the virtuous and the learned. 2.217.
Just as a man obtains water by digging with a spade, so too does one who is intent on service obtain knowledge residing in the teacher. 2.218

This is the fruit of the entire procedure of service (*śuśrūṣā*). It is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the injunction regarding self-study (*svādhyāya*), by means of propitiating the teacher. Just as a certain man, digging the earth with a spade or a hoe, obtains water without difficulty, so too does this person, devoted to serving the teacher and intent on attending to him, acquire the knowledge residing in the teacher. (2.218)
He may be shaven-headed or wear matted locks, or he may have his hair tied in a topknot; the sun must never set or rise while he is still within a village. 2.219.

He should have his hair shaved entirely, becoming *muṇḍaḥ*; or he may be *jaṭilaḥ*. *Jaṭā* refers to hairs that are extremely matted together; one who possesses such is a *jaṭilaḥ*. A *śikhājaṭaḥ* is one whose *śikhā* (topknot) itself constitutes a *jaṭā*. He should maintain a topknot in the form of a *jaṭā*, or he may be *muṇḍaḥ* as prescribed. Furthermore, he should act in such a way that while staying in a village, the sun does not set upon him—that is, it does not go down. The mention of "village" is intended to include the "town" (*nagara*) as well. He should ensure that the time of sunset occurs in the forest. Likewise, he should act so that for him, the student, the rising of the sun also occurs in the forest, just as it does for one staying in the forest. This refers to the student under discussion here.

Others, however, explain that the word *grāma* refers to village-dwelling practices such as sleeping and so forth, and thus [the rule] means "he should not set [the sun] while engaged in these. Accordingly, he says later on, "while lying down. Therefore, this is a prohibition against sleeping during the two twilights (*saṃdhyā*), not a prohibition against staying in the forest at those times. For a young student (*brahmacārī*) might be afraid. Gautama, however, has stated that the status of being "outside the twilights" (*bahiḥsaṃdhya*) begins after the *godāna* ceremony (GDh 2.10). The *godāna* vow occurs at the sixteenth year, and by then, having attained that age, he is able to perform the twilight worship in the forest. (2.219)
If the sun should rise while he is sleeping out of his own will,
or if it should set while he is unaware of it, he shall fast for the day while reciting prayers.

In this case, one should perform the following expiation (*prāyaścitta*): If the sun should rise while a celibate student (*brahmacārin*) is lying down, having fallen under the power of sleep, it would cause him to be affected by the fault of being overtaken by its rising. [The term *abhi* is used here as a *karmapravacanīya* according to Pāṇini 1.4.91, *abhir abhāge*. Hence, the accusative case in *śayānam*. Thus, it refers to one who is asleep in such a state; or rather, it is a characteristic mark indicating that if the sun should rise during the time of sleep, he should fast for the day while muttering prayers (*japann upavased dinam*).

Some say: "If one transgresses [the time for bathing] in the morning, there shall be recitation (*japa*) and fasting during the day, while eating occurs at night; but if one transgresses in the evening, there shall be recitation and fasting during the night, while eating occurs in the morning. The word "day" (*dina*) is used for the sake of illustration. They also cite the statement of Gautama: "He should stand during the day without eating, and from sunset until the following dawn, he should remain reciting the *Sāvitrī* mantra" (GDh 23.21).

That is incorrect. In both cases, it is proper that the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) be performed during the day alone, because there is no evidence that the word "day" (*dina*) is intended merely for illustration. For this [word], being dependent on that [context], does not convey its own primary meaning; rather, it is independent. Therefore, an option (*vikalpa*) is appropriate. In that regard, he for whom no illness arises while remaining awake the entire night shall recite at night; another, however, shall do so only by day. Furthermore, according to the statement of Gautama, the recitation (*japa*) is of the *Sāvitrī* alone. But how can Gautama be taken as an authority in this matter?

It is said in reply: this statement, "he should mutter," is dependent [on further specification], because that which is to be muttered has not been specified. When there is such a dependence, the understanding of a specific detail is appropriate based on another scriptural passage (*śruti*). But here, time is specified; since there is no dependence on any other time, Gautama does not require it. Alternatively, because the expiation for the omission of the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) is prescribed, the muttering of the *Sāvitrī* is already established. And it is logical that there is nothing superior to the *Sāvitrī*.

[542] By acting according to one's will: he who sleeps during the time of twilight (*saṃdhyā*) knowing [it to be so]. [543] Through lack of awareness: for one who has slept long, the failure to realize "this is the time of twilight" is lack of awareness. This is what is meant: this very penance applies to a transgression committed intentionally or through negligence. Furthermore, for one who neglects the twilight prayers of sunrise and sunset, the penance is fasting, as stated in the rule: "the omission of obligatory rites. Alternatively, when one transgresses the scriptures out of a desire to act as one pleases, that itself constitutes a lack of awareness. 2.220.
For he who goes to sleep while the sun is setting, or wakes up while the sun is rising, if he does not perform an expiation, he becomes joined with great sin. (2.221)

This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding the previously mentioned rule for expiation (*prāyaścitta*). "Corrupted by the setting" means one who has been overtaken by the sun at sunset; likewise for "overtaken by the rising. If one does not perform the aforementioned expiation, then one becomes connected with great sin, not a minor one. That which is called invisible sin (*adṛṣṭa-pāpa*) is the cause for experiencing sufferings such as those in hell. (2.221)
Having sipped water and being purified, he should always, with a concentrated mind, attend to both twilights in a clean place, reciting the prayers to be recited according to the rule. (2.222)

Thus, there is a great fault in the rising and setting [of the sun]. Therefore, having sipped water (ācamya), being pure, intent, and composed—with the distractions of the mind and its activities removed—one should worship both twilights (*saṃdhye*) while reciting the *japya* consisting of the *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī* in a clean place. Here, it is the two twilights themselves that are to be worshipped; and "worship" (*upāsana*) in this context refers to a particular state of mental disposition (*bhāvaviśeṣa*). Alternatively, one should worship the Lord Savitṛ at both twilights; for the mantra has him as its deity, and therefore one should worship him alone. With all conceptual constructions withdrawn, one should become single-mindedly focused on him. This is a restatement (*anuvāda*) supplementary to the previously mentioned injunction; only the act of worship (*upāsana*) is what is to be enjoined.

Others, however, say: "This verse is intended as an injunction for [staying] in a clean place. For them, there is a redundancy; for it has already been enjoined that "every action must be performed by one who is pure," and what purity can there be when one is in contact with an impure place? (2.222)
If a woman or a person of lower birth should practice anything that is beneficial, one should diligently perform all of that, provided it is where his mind finds delight. (2.223)

If the teacher’s wife (*ācāryānī*) is a woman, or if a junior (*avarajaḥ*), that is, a younger person, having learned from the teacher what is beneficial—the three aims of life beginning with *dharma*—should practice it, he should perform all of that. For it is possible that both of them have acquired thorough knowledge through their association with that teacher. Or, if a *śūdra* who is the teacher’s servant is a junior, and he should instruct him, saying: "In this way, the anus and penis are washed with clay and water; wash your hands skillfully; you have forgotten the sequence of clay and water; your teacher was seen by me many times while I was giving him water for the washing of the anus; first he performs purification with water, and then with clay"—if he should instruct him in such matters, [the pupil] should practice accordingly, being endowed with such conduct. Likewise, if the teacher’s wife should teach him the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), he should perform all of that with diligence and faith. He should not despise it, thinking, "This is practiced by women and *śūdras*."

The phrase "one should practice" (*samācaret*) here intends precisely an instruction preceded by traditional practice (*samācāra*). As he will state: "Dharma, purity... [these] are to be accepted from all sources" (MDh 2.240). Sometimes it is the teacher himself who instructs: "O Brāhmaṇī, cause this one who stands in the place of a son to perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) according to the rules. And he should say: "Clay and water must be given for the purpose of purifying his urine and feces. In that case, his word is to be followed, such as: "Take the clay," or "Wash with water. Alternatively, in the house of the teacher, the purification of metal, stone, and water, etc., which is practiced by women and Śūdras, is to be regarded as authoritative. This verse is appropriately intended to establish the authority of such practices related to women and Śūdras.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the authority of every practice (*ācāra*) connected with those who know the Veda is established? [Reply: This has not been stated. For not even the slightest practice of those who do not know the Veda becomes authoritative. If there exists a basis consisting of a connection with those who know the Veda, then that alone is the authority; what is the use of mentioning women? Furthermore, in such a context, the authority of the practices of women and *śūdras* is not intended. Had that been the case, it would have been mentioned in the very section dealing with the definition of authority. Therefore, the ultimate point is that this introductory discussion (*upodghāta*) is for the purpose of defining the category of the "good" (*śreyas*).

Or rather, this is a restatement of the authority of the teacher’s words: even what a woman or a Śūdra might say is fit to be practiced, how much more so that which is taught by a teacher? And as for that in which his mind may find delight and satisfaction—this too has been explained under the rule "satisfaction of the self" (MDh 2.6). In any case, this verse does not have much practical purpose. 2.223.
Some say that the good consists of dharma and artha; others, of kāma and artha; and still others, of dharma alone.
Or, in this world, artha alone is the highest good; such is the established position regarding the three aims of life (trivarga).

"That which is praiseworthy, that which, when practiced, does not harm one in this world or the next, and that which is called the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) in the world—what indeed is it? Thus he explains, acting as a friend. This matter is not rooted in the Veda, nor is it a definition of a term like the word "teacher" (*ācārya*). Rather, every person acts out of a desire for the highest good; therefore, this is stated: "This is the highest good; for its sake, effort must be made. In this regard, he first sets forth various opposing views.

According to the view of some, *dharma* and *artha* constitute the highest good (*śreyas*). *Dharma* consists of the injunctions and prohibitions prescribed by the scriptures; *artha* consists of cattle, land, gold, and so forth. This alone is the highest good, because human pleasure is dependent upon these. Another view holds that *kāma* and *artha* constitute it. *Kāma* (pleasure) is indeed the primary human goal (*puruṣārtha*), for pleasure is the highest good, and *artha* is also such because it is a means to that end. Thus the Cārvākas say: "Pleasure alone is the sole human goal; *artha* is its means, and *dharma* exists [only] if it serves that purpose."

Dharma alone is superior to all things, because everything has its root in it. And it is said: "From dharma come both wealth and pleasure" (MBh 18.5.49). As for wealth alone, that is the view of merchants who live by trade.

The established conclusion, however, is that the *trivarga* (the threefold set) is the settled rule. Therefore, even wealth (*artha*) and pleasure (*kāma*) should be pursued provided they do not conflict with dharma, but not if they do so conflict. And thus says Gautama: "One should not let the forenoon, midday, or afternoon pass fruitlessly; one should devote them to dharma, artha, and kāma according to one's ability" (GDh 9.46). A group consisting of three is a *trivarga*. This term is conventionally used for these three when taken together. (2.224)
The teacher, the father, the mother, and an elder brother must not be treated with contempt, even by one who is distressed; this is especially true for a Brāhmaṇa. (2.225)

No one else whatsoever should be treated with contempt, yet these [brahmins] especially so; the meaning is that there is an excess of penance in this case. "By one who is afflicted" means by one who is tormented by them. "Contempt" (avamāna) means disrespect, the failure to perform the honor due to them, and humiliation known as disregard. The mention of "brahmin" is for the sake of completion. 2.225.
The teacher is the embodiment of Brahmā; the father is the embodiment of Prajāpati;
the mother is indeed the embodiment of the Earth; and one's own brother is the embodiment of oneself. (2.226)

This is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for what precedes. That which is the Supreme Brahman, well-known from the Vedāntas and the Upaniṣads—of that, the teacher is the *mūrti*, meaning his body; he is like a physical form. He is the father of Prajāpati Hiraṇyagarbha. This earth itself is his mother, due to the common quality of bearing a heavy burden. And his own brother is his uterine sibling, in relation to the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) who is the Self; this is a eulogy. All these, being of the nature of deities and endowed with greatness, destroy [one] when they are disregarded, and when propitiated, they endow one with desired objects. Thus is the praise: "The teacher and the others are equal to those. (2.226)
The suffering that parents endure for the sake of the birth of human beings cannot be repaid even in a hundred years. (2.227)

This is another praise by way of restating the actual facts: The mother and father undergo suffering and hardship for their children from the time of conception until the tenth year. The mother’s hardship consists of carrying the fetus; her labor at birth is life-threatening; and the care required for the newborn is also a source of toil. This is experienced by everyone for themselves. For the father as well, this extends from the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) until the explanation of the meaning of the Vedas. Here, the word "birth" (*saṃbhava*) refers to the period beginning from conception; for that [conception itself] does not bring about hardship, but rather these subsequent rites, which must be accomplished through effort. It is impossible to discharge that debt—that is, to achieve a state of equality through a return favor—through even hundreds of years or many lifetimes, let alone in a single lifetime. Even by the gift of incalculable wealth or by rescuing them from great calamity, one cannot fully repay the debt owed to one's mother and father. (2.227)
One should always do what is pleasing to those two and to the teacher at all times; when these three are satisfied, all ascetic toil is fully accomplished. (2.228)

Therefore, one should always, for as long as life lasts, do whatever is pleasing to those two—mother and father—and to the teacher; one should not consider oneself to have fulfilled one's duty by doing so only once, twice, or thrice. When those three—the teacher and the others—are satisfied and propitiated through devotion, the fruit that is obtained by performing all forms of austerity, such as the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances, for many groups of years, is obtained simply from their satisfaction. (2.228)
Service to these three is said to be the highest austerity;
one should not practice any other duty without being authorized by them. (2.229)

How, then, can the fruit of austerity be attained through service to one's mother and others without practicing austerity? For this is the highest of all austerities: serving their feet. Without being permitted by them, a young student might perform other forms of dharma that conflict with such service—such as bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and so forth, or vows and fasts that wither the body and cause mental distress to them. Even when performing the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, permission must be obtained, since the prohibition against showing disrespect has been established. Furthermore, in great undertakings that are accomplished through the expenditure of much wealth and effort, those who are bewildered might become objects of contempt. However, in the performance of obligatory daily rites (*nityakarman*), permission is not of assistance. (2.229)
For these indeed are the three worlds; these indeed are the three stages of life (āśramas);
these indeed are the three Vedas; and these are said to be the three sacred fires. || 2.230 ||

This is stated because of the non-difference between cause and effect. Because they are the cause for attaining the three worlds, they themselves are called the "three worlds. And those same three are the other three stages of life (*āśrama*) beginning with the first stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*). Whatever fruit is obtained through the three stages of life beginning with the householder's life (*gārhasthya*), that is obtained when those three [elders] are satisfied. They themselves are the "three Vedas," because their fruit is equal to the recitation of the three Vedas. They themselves are the "three fires," because by serving them one obtains the fruit of performing rites accomplished through fire. This too is merely a form of praise. (2.230)
The father is indeed the Gārhapatya fire, and the mother is remembered as the Dakṣiṇa fire;
the teacher, however, is the Āhavanīya fire—this triad of fires is most venerable. (2.231)

This designation of the father and others as the *gārhapatya* fire and so forth is based on a certain commonality. The "threefold fire" (*agnitretā*) is the threefold consecrated fire (*ādhānāgnitretā*), which is most excellent and yields great fruit. The etymological derivation of the word *tretā* is: that which has gone (*itā*) to, or been attained for the purpose of protection (*trāṇa*), is *tretā*. || 2.231 ||
By being vigilant regarding these three, a householder may conquer the three worlds;
shining with his own body, he rejoices in heaven like a god. (2.232)

By being heedful toward these and not failing in their service, and by thus serving them, one may conquer the three worlds, take possession of them, and attain sovereignty over them. [This applies to] the householder; for the service rendered by a son who is in the stage of a householder is of benefit to his father and others, since at that time they have become old. Shining, beautiful, or radiant with his own splendor, he rejoices like a god—that is, like the sun—in the heavenly world. (2.232)
By devotion to one's mother one attains this world; by devotion to one's father, the middle world; and by service to one's teacher, one likewise reaches the world of Brahmā. (2.233)

This world is the earth. Because it bears weight, the mother is equal to the earth. The intermediate world, the atmosphere, is [equal] to the father because of devotion to the father; Prajāpati is called "father. And according to the etymologists (*nairukta*), Prajāpati occupies the middle station, for he is either the protector (*pātā*) or the guardian (*pālayitā*) of creatures through the act of raining. The world of Brahman is the world of Āditya; for there is the instruction that "Āditya is Brahman. "World" (*loka*) means a particular place; he partakes of—that is, reaches—that [world].

These are merely explanatory statements (*arthavāda*); one should not adhere to them as literal injunctions. Furthermore, one who merely desires worldly sovereignty has no entitlement to propitiate him. This is not an optional rite (*kāmya-vidhi*). Here, the fatherhood itself is the sole cause; failure to perform it constitutes a transgression of the scripture. (2.233)
All duties are honored by him who honors these three;
but for him who honors them not, all ritual actions are fruitless. (2.234)

"Respected" means honored. By the word "respected," one's intent to reciprocate is indicated; for he who is respected strives to repay that kindness once he is fully satisfied. Alternatively, "respected" is said to mean "fully satisfied. Since Dharma is infinite, complete satisfaction is impossible; therefore, it indicates a readiness to bestow rewards. All his actions quickly yield fruit when these three are respected and satisfied through service. However, if these are not propitiated, whatever auspicious action is performed by one desiring a result, all of it is fruitless. "All actions" refers to all rites prescribed by the Vedas (*śrauta*) and the Smṛtis (*smārta*).

This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). For the rule of propitiation is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*); by transgressing it, the person incurs sin and is obstructed from enjoying the desired fruits, even when those fruits have been acquired through [other] actions. Therefore it is said: "All his actions are fruitless" (2.234).
As long as those three live, he should not attend to anyone else; he should constantly perform service for them alone, devoted to their pleasure and welfare. (2.235)

The meaning of this verse has been explained. It was stated that one should not perform any other action, whether visible or invisible, without their permission. One should always practice service toward them alone, being devoted to what is pleasing and beneficial. That which is both pleasing and beneficial is intended: that which causes delight is "pleasing," and that which provides protection is "beneficial. (2.235)
Whatever one may perform for the sake of the next world without causing them distress, that one should report to them through thought, word, and deed. (2.236)

That which bears fruit in another world, in a future birth, is called *pāratrya*; this is a Vedic (archaic) form. Whatever other duty one should perform without contradicting service [to the elders], that one should report to them—that is, one should make them aware of it. The inclusion of the term "without contradiction" (*anuparodha*) is for this purpose: regarding that which is contrary to their interests, permission must not be sought at all. This is intended to prevent the case where someone of a straightforward nature, when requested, disregards his own or others' duty and grants permission; this rule is meant to avoid such an occurrence. [This reporting is done] through mind, speech, and action. Reporting is not for the sake of some unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭa*); rather, one should demonstrate through action exactly the kind of consent that has been granted.
Alternatively, the connection should be made as follows: whatever one performs for the sake of the next world through actions of mind, speech, and body, all that one should offer to them. (2.236)
For it is within these three that a man’s duty is fully accomplished;
this is the supreme dharma manifestly, while any other is called a secondary dharma (upadharma). 2.237.

The word *iti* signifies completion and implies totality. Whatever duty must be performed by a person, and whatever human goal (*puruṣārtha*) there may be, all that is completed—that is, fully accomplished—when these [teachers] are propitiated. This is the supreme and most excellent *dharma* because it is direct; whereas other duties such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice are secondary (*upadharma*), standing in the place of attendants rather than being like the king himself—this is the praise. The prohibition against showing disrespect, acting for their pleasure and welfare, the non-performance of what is contrary to their interests, and likewise the non-performance of even what is not forbidden but unauthorized—all this constitutes the remaining collection of verses, which are explanatory statements (*arthavāda*). (2.237)

One who possesses faith should acquire auspicious knowledge even from a lowly person; one should accept the supreme Dharma even from an outcaste, and a jewel of a woman even from a base family. (2.238)

A disciple who is faithful—whose inner self is embraced by a sense of conviction—and who is diligent, may learn auspicious knowledge, such as the science of logic beginning with the Nyāya-śāstra; or else, that which merely shines, being adorned with the pure sciences of poetry, dramaturgy (Bharata), and so forth, or even the science of mantras, though not directly useful for dharma—he may acquire and learn that even from a low-born person of inferior caste.

But in this context, auspicious Vedic knowledge is not to be understood; for there will be a rule for times of distress (*āpadi*), whereas it is not desired at all when there is no distress. As for that which is inauspicious—such as the *śāmbhavī* [mantra], or illusion, trickery, and the like—that is never [permitted].

And the last is the *caṇḍāla*; even beyond that is the "dharma which is other," meaning worldly dharma as distinct from that based on the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. The word "dharma" is also used in the sense of a settled rule (*vyavasthā*). For example, if even a *caṇḍāla* says: "This is the rule here"—such as, "Do not stay long in this place," "Do not bathe in this water," or "This is the custom of the villagers, or a boundary established by the king"—one should not think: "The teacher's word must be carried out by me; fie upon this wretched *caṇḍāla* who commands me!"

Furthermore, one should not entertain the following thought: "The supreme dharma is the knowledge of the reality of Brahman; for such knowledge is impossible for outcasts (caṇḍāla) and others because they lack knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas, nor is it possible for them through any other means, since there is no instruction regarding Brahman that consists of syllables like those of a mantra for scorpions."

"Like a jewel among women" (*strīratnam*). This may be analyzed as "she who is both a woman and a jewel," according to Pāṇini 2.1.56 (*upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ*) or 2.1.57 (*viśe�ṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*). When any excellent object is called a "jewel," then it is a case of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). However, if only emeralds, rubies, and the like are denoted by the word "jewel," and its application elsewhere [to a woman] is based on a commonality of excellence, then it is a case of comparison (*upamita*). A woman who possesses an abundance of radiance, physical form, and charm, or one who possesses auspicious marks such as offspring, much wealth, and sons—she may be taken even from a low family or one deficient in ritual acts. This serves as an introductory statement (*upodghāta*) for the rule "not from a non-Brahmin" (MDh 2.241); however, it is presented here because [such a woman] might not otherwise be available. (2.238)
Nectar should be taken even from poison; well-spoken words even from a child;
virtuous conduct even from an enemy; and gold even from filth. (2.239)

This is a supplement to the preceding injunction: "In times of distress, one may study even from a non-Brāhmaṇa" (MDh 2.141). By this, a common worldly proverb is cited as an illustration; for thus do people in the world say: "That which is good should be accepted even from that which is bad."

Even within poison, that which is nectar must certainly be accepted, just as a swan extracts milk from water. This was said with reference to certain elixirs (*rasāyana*) in which poison is present. Even a child, when he spontaneously utters some well-spoken word or an auspicious blessing at the start of a journey or similar occasion, that should be accepted. Even from an enemy or the like, whatever conduct of the virtuous constitutes the practice of the refined (*śiṣṭa*), that should not be rejected on the grounds that "this was performed by one who is hateful. This is a very well-known illustration: gold is [extracted] even from impurity; just as these [gems] are taken even from an unworthy source, so too is Vedic study [to be taken] even from a non-Brahmin. (2.239)
Women, jewels, as well as knowledge, dharma, purity, eloquent speech, and various arts—these are to be accepted from everyone. (2.240)

Precious gems and jewels, even when obtained from Śambaras, Pulindas, and others, are pure; likewise, so too are knowledge and the like. Furthermore, crafts such as the intricate cutting of leaves—which are non-defective and not censurable—such as the washing of clothes, the dyeing of cloth, and weaving, are to be accepted and taken up by those characterized by absolute fortitude, regardless of the specific caste of the source. This is because of the numerous scriptural statements such as "Even from poison, nectar [may be taken]" (MDh 2.239); since they follow the same introductory context, all these are *arthavādas* (explanatory passages). 2.240.
In times of distress, study from one who is not a Brahmin is permitted;
however, he must follow the teacher and serve him as long as the study continues. (2.241)

But here is the rule [578]: *āpad* means the state of being a non-Brāhmaṇa teacher. *Āpatkālaḥ* is the time of distress (*āpad*). Although it would have been sufficient to say simply *āpad*, the inclusion of the word *kāla* is for the purpose of completing the meter. There is an alternative reading: *āpatkalpa*. *Kalpa* means arrangement; in times of distress, this arrangement is prescribed or taught. When a teacher, having already begun instruction, leaves his pupil—either due to a penance or some other cause—and goes to another country, and no other Brāhmaṇa teacher can be found in that region, and because of the pupil's youth it is impossible to travel to a distant land, then study may be undertaken from a non-Brāhmaṇa, namely a Kṣatriya, or in his absence, from a Vaiśya. Because the subject under discussion is the Veda—as in the verse, "the entire Veda" (MDh 2.165)—the term "Veda" is specifically enjoined here.

Although here the term *abrāhmaṇa* denotes the human nature residing in the three [other] castes other than the Brāhmaṇa caste, nevertheless, the Śūdra is not included here, because he lacks the qualification for teaching. Teaching presupposes study. Now, one might argue: "By transgressing the scriptures, it is possible even for a Śūdra to have studied the Veda, just as it is possible for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas to be teachers. That too is not so; for a distinction of bodies (*śarīrabheda*) is recorded for him (the Śūdra) regarding the retention [of the Veda]. Therefore, from the severity of the punishment, this great misdeed is inferred. Through the habitual performance of censured acts and through association with them, there would be a falling away (*patana*) and extreme corruption for the religious student (*brahmacārin*). If it is argued that "there is an equal fault [in associating] because the prohibition of teaching applies equally to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas," there is a distinction in this case. Where the punishment and penance (*prāyaścitta*) are heavy, there is a great fault; where they are light, the fault is small. Furthermore, there are no heavy punishments or penances for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas in the act of teaching, as there are for a Śūdra. Moreover, there are two censured acts—studying and teaching—whereas for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas there is only one. Association with a prohibited teacher is permitted by this very [text], and thus it does not cause a fault. However, there is no authority whatsoever for association with a Śūdra who has engaged in prohibited study.

And "following after" (*anuvrajyā*) means service (*śuśrūṣā*). To exclude other forms of service such as prostration or washing the feet, it is specified that "service consists solely in following after, and nothing else. This continues until the study is completed and until [the text] has been mastered. (2.241)
A disciple desiring the unsurpassed goal should not dwell for life with a teacher who is not a Brahmin, nor even with a Brahmin who has not mastered the Vedas. (2.242)

Residence with a non-Brahmin teacher for the purpose of study was previously mentioned; that which might apply even to a *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong student) is here specifically prohibited. "Ultimate residence" means residing for as long as one lives. "He shall not reside" means he shall not do so. Regarding the expression "he shall reside," because of the relationship between the general and the particular, the connection should be understood as "he shall reside [with a Brahmin]. Residence refers to that which pertains to a teacher; he should reside there. Once his studies are completed, he should go elsewhere.
Now, since only study was permitted, from where could the possibility of ultimate residence have arisen?
This is not a fault; for it has been stated that his residence is with a guru, and a teacher is called a "guru. Therefore, this doubt arises.

"Or a Brahmin who is not learned (*anūcāna*). The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "also. Even if one is a Brahmin, if he is not today learned—meaning he is neither endowed with proper conduct and noble lineage nor habituated to exposition and study—then [he is unfit]. By the term "learning through recitation" (*anuvacana*), these other qualities are also indicated; for since the lack of eligibility (*arhābhāva*) is established precisely because of the absence of one who can recite, the prohibition of residence is already proven. Here, "goal" (*gati*) is intended to mean the attainment of supreme happiness. "Unsurpassed" (*anuttamā*): desiring that which has no other superior, namely liberation in the form of the bliss of the Supreme Self. (2.242)
But if he should desire to dwell permanently in the teacher's family,
he should attend upon him diligently until the liberation from the body.

If he should find pleasure in lifelong residence in the teacher’s family—that is, in perpetual celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya*)—then, being disciplined and devoted to that end, he should serve this teacher until the release from his prosperity, meaning as long as the body is maintained. (2.243)
But that Brahmin who serves his teacher until the end of his body goes straightway to the eternal abode of Brahmā. (2.244)

This is the injunction regarding the fruit of lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya*). "The completion of the body" means the renunciation of life. He who serves and attends upon his teacher until that time—that Brahmin goes to the eternal abode, the seat, the dwelling place of Brahman; that is to say, he does not return again to the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). "Directly" means by an unobstructed path; he is not hindered by another state of existence, such as birth as an animal or as a human being. According to the perspective of the *Itihāsas*, the word "Brahman" refers to a specific deity with four faces; his abode is a particular place located in heaven. However, for the proponents of Vedānta, "Brahman" is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); his "abode" is his very own nature, which is the attainment of that state of being. (2.244)

One who knows the Dharma should not provide anything to the teacher beforehand; however, when he is about to perform the final bath and has been authorized by the teacher, he should procure a gift for the teacher according to his ability. (2.245)

This [rule] prohibits the giving of wealth to the teacher by the *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong student), because the giving of wealth to the teacher is prescribed for one who is about to perform the ritual bath (*snāsyan*). Furthermore, there is no ritual bath for the *naiṣṭhika*. And it is the *naiṣṭhika* alone who is the subject under discussion here. As for the *upakurvāṇa* (temporary student), however, from the time of initiation (*upanayana*) until the ritual bath, giving exists indeed; provided that it is possible, he should give according to his ability.

Before the bath, he should do something to assist the teacher; that is, he should give. The verbal root *dā* (to give) is here used with a prefix (*upa*), and therefore the fourth case is employed for its object. Alternatively, according to the rule "the mention of the action itself must also be made," it constitutes a *saṃpradāna* (recipient). The phrase "knower of dharma" (*dharmavit*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*). But when the time for the bath has arrived and he is about to bathe (*snāsyan*), he should bring whatever has been commanded by the teacher, such as "bring this object. Then, according to his ability—that is, as much as he is able—he should bring for the sake of the teacher (*gurvartham*). "For the sake of the teacher" means "this belongs to the teacher. He should bring or present that which is necessary for the teacher.
But is this not a prohibition against the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) performing services for his teacher?

For these are not two separate sentences, such that one would be a prohibition and the other an injunction regarding service to the teacher. The injunction is: "At the time of the bath, service to the teacher must necessarily be performed"; the prohibition is supplementary to that. Furthermore, if there were a prohibition against all assistance, then the injunction for general service would become meaningless. Moreover, "assistance" does not consist solely of giving gifts, such that only financial assistance would be forbidden while other forms, such as doing what is pleasant or beneficial, would not be. As for its being an *arthavāda* (a commendatory statement), the fact that it does not state a literal fact is not a defect; indeed, a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) is perceived here. (2.245)
Bringing pleasure to his guru, he may offer a field, gold, a cow, a horse, a parasol, a footstool, or even at the very least, grain, garments, or vegetables. (2.246)

It has been stated and indicated that one should perform what is for the sake of the teacher (*gurvartha*); however, not everything must be done—this is the purpose of this verse. If the teacher should command something contrary [to dharma], such as, "Bring the wife of so-and-so," or "Give away your entire property," that must not be done. What then? "Field" (*kṣetra*) refers to a field of grain, that is, land for a dwelling. "Gold" (*hiraṇya*) means gold. The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of an option; they are not to be given together. At the very least, in the absence of anything else, even an umbrella and sandals. Because of the use of a copulative compound (*dvandva*), they are to be given as a set. Regarding "clothes" (*vāsāṃsi*), the specific number is not intended to be significant. "Bringing pleasure" (*prītim āharan*) connects with the preceding phrase "he should bring" (*etad āharet*). Alternatively, in the reading *prītam āharet*, the action is completed right there. Or, *prītim āvahet*. One should bring grain and so forth in order to produce pleasure. Or rather, pleasure itself is mentioned as something to be brought independently. Consequently, it is established that the mention of specific items is merely illustrative (*pradarśanārthatā*). It is understood that whatever else is of this kind and produces pleasure—such as jewels, pearls, coral, elephants, horses, carriages, chariots, and so forth—that too may be given. And thus says Gautama: "At the end of his studies, the teacher is to be invited with wealth" (GDh 2.48). He should bring it if he possesses it and it has come to him by his own power; if not, he should acquire it through begging and other means. (2.246)

But when the teacher has indeed passed away, one should behave toward the teacher’s son who possesses good qualities, or toward the teacher’s wife, or toward a sapinda relative, exactly as toward the teacher. (2.247)

This is the instruction for the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*). In the absence of his teacher, he should live with the teacher’s son—who is endowed with qualities such as being learned in the Vedas—or with the teacher’s wife, that is, the teacher’s consort (*ācāryāṇī*), or even with one who is a *sapiṇḍa* relative of the teacher himself. And there, he should conduct himself toward them as toward the teacher, performing everything such as the offering of alms-food and so forth. Grammarians record that the word *dāra* ends in the plural and denotes a wife; however, the authors of the *Smṛtis* also employ it in the singular, as in: "When one has a wife endowed with virtue and offspring, one should not take another" (ĀpDh 2.11.12). || 2.247 ||
When these are not available, one who is devoted to standing, sitting, and walking, and who performs service to the sacred fire, shall perfect his own body. (2.248)

The non-existence of all [these qualities] is their absence, or alternatively, their deficiency in virtues. When these are absent, one should apply oneself to the service of the fires: smearing the fire-sanctuary, fueling the fires, and—due to the rule of remaining in proximity like a teacher—sitting day and night like a servant. This is the service of the fires; performing it, one should perfect the body, that is, exhaust the physical frame. Just as a blind man is called "one who has eyes," so too one should "perfect" [the practice]. Standing and sitting constitute his movement (*vihāra*); possessing this, he should never merely sit, but should move in this manner.

Others, however, think: "The posture for staying (*sthāna*) is that seat such as the *svastika* used at the time of meditation; the 'wandering' (*vihāra*) is something else, such as going for alms. (2.248)
The Brahmin who conducts himself in this way, with his celibacy unimpaired, goes to the highest station and is not born here again. || 2.249 ||

The word "thus" refers back to the lifelong practice of celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-vṛtti*). He who thus practices celibacy without failing—that is, without stumbling—attains the highest station, which is characterized by the realization of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). He is not born again here; he does not enter into transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*); he becomes one with the nature of Brahman. (2.249)
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Mānava Dharmaśāstra*, in the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu;
thus [ends] the commentary on Manu composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi.

Madhav Deshpande notes in a private communication: "The *Dhātupāṭha* as given in the NSP edition of the *Siddhāntakaumudī* with the *Tattvabodhinī*, 7th ed., 1933, p. 734, lists two different roots: 1) *ḍudhāñ* in the sense of holding and nourishing (*juhotyādi*), and 2) *dhīṅ* in the sense of support (*divādi*). While *dhīyate* can be a passive form of *dhā-dadhāti*, it can also be a simple middle form of *dhī-dhīyate* from the fourth conjugation. It appears that Medhātithi prefers the latter interpretation."
